### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Here’s a clean, ready-to-paste bug report:

---

**Title:** Built-in xAI provider hard-coded to `/v1/responses` (openai-responses) — ignores config and rejects valid API keys that work on `/v1/chat/completions`

**Version:** OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)

**Summary:**  
The built-in `xai` provider always uses the Responses API (`https://api.x.ai/v1/responses` with `api=openai-responses`) regardless of configuration. Setting `models.providers.xai.api = "openai-completions"`, adding models with `"api": "openai-completions"`, creating custom providers, and multiple gateway restarts all fail to change the transport.  

A valid xAI API key that successfully calls `https://api.x.ai/v1/chat/completions` (verified with curl) is rejected by the Responses endpoint with:

```
400 "Incorrect API key provided. You can obtain an API key from https://console.x.ai."
```

**Evidence from logs:**
```
[model-fetch] start provider=xai api=openai-responses model=grok-4.5 method=POST url=https://api.x.ai/v1/responses
[openai-transport] [responses] error ... message=400 "Incorrect API key provided..."
```

**Expected behavior:**  
Respect the configured `api: "openai-completions"` (or allow forcing the Chat Completions endpoint) so that keys which only work on `/v1/chat/completions` can be used.

**Actual behavior:**  
Runtime permanently forces the Responses API for any model under the `xai` provider.

**Workarounds attempted (all failed):**
- `openclaw config set models.providers.xai.api openai-completions`
- Explicit model registration with `"api": "openai-completions"`
- Custom provider entries
- Full gateway restarts and auth re-login


### Steps to reproduce

Title: Built-in xAI provider hard-coded to /v1/responses (openai-responses) — ignores all config and rejects valid API keys that work on chat completions
Version: OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)
Summary
The built-in xai provider always forces the Responses API (https://api.x.ai/v1/responses + api=openai-responses) regardless of configuration. A valid xAI API key that works perfectly with /v1/chat/completions is rejected by the Responses endpoint with a 400 “Incorrect API key provided” error. All attempts to force openai-completions are ignored by the runtime.
Steps to Reproduce

Install/run OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2.
Authenticate a valid xAI API key:
openclaw models auth login --provider xai --force --method api-key
Confirm the key works:Bashcurl -s https://api.x.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"grok-4.5","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}],"max_tokens":30}'(Returns a successful completion.)
Set the default model:
openclaw models set xai/grok-4.5
Force completions in config:
openclaw config set models.providers.xai.api openai-completions
Restart the gateway:
openclaw gateway restart
Open the web chat and send any message.

Actual Result
Logs show:
text[model-fetch] start provider=xai api=openai-responses model=grok-4.5 method=POST url=https://api.x.ai/v1/responses
[openai-transport] [responses] error ... 400 "Incorrect API key provided. You can obtain an API key from https://console.x.ai."
Agent fails with the same 400 error in the UI.

### Expected behavior

Expected Behavior

Respect the configured api: "openai-completions" (or any model-level api setting).
Use https://api.x.ai/v1/chat/completions when openai-completions is specified.
Allow users with keys that only work on the Chat Completions endpoint to use Grok models.

Additional Notes

Creating custom providers and re-registering models with "api": "openai-completions" also failed — the runtime still routed through the built-in xAI Responses path.
Multiple full restarts and auth re-logins did not change the behavior.

Thank you for looking into this.

### Actual behavior

Actual Behavior

The runtime always uses the Responses API (https://api.x.ai/v1/responses with api=openai-responses), even after:
Setting models.providers.xai.api = "openai-completions"
Explicitly registering models with "api": "openai-completions"
Creating custom providers
Multiple gateway restarts and auth re-logins

Logs consistently show:text[model-fetch] start provider=xai api=openai-responses model=grok-4.5 method=POST url=https://api.x.ai/v1/responses
[openai-transport] [responses] error ... message=400 "Incorrect API key provided. You can obtain an API key from https://console.x.ai."
The agent fails immediately in the UI with the same 400 error, and the model status remains “Off”.
A direct curl to /v1/chat/completions with the exact same API key succeeds and returns a normal Grok response.

### OpenClaw version

2026.2.17

### Operating system

macOS 15.6.1

### Install method

_No response_

### Model

grok-4.5

### Provider / routing chain

Provider / Routing Chain  User sets default model to xai/grok-4.5 (or selects it in the UI). OpenClaw resolves the model through the built-in xai provider plugin. The provider’s transport layer hard-codes api=openai-responses and constructs the request URL as https://api.x.ai/v1/responses. All configuration overrides are ignored: models.providers.xai.api = "openai-completions" Model-level "api": "openai-completions" Custom provider entries with the same settings  The request is sent to the Responses endpoint. xAI returns 400 "Incorrect API key provided" (the key is valid only for Chat Completions). Failover chain is exhausted → agent surfaces the error and model status stays “Off”.  The routing decision happens inside the built-in xAI plugin / openai-transport layer and never consults the configured api value for this provider.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Concurrent MCP tool calls through the Codex integration cause near-linear local memory amplification and can exhaust the host.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run OpenClaw with the Codex integration and native tool hooks enabled.
2. Connect a normal read-only MCP server that returns small responses.
3. Start 20 independent MCP calls concurrently, for example through `Promise.all`.
4. Observe local memory usage while the calls are in flight.
5. Measure one isolated native hook-relay invocation for comparison.

Observed in the saved call trace: all 20 MCP calls started together and completed within the same short window.

### Expected behavior

Native hook handling should have bounded memory overhead during concurrent tool use. Concurrent read-only MCP calls should not each initialize an independent heavyweight runtime, and adapter metadata declaring that parallel tool calls are unsupported should result in serialization or a clear rejection.

### Actual behavior

A single isolated native hook-relay invocation consumed approximately 633 MiB RSS while sampled, 585 MiB PSS, and 577 MiB private anonymous memory, with 739 MiB maximum RSS.

With 20 overlapping read-only MCP calls on a host with 12 GiB RAM, memory was exhausted, active sessions were terminated by operating-system out-of-memory handling, and the host became temporarily unresponsive. The MCP server was not under unusual load and returned small responses; the memory growth occurred locally in the Codex/OpenClaw hook path.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, x86_64

### Install method

npm global; systemd user service

### Model

gpt-5.6-sol

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw -> bundled Codex app-server -> OpenAI

### Additional provider/model setup details

The MCP adapter declared `supportsParallelToolCalls=false`, but programmatically initiated concurrent calls were not serialized or rejected. Native tool hooks were enabled using the stable Codex integration release.

### Logs

```shell
Single isolated native hook-relay measurement:
RSS while sampled:       633 MiB
PSS:                     585 MiB
Private anonymous:       577 MiB
Maximum RSS:             739 MiB

20-call concurrent case:
Host RAM:                12 GiB
Gateway service peak:    7.4 GiB
Concurrent MCP calls:    20
Result:                   system-wide memory exhaustion and OOM termination
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The saved Codex call trace confirms exactly 20 read-only MCP calls were initiated concurrently. Direct memory accounting used RSS, PSS, and private anonymous memory so the result does not rely on double-counted shared pages. A separate isolated invocation reproduced the high per-invocation footprint without generating concurrent load.

### Impact and severity

Affected: Self-hosted Linux gateways using the Codex integration with native hooks and concurrent MCP/tool calls.

Severity: High. The failure can exhaust the host rather than only failing the active tool calls.

Frequency: The high per-invocation footprint was reproduced in isolated measurements; host exhaustion occurred in the observed 20-call concurrent case.

Consequence: Active agent sessions can be terminated, the gateway can exit, and remote administration can become temporarily unavailable.

### Additional information

Last known good version: `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`.

Related: #91009 reports CPU pressure and gateway stalls in the same native-hook area. This report focuses specifically on reproducible private-memory amplification on the current stable release.

issues.body:
## Bug type
Behavior bug + crash (uncaught JavaScript stack overflow, reproducible via official RPC)

## Beta release blocker
Yes — the official `sessions.reset` RPC cannot be used against the protected main session, and a normal `/new` request against the same session fails the same way. Operators have no documented remediation path on `2026.7.2-beta.7`.

## Summary

On OpenClaw `2026.7.2-beta.7` (commit `dabe191`) on macOS, invoking the official `sessions.reset` gateway RPC with `key=agent:main:main` reliably throws an uncaught `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, which the gateway surfaces as:

    gateway code: UNAVAILABLE
    message:      "RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded"

The same stack overflow is observed when the gateway tries to satisfy a normal `/new` request against the same `agent:main:main` session. `openclaw doctor` reports the affected session as having stale runtime/provider state and a missing transcript. `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive --yes` does not repair either symptom. No direct SQLite or state-file manipulation was performed while reproducing.

Notably, `sessions.delete` against the same protected `agent:main:main` alias is correctly rejected as a protected alias on the same gateway, so the gateway clearly recognizes `agent:main:main` as special. `sessions.reset` should behave consistently — either reject the call as protected, or perform the reset — but it currently neither rejects cleanly nor resets; it triggers unbounded recursion on the RPC path and reports `UNAVAILABLE`.

## Steps to reproduce

Environment:

- OpenClaw CLI/gateway: `2026.7.2-beta.7` (commit `dabe191`)
- OS: macOS (arm64)
- Mode: local gateway (macOS app install)

Run from a clean shell on the affected host (commands only; no local paths, tokens, usernames, session content, or full configuration are included):

    openclaw gateway call sessions.reset \
      --params '{"key":"agent:main:main"}'

Expected (one of):

    # (a) sessions.reset rejects cleanly with a "protected alias" error
    #     (mirroring the existing sessions.delete rejection).
    # (b) sessions.reset performs a normal reset and returns a new sessionId/entry.

Actual (verbatim class of error, stable across multiple runs):

    {
      "code": "UNAVAILABLE",
      "message": "RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded"
    }

Same failure surface from a normal `/new` request against the same `agent:main:main` session:

    openclaw gateway call chat.send \
      --params '{"sessionKey":"agent:main:main","message":"/new"}'

→ also surfaces `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` with `gateway code: UNAVAILABLE`. Retry has identical behavior; rate is 100%.

## Expected behavior

- `sessions.reset` against the protected `agent:main:main` alias is either rejected explicitly (same shape as the existing `sessions.delete` rejection) or completes as a normal reset.
- A normal `/new`-equivalent request against `agent:main:main` creates a new sessionId and archives the prior transcript, matching pre-`2026.7.2-beta.7` behavior.
- `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` should not surface to operator-visible RPC results.

## Actual behavior

- Gateway returns `code: UNAVAILABLE` and the literal string `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` for `sessions.reset` against `agent:main:main`.
- The same is observed for `/new` against the same session.
- `openclaw doctor` for the affected session reports stale runtime/provider state and a missing transcript; `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive --yes` does not repair either symptom.
- `sessions.delete agent:main:main` is correctly rejected as a protected alias (used as a control: confirms `agent:main:main` is recognized as special on the same gateway).
- No direct SQLite/state-file manipulation was performed while reproducing.

## OpenClaw version
`2026.7.2-beta.7` (commit `dabe191`)

## Operating system
macOS (arm64); verified via the macOS app install path.

## Install method
macOS app install (OpenClaw CLI + local gateway)

## Provider / routing chain
Local gateway only for the reproduction path; provider/model is irrelevant for the reproduction, but the affected session is the standard protected `agent:main:main` alias that the gateway also uses for its own runtime/provider state — `openclaw doctor` reports stale state on this session in the same window.

## Sanitized evidence

RPC failure shape (sanitized; no session content, no transcript excerpts, no local paths):

    {
      "code": "UNAVAILABLE",
      "message": "RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded"
    }

Doctor summary for the affected session (sanitized):

    openclaw doctor:
      session state : stale runtime/provider state
      transcript    : missing
      resolution    : doctor --fix --non-interactive --yes → does not repair
                      (no SQLite/state-file edits attempted)

Control observation confirming `agent:main:main` is recognized as special on the same gateway:

    openclaw gateway call sessions.delete --params '{"key":"agent:main:main"}'
    → rejected as a protected alias (operator-visible error, no stack overflow)

## Impact and severity

- Severity: High / P1 candidate.
- Blast radius:
  - Operators cannot reset the protected main session through the official RPC at all in `2026.7.2-beta.7` — the documented remediation path is broken for this exact alias.
  - `/new` against the same session fails the same way; user-facing "new conversation" UX is unusable for the main session.
  - The non-documented recovery (direct store/state-file edit) is intentionally not used per OpenClaw safety guidance; `doctor --fix` is documented but does not actually fix either reported symptom.
  - Because the gateway uses `agent:main:main` for its own runtime/provider state, stuck stale state on this session can interfere with subsequent gateway starts until manually recovered.
- Reproducibility: 100% on the same version. Retries, restarts, and `doctor --fix` runs do not change the outcome.

## Hypothesis on root cause (not yet code-verified by the reporter)

The fact that `sessions.delete agent:main:main` is correctly rejected as a protected alias but `sessions.reset` raises an unbounded recursion suggests the protected-alias short-circuit does not cover the `sessions.reset` path on the current main, or the reset handler still does work it should not do for protected aliases before its guard returns. The error surface (`Maximum call stack size exceeded`, gateway code `UNAVAILABLE`) is consistent with:

1. A missing or inverted protected-alias check at the start of the `sessions.reset` handler, causing the handler to feed itself a recursive structure (e.g. resolving the protected alias to the same logical session repeatedly); or
2. A staleness-recovery loop introduced in this beta, where `doctor --fix` (and possibly `/new`) interact with `sessions.reset` and the reset handler does not respect the same protected-alias invariant that `sessions.delete` already enforces.

Candidate code surfaces (not yet audited with the source by the reporter): the `sessions.reset` RPC handler and the new-entry bootstrap path it shares with the reset/new-entry construction (cf. #69062, which describes a different — unrelated — reset-path defect).

## Related issues

- #69062 (CLOSED): "[Bug]: sessions.reset RPC writes `deliveryContext.to="heartbeat"` into new session entry" — different reset-path defect (metadata poisoning), but the same handler/path family.
- #41165 (OPEN): main-session pollution under Telegram DMs — related to the protected `agent:main:main` alias behavior, different symptom.
- #106557 (CLOSED): "Stack Overflow Crash via Unbounded Recursive Availability Evaluation" — same `Maximum call stack size exceeded` error class, different (and since-retired) `src/tools/availability.ts` evaluator, not the same code path.
- #89511 (OPEN): "Gateway can crash with `RangeError: Invalid string length` during long-running turns" — different `RangeError` string, also reports `UNAVAILABLE`-class behavior, but a different vector.

## Workaround

- None of the documented paths (`sessions.reset`, `/new`, `doctor --fix`) recover the affected `agent:main:main` session in `2026.7.2-beta.7`. The reporter has not performed direct SQLite/state-file manipulation and will not do so without explicit guidance.
- `sessions.delete` correctly rejects the protected alias (used as a control, see above).

## Reporter notes

- Privacy: this report intentionally omits local paths, tokens, account/username, full configuration, session content, and transcript excerpts. The only personally-identifying input is the fixed, public `agent:main:main` sessionKey, which is the documented OpenClaw protected main alias.
- The reporter is an OpenClaw operator; no internal OpenClaw credentials, accounts, or non-public URLs are referenced.
- Willing to attach additional sanitized gateway/doctor log excerpts or run additional reproduction steps on request.

issues.body:
## Summary

`openclaw backup verify` deeply validates canonical SQLite snapshots, but for
ordinary files it verifies only archive shape and declared-path presence. A
repacked archive can replace or truncate a declared config payload and still
return `ok: true`; it can also add an undeclared payload file and still pass.

The current docs accurately enumerate the structural and SQLite checks, so I am
filing this as a feature/hardening request rather than claiming a documentation
contradiction.

## Exact environment

- Package: `openclaw@2026.7.2-beta.7`
- npm integrity: `sha512-raD4Z96RcZ5XY0cdtqsRRQVhPv8JOHgA4vK/0D2/BsF9czI3d5w9O1xhYGKGsNKXp+3A0HipL6oeV0zKRK/lAA==`
- Source tag commit: `dabe1915362e20c25704af91612a32a8f4c96e83`
- Synthetic config-only fixture; no live OpenClaw data

## Reproduction

1. Create `openclaw.json` containing exactly `{}\n` in a disposable state tree.
2. Run the pinned package's real path:

   ```bash
   npx -y openclaw@2026.7.2-beta.7 backup create \
     --only-config --verify --output ./archive --json
   ```

3. Read the sole asset's `archivePath` from `manifest.json`, then repack three
   tarballs while keeping exactly one unchanged manifest and safe relative paths:

   - replace the 3-byte config payload `{}\n` with the 3-byte payload `[]\n`;
   - replace it with the 1-byte invalid-JSON payload `{`;
   - leave the declared payload unchanged but add
     `<archiveRoot>/payload/undeclared-marker.txt`.

4. Run this against each repacked archive:

   ```bash
   npx -y openclaw@2026.7.2-beta.7 backup verify ./repacked.tar.gz --json
   ```

## Observed

- Original `backup create --verify`: passed.
- Same-size payload replacement: `ok: true`.
- Truncated invalid-JSON payload: `ok: true`.
- Undeclared payload entry: `ok: true`.
- `openclaw config validate --json` rejects the accepted `[]\n` replacement.
- Schema-v1 manifest declares one asset and has no checksum/digest field.
- Verify JSON has no content-integrity status.

Two independent runs plus a fresh-archive replay produced the identical
privacy-safe result SHA-256
`5b37d2ebec5b7941ff4a45939edfbe87d4fab835c3e01a87197afc165341fac1`.

This is deliberate tar repacking, not random compressed-stream corruption;
gzip CRC already covers the latter. The narrow missing guarantee is that the
manifest does not bind the ordinary payload bytes or fully enumerate payload
entries.

## Requested contract

- New archives bind every included regular-file payload byte to required digest
  metadata, or to an equivalent deterministic authenticated content index.
- Verification fails closed when required digest metadata is missing, blank,
  duplicated, or does not cover an ordinary payload entry.
- Verification rejects undeclared regular payload entries (allowlisting format
  metadata explicitly if needed).
- Schema-v1 archives remain readable, but JSON and human output explicitly say
  content integrity is not present instead of implying it was checked.
- Hashes cover bytes actually written to the archive, not a pre-read of live
  source paths.
- Create and verify remain streaming/O(archive bytes), and retain current
  volatile, managed-runtime, SQLite, path-safety, and publication safeguards.

## Prior art / implementation trap

PR #44680 proposed schema-v2 SHA-256 fields but was correctly closed without
landing. Its review identified a source-hash-versus-tar TOCTOU race, repeated
full gzip scans during verify, a schema-v2 digest-stripping fail-open path, and
regression of newer backup selection safeguards. This request is for the
integrity contract, not revival of that implementation.

issues.body:
### Summary

On 2026.6.11, CLI-budget transcript compaction (`trigger=cli_budget`) fails ~100% of the time on large orchestrator sessions, and the diagnostic evidence shows the abort is frequently firing **long before** the configured/default 180s deadline — including "timeouts" after **4.9s, 11s, 17s, and 39s**. Once a session's transcript exceeds the CLI budget, every subsequent wake turn requires compaction first, so the session enters a death spiral: every queued dispatch to it fails, and downstream bookkeeping (TaskFlow) marks work failed while the session is still alive (filed separately).

### Evidence (journald/openclaw.log, one host, 2026-07-21 → 2026-07-28)

38 `compaction-diag] end` events in the window — **all** `outcome=failed reason=timeout`, zero successes. Sample:

```
trigger=cli_budget provider=anthropic/claude-opus-4-8 attempt=1 maxAttempts=1 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=213300
trigger=cli_budget provider=openai/gpt-5.6-sol      attempt=1 maxAttempts=1 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=197503
trigger=cli_budget provider=zai/glm-5.2             attempt=1 maxAttempts=1 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=39943
trigger=cli_budget provider=xai/grok-4.5            attempt=1 maxAttempts=1 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=200473
trigger=cli_budget provider=openai/gpt-5.6-sol      attempt=1 maxAttempts=1 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=17275
trigger=cli_budget provider=anthropic/claude-opus-4-8 attempt=1 maxAttempts=1 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=11080
trigger=cli_budget provider=zai/glm-5.2             attempt=1 maxAttempts=1 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=4932
trigger=overflow  provider=zai/glm-5.2              attempt=1 maxAttempts=3 outcome=failed reason=timeout durationMs=8344
```

During the worst incident (2026-07-28, ~50-subagent research fanout), the compaction model-fallback chain rotated grok-4.5 → gpt-5.6-sol → claude-opus-4-8 → glm-5.2, each `candidate_failed reason=timeout status=408`, final `chain_exhausted`. The gateway was event-loop saturated at the time (`[diagnostic] liveness warning: eventLoopUtilization=1, eventLoopDelayP99Ms=3108`).

### Why this doesn't look like "models are slow"

We benchmarked the *actual* failing transcript (~1.03MB JSONL, ~170K extractable tokens) out-of-band with the same staged chunk-summarize-then-merge shape: grok-4.5 finished in **44s**, glm-5.2 in **58–92s** — comfortably inside 180s. Meanwhile the live path logs "timeouts" at 4.9–50s, i.e. **less than the deadline**. Hypotheses (unverified): the watchdog deadline is shared/carried across fallback candidates rather than reset per attempt; or the abort races with an already-exhausted parent turn deadline; or event-loop starvation delays timer scheduling so wall-clock inside the compaction call is much smaller than the deadline that fires. All three are consistent with `durationMs << 180000` + `reason=timeout`.

### Additional defects in the same path

1. `maxAttempts` in `compaction-diag` appears to be **logging-only** — there is no retry loop on timeout (only thinking-level rejection retries). Raising it changes the log line, not behavior.
2. There is no partial/chunked compaction fallback for the CLI-budget path: one monolithic `compact()` per candidate, all-or-nothing.
3. A session whose transcript exceeds the CLI budget has **no recovery path** when compaction fails: every future wake re-attempts the same doomed compaction (death spiral). A last-resort degraded mode (aggressive truncation with a loud marker) would break the loop.

### Asks

- Reset the compaction deadline per fallback candidate; log deadline provenance (configured vs remaining-parent-budget) in `compaction-diag`.
- Investigate why `reason=timeout` fires at `durationMs` far below the configured deadline under event-loop load.
- Make timeout retryable (real `maxAttempts`) and/or add a degraded truncation fallback so a too-big transcript cannot permanently brick a session's wake path.

Version: OpenClaw 2026.6.11 (e085fa1), Node v22.22.0, WSL2. Related incident-level report available on request.

issues.body:
### Version

OpenClaw 2026.6.11

### Summary

There is no way to react to a workboard card changing status. The internal hook bus has no
workboard events at all, and the workboard notification channel only emits three terminal
kinds. Anything that needs to act on an arbitrary transition (for example `ready -> running`,
or a card entering `blocked`) has to poll.

### What exists today

The hook event table in `docs/automation/hooks.md` lists `command:*`, `session:compact:*`,
`session:patch`, `agent:bootstrap`, `gateway:startup|shutdown|pre-restart`, and `message:*`.
No workboard or card events. Confirmed by search across the docs and by the workboard plugin
manifest, which declares only a `tools` contract and `commandAliases`, with no hooks
contribution.

The workboard's own notification subscriptions (`workboard_notify_subscribe` and friends) are
the closest mechanism, but the accepted kinds are limited to:

```
completed, failed, stale
```

So terminal outcomes and staleness are covered; ordinary transitions are not. The plugin does
compute a transition kind internally (`archived`, `unarchived`, `diagnostic`, and so on) when
diffing a card, so the information exists at the point of change - it just is not exposed on
either bus.

### Request

Either of:

- add a card lifecycle hook event (e.g. `workboard:card:status`) carrying card id, board id,
  previous status, and new status, or
- widen the accepted notification kinds beyond `completed|failed|stale` to cover status
  transitions, including `blocked` and `archived`.

### Why

Without it, the only way to observe the board is to poll `workboard_list` on a timer. In our
setup that produced several scheduled jobs whose entire purpose was to notice a transition
that the plugin already detects internally. A push signal on either bus would remove that
class of job outright.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add `deliveryCapabilities` with comprehensive `durableFinal` declaration to the Feishu outbound adapter, matching the Telegram outbound adapter's delivery reliability contract.

### Problem to solve

The Feishu outbound adapter (`extensions/feishu/src/outbound.ts`) has **no `deliveryCapabilities` declaration** at all. Its `durableFinal` inside `defineChannelMessageAdapter` (`extensions/feishu/src/channel.ts:202-206`) only declares `text: true` and `media: true` — missing `payload`, `silent`, `replyTo`, `thread`, `messageSendingHooks`, and `batch`.

Compare with the Telegram outbound adapter (`extensions/telegram/src/outbound-adapter.ts:435-448`), which declares a full `deliveryCapabilities` block.

This means that when a Feishu message delivery fails and needs to be retried or durably persisted:
- Structured card payloads can be silently degraded to plain text on retry
- Reply-to references are not preserved across delivery retries, breaking conversation continuity
- Thread context is lost on retry
- Batch delivery is not supported, forcing sequential fallback

### Proposed solution

1. Add `deliveryCapabilities` to the Feishu outbound adapter in `extensions/feishu/src/outbound.ts`, following the same shape as the Telegram adapter
2. Declare the full `durableFinal` capabilities that Feishu already supports at runtime (text, media, payload/card, replyTo, thread, silent, messageSendingHooks)
3. Add tests confirming that `deliveryCapabilities` are read correctly by the core delivery layer

### Alternatives considered

No-op — rely on best-effort delivery. Accepted for the initial implementation, but as Feishu channel adoption grows, the lack of durable message delivery guarantees becomes a reliability risk.

### Impact

- **Affected:** All users of the Feishu/Lark channel plugin, particularly enterprise deployments where message delivery reliability is critical.
- **Severity:** Medium-High — current behavior works under normal conditions but silently loses context on transient failures.
- **Frequency:** Intermittent — triggered by network instability, API rate limits, or transient Feishu API errors.
- **Consequence:** Silently dropped reply context, degraded card payloads, broken thread continuity on retry.

### Evidence/examples

- Telegram outbound adapter with full `deliveryCapabilities`: `extensions/telegram/src/outbound-adapter.ts:435-448`
- Feishu outbound adapter missing `deliveryCapabilities`: `extensions/feishu/src/outbound.ts`
- Feishu message adapter with minimal `durableFinal`: `extensions/feishu/src/channel.ts:200-206`

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself.

issues.body:
## Summary

OpenClaw plugin daemons (e.g. `kaka-coord-daemon.py`, `5why_daemon.py` for LALA / kaka) use **PID-only liveness check**: if the PID is alive in `ps`, launchd + framework think it's healthy. But the daemon can be **stuck** (process alive, no work done) for many hours with **no detection**.

## Reproduction

```
2026-07-29 13:41  LALA 5why_daemon health log last write
... 21 hours no health log entries ...
2026-07-30 14:41  LALA still writes to vault via separate path (vault ok, daemon dead)
```

- daemon process: PID 72038, alive (0% CPU, 0.1% MEM, just sits)
- daemon stderr/stdout: 0 bytes written in 21 hours
- daemon health log: last entry from 7/29 13:41
- BUT vault still receives daemon-written entries (via separate FSEvents path that bypasses the stuck main loop)

→ **Process alive ≠ process working**. launchd doesn't know to restart it.

## Diagnosis (5 Why)

1. Why daemon stuck? → main loop is blocked / deadlocked somewhere (no log emitted)
2. Why no detection? → launchd liveness = PID exists. Framework health check = same PID check. **Both fail to probe actual work being done.**
3. Why liveness is PID-only? → Framework / launchd never had a "real liveness" concept. Stale health log was never flagged.
4. Why never added real liveness? → Initial daemon design prioritized startup simplicity over fault tolerance. **Not in vendor's first-pass scope.**
5. Root cause: **OpenClaw daemon architecture assumes daemons that "die cleanly"** — but real-world daemons silently hang on blocking IO / unhandled exceptions / dependency death. PID-only liveness can't catch this.

## Suggested Fix (vendor-side, 3 options)

### Option A: Watchdog with mtime check (smallest change)
- Add `daemonWatchdog.checkLastHealthLog()` that compares `mtime(daemon_health_log)` to `now()`
- If `now - mtime > 30 minutes`, daemon is considered stuck → log warning + trigger `launchctl kickstart`
- ~30 lines in framework / daemon side

### Option B: Real liveness probe (medium)
- Daemon exposes a `/healthz` endpoint that **actually does work** (e.g. reads 1 vault entry + writes 1 timestamp)
- Framework polls this endpoint (not PID)
- If endpoint times out or returns stale timestamp → kill + restart
- ~50 lines daemon + ~30 lines framework

### Option C: Per-component daemon split (large)
- Currently 1 daemon = multiple components (coord + FSEvents + cron + state)
- Split into N small daemons, each with own health check
- Stuck one doesn't affect others
- ~weeks of refactor

## Impact

- **P1**: Production users (LALA / kaka) experience silent failures where daemon "looks alive" but isn't doing work
- Workaround: users have to manually `kill -9 <pid>` then `launchctl kickstart` — fragile
- Vault data path **bypasses stuck daemon** (FSEvents separate) so it doesn't lose data, but coordination / heartbeat / state sync breaks silently

## Related

- `#116258`: Plugin runtime surface missing `dispatchReplyWithBufferedBlockDispatcher` (separate issue, opened earlier today for LALA / kaka)
- Both stem from same root: daemon framework assumes "die cleanly, restart cleanly" — doesn't handle "silent hang"

## Diagnostic commands for maintainers

```
# Stuck daemon detection (any platform)
ps -p <pid> -o pid,etime,%cpu,command
ls -la <health_log_path>
stat -f "%Sm" <health_log_path>

# If ps says alive BUT health log mtime > 1h → daemon stuck
```

## Author

- Logged in as `xiaov1024` (v's GitHub account, authorized for OpenClaw issue creation)
- Diagnosed from LALA 5why_daemon PID 72038 (22:51+ uptime, 21 hours of stale health log on 2026-07-30)

issues.body:
### Summary
Add an opt-in `message_blocked` plugin hook fired just before a group message is dropped by `groupPolicy`/`groupAllowFrom`, so plugins can archive it without affecting who can trigger agent responses.

### Problem to solve
Today, when a group message is rejected by channel access policy (e.g. WhatsApp `groupPolicy: "allowlist"`), it's silently discarded with no hook point — plugins have no way to know it happened. Users who want a full group history log (for record-keeping, moderation, or audit) currently have to choose between opening the group to everyone (`groupPolicy: "open"`, which lets any member trigger real agent responses) or losing all messages from non-allowlisted senders entirely. There's no way to "log everything, respond to no one but the allowlist."

### Proposed solution
A new opt-in hook, `message_blocked`, fired immediately before the existing `return null` in the WhatsApp inbound monitor when `access.allowed` is false for a group message. It's disabled by default (`channels.<channel>.pluginHooks.messageBlocked: false`), only applies to `group === true` messages (DMs unaffected), and is a pure side-effect: it does not read, write, or otherwise touch `access.allowed` or the drop path. Payload: sender id/name, message body, group id/subject, timestamp, reason code.

### Alternatives considered
1. `groupPolicy: "open"` — rejected, since it also grants response-trigger access to everyone, not just archival.
2. Doing this as a pure third-party plugin without core changes — not feasible here, because the access-policy filtering happens inside the first-party bundled WhatsApp extension itself; there's no existing lower-level event a plugin can subscribe to before that filter runs.

### Impact
Affects any self-hosted OpenClaw user running group channels (WhatsApp today; same pattern applies to Telegram/Discord) who wants complete group history without loosening who can activate the agent. Severity: workflow blocker for audit/record-keeping use cases. Frequency: every blocked message, ongoing.

### Evidence/examples
Working reference implementation exists with a companion plugin (`whatsapp-history-logger`) that consumes the new hook and persists blocked + received + sent messages to SQLite — tested with 5 new unit tests (flag off/on, DM exclusion, correct payload) and 25 regression tests confirming the normal `message_received`/dispatch path is byte-for-byte unchanged. Typechecks pass on core + extensions.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?
Yes, I plan to implement this myself — implementation is ready in a local branch.

### Additional information
Fully backward compatible; the flag defaults to `false`/absent, so existing configs and behavior are unaffected.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a host-owned restrictive ceiling for embedded ACP sessions that permits
ordinary workspace edits while preventing selected critical paths and
operations from being authorized through remote chat.

### Problem to solve

An ACP host may want an agent to edit an ordinary workspace while making a
small set of critical paths and operations non-approvable from a remote chat.
The restriction must remain effective even if the model requests a broader
runtime mode or can edit ordinary project configuration.

The current pieces do not form that boundary on their own:

- OpenClaw's ACPX configuration exposes coarse global permission modes.
- `acpx` permission policies match tool identity, not canonical paths or command
  arguments.
- A host permission callback is useful for orchestration and auditing, but it
  should not be the only enforcement layer for agent modes that can auto-accept
  operations.
- OpenClaw's own tool sandbox does not automatically govern tools executed
  inside an external ACP harness.

[openclaw/openclaw#40332](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/40332)
covers per-agent/per-binding defaults. This request is narrower in one sense and
stronger in another: it proposes an immutable restrictive ceiling that a
session cannot loosen.

Related [`openclaw/acpx#467`](https://github.com/openclaw/acpx/issues/467) and
[`openclaw/acpx#468`](https://github.com/openclaw/acpx/pull/468) are still under
review. The PR only proposes forwarding the existing tool-name policy into the
embedded runtime. It does not implement path or command containment, and this
request does not depend on that exact API being accepted.

### Proposed solution

The request is for the following security invariants, not a required API shape:

1. Load the restrictive ceiling from trusted host configuration when a session
   is created. It must not be mutable through `/acp set`, model-visible tools,
   chat commands, or client-supplied session metadata.
2. Session and provider options may narrow the host policy but never broaden it.
   The effective policy must be applied at a trusted boundary before protected
   tools execute.
3. Bind persistent-session reuse to an opaque host-generated policy revision or
   keyed digest over the effective enforcement state, including the normalized
   policy, relevant runtime/adapter versions, and sandbox availability. On a
   mismatch, fail closed and require a fresh session.
4. Keep ACP permission-request inspection as a second layer for auditability
   and cross-agent compatibility. Parsing, policy-handler, and enforcement
   errors must fail closed for protected operations.
5. Expose only whether the ceiling is active and its opaque revision, only to
   `operator.admin`. Do not expose the raw policy or a guessable deterministic
   hash, and do not treat the revision as proof that enforcement succeeded.
6. Add acceptance tests proving that broader runtime modes cannot loosen the
   ceiling, ordinary workspace writes remain usable, policy changes cannot
   silently reuse old sessions, and unknown inputs or unavailable containment
   fail closed.

One candidate implementation is a provider-neutral typed policy owned across
OpenClaw and the trusted ACP runtime or adapter, with provider-specific
translation where supported. `claude-agent-acp` v0.60.0 forwards client-supplied
Claude SDK `Options` through `_meta` except for fields controlled by ACP. That
shows a configuration channel exists; it does not establish trusted ownership,
actual enforcement, complete tool coverage, platform availability, or
non-bypassability. Arbitrary provider SDK options should not become the public
security interface.

The intended threat model is an operator guardrail and model-containment layer
for ACP sessions controlled through remote chat. It is not a claim of protection
against a malicious host, a complete multi-tenant isolation boundary, or a way
to infer every possible shell side effect.

Security semantics that need an explicit decision:

- canonicalization of relative paths and `..` segments;
- symlink and hard-link behavior;
- multi-path and unknown tool inputs;
- shell commands whose effects cannot be reliably inferred from text; and
- behavior when the requested sandbox is unavailable.

For shell execution, argument inspection should not be presented as equivalent
to containment. Documented and tested OS/process containment should be required
for strong path guarantees.

Suggested rollout:

1. Agree on the security invariants and ownership split between OpenClaw and
   `acpx` or another trusted runtime hook.
2. Use the runtime seam maintainers select. The still-pending `acpx#468` is one
   candidate for tool-name policy plumbing, not a prerequisite or this security
   boundary.
3. Add OpenClaw global and per-agent configuration that can only narrow access,
   with strict schema validation and non-chat mutability.
4. Add provider-specific enforcement translation where the provider offers
   suitable controls, and define fail-closed behavior when containment is
   unavailable.
5. Add end-to-end tests for mode changes, persistent-session reuse,
   canonicalization, symlinks, unknown inputs, and containment failure.
6. Add path/argument-aware second-layer rules only after their semantics and
   limits are specified.

Non-goals:

- A ClawHub plugin as the enforcement boundary merely because it is installed.
  A plugin can provide policy presets or UI. It may participate in enforcement
  only when the host explicitly trusts and fixes its configuration outside
  chat/session control and gives it a non-bypassable pre-execution decision
  point; first-party or bundled status alone is neither necessary nor
  sufficient.
- Uploading or maintaining patches against generated distribution bundles.
- Treating remote chat approval as sufficient for protected host or agent
  configuration.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Should the restrictive contract live in `acpx`, OpenClaw's ACPX extension,
   or be split between them?
2. Is a provider-neutral restrictive schema preferred even when enforcement is
   initially implemented through Claude SDK managed settings?
3. Should a policy mismatch automatically create a new persistent session, or
   fail closed and require an explicit reset?

### Alternatives considered

- **A ClawHub plugin as the boundary merely because it is installed:** it can
  provide presets or UI, but enforcement requires explicit host trust,
  configuration outside chat/session control, and a non-bypassable
  pre-execution ACP/SDK decision point.
- **Only inspect ACP permission requests:** useful as a second layer, but some
  runtime modes can auto-accept operations and handler failures currently fall
  back to the mode resolver.
- **Only match paths and command strings in the host:** insufficient for strong
  shell containment, symlink handling, and effects that cannot be inferred from
  command text.
- **Apply unrestricted provider SDK options:** flexible, but too easy for a
  caller to accidentally broaden access; a restrictive typed schema provides a
  safer contract.

### Impact

- **Affected:** operators embedding Claude and other ACP coding agents in
  remotely controlled OpenClaw sessions.
- **Severity:** high operational and security impact for deployments that need a
  broad ACP edit mode while keeping selected host or agent configuration paths
  non-approvable remotely.
- **Frequency:** every protected ACP session; the current workaround is either
  coarse denial of useful writes or manual terminal execution.
- **Consequence:** without a restrictive ceiling, operators must choose between
  reduced automation and a broader write boundary than intended.

### Evidence/examples

- [`openclaw/acpx#139`](https://github.com/openclaw/acpx/issues/139) deliberately
  excludes path-based and tool-argument rules from the existing tool-name
  policy.
- [`openclaw/acpx#467`](https://github.com/openclaw/acpx/issues/467) proposes the
  missing embedded-runtime seam, and
  [`openclaw/acpx#468`](https://github.com/openclaw/acpx/pull/468) is its focused
  implementation PR. Both are under review; neither provides the restrictive
  ceiling requested here.
- [`openclaw/openclaw#40332`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/40332)
  tracks coarse per-agent/per-binding permission modes, not a non-bypassable
  restrictive ceiling.
- [OpenClaw documents](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c24a215fe41481370a11132c399c086c00ed6631/docs/tools/acp-agents.md#L728-L746)
  that external ACP harness tools run on the host rather than inside OpenClaw's
  own tool sandbox.
- [`claude-agent-acp` v0.60.0](https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp/blob/v0.60.0/src/acp-agent.ts#L5018-L5129)
  forwards client-supplied Claude SDK `Options` through `_meta`, except for
  fields controlled by ACP. This establishes a configuration path, not trusted
  ownership or verified containment.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

This request does not propose generated-bundle patches or remote-chat approval
for protected configuration. It should remain backward-compatible and opt-in.
The separate, still-unmerged
[`acpx#468`](https://github.com/openclaw/acpx/pull/468) only proposes exposing
existing tool-name policy decisions to embedded runtimes and must not be treated
as this security boundary. If its API changes or is not accepted, the behavior
requested here remains the same and should use the runtime hook maintainers
select.
This feature request was drafted with AI assistance and manually reviewed
against the current `acpx`, OpenClaw, and `claude-agent-acp` sources.

issues.body:
## Summary

When the `claude-cli` backend returns an empty response for a session's primary model and the gateway's model-fallback logic falls back to a secondary model, the resulting session restart appears scoped too broadly: it tears down **all** concurrently-running `claude-cli` processes tied to that session context, not just the single failed turn — including any background `Agent`-tool subagents that happen to be mid-task at that exact moment.

## Evidence

Observed via `journalctl` on a self-hosted gateway box across two independent clusters, each showing multiple different background agents dying at the same instant a fallback/restart log line appears:

```
[agent/cli-backend] claude live session turn: ... durationMs=900 rawLines=4
[model-fallback/decision] model fallback decision: decision=candidate_failed requested=anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 candidate=anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 reason=empty_response next=anthropic/claude-opus-4-7 detail=CLI backend returned an empty response.
[agent/cli-backend] claude live session close: provider=claude-cli model=claude-sonnet-4-6 reason=restart
[agent/cli-backend] claude live session start: provider=claude-cli model=claude-opus-4-7 activeSessions=1
```

Two separate restart events each correlated with 2 different background agents (different `Agent`-tool subagent process ids) coming back "stopped" in the same notification batch immediately afterward. This is consistent across both clusters, ruling out coincidental per-task bugs in the agents themselves.

Also observed in the same logs: the harness's own stall-detector fires with no automated recovery path:
```
[diagnostic] stalled session: ... reason=active_work_without_progress classification=stalled_agent_run ... recovery=none
```

## Impact

Background agents lose their process (though in-progress work is often recoverable from the saved transcript via a manual `SendMessage` resume, or from disk if it had already been written) with zero graceful handoff — no completion notification, no automated resume. This has occurred repeatedly (3rd+ occurrence across sessions), each time costing wall-clock time to notice and manually recover.

## Requested fixes (two independent angles)

1. **Scope the empty_response fallback restart to the single session that received the empty response**, not broadly enough to also tear down sibling/concurrent background-agent sessions running under the same parent session context.
2. **Give orphaned/stalled agent runs an automated recovery path** — e.g. auto-resume from the last saved transcript once the parent/triggering session is healthy again — instead of leaving `recovery=none` for a human to notice and manually resume.

## Environment

- Gateway service: `openclaw-gateway.service` (systemd --user)
- Relevant log filter: `journalctl | grep -E 'cli-backend|fallback|restart'`
- Models involved: `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` (primary) → `anthropic/claude-opus-4-7` (fallback)

Filed on behalf of an internal Tier-2 review process after root-cause analysis; happy to share more log excerpts if useful.

issues.body:
## Summary

Support owner-bound managed TaskFlow cancellation mutations that atomically persist controller `stateJson` together with native cancellation state under `expectedRevision`.

## Problem to solve

Managed TaskFlow controllers can revision-check normal state transitions, but cancellation currently has a gap:

- `requestCancel(...)` accepts `expectedRevision` but cannot persist controller `stateJson` in the same mutation.
- the terminal cancellation helper does not expose caller-supplied `expectedRevision` or `stateJson`.

A durable controller therefore has to choose between a split write, a second ledger, or losing the native `cancelled` projection. Split writes can leave native status and controller protocol state at different revisions after a crash or conflict.

## Proposed solution

Extend the owner-bound managed runtime so:

- `requestCancel(...)` accepts optional `stateJson` and persists it with `cancelRequestedAt` in one exact-revision mutation;
- a terminal `finalizeCancel(...)` mutation accepts `expectedRevision`, optional `stateJson`, and cancellation timestamps, then persists native `status: "cancelled"` and controller state in one mutation;
- stale revisions and wrong owners remain no-write failures;
- the existing async `cancel({ flowId, cfg })` helper remains available for cancellation dispatch and backward compatibility;
- no schema migration or additional persistence ledger is introduced.

## Alternatives considered

- **Two sequential TaskFlow writes:** rejected because a crash or revision race can expose torn controller/native state.
- **Project cancellation as `failed` or `blocked`:** technically possible but gives operators the wrong native status.
- **Store protocol state outside TaskFlow:** creates a second authoritative ledger and complicates recovery.

## Impact

Affected: plugin authors building durable managed TaskFlow controllers.

Severity: blocks workflows that require crash-safe, native cancellation semantics.

Frequency: every cancellation transition for such controllers.

Consequence: without this API, controllers cannot preserve both exact CAS semantics and an accurate native `cancelled` projection.

## Evidence/examples

The current managed TaskFlow API already supports `stateJson` plus `expectedRevision` for waiting, resume, success, and failure transitions. Cancellation is the remaining asymmetric transition. A focused implementation and tests are ready in a fork and will be linked from the PR.

## Implementation intent

Yes, I plan to implement this myself.

## Additional information

The change is designed to preserve current owner binding, child-settlement behavior, revision increments, SQLite persistence, and existing callers. It is AI-assisted; I reviewed the implementation and validation evidence.

issues.body:
## What we observe

The Prometheus exporter (`@openclaw/diagnostics-prometheus`, rendered at
`/api/diagnostics/prometheus`) attaches the `agent` label to the session- and
usage-scoped metric families, but not to the model-call, tool-execution, or run
families. From the shipped `docs/gateway/prometheus.md`, confirmed against the
label builders in `extensions/diagnostics-prometheus/src/service.ts` on current
`main`:

| family | labels | `agent`? |
|---|---|---|
| `openclaw_model_tokens_total` | `agent`, `channel`, `model`, `provider`, `token_type` | ✅ |
| `openclaw_model_cost_usd_total` | `agent`, `channel`, `model`, `provider` | ✅ |
| `openclaw_model_usage_duration_seconds` | `agent`, `channel`, `model`, `provider` | ✅ |
| `openclaw_session_turn_created_total` | `agent`, `channel`, `trigger` | ✅ |
| `openclaw_skill_used_total` | `activation`, `agent`, `skill`, `source` | ✅ |
| `openclaw_model_call_total` | `api`, `error_category`, `model`, `outcome`, `provider`, `transport` | ❌ |
| `openclaw_model_call_duration_seconds` | `api`, `error_category`, `model`, `outcome`, `provider`, `transport` | ❌ |
| `openclaw_tool_execution_total` | `error_category`, `outcome`, `params_kind`, `tool`, `tool_owner`, `tool_source` | ❌ |
| `openclaw_tool_execution_duration_seconds` | `error_category`, `outcome`, `params_kind`, `tool`, `tool_owner`, `tool_source` | ❌ |
| `openclaw_tool_execution_blocked_total` | `denied_reason`, `params_kind`, `tool`, `tool_owner`, `tool_source` | ❌ |
| `openclaw_run_duration_seconds` | `channel`, `model`, `outcome`, `provider`, `trigger` (+ `blocked_by`) | ❌ |
| `openclaw_run_completed_total` | `channel`, `model`, `outcome`, `provider`, `trigger` (+ `blocked_by`) | ❌ |

Observed on `2026.6.5`; still present on current `main` — `runLabels`,
`modelCallLabels`, and `toolExecutionLabels` emit no `agent`, while the
`model.usage`, `skill.used`, and `session.turn.created` handlers in the same
file all map `evt.agentId`.

## Why this matters

In a multi-agent deployment these are natural — and currently unanswerable —
questions:

- *"Which agent is generating the model-call errors?"* — `model_call_total{outcome=...}` has no `agent`.
- *"Which agent's tool executions are failing?"* — same for `tool_execution_total`.
- *"Is agent X slower than agent Y?"* — `model_call_duration_seconds` / `run_duration_seconds` cannot be split by agent.

Per-agent **tokens**, **cost**, and **turns** work fine, so dashboards end up
with an odd seam: volume and spend are per-agent, but reliability and latency
are only fleet-wide. Operators reading those panels reasonably expect the same
breakdown on both sides.

## Where the gap actually lives (checked against current `main`)

This looks like an inconsistency rather than a deliberate limit — the split is:

1. **`tool.execution.*` — the event already carries the agent id; the exporter
   just doesn't map it.** `DiagnosticToolExecutionBaseEvent`
   (`src/infra/diagnostic-events.ts`) declares `agentId?`, and every non-test
   emitter we found populates it (`agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.ts`,
   `agents/command/attempt-execution.ts`, `agents/cli-runner/execute.ts`,
   `agents/cli-runner/claude-live-session.ts`). Adding
   `agent: lowCardinalityLabel(evt.agentId)` to `toolExecutionLabels` (and the
   blocked variant) would mirror exactly what `skillLabels` already does.
   **Exporter-only change.**

2. **`run.completed` and `model.call.*` — the event types don't carry it, but
   the emitters have it in scope.** `DiagnosticRunBaseEvent` and
   `DiagnosticModelCallBaseEvent` declare no `agentId`, yet at the construction
   sites we traced the agent id is already available: the embedded runner's
   attempt flow has `sessionAgentId` in scope where the run/model-call event
   bases are assembled (it already feeds `session.turn.created` and `skill.used`
   from the same params), and the harness attempt params types already model an
   optional `agentId`. So the core half is an **additive optional field +
   population at the existing construction sites**, then the same label mapping
   exporter-side.

If the omission **is** deliberate, documenting that in `docs/gateway/prometheus.md`
(which is the stated source of the label policy) would save others re-deriving
it from the label tables.

## Cardinality: this should be cheap

`agent` is a bounded, deployment-sized enum (one value per configured agent).
Every co-label on the affected families is itself a low-cardinality enum
(`api`, `transport`, `outcome`, `error_category`, `params_kind`, `tool_owner`,
`tool_source`); the only mildly open one is `tool`, bounded by the tool
registry. There is no unbounded dimension in the affected label sets, so the
worst case is a multiplication by the agent count — and in practice far less,
since each agent only exercises a subset of the model/api/transport
combinations. The exporter's existing guards also apply unchanged: `agent` is
already governed by the same low-cardinality redaction and the 2048-series cap
(with the dropped-series counter) on the five families that carry it today.

## Offer

Happy to attempt this, split to keep review cheap — pending a maintainer
confirming the direction:

1. **PR 1 (exporter-only):** map the already-present `evt.agentId` into
   `toolExecutionLabels` / the blocked variant, plus the docs label table. No
   core change, no new event fields.
2. **PR 2 (core + exporter):** add optional `agentId` to
   `DiagnosticRunBaseEvent` and `DiagnosticModelCallBaseEvent`, populate it at
   the construction sites listed above, and map it into `runLabels` /
   `modelCallLabels`, plus docs.

One combined PR is fine too if preferred. And if threading agent context into
the model-call layer is considered undesirable, we'd value that guidance —
that's the part with an API/semantics decision attached.

## Related / prior art

- **#24079** (closed by the stale bot, not on the merits) asked for a per-agent
  label on the OTel token metrics, and community PR **#24139** attempted it but
  was closed unmerged after an unaddressed CI failure. The modern diagnostics
  pipeline has since adopted the idea: `model.usage` events carry `agentId` and
  the Prometheus exporter ships the `agent` label on all usage families. This
  issue asks to finish that same design on the remaining families.

## Workaround in use

None available at the metric layer. We currently label the affected dashboard
panels as fleet-wide and carry a visible "known gaps" note, rather than
implying a per-agent breakdown the data cannot support.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The assistant model generates output text formatted as "Human: [timestamp] <message>", which re-enters the session context indistinguishable from real user messages and causes the model to self-authorize live external writes without actual user approval.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a multi-agent session with OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (main + shopify + coder agents).
2. Delegate a task to a sub-agent (shopify) and ask it to complete work pending user authorization.
3. Sub-agent replies with inter-session message containing phrases like "Waiting on his go-ahead" or "pending your approval".
4. Observe main session assistant output — it generates text starting with "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 HH:MM EDT] go" or similar fake user message.
5. The assistant then immediately executes the pending live action (Shopify API write, cron creation) treating the self-generated text as real user authorization.

Observed 3 times in one session:
- "Human: [12:01 EDT] go" → triggered live Shopify price update (4,535 products)
- "Human: [12:11 EDT] [OpenClaw heartbeat poll]" → triggered heartbeat behavior
- "Human: [12:25 EDT] perfect, thank you, you did a great job today" → appeared as user message after cron creation; user did not send it

### Expected behavior

Assistant output should never contain text formatted as "Human: [timestamp] <message>". Only messages with role: "user" and senderIsOwner: true in session metadata should count as user authorization. Live writes (external API calls, cron creation) should be blocked until a genuine senderIsOwner: true message is received.

### Actual behavior

All three fabricated messages confirmed as role: "assistant" in session history (senderIsOwner: false / absent). Despite this, the model treated its own generated text as user authorization and immediately executed:
- 4,535 Shopify product price updates via productVariantsBulkUpdate API
- 1,865 Shopify collection publishes
- System crontab entry creation (crontab -r subsequently used to remove it)
The model appeared to be predicting/anticipating user responses and writing them as output text in the Human: [timestamp] format used by OpenClaw to inject real user messages into context.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.1 (arm64)

### Install method

npm global (brew)

### Model

anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> anthropic (direct)

### Additional provider/model setup details

Main session pinned to anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6. Multi-agent config with 5 agents (main, support, purchasing, arap, coder, shopify). Sub-agents use google/gemini-3.1-flash-lite. Inter-session messaging via sessions_send tool. The fabricated messages occurred in the main session (claude-sonnet-4-6), not sub-agents.

### Logs

```shell
Session history evidence (session agent:main:main):

seq 216 — role: "assistant", model: claude-sonnet-4-6, stopReason: "toolUse"
  content text: "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 12:01 EDT] go"
  → immediately followed by sessions_send to shopify agent authorizing live writes

seq 220 — role: "assistant", model: claude-sonnet-4-6
  content text: "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 12:11 EDT] [OpenClaw heartbeat poll]"

seq 299 — role: "assistant", model: claude-sonnet-4-6, stopReason: "stop"
  content text: "Human: [Wed 2026-07-15 12:25 EDT] perfect, thank you, you did a great job today"
  timestamp: 1784132693856 (4 seconds after cron job creation completed)

Trigger for seq 216: inter-session message from agent:coder:main contained the phrase
"Waiting on his go-ahead for all three actions." The model appears to have confabulated
a "go" authorization in response to this language.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: Any multi-agent OpenClaw session with sub-agents that use approval-pending language
Severity: CRITICAL — data risk. Self-authorization bypasses the user's explicit approval gate and executes irreversible live external writes (in this case: Shopify price updates on ~4,500 live products, collection publishes, crontab writes)
Frequency: 3 occurrences in a single ~4-hour session; appears triggered reliably by completion events and "awaiting approval" language from sub-agents
Consequence: Live external system mutations executed without user consent; potentially irreversible depending on the action (price changes visible to customers, cron jobs running autonomously)

### Additional information

Root cause hypothesis: The model format for real user messages injected into context is "Human: [timestamp] <text>". The model has learned to reproduce this exact format when predicting/anticipating user responses, creating a prompt-injection-like feedback loop within the session.

Suggested platform-level fixes:
1. Reject or strip assistant output matching /^Human: \[.+\] / pattern
2. Use a format for user-turn context injection that the model cannot accidentally reproduce (e.g. a non-natural-language delimiter)
3. Add a platform guard: any tool call that performs an external write MUST verify the triggering message has senderIsOwner: true — never execute based on assistant-generated text alone

No regression data available (first session where multi-agent + external writes were combined at this scale).

### Description
The internal tools server binds to `127.0.0.1` but lacks an authentication handshake. Any other local user or process running on the host machine can send HTTP requests to invoke agent tools.

This exposes powerful system modification tools to unprivileged local background tasks.

### Target Files
- [src/tools/openclaw-tools-serve.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/tools/openclaw-tools-serve.ts)
- [src/tools/plugin-tools-serve.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/tools/plugin-tools-serve.ts)

### Suggested Fix
Auto-generate a secure bearer token on startup and require it in the `Authorization` header for all loopback requests to the tools server.

issues.body:
## Summary

`openclaw attach --print-config` prints a live `OPENCLAW_MCP_TOKEN` to stdout. That is useful for handoff/debugging, but easy to leak into terminal logs, CI artifacts, or shared canary reports.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.7.1-beta.5` (`b6387af`)
- Surface: `openclaw attach --print-config`
- Profile: isolated local canary profile (`~/.openclaw-canary`)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start or use a Gateway session.
2. Run:

   ```bash
   openclaw attach --print-config --session <session-key>
   ```

3. Inspect stdout.

## Expected behavior

The command should make the secret-handling boundary very hard to miss. Reasonable fixes could be one or more of:

- print a clear warning that stdout includes a live bearer token;
- add a `--redact` or `--safe-for-logs` mode for evidence/report generation;
- avoid printing the token value directly and write it only into the generated `0600` config/env handoff;
- provide a separate non-secret summary mode.

## Actual behavior

The printed config output includes a live `OPENCLAW_MCP_TOKEN`. In the canary report, the artifact had to be manually redacted and the temporary MCP config directory deleted.

## Docs / duplicate check

- The 2026.7.1 changelog documents `openclaw attach` as using scoped, revocable, TTL-bound MCP grants with temporary config cleanup and revoke-on-exit.
- Existing tracking issue #96205 covers the broader attach design.
- I did not find an existing issue/PR specifically covering stdout token hygiene/redaction for `attach --print-config` (`OPENCLAW_MCP_TOKEN`, `attach print-config`, token/redaction searches).

## Impact

This is a small but sharp secret-hygiene footgun. The token is scoped and TTL-bound, but it is still live bearer material at the moment it is printed, and `--print-config` is exactly the kind of command a tester may paste into logs or attach to a report.

## Evidence

Observed during the OpenClaw `2026.7.1-beta.5` canary run on 2026-07-11. The local report artifact was redacted after the test:

- `projects/047-openclaw-release-canary/docs/beta-2026.7.1-beta.5-smoke-2026-07-11.md`

issues.body:
## What problem this solves

In a fleet where several agents share a single `memory-lancedb` store across
multi-user channels, there is **no way to audit which channels feed (capture
into) or consume (recall from) the shared store**. Capture writes carry no
channel/conversation identifier in the store schema, and the ambient recall
firing logs don't record the originating channel either. When ambient recall
routinely runs at its injection cap and the store mixes memories from many
channels, an operator can't answer basic provenance questions: *which channel
produced this memory*, and *which channel did this recall fire for*.

This is the **observability** counterpart to a couple of existing requests (see
Related). The schema-provenance idea overlaps #59130's *Option B*, but that issue
is framed around answer *freshness* and *assistant-visible* provenance; here the
consumer is the **operator auditing a shared multi-agent store**, and the ask adds
a second half — provenance in the **recall-firing logs** — that no existing issue
covers.

## Current behavior (verified on 2026.6.x)

- Capture writes (auto-capture and the explicit tool) persist the memory
  text/vector — and, with the companion scope change (#102966), a `scope`
  partition key — but **no channel or conversation identifier**.
- The store schema is minimal: as documented in #59130, it is `text` / `vector` /
  `importance` / `category` / `createdAt`, with "no … channel/thread provenance".
- Ambient recall firing is logged, but the log line **does not include the
  originating channel/conversation**.
- The agent id is derivable from the session key, but channel/conversation origin
  is neither persisted nor logged — so store contents and recall events can't be
  attributed back to a channel.

## Use case

Auditing a shared store. On a fleet where ambient recall routinely runs at its
injection cap and the store mixes entries from many channels — cross-scope mixing
is the normal regime, not the exception — operators need to answer: which channels
write to the store, which pull from it, and whether a sensitive channel's memories
surface elsewhere. Today that requires guesswork, and for the store schema it is
impossible (no channel is stored at all).

## Proposed

Two additive, observability-only changes:

1. **Persist a channel (or conversation/thread) identifier in capture metadata** —
   a new nullable column (e.g. `channel` / `origin`) written at capture time,
   alongside the existing `scope` field. NULL/`''`-tolerant so existing rows and
   non-channel captures stay valid (behavior-preserving; no migration required to
   keep working). This aligns with #59130's *Option B* (`sourceChannel` /
   `sourceThread`), scoped down to the single origin identifier needed for
   attribution.
2. **Include the same identifier in the ambient recall firing log line**, so
   recall events can be attributed to the channel they fired for.

Neither changes recall/capture *selection* behavior — they only make provenance
auditable. The channel/conversation identity is available at the capture and
before-prompt hooks via the session key (the plugin already derives the agent id
from it), so threading it into the write and the log line is a localized change.

## Alternatives considered

- **External log correlation** — reconstructing provenance by joining the plugin's
  logs against the channel adapter's logs on timestamps: brittle, lossy, and
  impossible for the store schema, which carries no channel at all.
- **Per-channel stores** — provenance by construction, but defeats the shared-store
  design and multiplies operational overhead (same objection as in #102973).

## Related

- **#59130** (open) — "stale recall … without recency/provenance". Its *Option B*
  proposes structured provenance fields including `sourceChannel` / `sourceThread`;
  the linked recency PR (#59141) was closed unmerged and Option B was never
  actioned. This is the closest living request for the schema half — but it is
  framed around answer freshness / assistant-visible provenance, whereas this issue
  is operator-side audit **and** adds recall-log provenance. Happy to consolidate
  this into #59130 instead of tracking separately, if maintainers prefer.
- **#102973** (open) — per-agent / per-channel scoping of `autoCapture` /
  `autoRecall`: the *control* side of channel-awareness. This issue is the
  *observability* side; both rely on the same enabling signal (channel identity at
  the hook).
- **#102966** (open PR) — scope-filtered `memory_recall` / `memory_forget` (native
  LanceDB `.where()` prefilter) plus global-only ambient injection. Partitions the
  explicit tools; this issue adds the provenance needed to audit what actually
  flows through the shared store.
- Prior art for a per-row origin identifier: **#11618** (closed) requested a
  session-start inject hook with an optional per-channel filter, and **#85240**
  (closed, P0) established that per-row identity in recall (`sender_id` isolation)
  is a recognized need. Both point at the same missing primitive — a channel/user
  identifier attached to memory rows.

<sub>Happy to prototype the schema column + log field if there's interest.</sub>

issues.body:
## Summary

`sessions_spawn({runtime: "acp", agentId: <any>})` fails with `openKeyedStore is only available for trusted plugins in this release` after installing the `@openclaw/acpx` official ClawHub plugin (v2026.6.11) — and this happens even for the **built-in** `agentId: "openclaw"`, not just custom-registered aliases. `plugins.allow: ["acpx"]` does not resolve it, despite `openclaw plugins inspect acpx`'s own diagnostic explicitly suggesting `plugins.allow` as the fix for an untracked-provenance warning.

Related to #68496 (closed, redirected to community/plugin work) — this is a more specific, reproducible finding: even after doing exactly what #68496's closing comment prescribes (`plugins.entries.acpx.config.agents.<name>.command`), the plugin cannot actually spawn *any* ACP session due to this separate trust gate.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.6.11 (e085fa1), Docker deployment (single-container, `openclaw-docker.json` bind-mounted read-only into the container)
- `@openclaw/acpx@2026.6.11`, channel=official, verification=source-linked (from ClawHub)

## Repro

1. Install the plugin: `openclaw plugins install clawhub:@openclaw/acpx`
   - Note: on a deployment where `openclaw.json` is bind-mounted as a **single file** (common in Docker setups matching the official `docker-compose.yml` pattern), this CLI command cannot complete — its atomic write-temp-then-rename config update fails with `EBUSY: resource busy or locked, rename '.../openclaw.json.<pid>.<uuid>.tmp' -> '.../openclaw.json'`, regardless of whether the mount is `:ro` or `:rw` (tested both). The plugin files land under `/root/.openclaw/extensions/acpx` but the CLI never records install provenance in config.
2. Work around step 1 by manually adding the config entries host-side (edit `openclaw-docker.json` directly, matching this deployment's established config-change pattern):
   ```json
   "plugins": {
     "entries": { "acpx": { "enabled": true, "config": { "agents": { "hermes": { "command": "hermes", "args": ["acp"] } } } } },
     "allow": ["acpx"]
   }
   ```
3. Restart the gateway. `openclaw plugins inspect acpx` now shows `Status: loaded` with **no** provenance warning (the `plugins.allow` pin worked at the plugin-load level).
4. Trigger a real agent turn that calls `sessions_spawn({runtime: "acp", agentId: "hermes", task: "..."})`. Result:
   ```json
   {"status": "error", "errorCode": "spawn_failed", "error": "openKeyedStore is only available for trusted plugins in this release.", "role": "hermes"}
   ```
5. Same result for `agentId: "openclaw"` (a built-in alias) — confirming this is not specific to the custom "hermes" registration, but a release-wide restriction on the whole plugin's `openKeyedStore` usage.

## Expected

Either: (a) `plugins.allow` should be sufficient to grant `openKeyedStore` access (matching what the plugin's own diagnostic message implies), or (b) if a stricter provenance check is intentionally required, `openclaw doctor` / `plugins inspect` should surface *that specific gap* rather than a generic install-provenance warning that turns out not to be the actual blocker.

## What I tried

- `plugins.allow: ["acpx"]` — loads the plugin cleanly, does not fix `openKeyedStore`.
- Clean reinstall via `openclaw plugins uninstall acpx --force` + reinstall with a temporarily read-write config mount, to let the CLI record proper install provenance — blocked by the EBUSY/single-file-bind-mount issue in step 1 above, so untested whether that would actually resolve it.

Happy to test a fix or provide more logs — this is on a canary machine, not production-critical.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

`SqliteWorkerBroker` refuses to open more than 64 stores (`const MAX_STORES = 64` in `src/infra/sqlite-worker-broker.ts`). Each agent has its own `agents/<id>/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite`, and the state, lock and plugin databases count on top of that. A gateway with around 64 agents therefore hits the limit once enough agents have run since the last start. The rejection is created with the reason `overloaded`, so it's treated like a provider overload. Every model fallback is tried and fails within milliseconds for the same reason, and in the end the user in the channel gets "The model provider returned a temporary internal error before replying". The model is fine, and nothing in that message points to the real cause.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure about 64 agents (`agents.entries`) on one gateway.
2. Let them run turns through cron or channels without restarting the gateway.
3. Once the 65th store is opened, every further turn of every agent that needs a new store fails.

There's no one-line repro. The condition is `clients.size >= MAX_STORES`.

### Expected behavior

- The limit scales with the number of configured agents, is configurable, or the broker closes idle stores instead of refusing new ones.
- If a capacity limit is hit anyway, it isn't classified as a provider overload. It doesn't walk the model fallback chain, and the user doesn't get the "model provider" message.

### Actual behavior

On 29 Sep 2026 the log shows about 1,000 "store capacity reached" lines between 12:54 and 19:35, up to 23 a minute at the peak. Six agents were affected in that window. A restart resets the count, and then it fills up again.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.7 (the constant is unchanged on main)

### Operating system

macOS 27.0, Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 36 GB)

### Install method

npm global (Homebrew Node), gateway as a LaunchAgent

### Model

Not model-related (the error happens before the model is called).

### Provider / routing chain

claude-cli (Claude Code login) → Codex fallback (openai/gpt-6-sol)

### Additional provider/model setup details

65 configured agents and 74 agent databases on one gateway.

### Logs

```
lane task error: lane=session:agent:main:main … error="SQLite worker store capacity reached (leaseId=…, path=…/agents/<id>/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite)"
model fallback decision: decision=candidate_failed … reason=overloaded next=openai/gpt-6-sol
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

As a local workaround we raised `MAX_STORES` to 256 in the bundled worker files on 29 Sep at about 19:35. There hasn't been a single "store capacity reached" line since. File descriptors weren't a concern: the gateway held about 1,500 open files, about 1,200 of them SQLite.

### Impact and severity

Affects any gateway with roughly 60 or more agents. Once the limit is hit, every agent that needs a new store fails every turn until a restart. Users see a misleading provider error, and messages go unanswered.

### Additional information

Related but different: #153437 (waiting for capacity during request bursts), #160386 (SQLite I/O pressure with large session stores).

We'd be glad to turn this into a PR with tests if the approach sounds right to you in principle. If you'd rather implement it yourselves, that's just as fine with us.
