issues.body:
### Environment
- OpenClaw 2026.5.20 (e510042)
- Provider: anthropic

### Summary
When an agent is pinned to a model string the gateway's internal price table does not recognize, the gateway writes `usage.cost.total: 0` (and every `usage.cost.*` sub-field = 0) into the session JSONL for **every** turn on that model. The token **counts** are recorded correctly — only the cost is zeroed. There is no warning at any level (no CLI output, no log line, no dashboard surface).

### Reproduction
1. Pin an agent to a model newer than the gateway build's price table — e.g. `claude-opus-4-8` on a 2026.5.20 runtime released before that model string.
2. Run any turn.
3. Inspect the session JSONL `message.usage`:
   - `input` / `output` / `cacheRead` / `cacheWrite` token counts -> populated (correct).
   - `cost` -> `{input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, total: 0}`.
4. Compare against a recognized model (`claude-sonnet-4-6`): `cost.total` is populated as expected.

### Impact
Any downstream consumer that trusts `usage.cost` silently under-counts to **zero** for the unrecognized model — cost dashboards, budget guardrails, per-agent attribution. In our deployment, every agent on the new model read $0 spend while the misattribution was invisible for ~a day (the spend was absorbed by the remaining recognized-model agents).

### Notes
The price table appears to be internal/upstream — it is **not configurable**. `models.providers.<provider>.models[]` entries accept only `id` and `name`; there is no price block, so an operator cannot patch the table locally to cover a new model string.

### Suggested remediation (either)
- A token-count x rate **fallback** when the model is unpriced (shipped default rates, or a configurable price block in the model registry), **or**
- An explicit **warning** at bootstrap / first use — e.g. `unknown model for pricing: <string>; usage.cost will be reported as zero` — so the gap is visible rather than silent.

issues.body:
## Problem

`pnpm test:coverage` exists and `test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts` defines V8 coverage thresholds, but the current default CI graph does not run `pnpm test:coverage` or an equivalent coverage-threshold lane. Normal `main`/PR validation runs many sharded Vitest configs, but it can stay green without proving the explicit coverage gate.

Noob explanation: tests can pass while the project quietly loses coverage. A coverage gate is the check that says "we still have enough tested code after this change." Right now OpenClaw has the command for that check, but default validation does not make GitHub run it automatically.

## Evidence from the 2026-06-03 auditor pass

- Issue creation snapshot: upstream `main` was `10830bc4a77cf12f0fcd36ba6c86459c7936cc98`.
- Closeout recheck snapshot: upstream `main` was `8de37e1ce4a98c165096f35ad3934388c62006f1`.
- `package.json` on `main` has `test:coverage`: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts --coverage`.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` on `main` does not contain `test:coverage`, `pnpm test:coverage`, `test:perf:budget`, or `pnpm test:perf` by literal command name.
- `docs/reference/test.md` documents `pnpm test:coverage` and says it is a default-unit-lane coverage gate with thresholds.
- Previous apparent duplicate PR #61166 was closed as opened on the wrong repo and did not land.

## Recommended test design

Start with a narrow, low-noise coverage guardrail before making it a required PR check:

1. Add a CI lane or scheduled/manual workflow that runs `pnpm test:coverage` on trusted `main` first and uploads `coverage/lcov.info` plus a text summary.
2. Add a small workflow/contract test that proves the coverage lane still references the package script instead of duplicating a raw Vitest command.
3. Keep the first version non-blocking or main-only until runtime/noise is known from several green runs.
4. After thresholds and wall time stabilize, promote it to a required default validation path for Node-relevant changes or a changed-coverage lane such as `pnpm test:coverage:changed` if that gives a better PR signal.
5. Do not mix this with the runtime performance workflow; `OpenClaw Performance` is already a separate report-oriented workflow and should keep its own baseline/regression policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- Default trusted validation runs an explicit coverage-threshold command or clearly documented equivalent.
- CI artifacts expose the coverage summary for humans.
- A repo test prevents the coverage guardrail from silently disappearing from the default validation path.
- The rollout plan states whether the first phase is advisory, main-only, scheduled, or PR-blocking.

## Summary

`openclaw status` shows all channels as `SETUP — configured; status unavailable in fast mode` in its Channels table, while the Overview section of the **same output** confirms the gateway is reachable at 33ms. 2. Observe the Channels table in the same output

4. Compare the two outputs

When `openclaw status` has already confirmed the gateway is reachable (as shown in its own Overview section), the Channels table should display live status fetched from that gateway — consistent with what `openclaw channels status` returns.

Gateway   local · ws://127.0.0.1:18789 (local loopback) · reachable 33ms

Running `openclaw channels status` immediately after returns:

- Feishu wukongim: enabled, configured, running
- Octo wukongim_bot: enabled, configured, running, in:1m ago, out:1m ago

`2026.5.28 (e932160)`

`macOS 26.2 (arm64)`

`pnpm (npm global)`

`claude-sonnet-4-6`

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a reliable, channel-aware way for OpenClaw to present shell/bash command blocks in chat responses so operators can copy commands safely and consistently.

### Problem to solve

Operational workflows often end with shell commands that need to be copied exactly: tail commands, jq filters, pruning commands, service restarts, diagnostic commands, and rollback snippets. Today agents commonly emit fenced Markdown such as ` ```bash ` blocks, but rendering and copy behavior can vary by chat surface.

For heavy operations users, command blocks are executable instructions. If line wrapping, escaping, language fences, or copy behavior are inconsistent, the user has to manually inspect and repair commands before running them.

### Proposed solution

Provide a first-class command-block rendering/convention for chat delivery, especially for shell snippets. Possible approaches:

- preserve fenced `bash` / `sh` blocks exactly across channel adapters
- normalize shell blocks before delivery so copy/paste does not introduce prompt text, escaped newlines, or lost indentation
- when a channel supports it, render command blocks as copyable code blocks
- when a channel does not support fenced code well, fall back to a plain text format optimized for safe copy/paste
- optionally add tests/fixtures for Telegram, Discord, Slack, Nextcloud Talk, and other chat adapters around fenced shell snippets

### Alternatives considered

Agents can avoid fenced blocks and send inline commands only, but that breaks down for multi-line shell, `jq`, heredocs, and diagnostic pipelines.

Users can manually repair pasted commands, but that defeats the purpose of using OpenClaw for operations support.

### Impact

Affected: Operators who use OpenClaw from chat surfaces and frequently receive shell commands or diagnostic snippets.

Severity: Medium. It is a UX/safety issue rather than a crash: poor command rendering slows operations and can cause incorrect commands to be copied.

Frequency: Recurs whenever a response includes multi-line shell commands or code fences.

Consequence: More manual verification, higher chance of copy/paste mistakes, and lower trust in chat-delivered operational instructions.

### Evidence/examples

A recent operational workflow required a live-monitoring command like:

```bash
latest=$(find ~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions -maxdepth 1 -name '*.trajectory.jsonl' -printf '%T@ %p\n' | sort -n | tail -1 | cut -d' ' -f2-)
tail -f "$latest" | jq -r '[.ts,.type,(.sessionKey // ""),(.data.name // .data.status // .data.provider // .data.modelId // "")] | @tsv'
```

This kind of command is common for OpenClaw operators and should be delivered in a way that is easy to copy safely from chat.

### Additional information

This is intentionally separate from the live-progress-log request. The progress-log issue is about the availability of an operator-friendly log view; this issue is about safe presentation of shell snippets in chat once OpenClaw suggests commands.

issues.body:
## Summary

We hit a production incident that started with the same Telegram/Codex stall symptoms tracked in #82274, but recovery exposed a separate state-path bug:

When OpenClaw CLI/session recovery is run from an agent/Codex environment whose `HOME` points at an isolated Codex home, session commands can read/write a shadow OpenClaw state tree instead of the gateway's real per-agent session store. The operator thinks sessions were reset, but the running gateway continues reading the canonical store and agents remain stuck in `typing...` / `status=running`.

This creates a nasty recovery split-brain during exactly the failure mode where operators are trying to unstick agents.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: `2026.5.12`
- Gateway: local systemd root runtime, listening on `127.0.0.1:18789`
- Codex CLI/app-server: `0.130.0`
- Channel involved: Telegram
- Model path involved: `openai/gpt-5.5`
- Related upstream incident: #82274

## Observed evidence

During the incident the gateway logs showed repeated runtime stalls:

```text
codex app-server turn idle timed out waiting for terminal event
codex app-server client retired after timed-out turn
timeout-compaction
active-memory timeout after 15000ms
before_prompt_build handler from active-memory failed: timed out after 15000ms
```

A recovery attempt then reset sessions from a CLI/tool context where `HOME` resolved under the Codex isolated home. That touched a shadow path like:

```text
$OPENCLAW_HOME/agents/<coordinator>/agent/codex-home/home/.openclaw/agents/<target-agent>/sessions/sessions.json
```

But the running gateway was using the canonical per-agent store:

```text
$OPENCLAW_HOME/agents/<target-agent>/sessions/sessions.json
```

Result: the shadow store looked reset, while the canonical store still had stale `status=running` sessions. Only after forcing the recovery with canonical env/path did the stuck agents clear.

## Why this is dangerous

- Recovery tools can report success against the wrong state tree.
- A stalled agent lane can survive an apparent reset.
- Operators can create multiple divergent session histories for the same agent.
- The failure mode is easy to trigger from ACP/Codex launcher contexts because `HOME` is intentionally isolated.

## Local mitigation applied

We mitigated by:

1. Backing up the shadow session directories.
2. Replacing the shadow `codex-home/home/.openclaw/agents/<agent>/sessions` directories with symlinks to the canonical `$OPENCLAW_HOME/agents/<agent>/sessions` directories.
3. Running future offline recovery with explicit canonical env:

```bash
HOME=/root \
OPENCLAW_CONFIG_DIR=/root/.openclaw \
OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=/root/.openclaw/openclaw.json \
openclaw ...
```

We also moved compaction/fallback away from the same Codex runtime and tightened active-memory timeouts as local blast-radius reduction, but that does not fix the underlying state-path split.

## Expected behavior

OpenClaw should not silently read/write a new state tree just because the process `HOME` is inside an isolated Codex/ACP home.

At minimum, session/state commands should do one of:

- derive the gateway home/config from `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_DIR` / `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` / the running gateway, not raw `~`;
- warn/refuse when `~/.openclaw` resolves under `agent/*/codex-home/home/.openclaw`;
- expose an explicit `--home` / `--config-dir` / `--store` for recovery tools;

issues.body:
## Summary

`diagnostics.otel.captureContent.{inputMessages,outputMessages,toolInputs,toolOutputs}` is documented but does nothing. The runtime emits only sanitized `paramsSummary` on the broadcast stream that bundled `diagnostics-otel` consumes — raw `inputMessages`, `toolInput`, and `toolResult` content never appear in OTel span attributes. Confirmed empirically against pre-bug traces from 2026-05-03 through 2026-05-04 with `captureContent: {enabled: true, inputMessages: true, outputMessages: true, toolInputs: true, toolOutputs: true}`: zero `openclaw.content.*` attributes on any span.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.5.3-1` (also confirmed on `2026.5.3` and earlier 5.2 releases)

## Reproduction

```bash
openclaw config set diagnostics.otel.enabled true
openclaw config set diagnostics.otel.captureContent.enabled true
openclaw config set diagnostics.otel.captureContent.inputMessages true
openclaw config set diagnostics.otel.captureContent.outputMessages true
openclaw config set diagnostics.otel.captureContent.toolInputs true
openclaw config set diagnostics.otel.captureContent.toolOutputs true
openclaw gateway restart --wait 30s

openclaw agent --message 'hello' --agent main --to '+15555550100' --json
```

## Observed

Spans reach the OTLP endpoint with `openclaw.run`, `model_call`, `tool.execution` names, but **no `openclaw.content.*`, `openclaw.input.*`, or `openclaw.output.*` attributes are populated**. Tool spans carry only `paramsSummary` (a hash + length, no actual values).

## Expected

Per docs (`/gateway/opentelemetry`), `captureContent: true` should populate raw input/output content as span attributes (size-capped, optionally redacted).

## Working approach (for reference)

We bypassed this by writing a separate plugin that subscribes to **public hooks** (`api.on("before_tool_call", ...)`, `api.on("llm_input", ...)`, etc.) — the hook arguments contain full unsanitized content because the runtime calls hook handlers with the real data, not the sanitized broadcast. Code: https://github.com/mjunaidca/tutorclaw/tree/main/plugins/tutorclaw-tracing

This works, but it means every operator who wants content visibility has to ship their own plugin. The bundled `diagnostics-otel`'s configuration knob is the natural seam — it just doesn't work today.

## Suggested fix

Either:
- (a) Wire `captureContent.*` flags through to actual content-emission paths so the documented config does what it claims; OR
- (b) Document `captureContent` as deprecated/no-op and point operators at the public-hook plugin pattern as the recommended approach.

## Related

Related to #77390 (bundled-only origin gate) — even if `captureContent` worked, externally-installed `diagnostics-otel` couldn't receive the events to attach attributes to.

issues.body:
Doing a retry-behavior test today — deliberately broken URLs (404, 500, 503, conn-refused, DNS-fail, slow-timeout) to see what the agent does on its own when fetches fail. Stood up a `python -m http.server` on 127.0.0.1 for the controllable cells.

web_fetch refused every URL pointing at 127.0.0.1, with this:

```
{"status":"error","tool":"web_fetch","error":"Blocked hostname or private/internal/special-use IP address"}
```

Right call, doing the SSRF check at the obvious place.

What I didn't expect was the model's response. Pretty much every cell where web_fetch refused, the next thing it did was switch to exec and curl the URL anyway. exec has no equivalent network filter so the request just went through. From the cell asking for /status/500 on localhost:

```
toolCall #1  web_fetch  {"url":"http://127.0.0.1:18760/status/500"}
toolResult              {"status":"error","tool":"web_fetch","error":"Blocked hostname or private/internal/special-use IP address"}
toolCall #2  exec       {"command":"curl -s -o /dev/null -w \"HTTP_CODE:%{http_code}\\n\" http://127.0.0.1:18760/status/500"}
toolResult              HTTP_CODE:500
```

This wasn't prompted. There was no instruction to "try another way" anywhere in the prompt or the workspace bootstrap. The model worked it out on its own as a normal fallback. Pattern hit four of the five local-IP cells in the probe (the fifth, conn-refused on a non-listening port, also failed via exec — but for a different reason).

Could be intentional. exec is a power tool, anyone enabling it has already opted into a wider surface than web_fetch alone. But if you're treating the SSRF check on web_fetch as a real boundary, this is going to surprise you — when exec is in the allowlist, the boundary is effectively cosmetic.

Two directions if it's not by design:

- mirror the URL/host blocklist on exec by inspecting argv. Cheap, brittle, takes the obvious path off the table. A model that wants to dodge it can use nc, python -m http.client, base64-encoded URLs, etc., but most won't bother.
- run exec inside a netns with no route to private/loopback. Categorical, harder to set up, probably wants the sandbox path.

Stack: openclaw 2026.4.9, vLLM Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on :8002 with `--tool-call-parser qwen3_xml`, `temperature=0`, `seed=42`. Repro is small — openclaw + http.server + a prompt asking the agent to fetch 127.0.0.1. Can share a minimal version of the probe harness if useful.

issues.body:
## Problem statement

The `allowConversationAccess` flag is set in `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` per-plugin under `plugins.entries.<id>.hooks.allowConversationAccess: true`. The flag is gated by config schema validation; non-bundled plugins must explicitly opt in or the gateway rejects their `agent_end` typed-hook subscriptions.

The PRoblem: the gateway's config schema doesn't know about the field unless explicitly extended. Smarter-Claw maintains TWO patches just to make this opt-in possible:

- `installer/patches/core/schema-allow-conversation-access.diff` (~12 LOC, JSON schema)
- `installer/patches/core/zod-schema-allow-conversation-access.diff` (~12 LOC, Zod schema)

Both patches add the same field declaration in two parallel locations — a recurring pattern that should be obviated.

## Proposed change

Make `allowConversationAccess` a declared field in the plugin manifest (`openclaw.plugin.json`) instead of in the host config:

```json
{
  "id": "smarter-claw",
  "name": "Smarter Claw",
  "permissions": {
    "conversationAccess": true
  }
}
```

The gateway reads the manifest at plugin load. If `permissions.conversationAccess` is true AND the plugin requests `agent_end` (or other conversation-access-gated hook), it's allowed. No host config flag needed; no schema patches needed.

For backward compatibility, the existing config flag continues to work (and overrides manifest if both present).

## Implementation sketch

```ts
// src/plugins/registry.ts (or similar)
function isConversationAccessAllowed(plugin: PluginManifest, config: PluginEntryConfig): boolean {
  if (config?.hooks?.allowConversationAccess === true) return true; // existing path
  if (plugin.permissions?.conversationAccess === true) return true; // NEW
  return false;
}
```

## Backward compatibility

Fully additive. Plugins that already set the config flag continue to work. New plugins can declare in manifest instead.

## What this saves Smarter-Claw

- Delete `installer/patches/core/schema-allow-conversation-access.diff`
- Delete `installer/patches/core/zod-schema-allow-conversation-access.diff`
- Move permission declaration to where it belongs (the plugin's own manifest)

## Why this matters beyond Smarter-Claw

This pattern recurs for any future capability gates. Currently each gate requires a parallel pair of patches (Zod + JSON schema). Manifest-declared permissions scale linearly without patch overhead — and put the permission disclosure in the plugin developer's own file (where security review can find it) rather than in the operator's config (where it's invisible).

## Tests proposed

- Plugin with `permissions.conversationAccess: true` in manifest can subscribe to `agent_end` without any config flag
- Plugin without the manifest field AND no config flag → existing rejection behavior
- Plugin with both → manifest value used (fallback to config if missing)

## Cross-link

Smarter-Claw RFC series:
- openclaw/openclaw#71260 (mergeSessionEntryWithPolicy)
- openclaw/openclaw#71426 (sessions.patch extension hook)
- openclaw/openclaw#71427 (tool-event subscription)

issues.body:
## Summary

`memoryFlush.softThresholdTokens` is documented as "Threshold distance to compaction (in tokens)" but the field name reads as an absolute arming level. Setting it to a large value (expecting later/less compaction) actually **lowers** the trigger threshold, producing *more* compactions. Additionally, no config-layer validation warns when `keepRecentTokens >= softThresholdTokens`, which causes post-compaction churn.

## Evidence

### Semantics inversion

On 2026-08-19, we set `softThresholdTokens=100000` expecting compaction to trigger later (at higher fill). The trigger formula (`agent-runner.runtime-C7BtnuJb.js:4486`):

```js
threshold = contextWindow - reserveTokensFloor(default 20000) - softThresholdTokens
```

With `contextWindow=200000`:
- `softThresholdTokens=35000` (original) → threshold=145000 (72.5% fill)
- `softThresholdTokens=100000` (our "raise") → threshold=80000 (40% fill) ← **more** compactions, not fewer

We got a compaction at 16:34 MYT on a session at 175k tokens — the session had just been compacted and was still above the 80k trigger. The field name reads as an absolute arming level ("the soft threshold is 100k tokens") but it is actually a **distance from the context window edge**. This inverted our fix: we expected later compaction and got earlier compaction.

### keepRecentTokens vs softThresholdTokens churn

Between 16:05 and 16:40 MYT, config had `keepRecentTokens=40000` above `softThresholdTokens=35000`. Post-compaction retained context (40k) + a single heavy tool turn (100k+ tokens) = 140k, above the 145k threshold. This produces compaction on nearly every message with no config-layer warning.

### Historical compaction data (all agents, Aug 5-19)

All 20 compactions found across all agent SQLite `transcript_events` have `fromHook=true`, with `tokensBefore` values:

| Bucket | Count |
|--------|-------|
| <50k   | 3     |
| 50-100k| 8     |
| 100-150k| 6    |
| 150-200k| 3   |

Many fired at 22k-77k — well below the 145k threshold — suggesting preflight compaction churn driven by projected token estimates including pending tool output.

## Proposed fixes

1. **Rename or alias the field.** `softThresholdTokens` reads as "the soft threshold" (an absolute level). It is actually a **distance from the context window edge**. Suggested: `softThresholdDistanceTokens` or document prominently in the schema description.

2. **Validation warnings** in `openclaw config validate` / config patch:
   - (a) Warn when `keepRecentTokens >= (contextWindow - reserveTokensFloor - softThresholdTokens)` — post-compaction retained tokens meet or exceed the trigger threshold, causing churn.
   - (b) Warn when `softThresholdTokens > contextWindow / 2` — the "soft" threshold has consumed more than half the context window, which is almost certainly a misconfiguration (as we experienced).

3. **Schema description update:** The current zod schema description (`schema-C9V-Q4n4.js:98`) says "Threshold distance to compaction (in tokens) that triggers pre-compaction memory flush execution." This is accurate but buried. Add a one-line callout in config docs.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.7.2-beta.7 (dabe191)
- macOS 26.6.1, node 26.3.1
- 9 agents, all morpheus/glm-5.2 (200k context window)

## Related issues

- #87136 — absolute token thresholds break when switching models
- #81856 — add absolute-token trigger (feature request)
- #120162 — safeguard compaction qualityGuard retry shares timeout budget
- #120455 — prepareCompaction refuses second pass

issues.body:
## Structured secret redaction masks non-secret JSON fields based on key name alone (e.g. Azure Log Analytics `SYN0002` error `token` field)

### Summary

`redactStructuredSecretValue` (via `shouldRedactStructuredPrimitiveField` / `isSensitiveFieldKey` in `redact-B9QQ4Wyz.js`) redacts any JSON field whose **key name** matches `STRUCTURED_SECRET_FIELD_RE` (`token`, `key`, `secret`, `session`, `signature`, `cookie`, etc.) to `"***"`, regardless of the field's actual content or the API it came from. This is correct for genuine credential-shaped output, but it also fires on unrelated third-party API responses that happen to reuse one of these words for something else entirely — destroying real diagnostic information in the process.

Concretely: Azure Monitor's Log Analytics query API returns syntax-error diagnostics shaped like

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "BadArgumentError",
    "innererror": {
      "code": "SyntaxError",
      "innererror": {
        "code": "SYN0002",
        "message": "Query could not be parsed at 'first' on line [1,60]",
        "line": 1,
        "pos": 60,
        "token": "first"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Here `token` is Azure's own name for "the specific parser token that caused the syntax error" — nothing to do with an API token/credential. Because the key is literally named `token`, the value gets masked to `"***"` before an agent session ever sees it, even though `"first"` is not sensitive in any sense.

### Environment

- Package: `openclaw`
- Version: `2026.7.1-2` (`0790d9f`)
- File: `dist/redact-B9QQ4Wyz.js`
- Relevant symbols: `STRUCTURED_SECRET_FIELD_RE` (line 460), `isSensitiveFieldKey`, `shouldRedactStructuredPrimitiveField`, `redactStructuredSecretValue`

### Reproduction

1. Have an agent (or any tool-execution path that runs captured JSON through the structured-redaction pipeline) run an Azure CLI Log Analytics query that hits a `SYN0002` syntax error, e.g.:

   ```bash
   az monitor log-analytics query -w "$LAW_GUID" \
     --analytics-query 'SentinelHealth | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | summarize first=min(TimeGenerated) | take 1' \
     -o json
   ```

2. **Expected:** the tool result contains Azure's real error body, including `"token": "first"`.
3. **Actual:** the tool result the agent sees contains `"token": "***"`.

Confirmed directly: running the identical `az` command outside the redaction path (plain shell, no agent tool-execution wrapper) returns the real value (`"token": "first"`). Running the same command through an agent session's `bash` tool returns `"token": "***"` for the exact same underlying API response. Nothing else about the request differs.

### Impact

An agent debugging its own query (or any downstream JSON-shaped tool output containing a `token`/`key`/`secret`/`session`/etc.-named field for non-credential reasons) loses the one piece of evidence a syntax/semantic error is built around. In this case the `message` field happened to also quote the token in prose ("...parsed at 'first'..."), so the agent could still recover — but that's incidental to this specific error shape, not guaranteed for other APIs or other error codes that might use one of the ~30 reserved key names in `STRUCTURED_SECRET_FIELD_RE` for a non-secret purpose.

This is a false positive in a security control, which is a worse failure mode than under-redaction here: it silently degrades agent capability (wrong/unexplainable failures, wasted retries) without any corresponding security benefit, since `"first"`/`"last"`/any KQL token name was never sensitive to begin with.

### Suggested fix

Key-name-only matching is too blunt for fields nested inside third-party API error/diagnostic payloads. Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. **Scope structured key-name redaction to trusted source paths** (e.g. resolved config/secrets objects, env dumps, auth headers) rather than applying it universally to *all* captured tool stdout/stderr JSON, regardless of which external system produced it.
2. **Combine key-name matching with a value-shape/entropy check** — a real secret is rarely a short dictionary word like `"first"`; requiring some minimum entropy or pattern match before masking a `token`/`key`-named field would eliminate this whole class of false positive while still catching actual credentials.
3. At minimum, special-case known non-secret uses of these key names from well-known SDKs/APIs (Azure Monitor's `SyntaxError.innererror.token` being one concrete example) so this doesn't need to be rediscovered API-by-API.

### Additional context

Found while debugging a SOC automation agent (`soc-lead`, running Sentinel KQL investigations via `az monitor log-analytics query`) that kept hitting `SYN0002` errors it couldn't self-diagnose from the tool output alone. Root KQL cause (`first`/`last` being reserved Kusto tokens, unrelated to this report) was fixed separately in our own docs; this report is specifically about the redaction behavior that obscured the diagnosis path.

Happy to provide the full (redacted-of-anything-actually-sensitive) session transcript if useful.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

With state on the PostgreSQL backend, a Gateway cannot start again after its host is replaced and the host-local client credential store (`client/credentials.sqlite`) is lost. Client credential preparation refuses until a matching backup is restored, and there is no supported path when no backup exists.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure `database.families.state.engine: "postgres"` with a reachable `database.postgres.connection`.
2. Run `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` once. This creates the PostgreSQL state store, the `state/openclaw.sqlite` anchor and `client/credentials.sqlite`.
3. Simulate a replaced host by deleting `client/` under the state directory. Keep the PostgreSQL store and `state/openclaw.sqlite`.
4. Run `openclaw doctor --client-credentials --repair --non-interactive --json`, or start the Gateway.

### Expected behavior

An operator can explicitly accept losing the old local device identity and pairing tokens and bind a fresh local credential store to the existing PostgreSQL state store, as a first bootstrap does. Ordinary startup can keep refusing.

### Actual behavior

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": {
    "type": "cli_error",
    "message": "Local credentials are missing; restore the matching client credential backup."
  }
}
```

Without that backup, the Gateway stays unable to start.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.5 (`main` 333b38de8770)

### Operating system

Linux containers with an ephemeral state directory (where this was found); reproduced locally on macOS 27 against PostgreSQL 18.

### Install method

docker; also pnpm build from source

### Model

Not applicable; this happens before any model call.

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable.

### Additional provider/model setup details

Not applicable.

### Logs

See Actual behavior; the refusal is the complete output.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Reproduction steps above use only the public CLI.

### Impact and severity

Affects operators who run PostgreSQL state on replaceable hosts such as Kubernetes pods. A routine host replacement without a backup of the local credential file leaves the Gateway unable to start. SQLite state is not affected.

### Additional information

A proposed fix is an explicit doctor flag, `--rebind-missing-credentials`, accepted only with `--client-credentials`. Gateway startup would never rebind. Present, mismatched or corrupt local stores and SQLite state would keep their existing refusals.

issues.body:
### Summary

Managed Tailscale Serve/Funnel always claims tailnet port 443 with no way to change it. On a host where another service already owns 443, the Gateway cannot start at all, and the only workaround (a hand-made `tailscale serve` on another port) silently breaks Tailscale identity auth.

### Problem to solve

`gateway.tailscale.mode: "serve"` hardcodes the tailnet-facing port to 443. `claimTailscaleRoute(mode, target)` receives only the *local* backend port and never passes `--https=<port>`, so the route is always claimed on 443.

That is fine on a dedicated host, but a reverse proxy bound to `0.0.0.0:443` also covers the Tailscale IP. The managed claim then fails and the Gateway refuses to start:

```
reason:         gateway.startup_failed
error.message:  sending serve config: updating config: listener already exists for port 443
```

The operator is left with two bad options:

1. **Give up the reverse proxy on 443.** Not viable when the host serves unrelated public vhosts.
2. **Set `gateway.tailscale.mode: "off"` and run `tailscale serve --https=8443 18789` by hand.** The route works and the dashboard loads, but every Gateway-authenticated request is rejected with 403.

Option 2 fails for a non-obvious reason. Tailscale identity headers are only trusted on the listener OpenClaw created itself. With `mode: "off"` the Gateway only has an ordinary listener, while the manual Serve still injects `x-forwarded-*`, and `ingress-attribution.ts` rejects that combination *before* `gateway.trustedProxies` is ever consulted:

```
[gateway] observed unattributable proxy-shaped traffic from 127.0.0.1;
Gateway-authenticated routes reject it, while plugin-authenticated routes ignore forwarded claims.
Configure gateway.trustedProxies narrowly and make the proxy overwrite or safely rebuild forwarded client headers.
```

That log line sends the operator toward `gateway.trustedProxies`, which cannot fix this case — the managed-listener check short-circuits first. Adding trusted proxies, tweaking headers, or widening auth all fail, because the real constraint is that the route must be *managed* to be trusted, and a managed route cannot avoid 443.

The practical symptom is the mobile app never completing authorization against a Gateway on a host that already uses 443. #89306 describes the same shape from the client side ("Deploy OpenClaw Docker with a custom domain and Nginx configured without exposing port 443, e.g. using port 8443") but was closed without a repro.

### Proposed solution

Add `gateway.tailscale.port` (default `443`) and thread it through to the managed claim as `--https=<port>`:

- `claimTailscaleRoute(mode, target, exposedPort?)` emits `--https=<port>` only for non-default ports, so the command operators see documented is unchanged in the default case.
- The port is kept in every published origin and log line (`https://<magicdns>:8443/`, `wss://<magicdns>:8443`), since clients dial the tailnet route directly.
- Config validation rejects ports Funnel cannot expose: Serve accepts any port, Funnel accepts only 443, 8443, and 10000.

This keeps the route managed, so identity-header attribution keeps working — which is the part the manual workaround loses.

```json5
{
  gateway: {
    bind: "loopback",
    tailscale: { mode: "serve", port: 8443 },
  },
}
```

### Alternatives considered

- **Trust identity headers from `gateway.trustedProxies` on the ordinary listener.** Rejected: it weakens the managed-ingress provenance guarantee that `ingress-attribution.ts` exists to enforce, for every deployment, to fix a port conflict.
- **Detect the 443 conflict and auto-pick a free port.** Silently changing a tailnet URL operators have to type is worse than failing; it also cannot be represented in config.
- **Document "don't run a reverse proxy on the Gateway host".** Doesn't help the docker + nginx setups this keeps hitting, and `docs/gateway/tailscale.md` already acknowledges custom Serve ports exist ("Doctor does not ... guess how to rewrite custom Serve ports").
- **A third-party plugin.** Not possible: the claim happens in Gateway startup, before any plugin surface.

### Impact

Operators running the Gateway on a host that already serves 443 (reverse proxy, docker + nginx, shared VPS) can use managed Tailscale ingress instead of choosing between a broken Gateway and a manual Serve that 403s. No behavior change for anyone who does not set the key — the default stays 443 and the emitted `tailscale serve` command is byte-identical.

### Evidence/examples

Reproduced on OpenClaw 2026.8.1, Ubuntu 24.04, Tailscale Serve, with nginx holding `0.0.0.0:443`:

- With `mode: "serve"`: `gateway.startup_failed` / `listener already exists for port 443` (quoted above, from `~/.openclaw/logs/stability/*-gateway.startup_failed.json`).
- With `mode: "off"` + manual `tailscale serve --https=8443 18789`: dashboard reachable, Android authorization returns 403, Gateway logs `observed unattributable proxy-shaped traffic from 127.0.0.1`.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

issues.body:
## Summary

`model_call_ended` (the plugin hook fired after every model stream completes/errors) carries no
field distinguishing a channel-dispatched guest turn from other model-invoking activity that goes
through the same diagnostic-event wrapper — specifically compaction and the runtime-event
scheduler detour (see #124180). A plugin using `model_call_ended` to drive guest-facing logic
(e.g. a circuit breaker that opens after N consecutive provider failures) cannot avoid counting
non-guest model-call outcomes toward that logic, because there is no `source`/`purpose`/`origin`
field on the event to filter on, and the two non-guest emitters we found run inside the *same*
session as the guest conversation, so `sessionKey` cannot discriminate either.

## Where this was found

Reviewing our own plugin's guest-facing circuit breaker (`model_call_ended` → count consecutive
`outcome: "error"` → open after 5), we needed to confirm whether non-guest model calls could
contaminate it. Traced the installed dist (`2026.7.1-2`, `0790d9f`) rather than guess:

- `compact-DLB4d8IL.js:1057`: `session.agent.streamFn = wrapStreamFnWithDiagnosticModelCallEvents(session.agent.streamFn, {runId: diagnosticCompactionRunId, ...})` — compaction wraps its own embedded-agent model call with the diagnostic-event wrapper.
- `selection-JInn13lc.js:13107` (the same file that defines `OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_EVENT_USER_PROMPT`, see #124180): `activeSession.agent.streamFn = wrapStreamFnWithDiagnosticModelCallEvents(activeSession.agent.streamFn, {runId: params.runId, ...})` — the runtime-event scheduler does the same.
- `attempt.model-diagnostic-events-CfZQM0hs.js:4892` (`wrapStreamFnWithDiagnosticModelCallEvents`): on stream completion or error, calls `dispatchModelCallEndedHook` (`:4706`), which — if `hookRunner.hasHooks("model_call_ended")` — calls `hookRunner.runModelCallEnded(event, hookCtx)`. This is the same hook a plugin registers via `api.on("model_call_ended", ...)`.

So: any plugin hook on `model_call_ended` receives events from at least three sources (real guest
turns, compaction, the runtime-event scheduler) with no way to tell them apart from the event
shape alone.

## What we checked for a discriminator, and why each didn't work

- **`sessionKey`**: identical for a guest turn and a compaction/runtime-event call on that same
  session — both non-guest sources operate on the guest's own session, not a separate one.
- **`runId`**: compaction uses a separately-named internal variable
  (`diagnosticCompactionRunId`) rather than a real agent-run id, but nothing in the event or its
  type marks it as such — a consumer can't distinguish "this runId came from
  diagnosticCompactionRunId" from "this runId came from a real agent run" without depending on an
  internal naming convention that isn't part of any documented contract. The runtime-event
  scheduler's call uses `params.runId` and flows through the *same* `onAgentRunStart` machinery a
  normal turn does, so its `runId` is not distinguishable from a genuine turn's at all.
- We did not find any `kind`/`type`/`origin`/`purpose` field on the `model_call_ended` event that
  would serve this purpose.

## Impact

Any plugin that uses `model_call_ended` for guest-facing bookkeeping (rate limiting, circuit
breakers, per-guest metrics, abuse detection) will have that bookkeeping silently affected by
OpenClaw's own internal model calls (compaction summaries, the runtime-event scheduler detour),
with no way to exclude them. In our case this means our safety-layer's circuit breaker *could* be
opened by a run of internal-call failures that have nothing to do with the guest-facing provider's
health — we have not observed this happening in production, but the mechanism for it to happen is
confirmed, not hypothetical.

## Suggested fix

Add a discriminator to the `model_call_ended` (and ideally `model_call_started`) event payload
identifying the call's origin — e.g. `source: "channel" | "compaction" | "runtime-event" | ...`,
or at minimum a boolean like `isGuestTurn`. Given `wrapStreamFnWithDiagnosticModelCallEvents` is
the single choke point all three call sites already go through, this looks like it could be a
narrow, low-risk addition at that one function rather than a change to each caller.

## What we're not asserting

We have not observed this contamination actually flip a breaker or otherwise cause a visible
production issue — this report is about a confirmed *mechanism*, from source, not an incident.
Happy to share the specific plugin-side code (`model_call_ended` handler) or more detail on the
citation trail above on request.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2` (`0790d9f`)
- Node `v24.19.0`, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS aarch64 (NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX)
- Channel: Telegram, polling mode
- Related: #124180 (runtime-event scheduler detour) — same file (`selection-JInn13lc.js`) surfaced
  in both investigations, independently.

issues.body:
## Summary

Add a Telegram-native `/ignore` command that keeps one human-only message out of agent context.

## Problem to solve

Shared Telegram chats often contain side conversations intended for other humans. Today those messages still enter OpenClaw's history and prompt context, which can distract the agent and cause later replies to reference irrelevant chatter.

## Proposed solution

Treat `/ignore <message>` and `/ignore@ThisBot <message>` as Telegram-native commands. After normal sender authorization, drop the update before reply-chain recording, media download/transcription, typing indicators, history compilation, or agent dispatch. Bare `/ignore` returns concise usage help.

The command is exact-token only: `/ignoreme`, inline mentions, and commands addressed to another bot remain ordinary messages. Albums are suppressed as a unit at the existing media-group flush boundary. A deliberate direct reply may reintroduce the replied-to Telegram quote for that turn, while the ignored ancestor is not recursively persisted into ambient history.

No new configuration or storage schema is introduced. Disabling native Telegram commands disables `/ignore` as well.

## Alternatives considered

- `/btw` controls whether the bot replies while retaining the message in context; it solves the opposite half of the workflow.
- A plugin hook runs too late to prevent history ingestion and media processing.
- Per-chat configuration, tombstones, or durable ignore tracking add complexity that is unnecessary for a one-update context-hygiene command.

## Impact

- Affected: people using OpenClaw in active Telegram groups and forum topics.
- Severity: recurring context pollution rather than data loss or a security boundary.
- Frequency: potentially daily in mixed human/agent conversations.
- Consequence: irrelevant agent context, confused follow-ups, and manual correction.

## Evidence/examples

The behavior follows existing Telegram ingress and native-command patterns, including foreign-bot command handling and early media policy checks. Local focused validation covers exact matching, foreign-bot and near-miss negatives, both album arrival orders, native-command disablement, reply-chain persistence, and Telegram bot ingress behavior.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself.

## Additional information

This is context hygiene, not deletion, secrecy, encryption, or message redaction. Telegram retains the original chat message normally.

issues.body:
### Summary

Allow users to use their browser's native Web Speech API for voice dictation in the WebUI input field without requiring OpenAI API keys or local Whisper backends.

### Problem to solve

Currently, clicking the microphone icon in the WebUI input field without a configured Realtime voice provider throws an error:

Error: Realtime voice provider "openai" is not configured

For self-hosted deployments without dedicated GPU resources for local Whisper inference or paid cloud API keys, there is no out-of-the-box way to use voice input. Users are forced to rely on browser extensions (Violentmonkey) or manual index.html patches via skill scripts to intercept the click event.

### Proposed solution

Add an option under Settings → Audio / Speech-to-Text (STT) in the OpenClaw Control UI to select Browser Web Speech API (Client-side Dictation).

When selected:

Clicking the microphone button in the prompt area triggers the browser's native SpeechRecognition / webkitSpeechRecognition API instead of initiating the WebRTC Realtime Talk pipeline.

The UI provides visual feedback (e.g., highlighting the microphone icon in red while recording).

Transcribed text is inserted directly into the prompt textarea, dispatching reactive state update events (input / change) to keep the UI in sync.

Privacy note: Add a brief label explaining that Chromium routes Web Speech requests via vendor endpoints (e.g., Google), keeping this feature as an explicit opt-in toggle.

### Alternatives considered

Server-side Whisper / Local STT: Requires significant local hardware resources or complex container setups, adding unnecessary friction for users who only need basic text dictation.

Manual Script Injection / Skill Hooks: Injecting custom JS into dist/ui/index.html via custom skills or reverse proxy rules is fragile and gets overwritten during OpenClaw updates.



### Impact

Affected users/systems: Self-hosted users, lightweight server instances, and users operating without paid voice API keys.

Severity: Annoying / Workflow friction (forces manual typing when voice dictation is preferred).

Frequency: Always occurs when clicking the microphone icon without configured cloud/local audio backends.

Consequence: Delays input, requires extra manual work or client-side browser extensions.

### Evidence/examples

Prior Art: Web interfaces like QwenPaw and Open WebUI natively offer client-side Web Speech API dictation as a zero-dependency alternative to server-side Whisper or cloud APIs.

Error Log: Error: Realtime voice provider "openai" is not configured when clicking the mic button in standard builds.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (live UI state is missing; persisted history is intact)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On the current `main` branch, Control UI / WebChat does not reliably show tool activity such as `exec` in real time. The tool call and its result become visible only after refreshing the page.

This makes an active tool-running turn look idle or incomplete even though the Gateway has recorded the events correctly.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run OpenClaw from a current `main` checkout.
2. Open Control UI / WebChat.
3. Send a prompt that triggers one or more tools, for example a multi-step request using `exec`.
4. Observe the chat while the tools are running and after they complete.
5. Refresh the page.

### Expected behavior

Tool-call activity and results should appear in the chat as the corresponding live `agent` / `session.tool` events arrive, without requiring a page refresh.

### Actual behavior

Some tool calls or results do not appear in the live UI. After refreshing, history hydration loads and displays them, showing that the events were persisted and that the failure is in the live Control UI rendering/reconciliation path rather than tool execution or transcript storage.

### OpenClaw version

Current `main` checkout (exact downstream checkout SHA was not captured).

### Surface

Control UI / WebChat

### Additional information

This appears related to, but distinct from:

- #92122, which concerned incorrect live ordering and was closed by #93184. In this report the activity is missing until refresh, rather than merely displayed out of order.
- #98540, where the composer appears idle while the Activity panel still shows running tools. In this report the live tool activity itself is not reliably rendered and only appears after refresh.
- #98461, which was closed as already implemented because current releases expose live tool activity over the Gateway WebSocket. The present behavior may therefore be a regression in consuming or reconciling those live events on `main`.

Likely investigation area: the Control UI live tool stream and history reconciliation/hydration path.

issues.body:
## Summary

Prompt cache hit-rate dropped to ~0% after upgrading to OpenClaw 2026.7.1 on proxy-like endpoints (starport / group3 / deepseek / bailian / grok). Root cause: the 7/25 release silently changed the default cache-key pass-through behavior for proxy-like endpoints, and the subsequent 7/29 fix only covered one model (`sol`), leaving ~17 other models broken.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)`
- macOS 26.3.1 (arm64)
- Node v24.x
- Config: `models.providers.*.models[].supportsPromptCacheKey` per-model flag

## Observed behavior

1. Before the 7/25 upgrade: prompt cache hit-rate ~90% on proxy endpoints (cache key forwarded).
2. After the 7/25 upgrade (silent): hit-rate dropped to ~0% — proxy-like endpoints started stripping the cache key from upstream requests.
3. The 7/29 fix added the flag back for **one** model (`sol`) only; the other ~17 models using proxy-like endpoints remained broken. No migration notice, no schema change surfaced in changelog.

## Root cause hypothesis

- The cache-key pass-through is enforced per-model via `supportsPromptCacheKey` with **no provider-level default and no wildcard**.
- Proxy-like endpoints (endpoints that forward to an upstream aggregator) now require the flag explicitly, but the upgrade changed the default behavior without a migration path or startup warning.
- Consequence: silent regression that is only detectable by monitoring hit-rate (no error logs).

## Reproduction steps

1. Configure a proxy-like provider (e.g. `starport`, `group3`) with multiple models.
2. Do NOT set `supportsPromptCacheKey` on each model (as was valid pre-upgrade).
3. Upgrade to 2026.7.1, run traffic, observe prompt cache hit-rate ~0%.

## Suggested fixes (any of)

1. **Provider-level default / wildcard**: allow `supportsPromptCacheKey: true` at provider scope (or `*`) instead of per-model only.
2. **Proxy-like endpoints default to pass-through**: if the endpoint type is an upstream proxy, keep forwarding cache keys by default unless explicitly disabled.
3. **Migration guard**: on upgrade, if existing models lack the flag and the previous default was pass-through, either preserve the old behavior or emit a startup warning listing affected models.

## Impact

Silent cost regression (prompt cache miss → full context re-encoding per request) with no visible error; only detectable by comparing hit-rate before/after upgrade. Affected our setup with ~18 models on 5 proxy-like providers.

## Related context

- Fix workaround applied on our side: scripted batch config patch adding `supportsPromptCacheKey: true` to all affected models, hot-applied via `config patch` (no restart). This is a workaround, not a fix.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a default-off Feishu option that natively mentions the current human sender on every group reply.

### Problem to solve

In busy Feishu group chats, an agent reply can be visually separated from the triggering message. Without a native mention, the person who asked may miss the answer or cannot tell which participant the bot is addressing. Prompting the model to type a name is not reliable and does not produce a native Feishu notification.

### Proposed solution

Add `channels.feishu.mentionSenderOnReply: true`, with the same option available per account. When enabled, automatic group replies include the inbound human sender as a required native mention recipient. Direct messages and proactive sends remain unchanged. Reuse the existing required-mention delivery path already used by Feishu bot-to-bot replies, including text chunking and static cards. Because Feishu streaming cards cannot carry native mention recipients, use normal text/static-card delivery for these replies.

The option remains off by default for backward compatibility.

### Alternatives considered

- Prompt-only name prefix: not deterministic and not a native mention.
- A plugin hook: `message_sending` can rewrite text but does not own Feishu mention recipients, so this would duplicate channel transport behavior.
- A new gate or approval layer: unrelated to delivery addressing and unnecessarily complex.

### Impact

- Affected: operators using OpenClaw in shared Feishu/Lark group chats.
- Severity: moderate usability issue.
- Frequency: every group reply when the operator wants explicit addressee notification.
- Consequence: missed or ambiguous replies in active groups.

### Evidence/examples

The Feishu channel already has a `requiredMentionTargets` path for bot-authored ingress replies. It attaches native mentions to text chunks and static cards and disables streaming cards when required mentions are present. The proposed change extends that existing path to human senders behind one default-off config flag.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself.

### Additional information

The implementation is intentionally channel-local and minimal: one config field and one condition at inbound reply-dispatch setup, plus tests, docs, and required generated config metadata.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug

### Is this a beta blocker?

No

### Summary

In Telegram `streaming.mode: "progress"` with commentary enabled, the first user-visible commentary/preamble can appear twice in the same progress bubble even though the model emitted the commentary only once.

The duplicate occurs when a provider bridge forwards the same normalized commentary as a streaming snapshot and then as a completed snapshot with different `itemId` values. `pushCommentaryProgress()` currently deduplicates by line ID, so both snapshots are appended.

### Reproduction steps

1. Configure Telegram progress commentary:

```json
{
  "streaming": {
    "mode": "progress",
    "progress": {
      "commentary": true,
      "label": false,
      "toolProgress": false
    }
  }
}
```

2. At the progress compositor boundary, send two adjacent preamble events containing the same normalized text but different item IDs:

```ts
await progress.pushCommentaryProgress("Checking the workspace", {
  itemId: "streaming-preamble",
});
await progress.pushCommentaryProgress("Checking   the workspace", {
  itemId: "completed-preamble",
});
```

3. Inspect the Telegram progress preview.

A provider-level instance presents the same shape: a streaming preamble snapshot followed by its completed snapshot under a different ID.

### Expected behavior

The adjacent snapshots represent one logical commentary message, so the progress bubble should contain:

```text
Checking the workspace
```

once.

### Actual behavior

The progress bubble contains the same first commentary twice. Later commentary messages are not duplicated unless they arrive in the same two-snapshot shape.

### Root cause

`pushCommentaryProgress()` creates a compositor line keyed by `itemId`. Existing `seenLineIds` and merge behavior correctly handle repeated updates under the same ID, but cannot recognize equivalent adjacent commentary when the provider changes IDs between streaming and completion snapshots.

The text has already been normalized, so the compositor sees equal `line.text` values but distinct `line.id` values and appends both.

### Proposed fix

Coalesce only an immediately adjacent `Commentary` line whose normalized text is identical. Replace the previous line with the newest line object so a later retraction using the completed item ID still works:

```ts
const previousLine = lines.at(-1);
if (
  typeof previousLine === "object" &&
  previousLine.label === "Commentary" &&
  previousLine.text === line.text
) {
  lines = [...lines.slice(0, -1), line];
  return false;
}
```

This is deliberately narrower than global text deduplication. Repeating the same commentary after an intervening tool or progress event remains valid and visible.

### Regression tests

A local source patch at `ee929dbb857c717a60f3b2b502db5a6dd31b5c11` adds:

- a core compositor test with identical normalized commentary and different IDs;
- a Telegram dispatch integration test using `streaming-preamble` and `completed-preamble` IDs.

Before the fix:

```text
pnpm exec vitest run src/channels/progress-draft-compositor.test.ts --config vitest.config.ts --pool forks --testTimeout 10000

FAIL 1 / 36: expected one occurrence, received two
```

After the fix:

```text
PASS src/channels/progress-draft-compositor.test.ts: 36 / 36
PASS extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch.progress-updates.test.ts: 25 / 25
```

A direct smoke against the generated runtime bundle produced `occurrences: 1` after the patch.

### OpenClaw version

`2026.7.2-beta.5 (ee929db)`

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.2 arm64, Node.js 26.0.0

### Installation method

Global npm installation under Homebrew Node

### Additional evidence

For the observed production occurrence:

- the native model transcript contained exactly one commentary item with the duplicated text;
- the channel ingress log contained one inbound Telegram update;
- the duplication was therefore introduced during progress rendering rather than by the model or duplicate inbound delivery.

Related but not duplicate: #111944 concerns commentary not being delivered at all. This report concerns delivered commentary being rendered twice when snapshot IDs change.

## Summary

Persisting an agent transcript can invalidate capability-bearing URLs by replacing ordinary query values such as `token`, `code`, and `signature` with redaction masks. The next turn then replays a broken magic link, OAuth callback, or pre-signed download URL instead of the URL that the user or tool supplied.

## Real environment observed

- OpenClaw `main` at `71f7f9e4c2e68b2c5f95c71c4972ca02933628b3`
- Windows 11
- Node.js `v22.22.3`
- SQLite transcript persistence path

## User-visible symptom

A URL can work during the turn in which it is produced, but after transcript persistence the agent sees query values replaced with `***` or a hinted mask. Any later instruction that asks the agent to reuse the stored URL fails because the capability value is gone.

## Source-level reproduction on current main

`redactTranscriptMessageForStorage` calls `redactTranscriptMessage` before the message is written. A current-main probe with:

```text
https://checkout.example/resume?token=opaque-magic-link&code=callback-code&signature=signed
```

produces persisted text equivalent to:

```text
https://checkout.example/resume?token=***&code=***&signature=***
```

The same behavior occurs for a URL stored inside structured tool-call arguments.

## Expected behavior

Transcript persistence should preserve URL query values so capability-bearing URLs remain replayable. Values that independently match a known credential shape, form-body secrets, structured credential fields, and Authorization headers must still be redacted. Log and tool-display redaction should continue masking URL query values.

## Actual behavior

Transcript redaction applies the log-oriented URL query rule at the persistence boundary, permanently replacing values based only on parameter names.

## Scope / non-goals

- Do not weaken log, tool-display, form-body, structured-field, or Authorization-header redaction.
- Do not preserve values that independently match known secret patterns such as `sk-...`.
- Do not add a user-facing disable-redaction switch.

## Proposed fix

Allow the transcript persistence path to skip only the built-in URL-query-name rule while retaining all value-pattern and structured secret redaction. Add regression coverage for plain transcript text and structured tool arguments, plus negative coverage for real secret shapes and non-URL credential surfaces.

## Duplicate search

Live searches across open and closed OpenClaw issues and PRs for transcript redaction, magic links, pre-signed URLs, and URL query persistence found no matching report or fix.

issues.body:
## Problem

When OpenClaw injects `Conversation context (untrusted, chronological)` into prompts, the model sees `#session:<uuid>` formatted lines. Occasionally, the model hallucinates additional content in this same format and appends it to its response.

OpenClaw then delivers the full response (including the hallucinated `#session:` markers) to the channel (e.g. Telegram). When the response is long enough to be split into multiple messages, the hallucinated conversation context at the end looks like a separate incoming message to the user — causing confusion and potential security concerns.

## Incident

On 2026-07-24, an agent (Donato) responded to a task request. At the end of its response, the model (Claude Opus 4.6) hallucinated a fake voice message transcription in `#session:<uuid>` format, using a real message ID from the session but with fabricated content and timestamp. This was delivered to Telegram as part of the bot's response, and the user interpreted it as an unauthorized message from someone else.

## Suggested fix

Strip or escape `#session:` / `#<uuid>` pattern markers from model responses before delivering to channels. These markers are internal OpenClaw metadata and should never appear in channel-delivered output.

Alternatively (or additionally):
- Detect when model output contains conversation-context-formatted blocks and strip them
- Add a post-processing pass that removes lines matching `^#session:[0-9a-f-]+ \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}` from final delivery text

## Environment

- OpenClaw v2026.7.1-2
- Model: claude-opus-4-6 (via claude-cli backend)
- Channel: Telegram

issues.body:
### Summary

`openclaw security audit` emits `config.secrets.gateway_password_in_config` ("Gateway password is stored in config", severity `warn`) even when `gateway.auth.password` is a **native file- or exec-source SecretRef** rather than a plaintext literal. With a SecretRef, the actual secret is **not** in the config — only a reference is — so this is a false positive, and it steers operators away from the (durable) file/exec provider forms toward the env form.

Version: OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4), macOS.

### Repro

```sh
# externalize the gateway password to a mode-0600 JSON file via a file provider
openclaw config set secrets.providers.local \
  --provider-source file --provider-path ~/.openclaw/secrets/service-secrets.json --provider-mode json
openclaw config set gateway.auth.password \
  --ref-provider local --ref-source file --ref-id /gatewayPassword

# config now holds a SecretRef, not a literal:
#   gateway.auth.password = {"source":"file","provider":"local","id":"/gatewayPassword"}
openclaw config validate      # -> valid
openclaw security audit       # -> STILL warns: config.secrets.gateway_password_in_config
```

### Expected

A resolved SecretRef (any provider source — `file`, `exec`, `env`) should be treated as **externalized** and not flagged as "stored in config" (or, at most, downgraded to `info`). Only a **plaintext literal** at `gateway.auth.password` should raise the `warn`.

### Where

`collectSecretsInConfigFindings` (the non-deep audit runtime) gates on:

```js
const password = normalizeOptionalString(cfg.gateway?.auth?.password) ?? "";
if (password && !looksLikeEnvRef(password)) findings.push({ checkId: "config.secrets.gateway_password_in_config", ... });
```

`looksLikeEnvRef(...)` only recognizes env-ref-shaped values, so file/exec SecretRef objects fall through and get flagged. The check should recognize a SecretRef object (regardless of `source`) as externalized before emitting the finding.

### Impact / why it matters

The check's remediation is "Prefer `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PASSWORD` (env)". On macOS the only place to inject that env var into the gateway process is the OpenClaw-generated `service-env/<label>.env`, which is stamped *"Generated by OpenClaw. Do not edit"* and regenerated on service reinstall/upgrade — so the env form is an upgrade-fragility footgun (the var gets wiped, gateway auth breaks). A durable **file/exec SecretRef** is the better externalization, but the audit currently won't recognize it as clean, nudging operators toward the fragile env path.

issues.body:
### Summary

There is currently no supported way for a plugin/hook to redirect an agent's outbound reply into a forum topic (`message_thread_id`) different from the inbound thread. A common pattern this blocks: a top-level group message arrives in General, code auto-creates a per-conversation forum topic for it, and the agent should reply natively inside that new topic. Today the reply always routes to the inbound thread (General); the only workaround is to copy/mirror the reply into the topic after the fact, which double-posts and loses formatting/attachment fidelity on the mirror path.

### Version

OpenClaw 2026.6.11

### Where the outbound thread is locked

The outbound reply thread is resolved solely from the inbound message context in `resolveRoutedDeliveryThreadId(params)` (auto-reply/reply/routed-delivery-thread.ts):

```
if (params.ctx.MessageThreadId != null) return params.ctx.MessageThreadId;
if (params.ctx.TransportThreadId != null) return params.ctx.TransportThreadId;
return parseSessionThreadInfoFast(params.sessionKey).threadId;
```

and the delivery site (channels/message delivery) builds the send target from `params.threadId` only:

```
...params.threadId !== void 0 ? { threadId: params.threadId } : {},
const deliveryTarget = deliveryHandler.buildTargetRef({ threadId: sendOverrides.threadId });
```

The outbound hooks that run before delivery cannot influence the thread:

- `message_sending` merges only `{ content, cancel, cancelReason, metadata }` (any returned threadId is dropped).
- `reply_payload_sending` returns `{ payload, cancel }` (no thread field consumed at the send site).
- `before_dispatch` exposes threadId as read-only context.

The `threadBindings` / `placement: "child"` subsystem does create child threads, but only for ACP/subagent spawns and `/thread` / `/acp spawn` commands (gated on `defaultTopLevelPlacement === "child"`, which Telegram defaults to `"current"`). It does not cover redirecting the main agent's reply for a regular top-level message into an auto-created topic within the same turn.

### Proposed

Allow one of the outbound hooks (`message_sending`, `reply_payload_sending`, or `before_dispatch`) to return an optional `threadId` that, when present, overrides `sendOverrides.threadId` at the delivery site. That lets a plugin route the reply natively into an auto-created forum topic without a post-send mirror. Alternatively, expose a config to set Telegram top-level placement to `"child"` for the main agent reply (not only ACP/subagent spawns).

### Impact

Without this, auto-topic patterns must mirror the reply after delivery, causing duplicate messages and degraded formatting/attachment fidelity on the mirrored copy.

issues.body:
# OpenClaw Bug Report: Duplicate Assistant Generation Attempts (MiMo Provider)

**Date:** 2026-07-15
**Reporter:** Kestrel (main agent), on behalf of Héctor Aldana
**Environment:** OpenClaw (local install), provider `xiaomi-token-plan`, model `mimo-v2.5-pro`, API family `openai-completions`

## Summary

Over 2026-07-13 through 2026-07-15, we observed persistent "looping" behavior with MiMo V2.5 Pro where the assistant appeared to repeat the same opening narrative text 2-3+ times per turn before eventually producing a final answer. Initial hypothesis was a MiMo-specific sampling/thinking-mode issue. After deep investigation (source tracing + live replay), we found the actual root cause is a **harness-level duplicate generation bug**, not a model sampling issue.

## Evidence

### 1. Config parameter `repetition_penalty` is silently dropped
Traced `extra-params-yKt6DsAs.js:createStreamFnWithExtraParams` in the compiled dist bundle. This function is the sole mapper from `agents.defaults.models.<model>.params` → the actual provider stream `options` object. It has an explicit allowlist:
- `temperature`, `topP`, `maxTokens`, `responseFormat`, `transport`, `cachedContent`
- `frequencyPenalty`/`frequency_penalty` (aliased)
- `presencePenalty`/`presence_penalty` (aliased)
- `seed`, `stop`, cache retention fields

`repetition_penalty` (and any other provider-specific param not on this list) is **never read, never mapped, never sent**. It's silently discarded. There is no generic passthrough mechanism for provider-specific sampling params outside this fixed allowlist.

**Impact:** We had `repetition_penalty: 1.2` configured for `xiaomi/mimo-v2.5-pro` for 2+ days, based on community-reported best practice for reducing MiMo's "Thought Loop" failure mode. It had zero effect the entire time because it never reached the API. This should either:
- (a) be documented clearly (config validation could warn on unrecognized/dropped param keys), or
- (b) supported via a generic passthrough for `openai-completions`-family providers, since the transport layer (`openai-transport-stream-D1R-kt0Q.js:buildOpenAICompletionsParams`) is a standard JSON body builder that could accept arbitrary extra top-level keys.

### 2. Duplicate assistant generation confirmed via session transcript

Session: `agent:main:default` (sessionId `a66b21be-a26b-4aff-a44c-44887d11aa24`), 2026-07-15.

The session log (`~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions/<id>.jsonl`) recorded **14 separate `openclaw:prompt-error` custom events** across the session, each with:
```json
{
  "error": "This operation was aborted | 20",
  "provider": "xiaomi",
  "model": "mimo-v2.5-pro",
  "api": "openai-completions"
}
```

Examining the message tree around one such event (timestamp `2026-07-15T14:36:24`):

| idx | ts | type | id | parentId | text preview |
|-----|----|----|----|----|----|
| 175 | 14:35:54.790 | assistant msg | `1d3337a5` | `75b962d2` (user msg) | "Héctor is asking if Owl (Fable 5) completed his assessment correctly. Let me che..." |
| 176 | 14:35:54.879 | toolResult | `c72032e3` | `1d3337a5` | (forbidden error from sessions_history) |
| 177 | 14:36:24.855 | assistant msg | `0dd56bf0` | `c72032e3` | "Héctor is asking if Owl (Fable 5) completed his assessment correctly. Let me che..." (**identical opening**) |
| 178 | 14:36:24.955 | `leaf` marker | — | `0dd56bf0` | branch point, `appendMode: "side"` |
| 179 | 14:36:24.958 | assistant msg | `f1c6be60` | `c72032e3` (**same parent as 177**) | "Héctor is asking if Owl (Fable 5) completed his assessment correctly. Let me che..." (**identical again**) |
| 180 | 14:36:25.007 | `openclaw:prompt-error` | — | — | `"This operation was aborted \| 20"` |

**Key finding:** messages 177 and 179 share the identical `parentId` (`c72032e3`, the tool result), and were generated **3 milliseconds apart**. Both begin with the same opening sentence. This is not one continuous generation stream self-repeating — it is **two independent assistant-turn generation attempts against the same parent context**, both surviving long enough to be appended to the session log, before an abort fires ~50ms after the second one starts.

This pattern (duplicate/near-duplicate assistant messages sharing a parentId, generated milliseconds apart, followed by an abort) recurred 14 times in a single session.

### 3. Ruled out model-level sampling randomness

Extracted the full 64-message conversation history from this exact session (including the trigger prompt that caused visible repetition in production) and replayed it directly against MiMo's raw `chat/completions` API (bypassing OpenClaw entirely), with multiple parameter combinations:
- No penalties
- `frequency_penalty=0.3, presence_penalty=0.3` (current config)
- `repetition_penalty=1.2` alone (to test if the raw API even respects it)
- Reasoning explicitly disabled

**Result: zero repetition detected in any of the raw API replays.** Every completion was clean, single-shot, no duplicated text chunks. This rules out "MiMo just samples repetitive text sometimes" as the explanation — the model does not reproduce the loop when called directly with the same context.

## Hypothesis for root cause

Something in OpenClaw's turn-execution loop for the `openai-completions` API family (possibly specific to `xiaomi`/`xiaomi-token-plan` provider handling, or to models with `reasoning: true` + `requiresThinkingAsText: true` compat flags, per the MiMo catalog entries) is:
1. Starting a generation attempt
2. Under some condition (unclear — possibly an idle-timeout race, a stream-parsing issue with MiMo's SSE format, or a retry-on-partial-failure path) starting a **second** generation attempt against the same parent/context before the first has resolved
3. Appending both attempts' visible text to the session transcript
4. Then aborting (with cause message literally `"20"` — meaning unclear, not found via source grep for `maxIterations`/retry-count/timeout constants matching that value)

This looks like a race condition or double-dispatch bug in the turn loop, specific to (or at least triggered more easily by) the MiMo/xiaomi-token-plan provider's `openai-completions` transport path — since testing on the same OpenClaw instance with Sonnet models does not exhibit this behavior (confirmed via side-by-side model testing on 2026-07-14).

## Suggested investigation areas for OpenClaw maintainers
1. Turn-loop dispatch logic for `openai-completions` API family — check for any code path where a stream abort/retry could re-invoke generation without properly cancelling/awaiting the prior attempt.
2. The `"This operation was aborted | 20"` cause chain — `formatErrorMessage` in `error-utils-lI9LxgyU.js` appends `cause.message` with ` | `; find where a cause with message `"20"` (likely a raw thrown number, not an Error) originates in the MiMo/xiaomi provider stream path.
3. Whether MiMo's specific SSE streaming format (given `requiresThinkingAsText: true` compat flag) interacts poorly with OpenClaw's idle-timeout/reconnect logic in a way that Anthropic/other providers don't trigger.
4. Consider adding a generic extraParams passthrough (or explicit warning) for unrecognized model `params` keys, since `repetition_penalty` was silently accepted in config but never used — this is a footgun for anyone trying to tune provider-specific sampling behavior.

## Workspace-side mitigations already applied (do not fully resolve the issue)
- `agents.defaults.thinkingDefault: "off"` — reduces but does not eliminate occurrence
- `frequency_penalty: 0.3`, `presence_penalty: 0.3` on `xiaomi/mimo-v2.5-pro` — confirmed reaching the API, unclear impact on this specific bug since it's not a sampling issue
- Removed dead `repetition_penalty` key (confirmed no-op)
- AGENTS.md prompt-level anti-loop discipline rules — these can't prevent a harness-level duplicate dispatch, only reduce narrative repetition within a single generation

issues.body:
## Problem

`gateway.auth.mode = "trusted-proxy"` verifies a per-request user identity (`authorizeTrustedProxy()` reads `trustedProxy.userHeader`, enforces `allowUsers`) — but the identity is discarded immediately after the yes/no auth gate. Nothing downstream can see *who* is connected:

- The connection object (`client.connect`) carries `role` and `scopes` but no verified user. Handlers receive `authResult.ok`/`.method`, never `authResult.user`.
- `sessions.list` / `sessions.changed` have no per-identity filter (`SessionsListParamsSchema`: limit/offset/activeMinutes/label/spawnedBy/agentId/search). Every operator connection sees **all** sessions.
- Session-bound RPCs (`chat.history`, `chat.send`, `sessions.messages.subscribe`, `sessions.preview`, `sessions.patch`) accept any session key from any operator connection.
- The pending device-pairing record (`buildPendingDevicePairingRequest`) and the `device.pair.requested` event (`DevicePairRequestedEventSchema`, `additionalProperties: false`) do not carry the verified user either.

This blocks any deployment where operator/UI clients are distributed to multiple end users (a first-party app shipped company-wide, incl. source) while the host stays trusted: client-side filtering is trivially removable, so the visibility boundary must be server-side. Existing options don't cover it — per-token identity (#43903) isn't shipped, and a front proxy (Pinchy-style) replaces rather than scopes the operator protocol.

## Proposal

1. **Retain the verified identity on the connection.** When `authMethod === "trusted-proxy"`, populate `connect.authUser` (or an equivalent `connect.identity`) from the verified `authResult.user` — server-verified, never client-supplied. No behavior change when the field is absent (token/password/local connections).

2. **Optional per-user session scoping.** A config switch (e.g. `gateway.sessionScope: "per-user"`) under which, for connections carrying a verified identity that is not an operator-admin:
   - `sessions.list` / `sessions.changed` return only sessions owned by that identity, plus a configurable shared class (channel/group/cron);
   - session-bound RPCs reject foreign session keys;
   - ownership resolves from the session-key peer / `origin.from` via an installation-provided identity map.
   Admin identities keep the full view. Defaults preserve today's behavior.

3. **Expose the identity on pairing.** Add an optional `authUser` to the pending pairing record, the pair-list response, and the `device.pair.requested` event, populated only under trusted-proxy. This lets out-of-band pairing approval (matching the requester against a second authenticated channel) bind to a trustworthy source instead of spoofable `ClientInfo` / ambiguous `remoteIp`.

## Why one issue

All three rest on the same missing primitive — the verified identity surviving past the auth gate. (1) is the enabler; (2) and (3) are the two consumers we need. Shipping (1) alone already unblocks downstream implementations.

## Interim

We run a local dist-patch (three anchored seams: retain-auth-user, an RPC guard, an outbound-event filter) consulting a host-side policy module, plus an ExecStartPre self-heal and a guard smoke. It is explicitly a stop-gap pending this platform support — we'll retire it on the first release that ships per-user scoping.

## Related

- #43903 — Support multiple gateway tokens for multi-user session isolation (overlaps the per-token-identity shape; this issue asks for the identity primitive independent of token mode)
- #92367 — scope-bound gateway auth tokens `gateway.auth.tokens[]` (same auth surface)
- #87953 — Trusted Proxy auth still requires device pairing (why (3) matters)
- #93581 — skip Control UI pairing for trusted-proxy authenticated operators (treats the trusted-proxy identity as strong)
