issues.body:
**Bug type:** Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)
**Beta release blocker:** No

## Summary

On a CLI backend (`claude-cli`), any cron job carrying a `toolsAllow` list has no shell at all: the backend disables Claude's native tools because the run is restricted, and OpenClaw's own `exec` is never offered on that surface to replace them, so the job silently loses the ability to run commands and the only remedy is an unrestricted `*` policy.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run an agent on the bundled `claude-cli` backend (`anthropic/claude-opus-5`).
2. From an agent turn, create a cron job with `payload.kind: "agentTurn"` whose message asks it to run a shell command. The job stores an explicit `toolsAllow` automatically (`toolsAllowIsDefault: true`), as documented in `docs/automation/cron-jobs.md:215`.
3. Force a run: `openclaw cron run <id> --expect-final`.
4. Read the run summary: `openclaw cron runs --id <id>`.

Observed summary text from run at `2026-08-17T06:21Z`:

```
No exec tool in this cron session, so the watcher script can't run.
Going to the GitHub API directly and computing the same signals the script does.
```

5. Attempt the obvious fix from the same agent turn — patch the job with `payload.toolsAllow` including `"exec"`. Fetch the job back: `exec` is gone. `process` and `read` are dropped in the same call. No error is returned.
6. Run `openclaw cron edit <id> --clear-tools` as an operator, then force a run again. The same job now completes in 15s using the shell.

## Expected behavior

A restricted cron job on a CLI backend should have some way to be granted a shell — either by allowlisting OpenClaw's `exec` for that job, or by keeping a mediated native shell — instead of being forced to choose between an unrestricted `*` policy and no command execution at all.

## Actual behavior

The two mechanisms combine into a dead end:

**1. Any `toolsAllow` disables the CLI's native tools.** From `docs/gateway/cli-backends.md:324`:

> Restricted runs such as cron jobs with `toolsAllow` require an exact backend-owned translation. The bundled `claude-cli` backend disables Claude's native tools and user, project, and local customizations […] It then exposes every allowed OpenClaw tool through the grant-scoped MCP server.

This is sound in isolation: OpenClaw cannot enforce an allowlist over a native shell it does not mediate.

**2. But OpenClaw's `exec` is not on that surface to take over.** In `dist/tool-resolution-No4drDPV.js` (2026.8.1-beta.2, `8f382a2`):

```js
// :46 — "loopback" is the bundled-MCP surface used by CLI backends
const nodeExecSurface = surface === "loopback" && params.includeNodeExecTool === true;

// :260 — on that surface the gateway-local exec is filtered out
openClawTools.filter((tool) => tool.name.trim().toLowerCase() !== "exec")
```

What remains is a node-only variant, whose own description states the assumption:

```js
// :305
description: "Execute a shell command on a connected OpenClaw node. This tool is
node-only; use the CLI native shell for Gateway-local commands. […]"
```

That assumption holds for interactive turns and breaks for restricted ones, because step 1 has already removed the native shell it points to.

**3. This also explains the silent strip in step 5.** The list a cron inherits from its creating turn is built from `inheritableTools`, which has `exec` removed just above:

```js
// :353
const inheritableTools = includeNodeExecTool ? tools.filter((t) => t.name !== "exec") : tools;
// :355
replaceWithEffectiveCronCreatorToolAllowlist(cronCreatorToolAllowlist, inheritableTools, …);
```

So an agent on a CLI backend cannot name `exec` when creating or patching a job: it is not in the surface it is capped to (`docs/automation/cron-jobs.md:215` — "Jobs created by an agent are capped to the tools available to that creating turn").

## OpenClaw version

2026.8.1-beta.2 (8f382a2)

## Operating system

Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie), aarch64

## Install method

npm global

## Model

anthropic/claude-opus-5

## Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> claude-cli (bundled CLI backend) -> anthropic

## Additional provider/model setup details

Default route is `models.default.primary: anthropic/claude-opus-5` with `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5` as fallback, both served through the bundled `claude-cli` backend (`cliBackends` is empty; no custom backend is configured). `tools.exec` is enabled globally as `{ "host": "gateway", "mode": "full" }`, which makes the absence of `exec` in the job's surface a routing consequence rather than a policy denial.

## Logs

```shell
# Before --clear-tools (run at 2026-08-17T06:21Z, duration 96670 ms, delivered=true)
$ openclaw cron runs --id <job-id> --limit 50
"No exec tool in this cron session, so the watcher script can't run.
 Going to the GitHub API directly and computing the same signals the script does."

# Patching toolsAllow from an agent turn: exec/process/read requested, none stored
$ openclaw cron get <job-id>
toolsAllow: ["automations","sessions","update_plan","sessions_list","sessions_history",
             "session_status","web_search","web_fetch","image","browser",
             "memory_search","memory_get"]
# requested but absent, with no error: exec, process, read

# Setting payload.toolsAllow to null does not clear it; the list is repopulated.

# After the operator workaround
$ openclaw cron edit <job-id> --clear-tools
$ openclaw cron get  <job-id>
toolsAllow: ["*"]

# Same job, same prompt, forced run at 2026-08-17T08:35Z (duration 15175 ms)
"I'll run the watcher script.\n\nHEARTBEAT_OK"
```

## Impact and severity

- **Affected surface:** every cron/automation `agentTurn` job running on a CLI backend that needs to execute a command — which includes every job created by an agent, since those always store an explicit `toolsAllow`.
- **Severity:** moderate. Nothing crashes, and there is a working operator workaround, but the least-privilege path is unavailable: the only configuration that grants a shell is `*`, which also grants everything else.
- **Frequency:** deterministic on this setup; reproduced across four runs of the same job (two before the workaround, two after).
- **Consequence:** operators who want a scheduled job to run one script must give that job unrestricted tool authority. Agents that create their own jobs cannot detect the problem at creation time, because the requested tool names are dropped without an error; the failure only surfaces at run time, as a model narrating that it has no shell.

## Suggested direction

Any one of these would close the gap; the first looks cheapest:

1. Keep the gateway-local `exec` available on the `loopback` surface when the run is restricted, so `toolsAllow: ["exec"]` becomes the precise grant that step 1 already assumes exists.
2. Include `exec` in `inheritableTools` for cron-creator capping on CLI backends, so an agent can at least name it.
3. Return an explicit validation error when a stored `toolsAllow` drops a requested tool name, instead of silently shortening the list.

## Related, but not duplicates

- #116059 — `capCronAgentTurnToolsAllow` silently strips `exec`/`write` on the MCP write path. Same visible symptom in step 5, different root cause: that report requires a `tools.deny` entry in the policy chain, states the CLI `--tools` path is unaffected, and confirms `exec` executes fine at run time. Here there is no `tools.deny`, `--tools exec` is rejected too, and the run genuinely has no shell.
- #60841 — `toolsAllow` cannot re-expose core tools in **embedded** cron runs filtered by a config allowlist. Adjacent, but the mechanism here is the CLI-backend loopback surface rather than a config allowlist, and it applies with no `tools.allow` configured.
- #89228, #92238 — `exec` unavailable in isolated cron sessions on other runtimes.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The agent prompt advertises Telegram inline buttons whenever `capabilities.inlineButtons` is any non-`off` scope, without regard for the current chat type, so a group turn under `inlineButtons: "dm"` is told to send buttons that the Telegram send runtime then rejects.

### Steps to reproduce

Source-verifiable on current `main`; no live run required to see the mismatch.

1. Set `channels.telegram.capabilities.inlineButtons: "dm"`.
2. Have the agent take a turn in a Telegram **group**.
3. Read the system prompt's Messaging section for that turn, then attempt a button send.

### Expected behavior

The prompt should advertise inline buttons only when the current target can actually accept them. Per `AGENTS.md`: "Never dead-end the agent: failure text states what to try next; unavailable tools are hidden by gating, not left to fail." A capability the runtime will reject for this target should not be presented as available for this turn.

### Actual behavior

The two sides disagree because only one of them is target-aware.

**Advertisement is scope-only.** `extensions/telegram/src/channel.ts:828` emits the capability for every non-`off` scope:

```ts
...(inlineButtonsScope === "off" ? [] : ["inlineButtons"]),
```

**The prompt gate is a plain boolean.** `src/agents/system-prompt.ts:1069` and `:658`:

```ts
const inlineButtonsEnabled = runtimeCapabilitiesLower.has("inlinebuttons");
```

with no chat-type condition on the line that teaches the button payload.

**The runtime is target-aware and rejects.** `extensions/telegram/src/action-runtime.ts:596-601`:

```ts
if (inlineButtonsScope === "dm" && targetType !== "direct") {
  throw new Error('Telegram inline buttons are limited to DMs when inlineButtons="dm".');
}
```

So under scope `dm` in a group, the model is shown the button shape, follows it, and the send throws. The symmetric case exists for scope `group` in a DM.

### OpenClaw version

Reproduced by reading `main` at `76e4ef68ced11426637a62964a06a54ee1754fa5`

### Operating system

macOS (Darwin 27.0.0)

### Install method

source checkout

### Model

Not model-specific; the mismatch is in prompt construction and capability resolution.

### Provider / routing chain

Not provider-specific.

### Additional provider/model setup details

The capability seam is the constraint. `ChannelAgentPromptAdapter.messageToolCapabilities` (`src/channels/plugins/types.core.ts:659`) receives only `{ cfg, accountId }`, and its caller `resolveChannelPromptCapabilities` (`src/agents/channel-tools.ts:135`) has no chat type either. A channel plugin therefore *cannot* answer "is this capability available for the current target?" even though its own runtime decides exactly that. Any fix likely needs the current chat type threaded to that seam, which is an additive optional field rather than a breaking change.

### Logs

```shell
No runtime logs. This is reported from source on the line references above; the
disagreement is visible without executing a turn.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

None; see the cited lines.

### Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Telegram operators using the scoped values `inlineButtons: "dm"` or `"group"`. The `all` and `off` scopes are unaffected, since for those the advertisement and the runtime agree.
- **Severity:** Moderate. The failure is loud (the send throws with a clear message) rather than silent, so it is well below the silent-drop class, but it dead-ends the agent on a path the prompt told it to take.
- **Frequency:** Deterministic for the mismatched scope/target combination.
- **Consequence:** a wasted model turn and a rejected send, on a configuration the operator set deliberately.

### Additional information

Found while addressing review feedback on #120330, which was correct to flag it. Filing separately because it is not introduced by that PR: #120330 touches no `extensions/telegram` files and changes no line of the capability gate, so the mismatch is present identically on `main` today. That PR does make the path easier to reach, by removing prompt wording that had discouraged same-destination `message(action=send)` in groups — which is how the issue surfaced.

Happy to implement the fix, in #120330 or on its own branch, once a maintainer indicates whether threading chat type into `messageToolCapabilities` is the shape they want.

_Filed by an AI agent (Claude) on behalf of the account owner. Every claim above is from the cited source lines._

issues.body:
## Summary

Make minimum-release-age exclusions reviewable exceptions with explicit
ownership and lifecycle context.

## Problem to solve

OpenClaw uses pnpm's two-day `minimumReleaseAge`, which is a useful default
supply-chain control. The current `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` list in
`pnpm-workspace.yaml` contains bare package names, patterns, and exact versions
without a machine-checkable owner, reason, or review/expiry date.

An emergency or compatibility exception can therefore remain indefinitely
after its original need has passed, and reviewers cannot distinguish a
temporary release unblock from a permanent compatibility policy.

## Desired outcome

Every release-age exclusion has reviewable context:

- responsible owner;
- reason for bypassing the default hold;
- date added; and
- expiry date or next-review date.

CI should fail when exclusions and their metadata drift. The maintainers should
choose whether the metadata lives in a companion file, structured comments, or
another repository-native mechanism that keeps `pnpm-workspace.yaml` valid.

This should preserve the ability to add urgent exceptions; it should not remove
the escape hatch or add downstream-specific approval policy.

## Alternatives considered

- Remove all exclusions: too disruptive and does not support urgent release
  needs.
- Leave rationale only in PR history: difficult to audit and easy to lose as
  the list evolves.

## Impact

Affected: dependency, security, and release maintainers.

Severity: medium. Permanent silent bypasses weaken the intended release-age
control.

Frequency: every install for each active exclusion.

## Evidence

Verified on OpenClaw `main` at
`493a3e46b3f2921269cfb0af5dfc86efb569ceaa`:

- `pnpm-workspace.yaml` sets `minimumReleaseAge: 2880`; and
- `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` is a plain list with no owner, reason, or lifecycle
  metadata.

## Implementation intent

Maybe, with maintainer guidance.

issues.body:
# Suspected synchronous transcript-projection reconcile stalling embedded bootstrap-context

## Summary

Profiling in #87509 showed a ~14–22s stall in the embedded bootstrap-context window (the
work `runEmbeddedAttempt` does before the first model turn). The extra-bootstrap glob path
was investigated and ruled out as the cause (it is off by default, already async, and a
~40KB workspace cannot produce 22s). A stronger suspect is the **synchronous
transcript-projection reconcile** that can run inside the same window.

## Details

`startSessionTranscriptIndexReconcile` (`src/config/sessions/session-transcript-reconcile.ts`)
drives a projection rebuild via `withCurrentProjectionSnapshot`. That rebuild is a
synchronous `better-sqlite3` operation whose cost scales with the size of the raw event log
for the session. It is reached from the SQLite session-accessor paths
(`session-accessor.sqlite-transcript-store.ts`, `session-accessor.sqlite-active-projection.ts`,
`session-transcript-search.ts`).

During embedded bootstrap-context prep, the runner consults session transcript state (for
example `hasCompletedBootstrapTurn`), which can touch these accessors and trigger a
reconcile. Because the rebuild is synchronous and proportional to the raw event log, a
session with a large accumulated event log can block the event loop for seconds — matching
the shape of the #87509 profile far better than the async glob path does.

## Repro / next step

- Re-attribute a real #87509-class incident using the new bootstrap substage instrumentation
  landed alongside the event-loop hardening PR: read the `substages=…` breakdown emitted for
  a slow bootstrap-context window (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`,
  `bootstrap-routing`, `continuation-scan`, `context-build`). A large `continuation-scan` /
  routing substage that correlates with a large session event log points here.
- Reproduce locally by copying a large real session store into an isolated
  `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, then starting an embedded run and measuring the bootstrap-context
  window while the projection for that session is stale (forcing a rebuild).
- If confirmed, the fix belongs at the reconcile owner: keep the synchronous commit section
  minimal and move the proportional rebuild work off the bootstrap-context critical path
  (defer, bound, or make it incremental) so it cannot block the first-turn window.

## Notes

This is a follow-up split out of the #87509 investigation. It is a suspected root cause to be
confirmed with the substage breakdown from a real incident, not a proven fix.

The original report contains two separate defects. **False-green accounting is fixed on main** by [PR #126010](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/126010), commit [`491dc7f8b1be`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/491dc7f8b1be8bf915da6d42775a88c7ea721490). On current [`605065ce7461`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/605065ce7461177e9b438c8d8917641a8e8380e0), [native project documents absent from OpenClaw's payload](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/605065ce7461177e9b438c8d8917641a8e8380e0/extensions/codex/src/app-server/attempt-context.ts#L251) are truthfully reported as `native_unverified` with null delivery counts; they are not declared delivered.

**Current sandbox delivery still needs a fresh observation.** The pinned dependency is Codex 0.160.0. Its [native project-instruction loader](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/core/src/agents_md.rs) reads the selected execution environment's filesystem and cwd, and OpenClaw's [sandbox filesystem bridge](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/605065ce7461177e9b438c8d8917641a8e8380e0/extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/filesystem.ts#L226) serves native file reads. A container cwd absent from the host no longer proves the old host-only discovery failure. [Our previous injection PR #120618](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/120618) is closed unmerged and should not be revived blindly, since reinjection could duplicate instructions now delivered natively.

Keep the remaining investigation bounded: a fresh remapped sandbox session, a synthetic AGENTS.md-only marker and sibling-file control, the selected environment/cwd, actual native instruction sources, and truthful report values. No current-version canary or production mutation was performed in this update; the historical reproductions below are retained as historical evidence.

---

## Summary

On a sandboxed Codex app-server run, `AGENTS.md` is delivered to nobody.

OpenClaw skips injecting it on the assumption that Codex loads it natively, but Codex cannot: the thread is started with the **container** workdir while the app-server process — and therefore its project-doc loader — runs on the **host**. The failure is silent, and `buildCodexContextFileStats` then reports the file as fully delivered, so nothing surfaces it.

Net effect: the entire `AGENTS.md` operating contract is missing from every sandboxed Codex turn, while `SOUL.md` / `IDENTITY.md` / `USER.md` arrive normally.

**Version:** `2026.7.2-beta.7`, Codex app-server `0.146.0`, docker sandbox, `workspaceAccess: "rw"`.

## Mechanism

`extensions/codex/src/app-server/attempt-context.ts` excludes the project doc from OpenClaw's own injection:

```ts
const CODEX_NATIVE_PROJECT_DOC_BASENAMES = new Set(["agents.md"]);
```

with the rationale stated in the developer-instruction preamble:

> "OpenClaw loaded these user-editable workspace files for the current turn. **Codex loads AGENTS.md natively.** SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md, and USER.md are provided as turn-scoped collaboration instructions so native Codex subagents do not inherit them. Those files are not repeated here."

That premise does not hold when the run is sandboxed:

```console
$ grep -o '"cwd":"[^"]*"' rollout-*.jsonl | head -1
"cwd":"/workspace"

$ ls -ld /workspace
ls: cannot access '/workspace': No such file or directory

$ ps aux | grep '[c]odex'      # app-server runs on the host
```

`/workspace` is the container workdir; it does not exist on the host. The loader walks a path that is not there, finds no project doc, and reports nothing.

## Why it goes unnoticed

`buildCodexContextFileStats` fills in the missing delivery as if it had happened:

```ts
if (injected === undefined && CODEX_NATIVE_PROJECT_DOC_BASENAMES.has(baseName)) {
  injectedChars = rawChars;
  truncated = false;
}
```

The system-prompt report therefore shows `AGENTS.md` with `injectedChars == rawChars` and `truncated: false` — a green signal for a file that was never sent. Any health check built on that report is blind to it.

The existing test `"routes AGENTS.md natively and MEMORY.md through tools"` passes because it uses a plain on-disk workspace with no sandbox, where `cwd` is a real host path and the native load does work.

## Reproduction

1. Run an agent through the Codex app-server with a docker sandbox and `workspaceAccess: "rw"`, so `containerWorkdir` differs from the host workspace path.
2. Put a phrase in `AGENTS.md` that appears in no other base file, e.g. `Capability is not authorization`.
3. Start a **new** thread — an existing one replays the developer prompt captured at creation — and grep the rollout:

```console
$ grep -c 'Capability is not authorization' rollout-*.jsonl
0
$ grep -c 'SOUL.md' rollout-*.jsonl
50
```

4. Ask the agent for something only `AGENTS.md` defines. It does not have it.

Observed on a real 50-request production turn: five phrases unique to `AGENTS.md` at **0** occurrences; `SOUL.md` and `USER.md` at 50 each. Reproduced on fresh sessions.

## Suggested fix

Two independent changes; the second is worth doing regardless of the first.

**1. Deliver the project doc when the workspace is remapped.** When the run is sandboxed the native loader cannot work, so `agents.md` should join the turn-scoped developer-instruction set. Unsandboxed runs keep the native path, so the no-double-copy intent and the pinning test are preserved:

```ts
function selectCodexWorkspaceTurnScopedDeveloperInstructionFiles(
  contextFiles: EmbeddedContextFile[],
  injectNativeProjectDoc = false,
): EmbeddedContextFile[] {
  const basenames = injectNativeProjectDoc
    ? new Set([
        ...CODEX_TURN_SCOPED_WORKSPACE_DEVELOPER_CONTEXT_BASENAMES,
        ...CODEX_NATIVE_PROJECT_DOC_BASENAMES,
      ])
    : CODEX_TURN_SCOPED_WORKSPACE_DEVELOPER_CONTEXT_BASENAMES;
  return selectCodexWorkspaceDeveloperInstructionFiles(contextFiles, basenames);
}
```

called with `params.sandboxed === true`. `selectCodexWorkspacePromptContextFiles` already excludes native project docs, so exactly one copy is delivered either way.

I have been running this exact change in production since today. The agent now recites content that only `AGENTS.md` defines, and the rollout shows the file arriving exactly once — same occurrence count as the other base files, single copy in the one developer message that carries it.

An alternative worth considering is giving the app-server a host-resolvable project-doc root instead of the container workdir, decoupling project-doc discovery from exec cwd. That is a larger change and I did not attempt it.

**2. Stop asserting an unverified delivery.** The `injectedChars = rawChars` branch turns a silent delivery failure into a green report. Reporting `injectedChars: 0`, or keeping `surface: "native_project_doc"` with an explicit "not verified" flag, would have made this visible immediately instead of days later.

## Related

Same class as the sandbox skill-path reports (#6346, #17924, #48011): a container-side path handed to a consumer that runs host-side. Those were closed as not planned; this one has a concrete mechanism, a reproduction, and a one-line conditional fix — and unlike a degraded lookup, it silently removes the agent's entire operating contract.

## Bug type

Behavior bug

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

On OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2, Fastmail MCP OAuth fails during authorization-code exchange with `invalid_request invalid signing_id`; reproduced twice, including after clearing all stored Fastmail OAuth credentials and starting a fresh authorization transaction.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an MCP server with:
   - URL: `https://api.fastmail.com/mcp`
   - Transport: `streamable-http`
   - Authentication: `oauth`
2. Run `openclaw mcp logout fastmail`.
3. Run `openclaw mcp login fastmail`.
4. Open the generated authorization URL and approve access in Fastmail.
5. Exchange the newly issued code with `openclaw mcp login fastmail --code <fresh-code>`.
6. Observe the CLI error.
7. Repeat the process with another freshly issued authorization code; observe the same error.

## Expected behavior

OpenClaw exchanges the freshly issued authorization code, saves the OAuth credentials, and reports `MCP OAuth credentials saved for "fastmail".`

## Actual behavior

The CLI exits during code exchange with:

```text
[openclaw] Could not start the CLI.
[openclaw] Reason: invalid_request invalid signing_id
```

## OpenClaw version

`2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)`

## Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS

## Install method

npm global, `openclaw@2026.7.1-2`

## Node.js version

v24.18.1

## Model

N/A — failure occurs in the MCP CLI before a model is invoked.

## Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw MCP OAuth client → Fastmail MCP/OAuth service

## Logs and supporting evidence

Before resetting, `openclaw mcp status --verbose` reported:

```text
- fastmail: streamable-http oauth
  launch: https://api.fastmail.com/mcp
  timeouts: connect=30000ms request=60000ms
  oauth: tokens=no client=yes
```

`openclaw mcp logout fastmail` then reported:

```text
MCP OAuth credentials cleared for "fastmail".
```

A newly initiated authorization transaction failed with the same `invalid_request invalid signing_id` response.

Two other OAuth MCP servers on the same OpenClaw installation report `tokens=yes client=yes`, so OAuth MCP authentication is not universally failing.

The configuration also emits an unrelated missing `GITHUB_MCP_PAT` warning. That warning does not stop MCP status, logout, or login from running and is not believed to be involved in the Fastmail exchange.

## Impact and severity

- Affected: Fastmail users attempting to connect through OpenClaw's native MCP OAuth flow.
- Severity: Workflow-blocking for the reporter.
- Frequency: 2/2 observed attempts, including one after clearing stored credentials.
- Consequence: Fastmail email and calendar tools cannot be connected through OAuth.
- Data risk: None observed.

## Additional information

It is not yet known whether the fault is in OpenClaw, Fastmail, or the interoperability between their OAuth implementations. No open OpenClaw issue matching `Fastmail`, `Fastmail MCP`, or `invalid signing_id` was found.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Several `macos-swift` suites assert wall-clock deadlines that a hosted GitHub runner cannot meet, so the job fails nondeterministically. The clearest is `BoundedProcessTests.swift:32`, which asserts an operation completes in under 2 seconds and measured `2.357511334` on CI.

This is visible without any external repro loop, because the `Swift test` step already retries 3× inside one job — and **the set of failing suites changes between those retries on identical code**. That divergence is the evidence: a code defect reproduces, a deadline race does not.

Fork PRs make it much more likely. `ci.yml` routes same-repo branches to `blacksmith-12vcpu-macos-26` but sends fork PRs to the hosted `macos-26` runner (`ci.yml:3007`), and these deadlines appear to be tuned for the faster machine.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open a PR from a fork that touches a path selecting `macos-swift` in `preflight`.
2. Let the `macos-swift` job run. The `Swift test` step retries up to 3× on its own.
3. Compare the failing suite set across those three attempts within the single job.

Measured on run [30863402064](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/30863402064), job `91850136345`, head `4d09189fcc8` — same commit, same runner, same job:

| `swift test` attempt | failing suites | issues |
|---|---|---|
| 1/3 | 7 — `AppStateVoiceEarsTests`, `BoundedCommandTests`, `BoundedProcessTests`, `DashboardWindowSmokeTests`, `MacNodeModeCoordinatorTests`, `QuickChatPowerFeaturesTests`, `RemoteGatewayProbeTests` | 11 |
| 2/3 | 4 — `BoundedCommandTests`, `BoundedProcessTests`, `DashboardWindowSmokeTests`, `RemoteGatewayProbeTests` | 6 |
| 3/3 | 5 — the four above plus `MacNodeModeCoordinatorTests` | 6 |

`AppStateVoiceEarsTests`, `QuickChatPowerFeaturesTests` and `MacNodeModeCoordinatorTests` drift in and out; four suites fail in all three.

Second observation on an unrelated diff — run [30863288585](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/30863288585), job `91849747565`, head `1271bfbd00a` — same `ContinuousClock` overruns with a partly different set of 11 suites, adding `PortGuardianRecordStoreTests`, `RemotePortTunnelTests`, `GatewayChannelConnectTests` and `MacNodeCodexThreadCatalogTests`.

### Expected behavior

`macos-swift` passes deterministically on any supported runner, or its timing assertions are expressed as generous upper bounds / relative measures that do not depend on runner speed.

### Actual behavior

Wall-clock assertions miss by fractions of a second and the job fails after exhausting all three retries:

```
BoundedProcessTests.swift:32:9:  Expectation failed: (ContinuousClock.now - startedAt → 2.357511334 seconds) < (.seconds(2) → 2.0 seconds)
BoundedProcessTests.swift:195:9: Expectation failed: (ContinuousClock.now - startedAt → 2.497009708 seconds) < (.seconds(2) → 2.0 seconds)
BoundedProcessTests.swift:121:9: Expectation failed: (ContinuousClock.now - startedAt → 3.970232792 seconds) < (.seconds(3) → 3.0 seconds)
RemoteGatewayProbeTests.swift:35:9: Expectation failed: (result → .failed("Remote gateway check timed out after 1000ms")) == (.ready(...))
BoundedCommandTests.swift:14:25: Expectation failed: output → nil
DashboardWindowSmokeTests.swift:118:9: Expectation failed
```

```
Test run with 1611 tests in 178 suites failed after 26.130 seconds with 6 issues.
swift test failed (attempt 3/3). Retrying…
##[error]Process completed with exit code 1.
```

Because `ci-gate` lists `macos-swift` under `REQUIRED_RESULTS`, this turns into a red required check on PRs whose diff cannot reach any of these surfaces.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.2 (observed against `main` at `1aea2df9351`; runs cited above are `4d09189fcc8` and `1271bfbd00a`)

### Operating system

macOS — GitHub-hosted `macos-26` runner

### Install method

Source checkout (CI)

### Model

n/a — CI test infrastructure, no model involved

### Provider / routing chain

n/a — CI test infrastructure, no provider involved

### Impact and severity

A required check fails on unrelated PRs, most often from forks, and a contributor cannot rerun it (`gh run rerun` returns `Must have admin rights to Repository`; pushing again just starts a fresh attempt 1). It costs maintainer reruns and makes red CI ambiguous — the signal stops distinguishing "this diff is broken" from "the runner was slow."

### Additional information

**I have not measured a local failure rate on unmodified `main`**, and want to be straight about that rather than imply a repro I did not run: this machine has Command Line Tools only, no Xcode, so `swift test` cannot run here at all. The evidence above is entirely CI-observed. The within-job retry divergence is the strongest form available and is better controlled than a local loop, since all three attempts run identical code on one runner — but a maintainer with a macOS toolchain could confirm the rate directly.

I deliberately have **not** opened a PR against these tests. `CONTRIBUTING.md` says test-only changes that make a red or flaky suite pass will be closed, and that is the right rule. Filing this instead.

Happy to do the work if a maintainer names the direction — either relaxing the deadlines to runner-independent bounds, or gating the timing-sensitive suites on runner class. The related budget half is [#119017](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/119017), which gives `macos-swift` a fork-aware timeout; that fixes the cancellation mode but not these assertions.

Surfaced while triaging red CI on [#118989](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/118989).

🤖 AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5). Human-reviewed before filing.

issues.body:
## Problem

The first session on a persistent node after a Gateway update can spend substantial time acquiring and preparing the current worker build. The node may be connected and available before that work has happened. In live macOS testing, first-use Start-to-active took about 59–68 seconds on two earlier builds; most of one measured interval preceded remote bundle publication. This does not establish a network-only bottleneck or a universal latency figure.

Simply installing earlier is incomplete: the existing remote retention snapshot only pins builds referenced by environments and placements. An otherwise unused prepared build can become collectible after its installation generation is acknowledged.

## Proposed behavior

Prepare the current sealed worker artifact through the existing installer when a consented persistent node reconnects. Retain one current artifact per Gateway namespace alongside existing live/recoverable placement pins, and let normal maintenance collect older unreferenced builds. Share an in-flight preparation with a concurrent Start, while preserving native integrity validation for later explicit dispatches.

A canceled Start releases its wait; disconnect, revoked hosting, replacement connection, cloud enrollment takeover, or Gateway shutdown closes the host preparation owner. Nodes prepare independently so one slow node does not block another. Cloud-enrolled execution modes keep their existing preparation owner. Failures should be visible without an automatic retry loop.

This proposes a bounded artifact-retention change, with no new schema, index, configuration option, or second artifact store. It does not promise that a newly provisioned cloud VM, a locked/asleep display, or every first tool call becomes ready in ten seconds.

## Validation

Exercise current-build retention across acknowledged maintenance passes, old-build cleanup, concurrent Start sharing, cancellation/replacement authority, live enrollment changes, and independent node progress. Measure session activation and successful tool use separately in live testing. No UI layout changes are required.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add explicit prompt caching (cachedContent) support to the google-vertex provider, matching the caching that already exists for the AI Studio (google-generative-ai) provider.

### Problem to solve

The Gemini prompt-cache path (google-prompt-cache.ts) only works for AI Studio. Vertex users re-send their full stable context on every request. We run a long-lived companion agent on google-vertex/gemini-3.6-flash with a ~50K-token stable prefix (system prompt + memory) per message; without explicit caching every message pays full input price for that prefix — on gemini-3.1-pro this cost roughly NT$1,000+/day (~US$30+) for one agent. Vertex implicit caching rarely hits for this workload.

### Proposed solution

Extend the existing Google prompt-cache layer to Vertex: create/refresh cachedContents via the Vertex REST endpoint ({location}-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/...), keyed by project/location/model + prefix hash. Authenticate with ADC access tokens (sentinel-guarded logging, single-flight refresh, clean global fetch so credentials never pass through model-request middleware). Fail open: skip caching when Vertex context or a token is unavailable. Attach the cachedContent reference to streaming requests — verified end-to-end, since the Vertex streaming path uses the raw REST transport.

### Alternatives considered

1) Switching agents from google-vertex to google-generative-ai just to get caching — works but gives up Vertex-specific benefits (GCP billing/credits, region control). 2) Relying on Vertex implicit caching — rarely hits for long-lived agents with large stable prefixes.

### Impact

Affected: anyone running always-on agents on google-vertex. Severity: cost — cached-token input pricing is ~75–90% cheaper, so savings are substantial for persistent agents. Frequency: every message of every Vertex session.

### Evidence/examples

Our workload: ~50K-token stable prefix re-sent every message; ~NT$1,000+/day for a single agent on gemini-3.1-pro without caching. A working implementation exists (13 Vertex unit tests, lint/type clean). Design question before PR: extensions/google/vertex-adc.ts already has a complete ADC resolver, but core cannot import plugin internals. Preferred seam — (1) a small self-contained ADC token helper in core (our current approach), or (2) a new core↔extension interface delegating to the existing resolver?

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information

Fully backward compatible with existing config keys; no behavior change when caching is unavailable.

## Description

A Codex close observer registered after the one-shot transport close transition never learns that the client is already terminal. A router or cleanup owner created in that acquire/use race can remain attached to a dead client.

## Expected behavior

Late close observers should receive the already-reached terminal state immediately and get a no-op disposer.

## Root cause and evidence

`addCloseHandler()` only stored callbacks for a future event and did not replay the current closed state. The fix immediately invokes late subscribers through the same isolated dispatch path. The fail-before regression observed zero calls after close; it now passes in the 112-test client/shared-client/router group.

Pinned reproduction: `c66ca2fbb2b038f4796abfa76bd52dcc3b675b02`. No public Plugin SDK or protocol boundary changes. Found and fixed during an AI-assisted QA campaign.

## Summary

When an agent enters a repetitive tool-call loop (e.g. due to a fast model tripping up on an edge case), the looping output is saved to the session transcript. If a subsequent agent turn — or a *different agent* — reads that transcript (via `session-search`, `memory_get`, or manual file read), the looping pattern is reinjected into the new context, causing the receiving agent to begin looping the same way. This persists across compaction resets because compaction summaries carry the pattern forward.

## Reproduction

1. Agent A (e.g. using `deepseek-v4-flash:cloud`) enters a repetitive loop — repeating the same tool calls and same assistant text many times
2. The loop output is saved to `agent-sessions/<agent>/<session-id>.jsonl`
3. Operator asks Agent A (or a different Agent B) to read the session transcript to diagnose/recover
4. The reading agent now begins repeating the same patterns — "Let me check..." repeated N times, identical tool calls, duplicate messages
5. Compaction does NOT break the cycle — the summary carries enough of the pattern forward to re-trigger it
6. Only a full context wipe (or compaction that strips raw transcript content) breaks the loop

## Evidence

- **Albert session `3fc4eab7`**: 553 lines, 259 assistant messages, 263 tool calls over ~5 hours. Same `session-search` queries repeated 27/21/16 times. Same `exec` command repeated 29 times. Same assistant text repeated 14 times. Compaction at L167 did not break the loop.
- **Cross-agent transmission**: The main agent (Clawdio, model `glm-5.2:cloud`) read Albert's looping transcript to diagnose the issue and immediately began repeating "You're right, let me dig deeper" 4 times in succession — the same repetition pattern. Compaction cleared it instantly.
- **Hermes comparison**: Same models (`glm-5.2:cloud`, `kimi-k2.6:cloud`) running through Hermes gateway with `max_turns: 60` and `tool_loop_guardrails` do not exhibit this behavior — the circuit breaker kills the loop before enough poisoned content accumulates to self-reinforce.

## Root Cause

Two issues compound:

1. **No circuit breaker**: `tools.loopDetection.enabled` defaults to `false`. With no loop detection, a tripped-up model can repeat indefinitely, generating a large volume of poisoned transcript content.

2. **Transcript reinjection as transmission vector**: Reading session transcripts (a normal diagnostic/recovery operation) injects the looping pattern into the reader's context. Compaction summaries preserve enough of the pattern to persist it. This makes the looping behavior *contagious* across agents and sessions.

## Related Issues

- #74973 — delivery-mirror assistant messages pollute LLM context causing infinite loop
- #69208 — Umbrella: duplicate transcript, replay, and context assembly across channels
- #90604 — signed thinking blocks poison session — permanent loop

## Suggested Mitigations

1. **Enable loop detection by default** (or at least enable the post-compaction guard by default — currently it's on, but the rolling-history detector is off)
2. **Compaction sanitization**: When summarizing session content for compaction, detect and truncate repetitive patterns (N identical tool calls, N identical assistant texts) rather than faithfully summarizing them. This would prevent the poison from surviving compaction.
3. **Session read sanitization**: When an agent reads a session transcript via `session-search` or file read, consider detecting and collapsing repetitive blocks in the output before they enter the reader's context.
4. **Document the diagnostic transmission vector**: Warn operators that asking a looping agent to read its own session history can reinject the looping pattern. Recovery should use a fresh session, not transcript replay.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)
- Models: `ollama/deepseek-v4-flash:cloud`, `ollama/kimi-k2.6:cloud`, `ollama/glm-5.2:cloud`
- `tools.loopDetection`: `{}` (enabled not set — defaults to false)
- `agents.defaults.compaction.mode`: `safeguard`

## Summary

On the official iOS app, configured wake words do not result in a visible or audible action when Talk is set to the default native route but no ElevenLabs credentials are configured. The UI makes the app look ready for wake-word use while the configured voice path is unusable.

## Observed setup

- iOS app: official build
- Speakerphone: enabled
- Wake words: `Viernes`, `Hey Viernes`
- Provider: **Gateway Default**
- Voice Mode: **ElevenLabs**
- Active Voice: **Not active**
- Transport: **Native**
- API Key: **Not configured**
- Show Talk Control: enabled

Saying either wake word produced no response.

## Expected behavior

At minimum, the iOS app should make the missing prerequisite explicit and report an actionable error/status rather than silently doing nothing.

Preferably, native iOS Talk/Wake should work without a paid/provider-specific TTS account:

1. Detect the wake phrase using the existing Apple Speech recognition path.
2. Send the following command/transcript to the active session.
3. Use `AVSpeechSynthesizer` / the built-in iOS system voice as a no-credential TTS fallback when Gateway TTS is unconfigured or unavailable.

This would make the native `Voice Wake` and `Talk` experience functional out of the box, with ElevenLabs/OpenAI Realtime remaining opt-in upgrades.

## Why this seems inconsistent

The iOS app exposes wake-word configuration and native transport, and current code already labels a `system` Talk provider as “iOS System Voice.” However, Gateway Default resolves to the shipped ElevenLabs route in this unconfigured state, yielding no active voice or feedback.

## Acceptance criteria

- A no-credential iOS configuration can complete: wake phrase → transcript/agent request → audible system-voice response.
- If that cannot be supported, the UI clearly says that a configured Gateway TTS provider is required and offers the relevant setup path.
- A wake-word match visibly updates status and surfaces diagnostics when speech/microphone permissions or provider readiness block it.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

**Environment**: openclaw 2026.6.11, Feishu channel, self-hosted; built-in `feishu_doc` tool (extensions/feishu).

**What happened**

During a task that appends 13 charts (image upload + caption append per chart) to a Feishu doc, the model batched up to 4 concurrent `feishu_doc` calls per turn. The Feishu API rate-limited the bursts:

- Three separate 429 responses on text appends (image uploads in the same batch succeeded), returned to the model verbatim as `{"error": "Request failed with status code 429"}`.
- One 504 on an append. 504 means the outcome is unknown — the write may or may not have landed. The tool surfaced it as a plain error; the model blind-retried the append, which produced a **duplicated caption block** in the document (verified: two identical h3+p pairs in the doc).

Because every retry decision is left to the model, the burst pattern continued (no pacing), the turn's wall time ballooned past the channel's 300s serial-queue release, and the document ended half-complete with duplicates.

**Suggested behavior**

Handle transient Feishu API errors at the tool layer, with a single responsibility layer for retries:

1. **Per-document write serialization** — one writer per doc token; concurrent write requests to the same doc get queued internally.
2. **429**: honor `Retry-After` (with jitter and a total wait budget per call), retry internally 2-3 times, and return a structured result: `{attempts, retry_handled, outcome: "committed"|"failed"}` so the model never blind-retries.
3. **504 / timeouts**: return `outcome: "unknown"` and do **not** auto-retry; the model (or the tool via a follow-up read) must verify whether the block landed before rewriting. Without an idempotency key, auto-retrying a 504 write is what creates duplicates.

This complements (but is distinct from) the empty-final-completion issue #111764 filed for the same incident.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Ask the agent to append a dozen images + captions to one Feishu doc; the model batches 3-4 concurrent feishu_doc append/upload calls per turn.
2. Observe Feishu 429 responses on some calls in each batch (`{"error": "Request failed with status code 429"}` returned to the model verbatim) while sibling calls succeed.
3. Observe an occasional 504 on an append; the model blind-retries it; compare the doc afterwards and find the appended block duplicated.

### Expected behavior

Transient Feishu API errors (429/504) are absorbed by the tool layer: writes to one document are serialized, 429s are retried internally honoring Retry-After within a wait budget, and 504s are reported as outcome-unknown without automatic rewrite. The model receives one final structured status per call instead of raw HTTP error strings. Reference: the same task's local chart generation (13/13) completed fine; only the uncoordinated write burst degraded.

### Actual behavior

Raw `{"error": "Request failed with status code 429"}` / `... 504` strings were returned to the model (3×429 at 14:54:54, 14:55:09, 14:55:33; 1×504 at 14:53:32 local). Image uploads in the same batches succeeded while text appends failed, leaving the doc half-complete (12/13 images, several captions missing); the model's blind retry after the 504 duplicated one caption block (two identical h3+p pairs verified in the document). No tool-level pacing occurred between batches.

### OpenClaw version

2026.6.11

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 (DGX Spark, arm64)

### Install method

npm global

### Model

deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro-202606

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> TokenHub (OpenAI-compatible gateway) -> deepseek (model side; the bug itself is in the Feishu tool layer)

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell
Redacted tool results from the session (timestamps local, UTC+8):

14:53:32 append -> {"error": "Request failed with status code 504"}
14:54:54 append -> {"error": "Request failed with status code 429"}   (sibling image upload in same batch: success)
14:55:09 append -> {"error": "Request failed with status code 429"}   (sibling image upload in same batch: success)
14:55:33 append -> {"error": "Request failed with status code 429"}   (sibling image upload in same batch: success)

Post-incident document audit: 12/13 images present, several captions missing, one caption duplicated (identical h3+p pair twice) — the duplicate matches the model's blind re-append after the 504.
```

issues.body:
# Agent tool call infinite loop + model.completed usage always 0

## Environment
- OpenClaw version: 2026.6.11 (e085fa1)
- OS: Windows
- Model: agent-plan/ark-code-latest

---

## Issue 1: Infinite tool call loop (positive feedback)

### Phenomenon
User sent **1 single message**:
> Check if OpenClaw needs updating, and perform the update if needed

Then the agent ran **45 model turns automatically** (no further user input), producing:
- 1498 total tool calls
- 1322 `exec` calls
- **The exact same 30 commands repeated 44 times in a row**

### Root Cause Analysis
Three factors combined to create a perfect positive feedback loop:
1. **Full context snapshot**: `messagesSnapshot` includes all previous tool calls + all tool outputs every turn
2. **Deterministic tool output**: All commands are read-only/idempotent (`npm view`, `openclaw --version`, reading local files), returning exactly the same output every time
3. **Model "double-check" obsession**: The model confirmed "already latest version", but then thought "maybe I missed something" and re-ran the exact same check sequence → same output → same decision → same re-run

### Evidence from trajectory
Exec command prefix counts (all integer multiples of 44 turns):
- Read file into variable: 572x = 13 per turn × 44 turns
- Search file content: 308x = 7 per turn × 44 turns
- List directory: 264x = 6 per turn × 44 turns
- `npm view openclaw version`: 45x = 1 per turn × 45 turns
- `openclaw --version`: 45x = 1 per turn × 45 turns

### Suggested Fix
Add runtime detection for **repeating identical tool call sequences**:
- If the agent outputs the exact same tool calls 2+ turns in a row → pause execution and ask user for direction
- Optional: Hard limit on automatic consecutive turns without user input (e.g., max 5 auto turns)

---

## Issue 2: `model.completed.usage` is always 0

### Phenomenon
In all `model.completed` events inside `messagesSnapshot`:
```json
{
  "usage": {
    "input": 0,
    "output": 0,
    "cacheRead": 0,
    "cacheWrite": 0,
    "totalTokens": 0,
    "cost": {
      "input": 0,
      "output": 0,
      "cacheRead": 0,
      "cacheWrite": 0,
      "total": 0
    }
  }
}
```

All fields are **always 0**, even for the 45-turn session that burned an estimated 500K+ tokens.

### Impact
- Dashboard token/cost statistics are **completely missing** for agent tool use sessions
- Users cannot detect runaway token consumption until they receive their API bill

### Suggested Fix
Populate `usage` fields from the actual model API response, or calculate approximate token counts from context length.

issues.body:
### Summary

Please add first-class native OpenClaw support for contextual embedding providers, so memory search can safely use models such as `voyage-context-4` without relying on a local wrapper around the native memory runtime.

The key request is not just "use a different embedding model". Contextual embedding providers need runtime semantics for document/chunk boundaries, contextual query mode, index identity, cache invalidation, diagnostics, and migration/rollback.

### Problem to solve

OpenClaw's current native memory path appears to model memory embeddings as ordinary single-text embeddings. On my host, native memory still reports the standard `voyage` / `voyage-4-large` backend and standard index identity.

That is not enough for provider-managed contextual embeddings. A model such as `voyage-context-4` should not be treated as a config-only replacement for `voyage-4-large`, because the provider needs document-level context and matching query/index semantics.

### Proposed solution

Add native support for contextual embedding backends in OpenClaw memory search.

The runtime should distinguish ordinary single-text embeddings from contextualized document/query embeddings at the provider/config level.

Suggested design points:

- Provider config can declare contextual embedding mode, not just provider/model/dimensions.
- Index identity includes:
  - provider
  - model
  - dimensions
  - source set
  - contextualization mode
  - corpus manifest digest
  - document/chunk boundary strategy
  - vector-store/cache version
- Switching between non-contextual and contextual models requires or performs a safe full reindex.
- Query embedding uses the matching contextual query mode.
- Query-mode mismatch hard-fails rather than silently degrading to weak cosine matches.
- Cache reuse fails closed across provider/model/contextualization/corpus-boundary changes.
- Diagnostics report contextual mode, corpus identity, index identity, and whether fallback was used.
- Rollback cleanly deactivates the contextual backend and returns to the previous native index without corrupting caches.

## Result Metadata

Memory search results should expose enough metadata for operators and agents to understand why a result is trusted:

- backend/provider/model
- contextualization mode
- source path
- source type
- document/corpus identity
- authority tier
- confidence or answerability
- fallback route, if any
- negative-result metadata when the system cannot answer safely

## Migration and Rollback Requirements

Native support should include an explicit migration path:

- detect existing non-contextual indexes
- require or perform a contextual reindex before contextual search is active
- record projected/actual embedding cost for large memory corpora
- preserve the previous native index until cutover is verified
- provide a rollback command or config path that returns to the previous native index
- prevent accidental mixed-mode search during migration

Cutover should be verifiable, not just a config flip.

## Privacy and Storage Requirements

Contextual vector indexes are durable derived-memory surfaces. They may contain inversion-susceptible vectors derived from private memory, so they should inherit the privacy tier of the source corpus.

Status artifacts should not contain raw memory text, raw query text, or secret values. Machine-readable status should contain bounded metadata only.

## Related Prior Issue

Related but not sufficient: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/3171

That issue asked for contextual retrieval by prepending document/section context to chunks at index time, and was closed as not planned. This request is broader and more specific to provider-managed contextual embeddings: native provider mode, document/chunk boundary identity, contextual query/index matching, cache/index migration, diagnostics, and rollback safety.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Native runtime can index and query a contextual embedding backend such as `voyage-context-4`.
- Config distinguishes contextual embedding providers from ordinary single-text embedding providers.
- Index identity prevents accidental reuse of incompatible `voyage-4-large` or non-contextual vectors.
- Switching contextualization mode requires or performs safe reindex before use.
- Query/index mode mismatch hard-fails.
- Diagnostics clearly report contextual mode and corpus identity.
- Search results expose bounded provenance and confidence metadata.
- Status artifacts do not contain raw memory text, raw query text, or secret values.
- Rollback to the previous native index is explicit and tested.

### Alternatives considered

## Existing Local Workaround

I currently use a local wrapper that keeps native OpenClaw generated/runtime bundles unchanged while adding a contextual memory path around the native runtime.

The wrapper provides:

- intent-aware routing
- fusion search
- provenance/quality metadata
- incremental contextual indexing
- corpus manifests
- feedback metadata
- healthcheck coverage

That local wrapper proves the direction, but it is not a substitute for first-class native runtime support.

### Impact

Without first-class runtime support, these failure modes are too easy:

- reusing stale non-contextual vectors after switching to a contextual model
- embedding chunks without the document context expected by the provider
- querying a contextual index with a non-contextual query embedding, or vice versa
- mixing indexes with incompatible document/chunk boundary strategies
- reporting generic memory status without corpus identity or contextualization mode
- making rollback depend on local wrapper behavior rather than a native migration contract

### Evidence/examples

_No response_

### Additional information

_No response_

issues.body:
### Summary / Problem Statement
In `src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts`, `writeFile` pipes the complete input Buffer directly as `stdin` into `runCheckedCommand`. For large assets (e.g., binaries or model weights), this duplicates the memory buffer and violates Node's `exec` payload limits, triggering Out-of-Memory crashes.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Vulnerable Code Location:** [src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts#L111)
- **Mechanics:**
  ```typescript
  const result = await runCheckedCommand("sh", [], { stdin: params.data }); // Huge buffer copied to stdin string
  ```

### Impact Analysis
- Process instability: large file uploads inside the sandbox crash the host gateway manager.
- Out-of-memory crashes on resource-constrained host machines.

### Proposed Solution
1. Stream large file payloads in chunks to the sandbox filesystem wrapper instead of passing the entire buffer via stdin.
2. Enforce a maximum file size write limit for direct buffer operations.

### Affected File References
- [fs-bridge.ts:L100-L120](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sandbox/fs-bridge.ts#L100-L120)

## What Problem This Solves

Android and Apple mobile implementations duplicate several deterministic
protocol and business-rule paths while the native UI and device integrations
must remain platform-owned. Existing near-duplicates already differ in edge
behavior, so an unplanned extraction risks a protocol regression.

## Proposed Solution

Create an evidence-backed, contract-first migration record before introducing
KMP. It defines the initial pure-logic boundary, a Swift-friendly SKIE plus
hand-written facade, ABI and Swift-parity gates, required Android/iOS proof,
and a per-PR net-negative production diff gate.

## Alternatives Considered

- Share mobile UI: rejected because platform-native UX and OS integrations are
  first-class requirements.
- Use Kotlin Swift Export as the production boundary: deferred because it is
  currently Alpha.
- Keep duplicate logic: rejected for deterministic protocol and business rules
  where a single source of truth has clear maintenance value.

## Impact

No runtime or UI behavior changes are proposed by the planning PR. The plan
gives maintainers a safe sequence for reducing future Android/iOS business-logic
duplication without exposing generated Kotlin APIs to Swift callers.

## Evidence

- Repository mapping found direct Talk directive and Bonjour parser overlap plus
  behavior differences that require characterization before extraction.
- Official Kotlin guidance supports incremental logic sharing while retaining
  native UI; Swift Export remains Alpha.
- Docs formatting, MDX, glossary, and link validation pass; autoreview reported
  no actionable findings.

issues.body:
## Summary

Add a Feishu/Lark-specific send path that can deliver text plus multiple images as a single Feishu interactive card.

## Problem to solve

When an OpenClaw agent sends text with multiple image attachments through the Feishu channel, the current agent-facing `message.send` path sends media sequentially / as separate parts rather than composing a single rich Feishu message.

This is hard to read and archive for workflows that naturally produce one coherent visual deliverable, such as:

- product page image sets,
- design review bundles,
- before/after comparisons,
- generated image batches with captions,
- step-by-step visual instructions.

`presentation` can already reach the Feishu card path for text-only cards, but the public presentation contract does not include an image block, and native Feishu card sanitization does not expose a safe image component path to agents.

## Proposed solution

For Feishu only, when a send payload contains text/presentation plus image attachments, the channel should be able to:

1. Upload each image to Feishu/Lark and obtain `image_key` / `img_key`.
2. Build a Feishu `interactive` card with markdown/text blocks and image elements.
3. Send it as one Feishu message via the existing card send path.
4. Fall back to the existing sequential media behavior if upload/card send fails.

Suggested design:

- Trigger only for Feishu sends with both textual content and image attachments, or use an explicit Feishu option if maintainers prefer opt-in behavior.
- Reuse the existing Feishu image upload helper where possible.
- Generate card content internally rather than allowing arbitrary unsanitized `channelData.feishu.card` image components from agents.
- Preserve the existing text-only `presentation` card behavior.
- Preserve existing multi-media fallback behavior on partial failure.

Pseudo-flow:

```ts
if (isFeishu && hasTextOrPresentation(payload) && hasImageAttachments(payload)) {
  const uploaded = await uploadImagesForFeishuCard(payload.attachments)
  const card = buildFeishuImageCard({ text, presentation, images: uploaded })
  return await sendCardFeishu({ card, ...target })
}
```

Likely implementation area:

- `extensions/feishu/src` outbound send/runtime code
- Published package: `@openclaw/feishu`

## Alternatives considered

- Keep sequential media sends: works reliably, but produces message bursts and loses the structure of a single deliverable.
- Expose arbitrary native Feishu card JSON to agents: powerful, but riskier because it expands sanitizer/security surface.
- Add a generic cross-channel image block to `presentation`: useful long term, but larger protocol/API surface than needed for a Feishu-first implementation.

## Impact

Affected users/systems/channels:

- Feishu/Lark channel users who deliver image bundles through OpenClaw agents.

Severity:

- Medium. Existing sends work, but the result is fragmented and less usable.

Frequency:

- Common for visual workflows, especially product pages, generated image sets, design reviews, and multi-step visual explanations.

Consequence:

- Extra manual cleanup, harder forwarding/archive, and worse readability compared with a single Feishu interactive card.

## Evidence/examples

I validated the underlying Feishu APIs against a real Feishu channel configuration:

- Uploaded two local JPEG images to Feishu image API successfully.
- Built a Feishu interactive card containing markdown text plus two image elements.
- Sent it as a single Feishu message successfully.
- The resulting message was an `interactive` Feishu message.

Observed successful test result:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "imageKeyCount": 2,
  "message_id": "om_x100b6bc4ae9124b8c2d946793d4bee6",
  "msg_type": "interactive"
}
```

I also confirmed that current `message.read` returns only the textual content for that interactive card. That is a separate read-path issue and is not required for this send-path feature.

## Additional information

Compatibility and safety suggestions:

- Keep this behavior Feishu-scoped; no cross-channel behavior change required for an initial implementation.
- Prefer a controlled image-card builder over exposing arbitrary native Feishu card JSON.
- Keep existing sequential media sending as fallback.
- Consider limits for image count, size, MIME type, and URL fetching policy if remote image URLs are supported.

issues.body:
## Summary

In a multi-account Discord setup, OpenClaw registers the same native slash commands for multiple Discord apps. In channels where only one OpenClaw account is enabled, Discord still shows duplicate commands from every installed app, for example several `/status` entries.

Runtime routing/auth is correct, but the command picker is noisy and forces the user to choose the right app manually.

## Expected behavior

OpenClaw should provide a supported way to make Discord command visibility match Discord account/channel routing.

Possible approaches:

- Sync Discord app command permissions from `channels.discord.accounts.*.guilds.*.channels`.
- Provide a CLI command to reconcile Discord command permissions per account.
- Let accounts register commands as guild-scoped/channel-aware where Discord supports it.
- Provide per-account command include/exclude or namespacing so generic commands do not collide across apps.

## Actual behavior

Each installed OpenClaw Discord app can expose the same global native commands in the Discord slash-command picker. A channel that is configured for one OpenClaw account can still show commands owned by other OpenClaw apps.

Those other apps may reject execution due to OpenClaw allowlists, but Discord still shows them as selectable options.

## Why this matters

Manual Discord integration permission setup is tedious with multiple OpenClaw accounts and channels. OpenClaw already has the account/channel routing config, so command visibility should ideally derive from that instead of requiring separate manual Discord setup.

Related: #78082 covers stale command cleanup when native commands are disabled. This request is broader: keep active native commands visible only where the corresponding account is meant to be used.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a first-class Agent Bundle export/import mechanism so agents can be moved between OpenClaw instances without manually rebuilding openclaw.json entries, workspace files, skills, bindings, and environment requirements.

### Problem to solve

Moving agents between OpenClaw instances is currently too difficult and error-prone.

A common workflow should be simple:

1. Create and test an agent locally.
2. Package or commit the tested agent.
3. Move it to another machine.
4. Import it there.
5. Run it without manually rebuilding configuration, workspace files, skills, bindings, and environment requirements.

Currently, agent-related state appears to be spread across multiple places, such as:

- openclaw.json
- agent definitions
- model assignments
- channel bindings
- workspace files such as AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, USER.md, TOOLS.md, IDENTITY.md
- required skills
- required environment variables
- runtime-managed workspace state

In addition, OpenClaw initializes workspaces as Git repositories. This makes it difficult to version a surrounding OpenClaw directory in Git, because nested .git directories conflict with an outer repository. Treating the workspace itself as a Git repository is possible, but it does not fully solve portability because not all agent-relevant configuration necessarily lives inside the workspace.

The result is that moving a tested agent from one machine to another can require duplicated manual work, remote editing of openclaw.json, manual skill installation, and careful reconstruction of bindings and environment requirements.

### Proposed solution

Add portable Agent Bundles.

Example commands:

openclaw agent export <agent-id> ./agent-bundles/<agent-id>
openclaw agent import ./agent-bundles/<agent-id>

or:

openclaw agent bundle create <agent-id> ./agent-bundles/<agent-id>
openclaw agent bundle install ./agent-bundles/<agent-id>

An agent bundle should contain portable, non-secret agent configuration, for example:

agent-bundles/
└── example-agent/
    ├── agent.bundle.json
    ├── workspace/
    │   ├── AGENTS.md
    │   ├── SOUL.md
    │   ├── USER.md
    │   ├── TOOLS.md
    │   └── IDENTITY.md
    ├── skills.txt
    └── README.md

The import command should:

- create or update the agent definition
- copy workspace files into the correct workspace location
- update openclaw.json or the internal agent registry as needed
- apply model assignment and context settings
- apply channel bindings if included
- check whether required skills are installed
- optionally install missing skills
- check whether required environment variables exist
- never import secrets, credentials, sessions, logs, completions, device state, caches, or runtime artifacts
- support a dry-run mode

Example:

openclaw agent import ./agent-bundles/example-agent --dry-run
openclaw agent import ./agent-bundles/example-agent --install-skills

### Alternatives considered

I tried treating the whole OpenClaw data directory as a Git repository, but this is unsafe because it contains runtime state, credentials, logs, caches, sessions, and nested workspace Git repositories.

I also considered treating the workspace itself as the only Git repository. That avoids the nested Git issue, but it does not fully solve portability because important agent configuration such as model assignments, bindings, skills, and environment requirements can live outside the workspace.

Manual copying or remote editing works, but it is error-prone and does not scale once multiple agents, sub-agents, skills, and machines are involved.

### Impact

Affected: Users who develop agents locally and deploy them to another OpenClaw instance, especially Docker/server setups and multi-agent or sub-agent workflows.

Severity: Medium to high. The current workflow is workable, but it creates significant operational friction and makes agent deployment error-prone.

Frequency: Recurring. This happens whenever an agent is moved, updated, tested locally and deployed remotely, or when a new machine needs to be initialized.

Consequence: Users must manually reconstruct or synchronize agent configuration, workspace files, skills, bindings, and environment requirements. This can lead to duplicated work, broken remote setups, inconsistent local/remote behavior, mistakes in openclaw.json, missing skills, and delayed deployments.

A portable Agent Bundle mechanism would reduce manual work and make agents easier to version, review, share, reproduce, and deploy safely.

### Evidence/examples

_No response_

### Additional information

_No response_

issues.body:
### Summary

Detect Cloudflare Sandbox / Cloudflare Containers runtime environments in `isContainerEnvironment()` by recognizing Cloudchamber cgroup paths such as `0::/cloudchamber_v2/<id>_oci`.

### Problem to solve

Cloudflare Sandbox containers do not currently match OpenClaw's container-environment heuristic.

On a live Cloudflare Sandbox container, `/proc/1/cgroup` was observed as:

```text
0::/cloudchamber_v2/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000_oci
```

The standard marker files were absent:

```text
/.dockerenv
/run/.containerenv
/var/run/.containerenv
```

As of OpenClaw `v2026.6.10`, `isContainerEnvironment()` detects Docker/Podman/Kubernetes/LXC-style cgroups and Fly.io marker env vars, but not the `cloudchamber_v2/..._oci` shape used by Cloudflare Sandbox. Source: [`src/infra/container-environment.ts` at `v2026.6.10`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.6.10/src/infra/container-environment.ts).

That means Cloudflare Sandbox is treated as an unmanaged host by any OpenClaw code path that depends on container detection. Recent restart-policy work makes the ordinary unmanaged restart path safer, but the platform is still classified incorrectly. That leaves downstream deployments relying on generic fallback behavior, explicit `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1`, or local wrapper guards rather than OpenClaw's existing container-specific intent.

### Proposed solution

Extend `isContainerEnvironment()` to recognize Cloudflare Sandbox / Cloudchamber cgroups generically, not just the currently observed versioned spelling. A minimal matcher could treat a `/proc/1/cgroup` path segment that starts with `cloudchamber` and is optionally versioned, such as `cloudchamber_v2/<id>_oci`, as a container signal.

Add regression coverage with a sample cgroup line:

```text
0::/cloudchamber_v2/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000_oci
```

If OpenClaw exposes diagnostics for detected runtime type, update that diagnostic text so operators can see Cloudflare Sandbox classified as a container rather than an unmanaged host.

### Alternatives considered

Set `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1` in Cloudflare Sandbox deployments.

This is a useful local workaround because OpenClaw checks it before container/supervisor detection in restart helpers. It does not fix the platform classification and requires every Cloudflare Sandbox deployment to know about an OpenClaw internals escape hatch.

Rely on the generic unmanaged restart fallback from [#83138](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/83138).

That mitigates ordinary unmanaged config restarts in `v2026.5.18+`, but it does not make `isContainerEnvironment()` accurate for Cloudflare Sandbox. Future detection-dependent behavior can still diverge unless the platform is recognized explicitly.

Fake Docker or supervisor marker files/env vars in the container.

That leaks OpenClaw detection details into deployment wrappers and can imply a supervisor/runtime that is not actually present.

### Impact

Affected: OpenClaw gateway deployments running inside Cloudflare Sandbox / Cloudflare Containers.

Severity: medium to high operationally, depending on OpenClaw version and wrapper architecture. Older OpenClaw versions can choose detached process respawn in this environment because the runtime is not detected as a container. Newer versions mitigate ordinary unmanaged restarts, but still classify the platform incorrectly.

Frequency: every OpenClaw startup and every code path that relies on `isContainerEnvironment()` for restart, bind, or diagnostic behavior.

Consequence: deployments need local mitigations such as `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1` and wrapper-level port/process guards. Without those mitigations on affected versions, a restart-classed config change can detach the serving gateway from its wrapper/supervisor, causing duplicate gateway launches and loss of wrapper-owned cleanup/sync hooks.

### Evidence/examples

Current detection source: [`src/infra/container-environment.ts` at `v2026.6.10`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.6.10/src/infra/container-environment.ts).

Related restart behavior source: [`src/infra/process-respawn.ts` at `v2026.6.10`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.6.10/src/infra/process-respawn.ts).

Related upstream items:

- [#73178](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/73178) fixed PID-1 behavior for detected container runtimes. This request is complementary: Cloudflare Sandbox should enter that detected-container category.
- [#65668](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/65668) / [#83138](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/83138) fixed ordinary unmanaged restarts by keeping them in-process. This request is not a duplicate because it asks for accurate Cloudflare Sandbox detection rather than relying on the unmanaged fallback.
- [#76239](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/76239) discussed Cloudflare Sandbox lifecycle behavior and was closed after current-version checks. This request is narrower: add `cloudchamber_v2` cgroup recognition to `isContainerEnvironment()`.
- [#80209](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/80209) is useful precedent: OpenClaw already added platform-specific detection for Fly Machines when the usual Docker/container markers were absent.
- [#94279](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/94279) / [#94310](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/94310) and [#95887](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/95887) are adjacent current work using containerized-environment detection to suppress or revise non-durable in-container update guidance. They are not duplicates, but they show `isContainerEnvironment()` remains an active shared signal.

Prior-art search performed on 2026-06-24: GitHub issue/PR searches for `cloudchamber` found no OpenClaw issue or PR covering this detection gap. Broader `Cloudflare Sandbox` searches found lifecycle reports, including #76239, but no `isContainerEnvironment()` / cgroup-detection fix. GitHub Discussion searches for `cloudchamber`, `Cloudflare Sandbox`, `isContainerEnvironment`, and `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN` returned no related OpenClaw discussions.

### Additional information

Cloudflare Sandbox is the SDK/runtime surface behind Cloudflare Containers. Cloudflare's public Sandbox concepts documentation describes sandbox lifecycle at https://developers.cloudflare.com/sandbox/concepts/sandboxes/.

The requested fix is intentionally small: recognize the Cloudchamber cgroup family and add a regression test for the observed `cloudchamber_v2/..._oci` shape, without changing the existing Docker/Podman/Kubernetes/LXC/Fly.io detection behavior.
