issues.body:
## Summary

The runtime treats `verboseDefault` and `elevatedDefault` as valid per-agent overrides (resolver, plugin-SDK types, status text, command handlers), but the strict zod entry schema does not declare them, so `openclaw config set agents.list.<idx>.verboseDefault on` (or `elevatedDefault`) is rejected with `Unrecognized key`. Only `agents.defaults.*` accepts these keys today, which forces a global default even when the operator only wants to change one agent.

`thinkingDefault`, `reasoningDefault`, and `fastModeDefault` are accepted per agent — they are listed in `AgentEntrySchema`. `verboseDefault`/`elevatedDefault` are missing from that same schema, despite the rest of the stack already supporting them.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.4.24 (cbcfdf6)`
- Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu VM)
- Config edited via `openclaw config set`

## Repro

```bash
# index 0 = any agent in agents.list, e.g. main
openclaw config set agents.list.0.verboseDefault on
# Error: Config validation failed: agents.list.0: Unrecognized key: "verboseDefault"

openclaw config set agents.list.0.elevatedDefault on
# Error: Config validation failed: agents.list.0: Unrecognized key: "elevatedDefault"
```

Same error when setting it in `openclaw.json` directly and running `openclaw config validate`.

`thinkingDefault` works as expected on the same path:

```bash
openclaw config set agents.list.0.thinkingDefault high
# OK
```

`agents.defaults.verboseDefault` and `agents.defaults.elevatedDefault` are also accepted and work as documented.

## Expected

Either (preferred): allow `verboseDefault` and `elevatedDefault` on per-agent entries the same way `thinkingDefault`, `reasoningDefault`, and `fastModeDefault` are allowed, since the rest of the codebase already resolves them per agent.

Or: explicitly document that these are global-only and remove the per-agent resolution paths and SDK types so the surface stays consistent.

## Evidence the rest of the stack already expects per-agent values

The strict schema is the only place the per-agent fields are missing. Everywhere else the resolver chain reads `entry.verboseDefault` / `agentCfg.verboseDefault` first and only then falls back to `agents.defaults.verboseDefault`:

- `dist/agent-scope-*.js`:
  ```js
  verboseDefault: entry.verboseDefault ?? agentDefaults?.verboseDefault,
  ```
- `dist/directive-handling.levels-*.js`:
  ```js
  currentVerboseLevel: params.sessionEntry?.verboseLevel ?? params.agentCfg?.verboseDefault,
  ```
- `dist/agent-command-*.js`:
  ```js
  const resolvedVerboseLevel = verboseOverride ?? persistedVerbose ?? agentCfg?.verboseDefault;
  ```
- `dist/get-reply-*.js`:
  ```js
  const resolvedVerboseLevel = directives.verboseLevel ?? targetSessionEntry?.verboseLevel ?? agentCfg?.verboseDefault;
  ```
- `dist/dispatch-*.js`:
  ```js
  fallbackLevel: normalizeVerboseLevel(
    sessionStoreEntry.entry?.verboseLevel
      ?? sessionAgentCfg?.verboseDefault
      ?? cfg.agents?.defaults?.verboseDefault
      ?? ""
  ) ?? "off"
  ```
- `dist/status-message-*.js`:
  ```js
  const verboseLevel = args.resolvedVerbose
    ?? args.sessionEntry?.verboseLevel
    ?? args.agent?.verboseDefault
    ?? "off";
  ```

The Plugin-SDK type definitions also document the per-agent fields:

- `dist/plugin-sdk/src/config/types.agents.d.ts`:
  ```ts
  /** Optional per-agent default verbosity level. */
  verboseDefault?: "off" | "on" | "full";
  ```
- `dist/plugin-sdk/src/config/zod-schema.agents.d.ts` (the published TS schema):
  ```ts
  verboseDefault: z.ZodOptional<z.ZodUnion<readonly [
    z.ZodLiteral<"off">, z.ZodLiteral<"on">, z.ZodLiteral<"full">
  ]>>;
  ```
- `dist/plugin-sdk/src/agents/agent-scope-config.d.ts`:
  ```ts
  verboseDefault?: AgentDefaultsConfig["verboseDefault"];
  ```

## Where the runtime schema diverges

`dist/zod-schema.agent-runtime-*.js` declares `AgentEntrySchema` as `z.object({...}).strict()` and only includes `thinkingDefault`, `reasoningDefault`, and `fastModeDefault`. `verboseDefault` and `elevatedDefault` are absent:

```js
const AgentEntrySchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  // ...
  thinkingDefault: z.enum(["off","minimal","low","medium","high","xhigh","adaptive","max"]).optional(),
  reasoningDefault: z.enum(["on","off","stream"]).optional(),
  fastModeDefault: z.boolean().optional(),
  // verboseDefault   <-- missing
  // elevatedDefault  <-- missing
  // ...
}).strict();
```

The defaults schema (`AgentDefaultsConfig` in `zod-schema-*.js`) does declare them:

```js
verboseDefault: z.union([
  z.literal("off"), z.literal("on"), z.literal("full")
]).optional(),
elevatedDefault: z.union([
  z.literal("off"), z.literal("on"), z.literal("ask"), z.literal("full")
]).optional(),
```

`openclaw config schema` confirms it at runtime — `agents.list[]` lists `thinkingDefault`, `reasoningDefault`, `fastModeDefault` but not `verboseDefault` or `elevatedDefault`.

## Documentation

`docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/config-agents` documents `verboseDefault` and `elevatedDefault` only under `agents.defaults.*`. There is no documented per-agent override for them, even though `thinkingDefault` is documented as available both at `agents.defaults.thinkingDefault` and `agents.list[].thinkingDefault`. The doc lookup at `https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/thinking` even references `Per-agent default (agents.list[].thinkingDefault in config)`, which sets the expected pattern.

## Suggested fix

Add the two fields to `AgentEntrySchema` in `zod-schema.agent-runtime`:

```js
verboseDefault: z.enum(["off", "on", "full"]).optional(),
elevatedDefault: z.enum(["off", "on", "ask", "full"]).optional(),
```

…and document them under `agents.list[]` in `gateway/config-agents.mdx` with the same precedence note used for `thinkingDefault` (per-agent overrides default, omitted falls back to `agents.defaults.*`).

## Workaround

Set the value globally via `agents.defaults.verboseDefault` / `elevatedDefault`. Per-agent toggling currently has to happen via runtime `/verbose` and `/elevated` slash commands per session, which doesn't survive new sessions.

issues.body:
## Summary

When an async/background exec approval follow-up cannot resume the original agent session, OpenClaw falls back to direct delivery and currently exposes an internal prefix to the user:

```text
Automatic session resume failed, so sending the status directly.
```

This is confusing because the underlying command may have succeeded. The failure is in the session handoff/delivery path, not necessarily in the command.

## Observed behavior

- Background/approved exec completes.
- Follow-up path attempts to resume the original agent session.
- If resume/follow-up fails, direct delivery is sent with the internal fallback prefix.
- The user sees the prefix in Telegram/DM output, sometimes while investigating approval/session issues.

In the installed runtime we found the string in the bash-tools chunk, not `dist/index.js`:

```text
/usr/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/bash-tools-MqL7r1OX.js:215:
return "Automatic session resume failed, so sending the status directly.\n\n";
```

We applied a local runtime mitigation by changing that return to `return "";`, but that is intentionally local and will be overwritten by updates.

## Expected behavior

1. Retry session resume/follow-up with short backoff before falling back, for example 500ms, 1500ms, 3000ms.
2. If direct delivery fallback is still needed, do not prefix the user-facing message with internal session-resume failure text.
3. Log the resume failure internally with enough metadata to debug, for example follow-up id, original session key/id, delivery target, and error cause.
4. Preserve the command result/status content in the fallback delivery.

## Why this matters

The current prefix makes successful command completions look like command failures. It also creates a noisy feedback loop: approval/follow-up failures surface while trying to diagnose approval/follow-up failures.

## Local workaround used

Runtime-only local patch:

```js
return "";
```

This only suppresses the user-facing prefix. It does not fix the deeper session handoff resilience issue.

## Suggested fix

Implement retry/backoff around the agent-session resume/follow-up call in the exec approval follow-up path, then fall back to direct delivery silently if all retries fail, with internal-only logging for the resume failure.

issues.title: [Feature] Add denylist mode to exec.security for balanced security

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: security
labels.description: Security documentation

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a denylist exec security mode that allows all commands by default and only blocks/requires approval for explicitly dangerous patterns.

### Problem to solve

The current exec.security has three modes: deny (blocks everything), allowlist (blocks unknown commands until manually approved), and full (allows everything). There is no middle ground.

allowlist mode creates severe approval fatigue in interactive agent workflows — every new command variant (even harmless ls, cat, curl, find) triggers an approval popup that blocks execution until the user manually responds. In a typical session, this means 10-20+ approval interruptions, each breaking the agent's flow and adding minutes of idle wait. Users end up switching to full mode just to get work done, losing all safety guardrails in the process.

### Proposed solution

Add denylist as a fourth exec.security enum value:

"exec": {
  "security": "denylist",
  "denyPatterns": [
    "rm -rf /",
    "rm -rf /*",
    "shutdown*",
    "reboot*",
    "mkfs*",
    "dd if=/dev/zero*",
    ":(){ :|:& };:",
    "chmod -R 777 /",
    "> /dev/sda"
  ]
}

Behavior:
All commands execute without approval by default (same as full)
Commands matching any denyPatterns entry are either blocked outright or escalated to require user approval (configurable via a denyAction: "block" | "ask" option)
Patterns support glob matching (e.g. rm -rf /*) and optionally regex
A sensible built-in default denylist is provided out of the box, users can extend or override it

### Alternatives considered

_No response_

### Impact

Affected users: All interactive agent users who rely on exec for daily workflows — especially power users running agents on personal machines via DM channels (Feishu, Discord, Telegram, etc.)
Severity: Blocks workflow. The approval loop makes multi-step tasks (web scraping, file exploration, build/test cycles, CLI tool usage) painfully slow. A 2-minute task can stretch to 20+ minutes waiting for approvals.
Frequency: Always. Every session with allowlist mode triggers multiple approval requests. It is not an edge case — it is the default experience for any non-trivial agent interaction.
Consequence:
Users abandon allowlist and switch to full mode, completely losing safety protection
Agent workflows are fragmented by approval timeouts (commands expire after ~2 minutes if the user doesn't respond)
Async command denials pile up, causing confusion about which commands ran and which didn't
The security model becomes binary (paranoid vs. wide-open) instead of offering a practical middle ground

### Evidence/examples

_No response_

### Additional information

_No response_

issues.body:
## Problem

A Feishu app can have only one reliable long-connection consumer for a given event stream. Feishu documents multiple long-connection clients for the same app as a cluster: a given event is delivered to one client, not broadcast to every client.

Today the bundled Feishu channel plugin owns the Gateway long connection but does not register `contact.user.*_v3` or `contact.department.*_v3` handlers. When a tenant enables those events, the Gateway can receive them and log that no handler exists. Starting a second listener for the same app is not reliable because either connection can receive the event.

This blocks a legitimate integration pattern: an in-process workflow plugin needs to react to organization changes while the Feishu channel plugin remains the only long-connection consumer.

## Evidence

- OpenClaw source: `extensions/feishu/src/monitor.account.ts` registers message, chat, drive, VC, reaction, menu and card handlers, but no contact user/department handlers.
- The bundled Webhooks plugin is external -> Gateway ingress, so it cannot receive a Feishu event already consumed by the Feishu channel.
- The public agent-events API is explicitly for sanitized agent workflow/UI events, not provider-native event delivery.
- Feishu cluster behavior is documented here: https://open.feishu.cn/document/server-docs/event-subscription-guide/event-subscription-configure-/request-url-configuration-case?lang=zh-CN

## Proposed capability (discussion requested before code)

Add a provider-owned, opt-in Feishu organization-event bridge. The Feishu channel remains the sole Lark SDK `EventDispatcher` owner and can register these six events when at least one in-process consumer subscribes:

- `contact.user.created_v3`
- `contact.user.updated_v3`
- `contact.user.deleted_v3`
- `contact.department.created_v3`
- `contact.department.updated_v3`
- `contact.department.deleted_v3`

The bridge should expose a narrowly scoped, typed in-process subscription surface owned by the Feishu plugin (not a core raw-event hook), with a minimal normalized envelope such as:

```ts
{ accountId, eventId, eventType, data }
```

A separate installed workflow plugin can then decide how to enqueue/forward the event. OpenClaw must not contain product-specific endpoint URLs, bearer tokens, or tenant logic.

## Constraints

- No second Feishu long connection for the same app.
- No new public inbound port.
- No product-specific FabricOS integration in the bundled Feishu plugin.
- Do not expose raw app credentials through the plugin API.
- Consumer failure must be isolated and logged; it must not break normal Feishu message handling.
- No configured/subscribed consumer means no additional contact event registration.

## Alternatives considered

1. **Second listener process** — rejected: Feishu cluster delivery means it races the Gateway and loses events.
2. **Use the bundled Webhooks plugin** — rejected: it is inbound HTTP to Gateway, the opposite direction.
3. **Add a global core raw-channel-event hook** — possible, but much broader than this requirement and would enlarge the core SDK contract for every channel.
4. **Add an arbitrary outbound URL to `channels.feishu` config** — possible, but introduces SSRF, secret, retry, and operational policy concerns; an installed in-process consumer is safer if the use case is accepted.

## Acceptance matrix

| Requirement | Evidence required |
| --- | --- |
| One Gateway connection owns Feishu delivery | Integration test proves one dispatcher registers all required handlers |
| Opt-in only | Test proves no contact handler is registered without a consumer |
| All six event types reach a typed subscriber | Unit test table for each type |
| Stable delivery key | Test validates `eventId` and `eventType` are preserved |
| Failure isolation | Throwing subscriber does not affect message handler or another subscriber |
| No competing listener / public port | Deployment instructions require neither |
| Real Feishu E2E | Tenant event -> one bridge delivery -> downstream sync run -> directory update, plus duplicate-event and failure proof |

## Request

Please confirm whether a Feishu-plugin-owned in-process subscription bridge is an acceptable extensibility boundary, and if so whether it should be exported from `@openclaw/feishu` or exposed through another supported plugin mechanism. I will not open an implementation PR until that boundary is agreed.

_This issue was prepared with Codex after reproducing the integration boundary; no tenant secrets, endpoints, or identities are included._

issues.body:
### Summary

On 2026.7.2-beta.7, every `sessions_spawn` call from our router agent is blocked before
dispatch with `error_code=tool_blocked`. The tool is built, offered to the model, and
permitted by every config knob we can find — it simply never executes. The same agent
successfully used the predecessor tool `collab.spawnAgent` on 2026-07-25 (beta.4 era),
so this looks like a regression introduced with the rename in the beta.5–beta.7 line.

Net effect: the agent cannot delegate to **any** sub-agent. All agent-to-agent
delegation from that agent is dead.

### Environment

- openclaw `2026.7.2-beta.7`
- macOS (Apple Silicon), gateway supervised externally by launchd
  (`OPENCLAW_SUPERVISOR_MODE=external`)
- Provider/model for the calling agent: anthropic / claude-opus-5
- Calling agent tools profile: `messaging`

### Diagnostic signature (the key detail)

From the gateway's own `audit_events` table. `sessions_spawn` emits
`tool.action.finished` with `status=blocked` and **never emits `tool.action.started`** —
i.e. it is rejected pre-dispatch. Every other tool from the same agent emits both.

```
-- sessions_spawn: 6 events, ALL blocked, ZERO started
ts                   agent_id     tool_name       action                 status   error_code
2026-08-12 20:25:45  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:45:28  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:45:33  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:50:07  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-13 16:50:11  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked
2026-08-14 14:45:11  core-router  sessions_spawn  tool.action.finished   blocked  tool_blocked

-- collab.spawnAgent (predecessor tool, same agent): dispatches normally
2026-07-25 10:50:54  collab.spawnAgent  tool.action.started    started
2026-07-25 10:50:54  collab.spawnAgent  tool.action.finished   succeeded

-- web_fetch (same agent, unrelated tool): dispatches normally
2026-08-08 22:19:41  web_fetch  tool.action.started   started
2026-08-08 22:19:42  web_fetch  tool.action.finished  failed
```

The 2026-08-12 occurrence is organic production traffic, not a synthetic probe.

### What we ruled out

All verified against the live config and the shipped `dist/`:

1. **Permission / allowlist.** `tools.agentToAgent = {enabled: true, allow: [main,
   core-router, personal-engine]}`; `tools.sessions.visibility = "all"`; the agent's
   `tools.alsoAllow` includes `sessions_spawn`, `sessions_send`, `sessions_yield`,
   `subagents`; `tools.deny` does not include it; `subagents.allowAgents` lists the
   intended target. Spawn depth is 0 against a default `maxSpawnDepth` of 1.
   `sessions_spawn` is not in `GATEWAY_OWNER_ONLY_CORE_TOOLS`, and the caller is the
   owner regardless.
2. **Tool availability.** `includeSubagentSpawnTool = !embedded ||
   options?.allowGatewaySubagentBinding === true`, and the gateway conversation path
   passes `allowGatewaySubagentBinding: true`, so the tool *is* built. The tool-policy
   availability predicate (`coreTools.has(tool)`) is satisfied — this is not the
   "shipped core tools but unavailable in the current runtime/provider/model/config"
   path (which we do see separately for a codex-runtime agent, as expected).
3. **Approvals.** The denial is not in the approval family. Per
   `agent-tools.before-tool-call-*.js`, specific reasons are
   `client-voice-confirmation`, `tool-loop`, and `plugin-approval`, with
   `plugin-before-tool-call` as the *default* fallback (`deniedReason ??
   "plugin-before-tool-call"`). No approvals/admission config gates `sessions_spawn`;
   the only approvals config present is an unrelated channel exec-approvals block.

### The observability gap (secondary ask)

We could not recover the actual denial reason anywhere:

- `audit_events` records `status`/`error_code` but no reason payload.
- `diagnostic_events` did not persist the tool-block payload; `capture_events` empty.
- Nothing in the gateway logs.

Because the reason is unavailable, the calling model *invents* one. Ours consistently
narrated a confident, entirely fabricated `deniedReason: "plugin-before-tool-call"` with
a reason string belonging to a completely different (shell/exec) policy — a string that
exists nowhere in the shipped code. That cost us significant debugging time chasing a
non-existent hook.

**Request:** persist `deniedReason` (and the blocking hook/plugin identity) on the
`tool.execution.blocked` audit row, or surface it in the tool result returned to the
model. A pre-dispatch block that is invisible to both operator and model is very hard
to diagnose.

### Regression window

- 2026-07-25: `collab.spawnAgent` **succeeds** (newest published build at that point was
  `2026.7.2-beta.4`, 2026-07-24).
- 2026-08-12 onward, on `2026.7.2-beta.7` (published 2026-08-02): `sessions_spawn`
  **always blocked**.

So the regression landed in beta.5 (2026-07-28), beta.6 (2026-08-01), or beta.7. The
2026.7.2 release highlights an approvals/admission gate, which seems like a plausible
neighbourhood, though we could not confirm it is the cause.

### Impact

Agent-to-agent delegation is completely unavailable from the affected agent. In a
router/specialist topology where the front-line agent intentionally holds a reduced
toolset and delegates everything else, this silently degrades the whole system to
"whatever the router can do alone" — and because the block is invisible, the model
apologises with a fabricated explanation instead of surfacing a real error.

### Questions

1. What sets `deniedReason` for a pre-dispatch `tool_blocked` on `sessions_spawn`, and
   what config (if any) is expected to permit it beyond `tools.agentToAgent` +
   `subagents.allowAgents`?
2. Was the `collab.spawnAgent` → `sessions_spawn` migration expected to require a config
   change that we've missed?
3. Is this fixed in `2026.8.1-beta.2`? (We could not adopt it to test: 8.1 moves the
   iMessage channel out of core into `@openclaw/imessage`, which is a larger migration
   than we can take right now on a production gateway whose primary channel is iMessage.)

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect behavior without a crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2`, two simple warm Codex app-server turns in the same Nextcloud Talk session showed a repeatable 19-21 second gap between `session.started` / `context.compiled` and `prompt.submitted`, before model or tool work began.

This is the same lifecycle phase previously reported in #84725, but the current latest-release samples are substantially slower than that issue's approximately 7.5 second warm-turn measurement. #84725 was closed as stale with a request to open a new issue with fresh reproduction details if the problem still occurs on the latest release.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2` with the bundled Codex app-server runtime and OpenAI OAuth.
2. Use a warm, long-lived Nextcloud Talk session with `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`.
3. Send a short request that requires at most one small local file read, or send a short status follow-up.
4. Inspect the session trajectory timestamps.

I reproduced the long pre-submit gap on 2/2 simple turns observed in this session:

```text
Sample A
2026-08-13T03:56:42.538Z  session.started
2026-08-13T03:56:42.540Z  context.compiled
2026-08-13T03:57:01.747Z  prompt.submitted
2026-08-13T03:57:21.626Z  tool.call (bash)
2026-08-13T03:57:21.755Z  tool.result
2026-08-13T03:57:30.155Z  model.completed / session.ended

context.compiled -> prompt.submitted: 19.207 s
session.started -> session.ended:       47.617 s

Sample B
2026-08-13T04:42:45.466Z  session.started
2026-08-13T04:42:45.468Z  context.compiled
2026-08-13T04:43:06.604Z  prompt.submitted
2026-08-13T04:43:30.109Z  tool.call (memory_search)
2026-08-13T04:43:42.723Z  tool.result
2026-08-13T04:43:46.325Z  model.completed / session.ended

context.compiled -> prompt.submitted: 21.136 s
session.started -> session.ended:       60.859 s
memory_search tool duration:            12.614 s (separate from pre-submit gap)
```

### Expected behavior

A warm turn should not spend 19-21 seconds in an unobservable phase after `context.compiled` and before `prompt.submitted`. If this setup work cannot be avoided, the trajectory should expose subphase timings sufficient to identify whether the delay is authentication, start-options resolution, dynamic-tool construction, shared-client startup, request serialization, or another step.

### Actual behavior

The user sees roughly 28-40 seconds of latency after sending these simple messages. The trajectory shows that 19-21 seconds occurs before `prompt.submitted`; model and tool durations account for later, separate portions of the turn.

There was no gateway crash or restart during either sample. The host was not CPU- or RAM-saturated during follow-up inspection. This report does not attribute the delay to native hooks, disk usage, or any specific internal subphase because the current trajectory does not prove that.

### OpenClaw version

`2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)`

### Operating system

Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie), x86_64

### Install method

npm global install; systemd user service

### Node.js version

`v22.22.3` (gateway service runtime)

### Model and provider

`openai/gpt-5.6-luna` through OpenAI OAuth and the bundled Codex app-server runtime

### Provider / channel chain

Nextcloud Talk -> OpenClaw gateway -> bundled Codex app-server over stdio -> OpenAI OAuth -> `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`

### Additional setup details

- Warm shared Codex app-server process
- Long-lived Nextcloud Talk group session
- The session had grown to approximately 155k tokens before manual compaction
- Gateway service remained active; follow-up host inspection showed low instantaneous load and approximately 3.9 GiB available memory
- Raw prompts, room IDs, usernames, hostnames, paths, and credentials are intentionally omitted

### Logs / evidence

The redacted timestamp sequence above is taken from the session trajectory. No error was emitted for the pre-submit interval.

Related lifecycle reports:

- #84725: same post-`session.started`, pre-`prompt.submitted` phase; closed stale with instructions to file a fresh latest-release reproduction
- #84640: earlier hidden delay before `session.started`; tracing improvement merged in #88101
- #95121: later delay after `prompt.submitted`; different phase from this report
- #72365: older `tools.effective` regression, fixed in `6ae2e9e9dcea5e57c3657537402020cdcbe36d4f`; this report persists on `2026.7.1-2`

### Impact

Interactive Nextcloud Talk commands feel stalled even when the requested work is trivial. Severity is medium: no data loss or crash, but every affected warm turn incurs tens of seconds of user-visible latency.

### Additional information

The large session size is a possible confounder, not a proven cause. Manual compaction reduced the session from approximately 155k tokens to approximately 1.6k tokens, but I do not yet have an equivalent controlled post-compaction reproduction, so whether context size causes the pre-submit gap is `NOT_ENOUGH_INFO`.

I also do not have a controlled same-model, same-session A/B measurement from an older OpenClaw release, so this report intentionally does not claim a confirmed version regression. It reports current latest-release behavior and the precisely observed lifecycle phase.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The signed easyclaw.app binary sends Apple Events without the com.apple.security.automation.apple-events entitlement in its code signature, causing macOS to block the process with a non-dismissible native consent dialog whenever an internal AppleEvent (e.g. via file open/save panel, QuickLook) is triggered.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run the signed macOS build of easyclaw.app (v1.3.93, build 1.3.93.1068) with an undecided or previously-reset Automation/AppleEvents TCC grant.
2. Use the app normally so that an internal component triggers a file open/save panel or QuickLook preview (these use AppKit/QuickLookUI XPC services that send AppleEvents via appleeventsd on the app's behalf).
3. Observe macOS's tccd log via `log stream --predicate 'process == "tccd"'` or `log show`.

### Expected behavior

Because the app is under the hardened runtime and does send AppleEvents, its code signature should declare the com.apple.security.automation.apple-events entitlement (ideally with a paired NSAppleEventsUsageDescription). This would let macOS surface a normal one-time consent prompt tied to an explicit user action, and allow the grant to persist without repeatedly blocking unrelated internal operations.

### Actual behavior

tccd log shows, verbatim:

Prompting policy for hardened runtime; service: kTCCServiceAppleEvents requires entitlement com.apple.security.automation.apple-events but it is missing for responsible={TCCDProcess: identifier=ai.easyclaw.desktop, pid=10529, auid=502, euid=502, responsible_path=/Applications/easyclaw.app/Contents/MacOS/easyclaw, binary_path=/Applications/easyclaw.app/Contents/MacOS/easyclaw}, accessing={TCCDProcess: identifier=com.apple.appkit.xpc.openAndSavePanelService, pid=18707, auid=502, euid=502, binary_path=/System/Library/Frameworks/AppKit.framework/Versions/C/XPCServices/com.apple.appkit.xpc.openAndSavePanelService.xpc/Contents/MacOS/com.apple.appkit.xpc.openAndSavePanelService}, requesting={TCCDProcess: identifier=com.apple.appleeventsd, pid=556, auid=55, euid=55, binary_path=/System/Library/CoreServices/appleeventsd}

This fired for both openAndSavePanelService and QuickLookUIService as responsible processes attributed to easyclaw.app, confirming the entitlement is genuinely absent from the app's code signature rather than a one-off consent decision. Because the app frequently runs unattended, this blocking dialog has no way to be dismissed programmatically and the process hangs until a human physically clicks the dialog on the machine.

### OpenClaw version

easyclaw.app 1.3.93 (build 1.3.93.1068); CLI reports OpenClaw 2026.4.14 (093aa0e)

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.1 (build 25F80), Apple Silicon (arm64)

### Install method

Signed macOS app bundle installed to /Applications/easyclaw.app; separate npm-installed CLI at a bundled Node path

### Model

N/A - not model-dependent, this is a code-signing/entitlement issue in the macOS app binary itself

### Provider / routing chain

N/A - occurs regardless of provider/model routing; triggered by AppKit/QuickLookUI system XPC services sending AppleEvents attributed to the easyclaw.app process

### Additional provider/model setup details

_No response_

### Logs

```shell

```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: any user running the signed macOS easyclaw.app build, especially unattended/headless setups where the app triggers automation-driven actions without a human present.
Severity: blocks workflow - a single unattended process hits an unresolvable, non-programmatic native dialog and hangs indefinitely, appearing as a frozen agent/tool call.
Frequency: deterministic whenever an internal AppleEvent-triggering action occurs (observed via openAndSavePanelService and QuickLookUIService as responsible processes) and the Automation grant is not already decided.
Consequence: unattended automation tasks silently stall until a human is physically present at the machine to click Allow/Deny, defeating the core unattended-operation use case.

### Additional information

Related but distinct from #112217, which documents a passive permission-status check triggering the prompt via `tell application "Terminal"`. This report is about the underlying entitlement being absent from the app's code signature itself, which affects any AppleEvent trigger (confirmed here via two different system XPC services), not just the passive status check page.

Suggested remediation: add com.apple.security.automation.apple-events to the app's entitlements plist (with a paired NSAppleEventsUsageDescription) and re-sign/re-notarize, so the OS can present a normal consent prompt tied to an explicit user action and persist the grant afterward.

issues.body:
### Summary

When an ACP harness advertises a `category: "model"` session config option, populate the Control UI composer from it instead of locking the model selector.

### Problem to solve

[#121993](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/121993) reported that the composer footer shows the owning agent's model in sessions where an external ACP harness answers. [PR #122264](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/122264) fixes the misattribution by projecting the canonical ACP identity and setting `modelSelectionLocked: true`.

That removes the wrong information, which is the important half. What it leaves is a locked, empty affordance in sessions where the harness is in fact offering a model list and accepting model changes. The operator can see that the model is not the agent's, but not which model is answering, nor switch it from the UI, even though the protocol carries both.

I filed #121993 and my evidence there pointed at the wrong surface, so this issue is partly a correction of my own report. There I cited the `models` field on `session/new`, which was ACP's unstable model API and has since been removed from the schema (see the [acp-go-sdk v0.13.5 notes](https://github.com/coder/acp-go-sdk/releases/tag/v0.13.5)). Building the composer on that would have been a mistake. The stable replacement is what this issue is about.

### Proposed solution

Drive the composer from session config options, gated on capability rather than on harness identity:

1. When the session's ACP details carry a config option with `category: "model"`, project its `currentValue` and `options` onto the session row alongside the ACP identity overlay from #122264.
2. Render that as the composer's model selector for the session, and route a change through `session/set_config_option` with the option's `configId`.
3. When no such option is advertised, keep #122264's behaviour exactly: project the canonical ACP identity and lock the selector.

The same shape generalises to `category: "mode"`, which Cursor also advertises, though that is out of scope here.

Nothing about this is harness-specific. The [ACP v2 migration guide](https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/v2/migration) states the stable categories are `mode`, `model`, `model_config` and `thought_level`, that "clients can use them for UX affordances", and instructs clients to "drive mode/model UI from `configOptions` (using `category`) via `session/set_config_option` and `config_option_update`".

### Alternatives considered

**Lock unconditionally, as #122264 does.** Correct and shippable, and strictly better than today. The concern is only that it hardens into an assumption that externally-answered sessions have no selectable model, when the protocol has a stable way to say otherwise and at least one harness already says it.

**Populate from `models` / `availableModels` on `session/new`.** This is what I originally suggested on #121993 and it should not be done: that surface was unstable and is removed, and `session/set_model` answers `-32601` on updated implementations.

**Leave model changes to chat commands only.** Works, and is what I use today, but it means the UI shows a control that is visibly inert while the capability exists underneath it.

### Impact

Control UI operators of ACP harness sessions get to see which model is answering and change it in place, instead of a locked selector, for any harness that advertises the capability. For harnesses that do not, behaviour is unchanged from #122264.

### Evidence/examples

The plumbing already exists on the gateway side, which is why I think this is small. `src/acp/control-plane/manager.runtime-controls.ts` already extracts option keys off the session details (`extractConfigOptionKeys(details?.configOptions)`) and advertises `session/set_config_option` as a control; `src/acp/control-plane/manager.runtime-options-commands.ts` already gates writes on `capabilities.controls.includes("session/set_config_option")`. `session/set_model` appears only in `docs/tools/acp-agents.md`. So the missing part is the session-row projection and the composer, which is the surface #122264 touches.

Measured against the harness, driving `cursor-agent acp` directly over stdio with no OpenClaw in the path (Cursor CLI `2026.08.04-aaa8809`, which negotiates protocol version 1 even when asked for 2):

```
session/new keys: sessionId, modes, models, configOptions
  removed surface  models:        33 entries
  stable surface   configOptions: 2 options (category=mode, category=model)
```

The stable option, verbatim and abridged:

```json
{
  "id": "model",
  "name": "Model",
  "description": "Controls which model variant is used for responses",
  "category": "model",
  "type": "select",
  "currentValue": "composer-2.5[fast=true]",
  "options": [
    { "value": "default[]", "name": "Auto" },
    { "value": "grok-4.5[effort=high,fast=true]", "name": "grok-4.5" },
    { "value": "composer-2.5[fast=true]", "name": "composer-2.5" },
    { "value": "claude-opus-5[thinking=true,context=300k,effort=high,fast=false]", "name": "claude-opus-5" },
    { "value": "gpt-5.6-sol[context=272k,reasoning=medium,fast=false]", "name": "gpt-5.6-sol" }
  ]
}
```

Worth noting for whoever picks this up: `currentValue` is not necessarily the OpenClaw-side default. Cursor persists the ACP selection globally in `~/.cursor/acp-config.json` as a single `selectedModelVariantId`, so a fresh session inherits the last choice unless a model is passed explicitly at spawn. Reading `currentValue` off the session, rather than inferring it from configuration, is the only reliable way to display it.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, not planning to at the moment. Filing it so the follow-up is recorded rather than buried in a PR thread. Happy to run further protocol probes against the Cursor harness if measurements would help whoever takes it.

### Additional information

Related: #121993 (the bug), #122264 (the lock fix). Observed on OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2` in a rootless container, with the Cursor CLI embedded as an ACP harness via `acpx`.

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Summary

The `sessions_send` tool does not accept any timeout-related parameter (`timeoutSeconds`, `runTimeoutSeconds`, or equivalent). Callers have no way to size the recipient session, and the recipient inherits `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` silently. This makes `sessions_send` unsuitable for long-running agent-to-agent dispatch.

## Steps to reproduce

1. From any session, call `sessions_send` with `timeoutSeconds: 1800` (or any timeout-related key).
2. Observe that `timeoutSeconds` is accepted but ignored — the recipient session still uses `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`.
3. Alternatively, call `sessions_send` with a task that requires >900s. Observe the recipient session times out at 900s.

## Expected behavior

`sessions_send` should accept a `timeoutSeconds` parameter (or equivalent) that overrides the recipient session's timeout for the duration of this dispatch. This would match the behavior of `sessions_spawn`, which is governed by `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds` (default 3600s).

## Actual behavior

`sessions_send` silently ignores any timeout-related parameter. The recipient session's timeout is resolved exclusively from `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`.

Comparing the two tools:

| Tool | Per-call timeout param | Effective timeout source |
|------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| `sessions_spawn` | `runTimeoutSeconds` (rejected with explicit error) | `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds` (default 3600s) |
| `sessions_send` | None (silently ignored) | `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` (default 900s) |

Evidence from the source (`openclaw-tools-*.js`):

```javascript
const UNSUPPORTED_SESSIONS_SPAWN_TIMEOUT_PARAM_KEYS = ["runTimeoutSeconds", "timeoutSeconds"];
// ...
const unsupportedTimeoutParam = UNSUPPORTED_SESSIONS_SPAWN_TIMEOUT_PARAM_KEYS.find(
  (key) => resolveSnakeCaseParamKey(params, key)
);
if (unsupportedTimeoutParam) throw new ToolInputError(
  `sessions_spawn does not support per-call "${unsupportedTimeoutParam}". Configure agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds instead.`
);
```

`sessions_spawn` explicitly rejects per-call timeout params (redirecting callers to config). `sessions_send` does not enforce this — it simply ignores them with no feedback.

## OpenClaw version

2026.7.1-2 (0790d9f)

## Operating system

Linux 6.8.0-137-generic (x86_64)

## Install method

npm global

## Model

zai/glm-5.2 (primary), minimax/MiniMax-M3 (fallback)

## Provider / routing chain

openclaw → z.ai API (openai-completions compatible)

## Additional provider/model setup details

Multi-agent configuration. `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds: 900`. `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds: 3600`. `sessions_send` has no per-call or per-target-agent timeout override.

## Logs

Recipient session timing showing the global default was applied:

```
session.started → 1786460663365 (epoch ms)
session.ended   → 1786461566796 (epoch ms)
runtimeMs       → 903431  (≈ 900s = agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds)
status          → "timeout"
```

The 903s runtime is deterministic evidence that the global 900s default was applied, not any per-call override.

## Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Multi-agent dispatchers that use `sessions_send` for long-running work
- **Severity:** Medium — blocks use cases that exceed 900s; requires workarounds (dispatch one card per session, or use `sessions_spawn` with different execution model)
- **Frequency:** Always (when dispatch exceeds 900s)
- **Consequence:** Either silent truncation (if caller passes `timeoutSeconds` and it's ignored) or premature timeout (if caller doesn't know the default).

## Additional information

**Asymmetry with `sessions_spawn`:** Both tools create sessions, but only `sessions_spawn` has a config field (`subagents.runTimeoutSeconds`) that callers can tune. `sessions_send` has no equivalent.

**Recommendation:** Either:

1. Add a per-call `timeoutSeconds` parameter to `sessions_send` that overrides the recipient's timeout for this dispatch, OR
2. Reject per-call timeout params explicitly with an error message (matching `sessions_spawn`'s behavior), OR
3. Document the timeout inheritance clearly so callers know to tune `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds` instead.

issues.body:
## Summary

Proposal to add an opt-in **daily maintenance window** to OpenClaw's cron subsystem that **defers non-roster cron and heartbeat work** during the window and **replays deferred work FIFO on phase exit**. The feature preserves the original PR #79192's operational surface but is re-anchored on the post-`#112585` split architecture (`heartbeat-cooldown.ts` + cron monitor rows + split `cron service`).

## Status

- v2 implementation completed and reviewed in PR #119575 (closed 2026-08-07).
- ClawSweeper cycle 3 verdict: "Pause for owner design — do not continue patch-level fixes until an owner decides whether this policy belongs in core and specifies its recovery contract."
- `@tyler6204` pinged 2026-08-06 08:52 UTC; no response at the time of close.
- This issue exists to drive the design discussion and reach an explicit owner verdict.

## What was built (preserved on branch `codex/maintenance-window-v2-2026q3`, head `7a63cae81e7`)

| Area | Change |
|---|---|
| Config schema | New additive `cron.maintenance` block: `window` (`start`, `end`, `timezone`, `roles`), `roster` (per-agent allow list), `replay` (`mode: "fifo" \| "drop"`, default `"fifo"`), `allowManualRun` (boolean, default `false`). |
| Policy core | `src/cron/maintenance-policy.ts` — phase resolution, role decision, retry-after calculation. |
| Deferred backlog | `src/cron/maintenance-deferred.ts` — FIFO queue with `push`, `drain`, `clear`, `size`, `snapshot`. |
| Status surface | `src/cron/maintenance-status.ts` — read-only report used by `cron.status` RPC. |
| Timer admission | `isRunnableJob` in `src/cron/service/timer-runnable.ts` consults the policy and records a deferral when the window is active. |
| Heartbeat wake | `evaluateWakeDeferral` in `src/infra/heartbeat-runner-scheduler.ts` resolves a per-agent `maintenanceWindow` and threads it into `shouldDeferWake`; `"maintenance-window"` is added to `RETRYABLE_GUARD_SKIP_REASONS`. |
| Manual run gate | `inspectManualRunPreflight` in `src/cron/service/ops-run-preparation.ts` returns a `maintenance-blocked` reason; `mode: "force"` always pierces. |
| Diagnostics | `applyJobResult` in `src/cron/service/timer-outcomes.ts` mirrors deferred entries into `job.state` so the protocol fields have a producer. |
| RPC surface | `CronJobStateSchema` (gateway-protocol) gains 3 read-only fields: `lastDeferredAtMs`, `lastDeferralReason`, `deferredMaintenanceCount`. |
| Operator docs | `docs/automation/maintenance-window.md`. |
| Tests | 66 new unit tests + 131 regression. `pnpm tsgo:core` + `pnpm tsgo:core:test` clean. |
| Evidence | `artifacts/pr79192-v2-maintenance-proof.mjs` exercises the real policy / queue / status modules (no mocks) across 5 scenarios. |

## Open design questions (where an owner verdict is needed)

1. **Should a daily maintenance window be a core-level cron policy at all?** Alternative: keep it as a per-deployment convention enforced outside the scheduler.
2. **Recovery contract on phase exit.** v2 picks **FIFO replay** (the most operator-friendly default), with `mode: "drop"` available. Is that the right default? Should we support a "skip if past due by >N" hybrid?
3. **Cross-midnight windows.** v2 explicitly **rejects** `start >= end` with a schema error. Is that the right ergonomic, or should we support `22:00–06:00` style windows?
4. **Hot reload of `cron.maintenance.*`.** v2 requires a cron service restart (the v2 docs say so); the project's general reload guidance is to hot-restart `CronService` on config changes. Should we treat `cron.maintenance.*` as a hot-reload-affecting field or document the restart requirement?
5. **Heartbeat / monitor rows during the window.** v2 defers all heartbeat wakes; the operator's monitor system still runs because it's not cron-scheduled. Is that the right split, or should the maintenance window also gate monitor wakeups?
6. **Manual run semantics.** v2 makes `cron run <job>` return `maintenance-blocked` unless `mode: "force"`; `allowManualRun: true` makes it pierce without force. Is that the right trust model?
7. **Configuration surface.** v2 introduces a top-level `cron.maintenance` block and 3 new `CronJobState` fields. Acceptable blast radius, or do we want a per-agent namespace (e.g. `agents.<id>.maintenance`) from day one?

## ClawSweeper actionable findings (preserved for whoever picks this up)

Carried forward from cycle 3 — these are the items the bot flagged even while asking us to pause for the owner decision:

- **P1** Record deferrals only after due-job admission checks (currently `isRunnableJob` records even jobs that would have been skipped for other reasons).
- **P1** Own the maintenance phase exit in the scheduler lifecycle (FIFO drain is implemented in the queue but not invoked from a scheduler-owned tick; the wake is also not driven by a phase-exit callback).
- **P1** Refresh heartbeat policy on `cron.maintenance.*` reload (current implementation requires a service restart; ClawSweeper flagged that as a contract contradiction).
- **P2** Compute phase transitions in the configured timezone with a zoned-instant resolver (current implementation adds a wall-minute delta to `nowMs`, which is wrong across DST).
- **P2** Publish the `cron.maintenance.*` schema alongside the operator docs (currently discoverable only via the docs page).

## Links

- Closed PR: #119575 (branch `codex/maintenance-window-v2-2026q3`, rebased on `upstream/main` `d85920c03e2`)
- Original closed PR: #79192 (closed by ClawSweeper as architecture-retired)
- v2 blueprint: `.pr79192-blueprint/rewrite-blueprint.md` in the worktree (7 design decisions D1–D7, rationale per decision)
- Evidence script: `artifacts/pr79192-v2-maintenance-proof.mjs` (5 scenarios, real module calls)
- Operator docs: `docs/automation/maintenance-window.md`

## How to revive

1. Owner confirms the feature direction (this issue, or a follow-up).
2. Address the 5 ClawSweeper findings above (the branch already contains the v2 baseline).
3. Re-open PR #119575 from the preserved branch — no rework needed.

If the answer is "not now" or "out of scope for core", please close this with a one-line verdict so the work stops cleanly and the cron/heartbeat-area maintainers have a clear signal.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add `brain: "codex-realtime"` as a Codex-specific Talk mode that continues an existing routed OpenClaw session through bundled Codex app-server Realtime V3 and subscription OAuth.

```json5
{
  talk: {
    realtime: {
      transport: "gateway-relay",
      brain: "codex-realtime",
      provider: "codex",
      providers: { codex: { voice: "arbor" } },
    },
  },
  plugins: {
    entries: {
      codex: { config: { appServer: { transport: "stdio" } } },
    },
  },
}
```

`brain` selects conversation/tool-turn ownership; `provider` selects realtime media. `codex-realtime` requires provider `codex` or an unset provider that resolves to Codex.

### Acceptance criteria

- Reuse each surface's existing canonical `agentId`, `sessionKey`, admission result, caller/session scope, sender identity, and voice-tool allowlist.
- Use the ordinary Codex harness/app-server attempt lifecycle and its existing workspace, sandbox, policy, MCP, native tool router, subagent monitor, timeout, and cleanup.
- Use Realtime V3 through the logged-in Codex subscription. App-server control uses `stdio`; app-server negotiates WebRTC internally.
- Reject V1/V2, explicit realtime API keys, conflicting providers, and non-stdio control transports for this brain.
- Work through the shared Talk realtime bridge. Legacy clients that send their existing `agent-consult` default must inherit configured Codex mode centrally; do not add Codex routing to individual channel/carrier handlers.
- Preserve existing Voice Call `sessionScope: per-call | per-phone`, caller admission, Discord admission, and meeting session mapping.
- Do not add custom turn handling, VAD, interruption, transcription, voice selection, tool routing, harness operations, lanes, persistence, or multi-speaker security policy.
- Reuse one shared WebRTC/Opus implementation with GPT-Live.
- Buffer bounded pre-connect/recovery audio, recover only the pinned established transport-reset shape, and fence stale media generations.
- Require Gateway-local placement for the process-local audio bridge and fail closed for an existing remote-worker placement.

### Scope

Out of scope: Discord SecretRef/autojoin/follow/requester rebinding/DAVE, Codex V1/V2 Platform-key support, a generic `agent-native` brain, other coding-agent realtime assumptions, a second media stack, new identity/session databases, new multi-speaker policy, and a Codex package upgrade.

OpenClaw already pins `@openai/codex` **0.147.0**. Matching upstream tag `rust-v0.147.0` (`be6e8eac029b183056b7e4402879f15d2c85f61b`) contains the required app-server V3/WebRTC subscription contract.

### Implementation and evidence

PR: #119001  
Final head: `5eb46f532619443263355ec3fe4cf20c51769a93`

- Local Docker gateway-relay E2E passed real virtual-microphone audio, native `pwd`, multi-turn memory, barge-in, and transport recovery.
- Local Discord bot-to-bot E2E passed speech, native tools, memory, long-session recovery, and existing text-channel transcript/tool-progress presentation in the dedicated test guild.
- Local Voice Call/Twilio-media websocket E2E passed real mu-law input and synthesized return audio without a real phone/network call.
- 606 focused assertions passed across all changed runtime boundaries. On the exact final head, 48 focused Codex/OpenAI media assertions, full `pnpm check`, strict production build smoke, dependency-ownership guards, Plugin SDK API/exports, formatting, and diff checks passed.
- Railway and the personal OpenClaw deployment were not touched.
- The shared Talk runtime now owns the existing WebRTC/Opus dependencies; the Codex plugin has no duplicate declarations. The resolved graph adds/removes/version-changes zero packages, while admin/secops approval remains required for the root declaration/ownership/lock change.
- [Redacted local-product evidence](https://gist.github.com/GoatInAHat/2b41e7e32bb5d89c8bc96bb632cd649e).

AI-assisted issue refinement.

issues.body:
### Summary

Request a distraction-free fullscreen chat mode on Android that hides all non-essential UI chrome (tab bar, app bar, status indicators), showing only chat messages and the input box.

### Problem to solve

On a Xiaomi 14 Ultra (6.73" 2K display), the current chat UI squeezes the actual chat content into a small portion of the screen. The bottom tab bar (Connect / Home / Chat / Canvas / etc.), top app bar, and other chrome take up significant space. When actively chatting, users don't need to see connection status or other tabs — they just want to read and type messages comfortably. The current layout wastes screen real estate and reduces readability, especially for longer conversations.

### Proposed solution

Add a "Fullscreen Chat Mode" toggle that can be activated from the Chat tab (e.g., a button in the header, a pinch-out gesture, or a long-press). In this mode:

- Show ONLY: chat message history + input box
- Hide: bottom tab bar, top app bar, status indicators, all other chrome
- Exit via: back button, swipe gesture, or a small floating exit button

This is similar to how WhatsApp, Telegram, and most messaging apps use the full screen for the conversation view.

### Alternatives considered

- Increasing font size / display scaling: doesn't help — the issue is layout proportions, not text size
- Using the web Control UI on mobile browser: not a native experience, clunky on phone
- Rotating to landscape: makes it even worse — the chat area nearly disappears completely in landscape mode

### Impact

Affected users: All Android app users, especially those on large-screen devices (tablets, large phones like Xiaomi 14 Ultra). iOS users likely face the same issue.

Severity: Annoying — significantly degrades the core chat experience on mobile. The chat feature is the primary use case of the app, yet it gets the least screen space.

Frequency: Always — every conversation on mobile is affected. This is not an edge case.

Consequence: Users struggle to read longer messages, see fewer messages on screen at once, and have a poor mobile chatting experience. This pushes users to switch to the web Control UI on a browser instead of using the native app, defeating the purpose of having a dedicated mobile app.

### Evidence/examples

_No response_

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only

_No response_

prs.title: fix: refresh activity recaps after runs with available credentials
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Activity recaps could call the utility model when a request arrived and again when its run ended. Gateways without a usable recap credential could also enter provider connection retries before reporting failure.

## User Impact

Recaps refresh after completed runs. A Gateway without a usable utility-model credential immediately shows the existing unavailable state and records `recap unavailable: no Gateway model credential`, without attempting inference or scheduling retries. Archive catch-up and requested Activity backfill remain available, and wait while a run is active.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remove transcript-triggered recap scheduling and the obsolete ongoing-refresh throttle. The queue uses the existing active-run projection for backfill admission and the existing published credential/catalog readiness for utility-model preflight, including fallback and native runtime credentials. Terminal events remain able to schedule catch-up before the run's cleanup finishes. Credential preflight shares the existing recap timeout and cleanup owner, so late preparation cannot dispatch after cancellation. Temporarily cooling-down credentials retain the existing execution retry path; only missing or failed credentials take the immediate unavailable path.

No new configuration, protocol, or durable state. Net production change: **+30 lines** across three files; the growth supplies the credential preflight and active-run guard, offset by removing the old scheduling path.

## Evidence

- Isolated Codex reviews of the feature and the CI correction found no actionable P0/P1 findings.
- Changed-file formatting, whitespace checks, and type-aware lint passed.
- Focused Gateway subscription regression: 2 cases passed (`pnpm test src/gateway/server-runtime-subscriptions.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 -t 'recaps only completed runs'`), 47.83 s wall time. Counts: start/input 0; run end 1 with credentials, 0 without. Unavailable state persists after advancing the scheduler by one hour. The final additional assertion checks credential preflight is not retried.
- Paired isolated Gateway runs against the same fake HTTP provider: baseline `b7b7415ae65` made **2 recap requests** for one turn; the candidate made **1**, with a current recap. Baseline startup was cold enough for the first `agent.wait` to time out; the run subsequently completed and its terminal recap was observed. Request counts, not latency, are the claim.
- CI corrections replayed locally: the two failed recap tests pass (`pnpm test src/gateway/session-activity-summaries.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 -t 'uses committed resident facts|does not let timeout'`), 195.79 s wall time (cold compilation dominated; test bodies ~5 s). The subscription regression, including the no-retry assertion, also passes, 50.72 s Vitest duration.
- Initial CI identified obsolete/incomplete test mocks, a test waiting for a deliberately absent publication, and preparation outside the existing deadline. The follow-up prunes the exception, completes the mock, waits for actual work settlement, and restores deadline ownership; no timeout or baseline was raised. The full subscription file passes all 65 cases locally. The shutdown fixture also explicitly supplies credential readiness; all four cancellation/cleanup cases pass (61.31 s wall time).
- Final credential-less recap route in a running isolated Gateway: the main fake-provider turn completed successfully, Activity published `unavailable`, the exact missing-credential diagnostic was logged, and the provider recorded **0 recap requests**. The scheduler regression additionally proves one preflight and no retries over an hour of injected time.
- Utility credential regression: cooldown is red with the old preflight; all 18 utility-completion tests pass with the fix, including missing/API/fallback/native credentials and preserving the unavailable UI route during cooldown (58.40 s wall time).
- PR CI supplies broad test and static validation.

prs.title: perf(sandbox): attribute slow setup and reuse clean failed-install source
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Slow sandboxed chat startup can report tens of seconds under `attempt.setup` without its nested worktree phases in the same line. A failed dependency installation also rebuilds the entire source checkout even when the installer left tracked files unchanged.

## User Impact

Slow-send diagnostics identify the setup work directly. Clean dependency-install failures reuse the validated source checkout after removing generated files; changed or unverified source still rebuilds. No configuration, schema, or authority changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

A recent startup had `attempt.setup=67201ms` and a separate earlier `worktree=23891ms`. The sandbox owner already recorded 67198ms, including 42428ms of template preparation, 24666ms of accumulated checkout work, and a dependency install that failed in 442ms. Its unattributed time was only 16ms. These nested timings overlap and must not be summed.

Request-owned checkpoints now separate setup policy, baseline waiting, workspace, skills, backend, and browser preparation. The worktree owner forwards its recorded durations as `detail.worktree.managed.*` and `detail.worktree.sandbox.*`; it does not remeasure them. Labels are fixed and elapsed timing is monotonic. The existing template validator removes partial dependencies and installer debris before reusing unchanged source, eliminating the second checkout in the clean-failure case.

Historical owner attribution (milliseconds; inclusive parents and accumulated children overlap):

| Owner phase | Duration | Meaning |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `attempt.setup` | 67,201 | Whole setup |
| `worktree.sandbox` | 67,198 | Sandbox preparation inside setup |
| `worktree.sandbox.reservation` | 63,850 | Inclusive allocation/preparation |
| `worktree.sandbox.templatePrepare` | 42,428 | Source, dependency install and fallback |
| `worktree.sandbox.checkout` | 24,666 | Accumulated checkout work, including rebuild |
| `worktree.sandbox.templateApply` | 12,339 | Clone prepared template |
| `worktree.sandbox.synchronizeProjection` | 4,271 | Reconcile canonical content |
| `worktree.sandbox.snapshot` | 3,260 | Initial projection manifest |
| `worktree.sandbox.containerStart` | 3,090 | Builder/runtime preparation |
| `worktree.sandbox.workspaceLayout` | 1,240 | Workspace/skills layout |
| `worktree.sandbox.setup` | 442 | Failed dependency installer |
| `worktree.sandbox.unattributed` | 16 | Outside the union of recorded owner phases |

The earlier chat `worktree=23891ms` surrounds a separate managed preparation (`durationMs=23622`, `unattributedMs=61`); it must not be subtracted from `attempt.setup`. The repeated “Native image: sandbox validation failed” warning validates prompt image-file paths, not container images. It occurs outside this setup boundary, with no retry loop in that validation path, so this change does not alter it.

## Evidence

- Regression: both new baseline-wait attribution cases fail on base because the slow-send line omits the phase; all 11 attempt-setup tests pass with the change.
- Regression: clean install failure and external-store fallback both perform two template creations on base and one with the fix. Successful and failed installers that change tracked source still rebuild. The existing tests verify original source/lockfile bytes and no installer debris.
- Focused verification: 30 tests passed across template recovery, slow-send diagnostics, workspace sandbox authority, and worktree timing. One earlier check aborted because source changed during worker compilation; the stable-source run passed.
- Review: independent subagent review (autoreview route unavailable), scoped clean through P2. The configured autoreview provider did not match the operator configuration; no configuration was changed.

### Measurement contract (recorded before paired runs)

Use a real isolated Gateway with synthetic model transport, 5,000 sessions, 6,000 retained runs, 5,000 distinct 4 KiB tracked files, managed worktrees, Podman session sandboxes, and synthetic plugin/Streamable HTTP MCP tools verified at the model boundary. Generate distinct same-tree commits so each of 32 cold samples per side prepares a cold dependency template; use four concurrent turns per 16-core side, keep the resident Gateway, and reuse the final four sessions for 200 warm turns. Report send-to-first-model-request p50/p99, sample counts, CPU, GC/work, promotion, loop tails and maximum pauses. Cold means session/template, not a fresh Gateway process.

Run concurrent pairs under one shared quiet lock and production guard, then swap interleaved CPU sets. Discard guard-interrupted pairs. Decide on paired means; reject at >=20% adverse mean or >=10% adverse in both pairs. Opposite-signed deltas or baselines differing by >5x are inconclusive, with absolute deltas and a third pair if gating. p99 needs 1,000 samples per side, p95 needs 200; smaller tails are context. Apply the GC collection-count, absolute pause-delta, and maximum-pause exceptions from the campaign rules.

The comparison uses candidate `127ddf47af7742f5e663a59baa3443bf97b70446` and baseline production `9538d3ab0bb5d1d5de262fe53ec0c24da0b2f0cc`, with the same benchmark harness on both sides. Its continuous whole-workload histogram supplies event-loop p99 and count, including cold session creation between cohorts.

### Measurement and landing decision

| Metric | Baseline | Candidate | Paired delta | Qualification |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Cold first-model p50 | 55,643.70 ms | 52,543.51 ms | −3,100.19 ms (−5.57%) | 32 turns/side |
| Cold first-model p99 | 114,349.72 ms | 114,231.09 ms | −118.64 ms (−0.10%) | Context: 32/32 samples |
| Warm first-model p50 | 3,774.47 ms | 3,564.26 ms | −210.21 ms (−5.57%) | 200 turns/side |
| Warm first-model p95 | 5,765.73 ms | 5,536.17 ms | −229.55 ms (−3.98%) | Eligible: 200/200 samples |
| Warm first-model p99 | 8,241.33 ms | 7,454.86 ms | −786.47 ms (−9.54%) | Context: 200/200 samples |
| Total observed GC/turn | 40.2196 ms | 40.3099 ms | +0.0903 ms (+0.22%) | Includes incremental GC; 1,954/2,037 events |
| Promotion/turn | 28.0124 MB | 28.0492 MB | +0.0368 MB (+0.13%) | Whole measured workload |
| Whole-loop p99 | 47.7757 ms | 45.1215 ms | −2.6542 ms (−5.56%) | Eligible: 62,744/63,110 samples |
| Whole-loop maximum | 296.7470 ms | 367.5259 ms | +70.7789 ms (+23.85%) | Context; loop p99 is the gate |
| Maximum single GC pause | 108.503 ms | 106.955 ms | −1.548 ms | Below max(50 ms, 2× baseline max) |
| Minor-GC p95 / p99 | 6.505 / 17.745 ms | 6.135 / 18.211 ms | −0.370 / +0.466 ms | 1,812/1,895 collections; final absolute-mean rule pending pair 2 |
| Major-GC p95 / p99 | 56.097 / 69.186 ms | 60.103 / 106.955 ms | +4.006 / +37.769 ms | Context: 71/71 collections, below percentile minima |
| Main-isolate CPU/turn | 555.39 ms | 531.14 ms | −24.25 ms (−4.37%) | Measured rounds |
| Gateway-process CPU/turn | 2,295.31 ms | 2,302.89 ms | +7.58 ms (+0.33%) | Measured rounds |
| Aggregate scope CPU/turn | 8,861.06 ms | 8,694.70 ms | −166.36 ms (−1.88%) | Common start through driver exit; excludes warmup/cleanup |
| Cold checkout mean | 2,112.44 ms | 1,055.19 ms | −1,057.25 ms (−50.05%) | 32 cold templates/side; two checkouts become one |

Both model-bound catalogs contained the synthetic plugin and MCP tools. No dropped diagnostic events, histogram samples, or collection errors occurred. Interleaved 16-core sets and sandbox-container placement were verified. The common barrier produced measurement starts 1 ms apart; first-cohort admission differed by 22.23 ms. One high-load minute (67.36) recovered without meeting the shared guard's three-consecutive-minute abort rule; both drivers and the orchestrator exited 0. This is a qualified first pair, not a completed performance verdict.

The small 20 MiB tracked-source fixture makes checkout much cheaper than the historical production case. Do not extrapolate its absolute saving to production. Mean owner-unattributed time fell from 1,205.79 to 105.05 ms because quiesce/resume now have labels; that is attribution coverage, not latency saved.

**paired measurement deferred: Team outage; simplification**. The lead explicitly authorized landing this duplicate-work removal without further pairs under the updated decision rule. The valid first pair showed no qualifying regression; it is not a completed swapped-pair estimate.

The first swapped attempt timed out during the initial cold cohort on both sides before completing a round. Its partial data is retained and excluded. Owner logs show progress: final setup completed at 164.495s on baseline and 159.721s on candidate, leaving insufficient time under the 170s observation ceiling. The prepared retry uses fresh cold fixtures and an identical, independently reviewed benchmark-only overlay: setup-image provider/turn deadlines increase to 600s and RPC observation to 610s. Workload, timestamps, and product source stay unchanged; pair 1 never reached its original deadlines. Overlay driver SHA-256: `b16beddfcea43656c0f8c2f293bf5d1e66f9258921531e4d3eeafd27310a8302`. The subsequent Team outage prevented the retry. The host has recovered, but no retry will run under the lead’s landing instruction; no complete swapped result exists.

### Captured live diagnostic signal

The real candidate sandbox emitted this synthetic slow-send excerpt during pair 1:

```text
detail.attempt.setup=22377ms
detail.attempt.setup.workspace=22376ms
detail.attempt.setup.workspace.sandbox=22357ms
detail.worktree.sandbox=22355ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.templatePrepare=18993ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.checkout=1016ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.containerStart=1592ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.setup=50ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.templateApply=303ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.snapshot=1191ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.synchronizeProjection=395ms
detail.worktree.sandbox.unattributed=23ms
```

These are nested/inclusive facts, not additive buckets. New fields are verified in a running isolated Gateway, **not yet in production**. Production observation requires the normal deployment; this lane does not restart or deploy a production Gateway.

Initial CI run 40037827662 passed the production checks but found an implicit-array-type error in the benchmark's nested summary construction. Two direct summaries fix that inference error without changing the reported samples. Pre-rebase [CI run 40039266721](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40039266721) passed all 88 jobs and verifies the repair. The required main rebase also brought a general chat diagnostic capture into this block; the independently reviewed resolution keeps ordinary chat and the dedicated attempt-setup capture correctly named and reported.

Changed-file lint/format, the `tsgo:core` lane (native tsrs), export-name collision guard, and the two source-closure files passed (22 closure tests). Focused test wall time was 45.42s for attempt setup, 64.75s across the four recovery/timing files, and 26.73s for closure checks; this includes compilation. Broad tests are delegated to PR CI; no Testbox/Crabbox lease was used under the lane's compute policy.

Runtime production delta is +90 lines: +81 for the explicitly requested continuous attribution and worktree-fact bridge, and +9 for source-only recovery while preserving the integrity rebuild. The deleted work is a complete second source checkout, not an alternate cached implementation. Benchmark fixtures and tests are separate from that runtime count.

The complete functional Gateway smoke passed plugin/MCP catalog assertions and a sandbox README read. It exercised a cold-template failed install and a warm reused sandbox. Added `runtimeQuiesce`/`runtimeResume` timings after that smoke exposed pause/resume work outside the existing worktree phases; both focused pause/resume behavior cases passed. These smoke timings are not paired performance evidence.

The final main rebase resolved a conflict in adjacent benchmark summary fields by preserving both sets. Independent review and focused lint/format passed; range-diff confirms the runtime changes remained identical. All paired measurements use this final head. Exact-head CI completed with the inherited failure below.

### Exact-head CI: inherited failure

[Run 40041421575](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40041421575) completed all 88 jobs. The only failing leaf was [checks-node-changed-compact-large-24](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40041421575/job/120713597642): two `progress-card-refresh.integration.test.ts` cases, “steers duplicate active refreshes…” with `unconfirmed=false/true`, expected an accepted retry but received `PROGRESS_CARD_REFRESH_TERMINAL`. The aggregate CI gate failed downstream; other jobs passed.

The same single file reproduced **2 failed / 7 passed on both PR head `127ddf47` and unchanged main baseline `9538d3ab`**, using CI's pinned OpenClaw Bun `1.4.4-canary.1+ef37c31de` in the isolated sandbox. Command: `OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=bun node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/progress-card-refresh.integration.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. No broad suite or CI rerun was used.

Main's #181953 moved steering after ACK. This fixture still completes the target run immediately after ACK, before awaiting its `queueMessage` call, so the hidden refresh can fall back and settle without changing the card. The failing test, fixture, and causal dispatch/receipt owners are byte-identical on baseline, PR head, and CI's tested merge `6dd740a1` (main parent `215cb73b`). All gateway-method source files are also unchanged between the replayed main baseline and that CI parent. This PR's instrumentation adds no receipt mutation or await on that path. That prior-head failure was baseline-attributed; it is not a claim of green CI. Final rebased-head CI is checked separately below.


### Final landing head

Rebased cleanly onto main `40e0e5ab151484228a9f6072ee9a20ede6db3fed`; final head `2a85d12991c761cfefbc3c3b5e9712ff0b3531de`. Range-diff shows only surrounding perf-fixture context changes; the reviewed runtime patch is unchanged. Measurements above remain evidence for the explicitly named pre-rebase source, not a claim of a new run. Exact-head [CI run 40058889539](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40058889539) completed successfully: 62 jobs passed and 26 were skipped. The earlier baseline-attributed progress-refresh failures did not recur. Independent rebase review confirmed the runtime diff is byte-for-byte unchanged and found no actionable P0–P2 issues.

## What Problem This Solves

Prevents auto-reply dedupe from treating whitespace-only media fields as deliverable content. Without this guard, a final assistant payload could retain duplicate text after a message-tool delivery.

## Why This Change Was Made

The runtime behavior is provided by the shared sendable-media resolver (canonical fix in [openclaw/openclaw#128372](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/128372)). This PR adds focused coverage at `buildReplyPayloads` for blank plural media, blank singular media, retained real media with a matching caption, and singular media when plural metadata is blank.

The local proof uses the production message-tool lifecycle and reply router. Completion delivery facts come from `subscribeEmbeddedAgentSession` and `runToolLifecycle`, then final payloads pass through `buildReplyPayloads`, `routeReply`, the durable outbound delivery core, and the Telegram Bot API adapter.

## User Impact

Regression coverage only; no shipped runtime behavior changes.

## Compatibility

Rebased cleanly onto pinned main `27f0857bf3c7362c8fb2d72e2d2e482e6dc3d628`. The three-file delta is a package command, a proof runner, and one focused regression test file. It changes no runtime implementation, persistent data format, database schema, migration, or upgrade path, so no stored-data migration is required.

The proof runner writes its config and media fixture under a temporary state directory and removes that directory in its `finally` cleanup. The tests use the repository's existing test registry and state lifecycle.

Review follow-up: removed the plain-text same-target assertion flagged in review because it repeats the exact case the repository's test cleanup intentionally removed. The four blank-media cases remain; the production-path proof independently checks message-tool delivery followed by a blank final.

## Evidence

- Exact head `2eb9db3847baeddd01f0a5e982074bb4d25ecff1`: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-payloads.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-payloads.blank-media.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --reporter=dot` — 2 files, 36 tests passed. The measured focused shard used 13.73 seconds, leaving 3,586.27 seconds under that fallback. Hosted CI does not expose a separately attributable duration for this individual test file.
- Exact-head changed preflight for `2eb9db3847baeddd01f0a5e982074bb4d25ecff1` ran `pnpm check:changed --base 27f0857bf3c7362c8fb2d72e2d2e482e6dc3d628 --timed` for 336.84s.
