prs.title: fix(plugins): keep plugin instance cleanup budget on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A plugin instance that is being torn down starts its cleanup deadline with `Date.now()`, then feeds the remaining budget into a `setTimeout`-based timeout that counts monotonic time. When the wall clock jumps during a cleanup (NTP adjustment, suspend/resume, VM clock drift), the cleanup budget is distorted: a clock rewind inflates the timeout so a stuck plugin hangs far past its 5s budget, and a clock jump forward shrinks it so a healthy cleanup is killed early.

- Problem: `src/plugins/plugin-instance.ts` seeds `deadline = Date.now() + SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS` and computes `Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now())` for each cleanup callback, mixing wall-clock arithmetic with monotonic `setTimeout` consumption.
- Solution: seed the deadline and read the remaining budget from `performance.now()` so the budget stays on the same monotonic clock as the `setTimeout` that bounds it.
- What changed: two lines in `runDisposalCleanup` in `src/plugins/plugin-instance.ts`, plus the regression test folded into the existing suite (now an outcome-based regression).
- What did NOT change: the deadline is a process-local closure (not serialized, persisted, or reported to any UI), so switching its clock source is safe.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cleanup deadline is bounded by `raceWithTimeout` (from `packages/retry`), which arms a `setTimeout` — a monotonic timer. The fix aligns both ends of the budget on the monotonic clock: `deadline = performance.now() + SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS` and `Math.max(0, deadline - performance.now())`. Because the value feeds a plain `setTimeout` (not `AbortSignal.timeout`), the sub-millisecond float is silently rounded and no `Math.floor` is required.

This is the same `wall-clock-remaining-budget` family as already-merged monotonic-clock fixes; the neighboring reload drain path (`server-plugin-reload-cleanup.ts`) was already migrated to `performance.now()`. The plugin instance cleanup path is the remaining wall-clock holdout in the plugin lifecycle.

## User Impact

Plugin shutdown is more reliable under system clock changes: a plugin whose cleanup actually makes progress is no longer mis-killed by a forward clock jump, and a genuinely stuck plugin is still bounded by its full 5s budget rather than hanging indefinitely on a rewind. No behavior changes when the clock is stable.

## Evidence

Real shipped-entry Gateway run (`startGatewayServer`) plus a real `PluginInstance` whose `onDispose` registers a cleanup that consumes **3.5s of real time then settles** (physical settlement). The plugin is loaded into the **Gateway's own active plugin registry** (the `registryOwner` singleton `server.close()` retires), and retirement is driven by the **shipped shutdown path**: `server.close()` → `closePluginRegistry` → `pluginRegistryOwner.close()` → `clearActivePluginRegistry()` → `disposePluginRegistryInstances()` → `createPluginHostRegistryRetirement` → `instance.dispose()` → `runDisposalCleanup` → `raceWithTimeout`. A wall-clock step is injected into `Date.now` between the deadline seed and the remaining-budget read (pre-fix only — fixed code reads `performance.now()` and never arms the injection). Observed outcome: the **raceWithTimeout budget** and the **shutdown log's "did not settle" failures** (the failures the shipped shutdown path reports).

Post-fix — all clock states keep a stable monotonic budget, 0 shutdown failures:
```
step=0      budgets: 5000, 4999ms   shutdown failures=0  settled ✓
step=+3000  budgets: 5000, 4999ms   shutdown failures=0  settled ✓
step=-3000  budgets: 5000, 4999ms   shutdown failures=0  settled ✓
```

Pre-fix (source reverted to `Date.now()`) — a forward jump collapses the budget and the shipped shutdown path reports mis-kill failures:
```
step=+3000  budgets: 5000, 1999ms   shutdown failures=2  settled ✓  → MIS-KILLED
step=0      budgets: 5000, 4999ms   shutdown failures=0  settled ✓
step=-3000  budgets: 5000, 7999ms   shutdown failures=0  settled ✓  (budget inflated)
```

`settled ✓` in every run — physical settlement is always preserved. The bug: a forward wall-clock jump shrinks the pre-fix budget to ~1999ms, so the healthy 3.5s cleanup is **reported by the shipped shutdown path as a "did not settle" failure** (2 failures in the shutdown log) even though it settles; post-fix the budget stays on the monotonic clock (~5000ms) and the same cleanup settles with **0 shutdown failures** in every clock state.

**Before / After**

| Clock state | Before (`Date.now()`) | After (`performance.now()`) |
|---|---|---|
| normal clock | 4999ms budget, 0 failures | 4999ms budget, 0 failures |
| clock rewind −3000ms | 7999ms budget (inflated) | 4999ms budget, 0 failures |
| clock jump +3000ms | **1999ms budget → healthy cleanup mis-killed (2 failures)** | 4999ms budget, 0 failures |

Regression test — `src/plugins/plugin-instance.test.ts` `it.each([0,-3_000,3_000])` was replaced (from a `raceWithTimeout`-argument spy) with an **outcome regression**: monotonic time advances with the fake timers, `Date.now` is stepped after the deadline is seeded, a 3.5s-settling cleanup is registered, and the observable result (0 errors + cleanup settled) is asserted. Pre-fix it is RED — the +3000ms case fails with `expected [1 error] to have length 0 but got 1` (healthy cleanup mis-killed); post-fix the full suite is GREEN (37/37).

What was not tested: an actual NTP/suspend clock change on a live gateway (the proof injects the jump into `Date.now` and observes the monotonic `setTimeout`); other plugin-lifecycle wall-clock deadlines (service start/drain/stop in `src/plugins/services.ts`) are tracked separately and not part of this change.

Open PR collision check: searched open PR titles/topics for the plugin-cleanup monotonic pattern and scanned changed-file lists of open PRs; no open PR touches `src/plugins/plugin-instance.ts`, and `origin/main` still contains the `Date.now()` deadline this fix replaces.

prs.title: fix(gateway): keep an astral MCP event description whole at the catalog cap
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`mcp.events.list` projects every catalog event with `event.description.slice(0, 4096)` (`src/gateway/server-methods/mcp-events.ts:43`). When an astral character starts at UTF-16 unit 4095, the slice keeps its high surrogate and drops the low one, so the RPC response carries a lone surrogate (`\uD83D`) instead of `😀`. The Control UI renders a trailing `�`, and non-JS consumers receive invalid Unicode.

Reproduced through a running Gateway's shipped `mcp.events.list` RPC against a loopback Streamable-HTTP MCP stub: on current main the projected description ends in a dangling high surrogate, on this head it ends at 4095 units with the pair intact.

Precedent: #176233, #176230 (same `truncateUtf16Safe` swap, merged 2026-10-22/23).

## Why This Change Was Made

The projection owner reuses the existing surrogate-safe truncation helper (`truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`) at the same 4096 cap. No new validator, option, config, dependency, or persistence surface.

Production LOC is `+2/-1` (net +1).
Classification: `behavior-preserving` — text at or under the cap is returned byte-identical; only a cut that would split a surrogate pair stops one unit earlier. Name, delivery, schema, page-size and cursor bounds are untouched.

## User Impact

Operators whose MCP Events server publishes descriptions containing emoji or other astral characters near the cap see the whole description instead of a trailing replacement character. Shorter descriptions and all non-description fields are unchanged.

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `5b6f05b2ee17262bbb0252c049c1020eff1a9228`

prs.title: fix(net-policy): match credential query-param spelling variants and remove ambiguous regex quantifiers
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two robustness problems in first-party code, both found by running dynamic tools over the repo rather than by reading it.

**Credential query-param spelling variants were not recognized.** `isSensitiveUrlQueryParamName` compared a lowercased name with `-` mapped to `_`, so `access-token` and `access_token` were recognized but `accessToken` was not — and camelCase is the spelling most JSON and JS APIs emit. Measured on current `origin/main` through the two production consumers, **15 of 16** credential spellings kept their value: `accessToken`, `refreshToken`, `idToken`, `authToken`, `clientSecret`, `appSecret`, `privateKey`, `hookToken`, `sessionToken`, `secretKey`, `webhookSecret`, `urlSignature`, `bearerToken`, `accesstoken`, `clientsecret`. Only `apiKey` was already covered, via the existing `apikey` entry. Those values reach gateway log lines (`redactSensitiveText`), MCP server descriptions (`src/agents/mcp-transport-config.ts`) and plugin manifest diagnostics (`src/infra/clawhub-plugin-manifest.ts`).

**Three regexes admitted exponentially many equivalent splits.** Each repeated a group whose own trailing optional whitespace overlapped the next repetition's leading whitespace, or alternated between overlapping Unicode properties. Either shape lets one subject be split many equivalent ways, so a non-matching subject degrades superlinearly instead of failing fast:

| Site | Note |
|---|---|
| `extensions/zalouser/src/text-styles-{source,ranges}.ts` | Blockquote-only line check, reached from outgoing message text. The **same literal appeared at three call sites**; now one shared constant. |
| `src/cli/command-format.ts` | Root-update detection joined a flag to its value with `[=\s]+`, letting the value matcher swallow the separator and consume the next ` --flag` chunk. |
| `extensions/telegram/src/text-width.ts` | Four overlapping Unicode properties in an alternation, folded into one character class. |

The Telegram one is **consistency, not a behavior fix**: grapheme segmentation already bounded it, because a cluster reaching that check either matches whole (no backtracking) or fails on its first character. Attacking the real entry point `renderTelegramMonospaceGrid` with thousands of joiners and variation selectors stayed in the low milliseconds, so I could not make it misbehave.

## What Changed

Spelling variants now collapse onto one canonical `_`-separated form at the single predicate every redaction path already funnels through: camelCase and PascalCase word starts, `.` alongside `-`, array and index subscripts, and the run-together spelling of each listed name, plus a small set of segment markers for `webhookSecret` / `url_signature`.

Scoped deliberately to avoid over-redacting debugging context:

- `token` and `key` are **not** segment markers, so `token_count`, `tokenCount`, `maxTokens` and `cacheKey` stay readable.
- `session_id` stays visible, matching the existing form-body expectation in `src/logging/redact.test.ts`.
- 52 non-credential names are pinned as must-not-redact.

Every normalization step is linear in the name's length (see the review follow-up below). For the three regexes, each repetition boundary is now forced: the run between `>` markers is spelled once, and the CLI matcher keeps the `=` and whitespace spellings separate so neither branch can cross whitespace.

## Review follow-up: normalization kept linear

The first revision of this PR traded one superlinear scan for two, which ClawSweeper caught. I confirmed it by measurement before changing anything — on `"[".repeat(n)` the bracket expression rescanned the remaining suffix at every `[` it could not close, and on `"A".repeat(n)` the acronym expression consumed the uppercase run and backtracked through it before failing its lowercase requirement:

| n | bracket scan | acronym scan | ms/n² (bracket) | ms/n² (acronym) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1.5 ms | 3.8 ms | 1.49 | 3.83 |
| 4,000 | 21.8 ms | 44.0 ms | 1.36 | 2.75 |
| 16,000 | 351.7 ms | 706.9 ms | 1.37 | 2.76 |

The flat ms/n² column is the quadratic signature, and query names are unbounded here because logging and URL diagnostics call this synchronously.

Subscript stripping is now a forward scan whose cursor only advances; it removes each `[` through the first following `]`, which is exactly what the expression accepted. The acronym boundary keeps its regex but takes the leading uppercase as a fixed-width lookbehind, leaving no run to backtrack through. After the fix, 1,000,000 characters cost about 1 ms where 16,000 previously cost 350 ms.

A first attempt at the bracket side — excluding `[` from the inner class — was **rejected by its own equivalence check**: it changed how spans nest and differed on 75,302 strings. The forward scan replaced it.

## Evidence

### Real behavior through the changed production consumers

Captured after the fix. Synthetic values only; no real endpoint, key, or personal data.

`redactSensitiveUrl` — the MCP server description and plugin manifest diagnostic path:

```text
in : https://mcp.example.test/sse?accessToken=s3cr3t-value-0123456789&model=sonnet&page=2
out: https://mcp.example.test/sse?accessToken=***&model=sonnet&page=2
in : https://mcp.example.test/sse?clientSecret=s3cr3t-value-0123456789&model=sonnet&page=2
out: https://mcp.example.test/sse?clientSecret=***&model=sonnet&page=2
in : https://mcp.example.test/sse?privateKey=s3cr3t-value-0123456789&model=sonnet&page=2
out: https://mcp.example.test/sse?privateKey=***&model=sonnet&page=2
in : https://mcp.example.test/sse?apiKey[]=s3cr3t-value-0123456789&model=sonnet&page=2
out: https://mcp.example.test/sse?apiKey%5B%5D=***&model=sonnet&page=2
in : https://mcp.example.test/sse?webhookSecret=s3cr3t-value-0123456789&model=sonnet&page=2
out: https://mcp.example.test/sse?webhookSecret=***&model=sonnet&page=2
```

`redactSensitiveText` — gateway log lines (this mode masks with a length hint rather than `***`):

```text
in : mcp: connecting upstream url=https://mcp.example.test/sse?accessToken=s3cr3t-value-0123456789 attempt=1
out: mcp: connecting upstream url=https://mcp.example.test/sse?accessToken=s3cr3t…6789 attempt=1
in : mcp: connecting upstream url=https://mcp.example.test/sse?clientSecret=s3cr3t-value-0123456789 attempt=1
out: mcp: connecting upstream url=https://mcp.example.test/sse?clientSecret=s3cr3t…6789 attempt=1
in : mcp: connecting upstream url=https://mcp.example.test/sse?privateKey=s3cr3t-value-0123456789 attempt=1
out: mcp: connecting upstream url=https://mcp.example.test/sse?privateKey=s3cr3t…6789 attempt=1
```

Ordinary context stays readable through both consumers, so the change does not blind the logs:

```text
in : https://api.example.test/v1/chat?token_count=1&maxTokens=2&cacheKey=3&sessionId=4&clientId=5&page=6
url: https://api.example.test/v1/chat?token_count=1&maxTokens=2&cacheKey=3&sessionId=4&clientId=5&page=6
log: request https://api.example.test/v1/chat?token_count=1&maxTokens=2&cacheKey=3&sessionId=4&clientId=5&page=6
```

Normalization cost on the unbounded names from the review finding, measured through `redactSensitiveUrl`: 40,000 unclosed subscripts → **9.7 ms**; a 40,000-character uppercase run → **2.6 ms**.

### Before/after through both consumers

Same 16 names, run against the `origin/main` version of the file and then against this branch:

| | `redactSensitiveText` (logging) | `redactSensitiveUrl` |
|---|---|---|
| `origin/main` | 15 of 16 leak | 15 of 16 leak |
| this branch | 0 leak | 0 leak |

### Equivalence checking

These are parsing predicates where a silent behavior change would be worse than the original problem, so every regex change was proven equivalent before landing:

- Subscript scan — exhaustive over `{[, ], a, A, 0, _}` to length 8 (2,015,538 strings) plus 500,000 random bracket-heavy names: **0 differences**.
- Acronym boundary — exhaustive over `{A, B, a, b, 0, _}` to length 7 (335,922 strings): **0 differences**.
- Blockquote matcher — exhaustive over `{>, space, tab, x}` to length 10 (1,398,100 strings) plus 500,000 random multi-space strings: **0 differences**. My first attempt here was also not equivalent (it broke tab separators) and this check caught it.
- Grapheme class — every Unicode code point (1.1M) plus 200,000 random strings: **0 differences**.
- CLI matcher — 585 realistic command tails. The only difference is `--profile= foo` (equals, then a space, then a value) no longer counting as a flag value. That spelling *is* the ambiguity, and it is not a shell invocation anyone writes; `--profile foo` and `--profile=foo` are unaffected.

### Regression tests

Each verified to fail on the pre-fix code for the intended reason and pass after:

- `packages/net-policy/src/redact-sensitive-url.test.ts` — 24 credential spelling variants (22 failed pre-fix); 14 non-credential names as negative controls (all already passed, so they guard against over-redaction); and two linear-time cases through the redaction owner, measured at **2.2 s and 4.4 s before, 6 ms after**.
- `src/cli/profile.test.ts` — wall-clock bound on repeated global flags (failed pre-fix on the timing assertion).
- `extensions/zalouser/src/text-styles-blocks.test.ts` — wall-clock bound at the `parseZalouserTextStyles` boundary.

Both timing tests keep their input modest so a reintroduced ambiguity still finishes and reports rather than hanging CI. One table row was dropped during review because it passed pre-fix and so proved nothing. No test was added for the Telegram change: it is equivalent over all code points, so a regression test could not fail on the pre-fix code, and the authoring gate in `.claude/skills/test-audit` rejects tests that never demonstrably failed.

### Checks and suites

`tsgo:core`, `tsgo:core:test`, `tsgo:extensions`, `tsgo:extensions:test`, `oxlint` (core + extensions), `oxfmt`, `git diff --check` — all clean.

Tests: `packages/net-policy` (89), `packages/gateway-client` (140), `src/logging`, `src/config` (502), `src/infra/net`, `extensions/zalouser` (236), `extensions/telegram`, `src/cli/profile.test.ts`, plus the redaction consumers in `src/config/schema.hints`, `src/config/redact-snapshot` and `src/agents/mcp-transport-config` — **0 failures**.

### One fixture entry changed

`src/logging/redact-byte-identity-fixture.json` pins byte-identical output over 250 recorded samples. Exactly **one** sample changes: its parameter name ends in `_secret`, which the canonical form now recognizes, so the value is masked rather than passed through. The other 249 are untouched, and the file keeps its compact formatting (parse→stringify is byte-identical on it, so the diff is one line).

## Known Limitation

Subscript forms are normalized for URL redaction, but **not** in free log text: `src/logging/redact.ts` builds its own `FORM_BODY_KEY` grammar that excludes `[` and `]`, so `apiKey[]=…` in a log line is not recognized as an assignment at all. This is pre-existing and unrelated to this change — `token[]` and `api_key[]` are equally unmasked there on current `origin/main`, which I verified directly. Widening that grammar would change a module with its own byte-identity contract across many samples, so I left it as a follow-up rather than growing this PR's scope.

## Scope Note

Per `SECURITY.md`, ReDoS that needs trusted operator configuration input is not a vulnerability under this project's trust model — which covers the CLI matcher, since it only runs when a container hint is configured — and the zalouser plugin is excluded from the shipped bundle. These are filed as hardening, not as a vulnerability report.

Separately, `pnpm audit` on current `main` is clean apart from two dev-only transitive advisories (`http-cache-semantics` via `sigstore`, and `braces` via `stylelint`/`lit-analyzer`, the latter with no published fix). Neither is runtime-reachable, so neither is touched here.

A live SSRF sweep was also run against `fetchWithSsrFGuard` using a real loopback server and the real `fetch`, covering 35 obfuscated host encodings (decimal, octal, hex, IPv4-mapped and 6to4/NAT64 IPv6, trailing dots, ideographic and fullwidth full stops, and `localhost` variants). **All 35 were blocked**, so nothing changed there. That result covers unchanged code and is reported only to say why no SSRF change was needed.

prs.body:
## Summary
- document the visibility-scope difference between `openclaw agents list` (config-scoped) and Gateway `agents.list` (runtime-scoped)
- describe both supported explicit roster shapes: canonical `agents.entries` and compatibility `agents.list`
- add focused regression coverage for implicit discovery and both explicit roster shapes
- keep runtime behavior unchanged (no visibility-surface expansion)

## Root cause
Chat/UI surfaces (iOS/Android/TUI) call Gateway `agents.list` through `listAgentsForGateway`, while `openclaw agents list` uses `buildAgentSummaries` from configuration.

When no explicit roster is configured, Gateway may include disk-discovered agent state directories. When an explicit roster exists through either `agents.entries` or `agents.list`, Gateway intentionally restricts visibility to that configured scope. The CLI remains configuration-scoped.

## Changes
- Updated `docs/cli/agents.md` to use the shared “explicit roster” concept.
- Documented `agents.entries` as the canonical shape and `agents.list` as a supported compatibility shape.
- Added regression coverage proving both explicit shapes exclude disk-only agents from Gateway and CLI output.
- Retained the existing test proving Gateway/CLI divergence when no explicit roster exists.

## Verification
Automated checks are running for current head `527b3dc072a621d18935cb887293f77d8e53980f`.

Targeted commands:
```bash
pnpm test src/gateway/session-utils.test.ts -t "gateway agents.list and CLI agents list intentionally diverge"
pnpm test src/gateway/agent-list-explicit-roster.test.ts
pnpm build
```

## Real behavior proof
A redacted current-head CLI/Gateway RPC transcript is still required before final merge approval. This PR description will be updated with that evidence after running the current head in a real local setup.

## Notes
- no plugin diagnostic changes
- no security/routing-filter bypass
- no changes to agent eligibility or authentication policy

prs.title: fix(telegram): route model-confirmation edit through rich funnel
prs.body:
Closes #123886

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with `richMessages: true` on their Telegram account and who complete the `/models` picker would see the final "✅ Model changed to…" confirmation rendered on top of / mixed with the stale rich-text markup from the picker's prior provider/model-list step, instead of a clean confirmation message. The picker's intermediate steps (provider list, model list, pagination) already fully replace the rich body correctly; only the terminal confirmation edit was affected.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `/models` picker sends its initial body as a rich message when `richMessages` is enabled, and every lifecycle edit to that message (provider list, model list, pagination) already routes through the rich funnel in `createTelegramCallbackMessageActions`. The final selection confirmation was the one exception: it always fell back to the legacy HTML `editMessageText` path. Editing a rich-sent message through that legacy text path does not fully replace the prior rich body — Telegram renders the new plain/HTML text mixed with the stale rich markup underneath it.

The fix converts the model-confirmation call site to author rich content via hand-built `RichText`/`InputRichBlock[]` when `richMessages` is enabled, following the existing `progress-draft-preview.ts` precedent for opting a `parse_mode: "HTML"` edit back onto the rich funnel:

- `TelegramCallbackRichTextOverride` lets `editCallbackMessage`/`editCallbackMessageWithButtons` accept an optional `richTextOverride`; when supplied, the edit routes through `getTelegramRichRawApi(bot.api).editMessageText(...)` with hand-built `rich_message` blocks instead of the legacy text funnel.
- `buildModelSelectionConfirmation` (new file) builds both the HTML and rich-block confirmation bodies from one shared text-building function, so the two representations can't drift apart — only model-id HTML-escaping and the runtime placeholder spelling differ per funnel.
- Non-rich accounts (`richMessages` disabled or unset) are unaffected; the legacy HTML path is unchanged for that funnel.

As a side effect of this fix, `bot-handlers.callback-router.ts` grew past the repo's 700-line oxlint `max-lines` cap, so the pre-existing ~290-line `handleTelegramModelCallback` function was extracted verbatim into a new file, `bot-handlers.model-callback.ts`, with no logic changes — pure file-split, kept in this PR so CI stays green (`AGENTS.md`: "Split files around ~700 LOC... never add a `max-lines` suppression").

This PR supersedes closed PR #124173, which introduced rich-block sending but left the confirmation edit on the legacy HTML path — ClawSweeper's own review of that PR classified it as `partial_overlap`, i.e. it fixed the picker's rich-block plumbing but not the actual reported bug (the confirmation still overlapped stale rich text). This change closes that exact gap.

## User Impact

Telegram operators with `richMessages: true` now see a single clean confirmation message when they finish the `/models` picker — no more stale/mixed rich-text markup left behind. Operators without `richMessages` enabled see no behavior change.

## Evidence

- Targeted tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/bot-handlers.callback-actions.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot-handlers.model-callback.ts extensions/telegram/src/model-confirmation-message.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot.test.ts` (and related callback-router/harness specs) — 151/151 passing, including a new regression test asserting `richTextOverride` routes through the rich funnel and 3 new `buildModelSelectionConfirmation` tests asserting HTML vs rich-block parity/escaping.
- Full extension suite: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram` — 3593/3594 passing; the 1 failure (`setup-surface.test.ts > accepts numeric sender ids only`) is a pre-existing, unrelated sandbox-locale artifact (`zh`-locale string vs expected English string), reproducible on `main` before this change.
- Typecheck: `pnpm tsgo:extensions` clean.
- Lint: `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on all touched/added files — exit 0, confirms the `max-lines` violation from the file-split is resolved (`bot-handlers.callback-router.ts` now 395 lines, down from 706).
- Format: `pnpm format` — no diff.
- Pre-land `$autoreview` (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, high reasoning): `autoreview clean: no accepted/actionable findings reported`, `overall: patch is correct (0.96)`.
- Live Telegram bot-to-bot proof was not feasible in this environment (no bot token configured); the mock-harness/unit proof above exercises the exact changed rich-funnel edit path per the ClawSweeper Review Policy real-behavior-proof gate for channel-visible changes.

## Update (commit 6973bab29b9)

Two fixes on top of the original commit:

- **ClawSweeper P1 finding addressed** — `editCallbackMessage`'s rich-routing branch previously fell back to `buildTelegramRichMarkdown(text)` for *any* rich-account callback edit that wasn't `parse_mode: "HTML"`, not just the model-picker confirmation. That silently ran markdown parsing over arbitrary un-authored text from approval receipts (`terminalizeApprovalMessage`), the plugin SDK's `respond.editMessage`, and the model picker's own intermediate pagination/provider-list/model-list/error edits — none of which are markdown-authored, so incidental `*`/`_`/backtick/`[` characters (e.g. in provider/model ids or user-controlled error text) could be reinterpreted as formatting instead of sent literally. Fixed by making rich routing strictly opt-in per call: it now only fires when the caller explicitly supplies `richTextOverride`'s hand-built blocks (as the model-picker confirmation does); every other caller — regardless of `richMessages`/`parse_mode` — stays on the legacy literal-text funnel, exactly as before this PR. `buildTelegramRichMarkdown` is no longer imported by this file (still used correctly elsewhere: streaming draft previews and the general outbound-delivery pipeline, where callers genuinely author markdown).
- **CI fixes**: `check-test-types` (two `bot-handlers.callback-actions.test.ts` blocks needed explicit `vi.fn<T>()` typing plus a null-check helper for `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`-safe `.mock.calls.at(0)` access) and `check-dependencies`/knip (`ModelSelectionConfirmationParams`/`ModelSelectionConfirmation` had no external importer and shouldn't have been exported).

**Correction to my earlier claiming comment on #123886**: I stated "clean typecheck" there; at that point `check-test-types` and `check-dependencies` were actually failing on CI (fixed now, in this commit). Apologies for the inaccurate evidence claim — flagging it here so the record is accurate.

### Updated evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/bot-handlers.callback-actions.test.ts` — 7/7 passing, including a rewritten test asserting plain-text edits with no `richTextOverride` stay on the legacy funnel even when `richMessages` is enabled (inverts the prior test, which asserted the now-fixed over-broad behavior), and updated fallback/error-path tests that now supply an explicit override to exercise the rich funnel.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram` (full extension suite) — 3593/3594 passing; same single pre-existing unrelated `setup-surface.test.ts` locale failure noted above, reproduced identically on this branch's pre-fix HEAD via `git stash`.
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions` and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` — both clean.
- `knip` production + all-exports check — clean, no new dead exports.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt` — no diff. `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on touched files — exit 0.
- Pre-land `$autoreview` (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, high reasoning) rerun on this commit: `autoreview clean: no accepted/actionable findings reported`, `overall: patch is correct (0.98)`.
- Live Telegram bot-to-bot proof remains not feasible in this environment (no bot token configured), unchanged from the original PR evidence.

## Update (commit a0dec118a21): delete-and-reply instead of legacy-edit on rich-edit failure

ClawSweeper's follow-up P2 finding on the prior commit: `editCallbackMessage`'s
catch block fell back to `legacyEditCallbackMessage(text, editParams)` whenever
the rich raw-API edit failed for a non-terminal reason. `richTextOverride` is
only ever supplied for a message that was itself sent as rich (the model
picker's final confirmation edit), so a legacy-text retry there reproduces the
exact stale-rich-markup symptom #123886 reported — the new text lands mixed
with the prior rich body instead of replacing it.

Fixed by extracting a shared `deleteAndReplyCallbackMessage` helper (delete
the rich-sent message, then send a plain reply) and using it both for this
new failure path and for `editCallbackMessageWithButtons`'s existing "no text
in the message" recovery, which had the same delete-then-reply logic inlined

On a Business callback whose rich edit fails, the replacement could be sent while deletion silently failed and was swallowed, leaving the stale interactive picker behind.

- Re-read `deleteCallbackMessage`: it called `bot.api.deleteMessage(chat_id, message_id)` unconditionally, while its siblings `legacyEditCallbackMessage` and `replyToCallbackChat` both forward `business_connection_id`.
- Checked grammY's typed API surface (`node_modules/grammy/out/core/api.d.ts`): `deleteMessage(chat_id, message_id, signal?)` has **no** `business_connection_id` parameter at all — unlike `editMessageText`/`sendMessage`/`editMessageReplyMarkup`, which all accept one.
- Cross-checked against the Telegram Bot API's own method list (`@grammyjs/types/methods.d.ts`): `deleteMessage` genuinely has no such field. Telegram instead exposes a dedicated method for this exact case, `deleteBusinessMessages(business_connection_id, message_ids)`, which grammY surfaces as `bot.api.deleteBusinessMessages(...)`. Deleting a business-sent message is a different Bot API call, not `deleteMessage` plus an extra field.

Fix: `deleteCallbackMessage` now calls `bot.api.deleteBusinessMessages(business_connection_id, [message_id])` when the callback carries business context, and falls back to the existing `bot.api.deleteMessage(chat_id, message_id)` otherwise.

Confirmed it fails against the pre-fix code (via `git stash` of the production change alone — `deleteBusinessMessages` is never called pre-fix) for the intended reason, then passes after the fix.

prs.title: fix(memory): prevent duplicate Gemini batch jobs after timeouts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Gemini native embedding-batch creation is non-idempotent. If a create response is lost or times out after the provider accepted it, an immediate retry can create a second paid remote job. The provider assigns the batch name only in the response and does not expose a caller-supplied idempotency key.

- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api#best-practices
- https://ai.google.dev/api/batch-api#method:-models.asyncbatchembedcontent

## What Changed

This version treats batch submission as a crash-recoverable ownership protocol:

- Memory Core persists an exclusive reservation in the published memory database before Gemini's non-idempotent create call.
- Acknowledged provider batch names are attached to that reservation as soon as they are returned.
- Each request set has a deterministic SHA-256 fingerprint; manifests retain content-independent custom IDs and chunk hashes, not source text, credentials, or vectors.
- Restarted managers adopt an acknowledged job only when its exact request fingerprint matches.
- Completed output is reconciled by stable chunk hash and published idempotently to the shared embedding cache, including when source enumeration has drifted since submission.
- Ambiguous create outcomes remain quarantined. Definitive non-ambiguous 4xx rejections (except 408) release the reservation.
- The reservation is cleared only after local cache/index publication commits.
- Closing a manager aborts local polling without cancelling or duplicating an accepted remote job.
- Gemini's native-batch failure mode remains fail-closed instead of fanning a large migration into synchronous paid requests.
- Status output exposes the submission, provider job, timestamps, and recovery state.
- Deliberate quarantine clearing requires both `--force` and `--clear-batch-quarantine`.

The ownership record lives in the published database while a shadow rebuild remains isolated. Independent managers serialize reservation changes through SQLite immediate transactions.

## User Impact

Interrupted Gemini memory migrations can resume acknowledged work without resubmitting already accepted requests. Operators get an explicit quarantine for genuinely ambiguous remote ownership instead of hidden duplicate spend or an uncontrolled synchronous fallback.

## Evidence

Exact candidate head: `ca2a3d6a9bcb7215a9dfba22f8407b06ab116206`

Candidate base at construction: `044cf2e6e027591e6361dbd2784a8b9c68959e18` (`upstream/main` at the time)

- Focused Google provider/lifecycle tests: **67/67 passed**.
- Memory integration tests: **235/235 passed**.
- Plugin contract suite: **1,117/1,117 passed**.
- Total: **1,419 tests passed**.
- Core and extension production/test TypeScript checks passed.
- Changed-file structural, dependency, formatting, documentation, SDK, and extension-boundary gates passed.
- Documentation validation passed: 1,294 MDX files, 13,239 internal links with 0 broken, and 1,224 config examples.
- Full production build passed, including 91 external plugins, 152 public SDK subpaths, CLI bootstrap, and Control UI performance gates.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- A secrets/logging audit found no credentials, request text, vectors, or authorization values added to logs.

The implementation has also been exercised against a real authenticated Gemini migration outside CI: completed jobs were reconciled, cache entries advanced, and a subsequent quota rejection occurred before a new provider job ID was assigned. Completed fingerprints were not replayed. No provider identifiers or credentials are included here.

## Scope

This PR intentionally adds no quota-size, parallelism, or retry-policy configuration. It does not alter production deployment files. Provider transport remains in the Google extension; Memory Core owns durable publication and recovery state.

## Required Before Ready/Merge

- Upstream CI must pass on this exact head.
- An independent exact-head review must complete; the author-side GCP environment does not currently have an independent Codex reviewer identity, so this is not being bypassed.
- Maintainers must approve the fail-closed ambiguity/quarantine contract and its operator-recovery tradeoff.

This PR is kept as a draft until those gates are satisfied.

prs.title: fix(net-policy): redact credentials in a nested URL embedded in text
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A credential inside a **nested** URL survives redaction as soon as any text precedes the outer URL:

```
redactSensitiveUrlLikeString(
  "fetching https://auth.test/a?redirect_uri=https://app.test/cb?access_token=<secret> now")
-> "fetching https://auth.test/a?redirect_uri=https://app.test/cb?access_token=<secret> now"

redactSensitiveUrlLikeString(
  "https://auth.test/a?redirect_uri=https://app.test/cb?access_token=<secret>")
-> "https://auth.test/a?redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.test%2Fcb%3Faccess_token%3D***"
```

One leading word is the whole difference. The nested-URL rules only run on the parsed-URL path (`parsedWholeUrl`); anything else falls to `redactUrlLikeFallback`, whose scan is

```js
.replace(/([?&])([^=&]+)=([^&]*)/g, ...)
```

The value class allows `?`, so `redirect_uri=https://app.test/cb?access_token=<secret>` is one value, the name `redirect_uri` is not a credential name, and the inner `access_token` is never classified. The `g` scan has already consumed past it.

This is reachable with whole lines, not just bare URLs. The call sites that pass a *message*
rather than a URL are the ones that land in the fallback — see **What this does not cover** below
for which of them I measured, and which turned out to be already safe on `main`.

An OAuth-style `redirect_uri=` or a callback URL carrying a token is the common shape.

## How It Was Found

A sentinel-secret fuzz over the production redaction entry points: credential-named assignments in 33 base names × 16 spelling mutations × 15 contexts, asserting the sentinel never survives, and only requiring redaction where the shared classifier itself calls the name a credential. 83,820 checks; the surviving shape was the nested URL. The scan also flagged the same input surviving `redactSensitiveText` — that is a separate gap in the logging path and is **not** addressed here.

## Fix

Nesting is handled in the replacer, not in the grammar. The key and value classes are
**byte-identical to `main`** (`[^=&]+` / `[^&]*`); a value is scanned for a nested assignment only
when its own name is not a credential:

```ts
function redactQueryAssignments(value: string, depth: number): string {
  return value.replace(
    /([?&])([^=&]+)=([^&]*)/g,
    (match, prefix: string, key: string, entryValue: string) => {
      if (isSensitiveUrlQueryParamName(key)) {
        return `${prefix}${key}=***`;
      }
      if (depth >= MAX_NESTED_URL_REDACTION_DEPTH || !entryValue.includes("?")) {
        return match;
      }
      return `${prefix}${key}=${redactQueryAssignments(entryValue, depth + 1)}`;
    },
  );
}
```

A sensitive value is still masked to the end of its `[^&]*` run, exactly as before, so the mask
boundary of an actual credential is never recomputed. Only `?` can open a nested assignment,
because `&` cannot appear inside a value. Recursion reuses the existing
`MAX_NESTED_URL_REDACTION_DEPTH` bound, and the regex literal lives inside the function so a
recursive call cannot share `lastIndex`. Because the sensitive branch is untouched, the change can
only *add* masking.

An earlier revision of this PR instead narrowed the fallback's classes to stop at `?` and at
whitespace. That was wrong twice over and was correctly caught in review: it truncated the mask of a
sensitive value that legitimately contains a raw `?` (`password=***?bravo`), and adding `\s` to the
*key* class stopped whitespace-spliced names (`access_ token=`) matching at all. Both class edits
are gone.

One consequence worth stating: trailing prose after a *masked* credential is consumed, because the
mask runs to the end of the `[^&]*` run. `main` already drops trailing prose that way for a
top-level sensitive parameter, so this matches existing behaviour rather than inventing
safer-looking output.

## Evidence

Additivity, sentinel differential against the merge base — leading prose × trailing prose × nesting
depth (0/1/2) × sensitive name × separator (`?`/`&`) × name-splice (none, space, NBSP, `+`):

```
DIFFERENTIAL 42336 inputs | 0 regressions | 4704 newly masked (11.1%)
```

0 regressions = no input where `main` hid the sentinel and this head leaks it.

Where the change bites — 5 leading prose forms × 5 trailing forms × 3 outer parameter names × 3
credential names × both separators:

```
main         total=450  leaks=270
this head    total=450  leaks=0
```

```
in : fetching https://h.test/p?redirect_uri=https://app.test/cb?access_token=<sentinel>
main: unchanged — credential in full
head: fetching https://h.test/p?redirect_uri=https://app.test/cb?access_token=***
```

A nested value with no credential is still returned byte-for-byte:

```
in : fetching https://auth.test/a?redirect_uri=https://app.test/cb?page=2 now
out: unchanged
```

### What this does *not* cover, measured

`redactSensitiveUrlLikeStringAtDepth` tries `new URL()` on the whole string first and only reaches
the changed fallback when that throws. So:

- a **bare URL** never reaches it — `redactQueryString` → `redactNestedUrlValue` already recursed on
  `main`;
- the **percent-encoded** nested form inside prose is already masked on `main` by
  `redactEncodedUrlLikeString`, which decodes and recurses.

I ran the shipped `src/snapshot/git-backup.ts:71` diagnostic end-to-end (`openclaw backup git
create --push` to an unreachable remote) and `main` produces a **byte-identical** masked line,
because git normalises the remote URL into the encoded form before it reaches the redactor. That
path is already safe; this PR does not change it.

The shape this PR does fix — prose carrying a *raw* nested query — is reached from the call sites
that pass a message rather than a URL, two of which document the risk themselves:
`src/agents/mcp-error.ts:29` (a remote MCP server's error text), `src/gateway/call.ts:230`
(*"the remote-controlled close reason, which can echo a credential-bearing URL"*),
`src/security/audit-gateway-probe.ts:54,58`, `src/commands/status-all.ts:447`, and the
`formatErrorMessage(...)` sites in `src/cli/daemon-cli/probe.ts`, `src/cli/local-state-owner.ts` and
`src/cli/logs-cli.ts:611`. I have not driven one of those to terminal output, because each needs a
cooperating remote; happy to build a synthetic MCP stub if that is the bar.

## Checks (Node 24.16.0)

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/net-policy/src
-> Test Files 4 passed (4), Tests 96 passed (96)

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/snapshot/git-backup.test.ts
-> 22 passed, 1 skipped          (the shipped consumer the review named)

oxlint, oxfmt --check on both changed files -> clean
run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json          -> exit 0
```

Four new regressions: a nested credential behind leading prose (plain and percent-encoded, two
prose shapes), a sensitive value that itself contains a `?` or a space, and a whitespace-spliced
credential name. The last two are the review's P1s.

The test file conflicted on the rebase because `main` converted it to flat `it.each` tables; I took
`main`'s version and re-added these cases in that style rather than restoring the old `describe`
blocks.

This touches a security-sensitive file, so it will need a maintainer `/allow-security-sensitive-change`.

prs.title: feat(plugins): let plugins react when a verified person first signs in
prs.body:
Related: guest onboarding (first-sign-in trigger, item 3 of the guest-onboarding project)

## What Problem This Solves

Plugins have no trustworthy signal that a person has just signed in to the Gateway for the first time, so a guest who signs in with a visitor invitation lands in Home with nothing set up for them.

## User Impact

User impact: no visible change on its own. Plugins can now register `api.on("user_first_sign_in", handler)` and receive one event per person after their first verified, admitted sign-in, with the profile id, display name, verified emails and GitHub account ids, and whether the profile is new. The follow-up visitor-access change uses it to create a guest's welcome session.

Delivery never blocks or fails sign-in, and it is at least once per handler plugin, so **handlers must be idempotent**. Profiles that existed before this change get one event on their next sign-in, with `isNewProfile: false`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway sign-in paths (HTTP request auth and the Control UI WebSocket connect, including deferred GitHub identity attachment) report an admitted sign-in to one owner, `src/gateway/user-first-sign-in.ts`, after the profile is durable and access policies have passed. Only trusted-proxy and Tailscale identities count; shared-secret operators, the Gateway owner profile, paired devices and nodes never do.

The owner records the first sign-in in the existing core plugin-state store (`core:user-sign-in`, retained namespace, no schema change), together with the plugins that had handlers at that moment. Each plugin's delivery stays pending until its handler resolves: failures and 60-second timeouts retry with backoff (5 s doubling, capped at one hour), and pending deliveries resume after `gateway_start` on the next Gateway start. Without any registered handler nothing is recorded, so Gateways without consumers do no extra work. Repeated sign-ins in one process skip the store after the first check.

To stay within the `hook-types.ts` line cap, the private channel-pairing hook types moved unchanged to `hook-channel-pairing.types.ts`. Docs: `docs/plugins/hooks/lifecycle.md#first-sign-in`, the hook reference table, and the SDK events overview.

When an administrator merges profiles, the merge target inherits the merged-in profile's first-sign-in record and any pending deliveries, so a merge never produces a second first-sign-in event.

Storage compatibility: no schema version, migration, or table change. Records live in the existing `plugin_state_entries` table under a new core-owned namespace, so existing databases load unchanged; profiles from before this change carry no record and receive one event on their next sign-in with `isNewProfile: false` (covered by tests).

Accepted edge cases: a plugin registered after someone's first sign-in does not receive it, and `isNewProfile` means "created at most one minute before the first sign-in".

## Evidence

- `src/gateway/user-first-sign-in.test.ts` (9 tests, real state database): fires once across repeated sign-ins and simulated restarts; a failing handler is retried after restart without redelivering to plugins that succeeded; in-process backoff retry; sign-in never waits on the handler; existing profiles report `isNewProfile: false` and late plugins are skipped; after `users.merge` the target keeps the merged-in profile's history and pending delivery (red without the merge handling); a real Cloudflare Access trusted-proxy HTTP sign-in delivers the verified email and GitHub account 101; a person denied by an access-policy plugin and a shared-secret operator record nothing; unverified auth methods record nothing.
- `src/gateway/server.auth.first-sign-in.test.ts`: a real Gateway server with trusted-proxy auth; two Control UI WebSocket sign-ins produce exactly one event. Removing the WebSocket call site makes this test fail.
- Consumer suites passed: `github-user-identity.oidc`, `github-user-identity`, `user-background-http.authority`, `hook-runner-global`, `hook-lifecycle-gates`, `wired-hooks-gateway`, `contracts/boundary-invariants`, `server-startup-observers`, `plugin-sdk/api-baseline`, `test/vitest-projects-config`.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, core test typecheck (`src` shard), oxlint on changed files, `pnpm plugin-sdk:check-exports`, line-cap ratchet and docs formatting all pass. A local autoreview pass reported no actionable findings.
- Unrelated CI failures under the Bun test runtime, reproduced locally with this PR's Gateway call sites reverted to the merge base: `server.chat-abort-settlement` (accepted-injection case) and `server-methods/progress-card-refresh.integration` (duplicate active refresh). `chat-send-message-injection.isolated-gateway` timed out once in CI and passes locally.
- Gap: not yet exercised on a live Gateway behind Cloudflare Access with a real consumer plugin; the visitor-access consumer and end-to-end guest proof land in follow-up PRs.

Requested by @jalehman.

## Work sessions

- [Original discussion with @jalehman](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/4ff43853-805b-4ab6-932c-1622ab5bb1d8)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/e651ad51-7e75-4b17-a801-a9e2bc02f80b)

## Worked on by

- @jalehman

prs.title: fix(update): report corrupt restart sentinel rows
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A present-but-unreadable restart sentinel row was treated as absent by the managed update helper. Operators lost the recovery context without any corruption-specific guidance. The helper now reports the shared reader's `invalid` state, keeps the row intact, and does not replay unverified context.

Closes #153501

## User Impact

After a failed managed update, corrupt JSON in `continuation_json` or `stats_json` now produces an actionable warning instead of silently dropping recovery context. Safe service recovery still proceeds, and the malformed row remains available for inspection.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared reader already distinguishes `missing`, `valid`, and `invalid` rows. The helper consumed that state but returned silently. This change reuses the existing owner result rather than parsing or rewriting the corrupt payload.

The warning is logged and recorded as a run warning:

`Restart sentinel metadata is unreadable; preserved the row and skipped its unverified recovery context. Run openclaw update repair on the Gateway host, then retry the update.`

## Evidence

- Added a managed-handoff regression test that writes truncated `continuation_json`, asserts the repair hint appears, and verifies the sentinel row is byte-for-byte unchanged.
- `pnpm test src/infra/update-managed-service-handoff-ownership.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 13 passed, 1 skipped.
- `pnpm test src/infra/restart-sentinel.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 39 passed.
- `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, `git diff --check`, and the line-cap ratchet pass.
- Test and core typechecks report only the pre-existing unrelated `src/snapshot/local-repository-directory-policy.ts:351` (`isVolumeRoot`) failure on `main`.

prs.title: fix(telegram): skip sticker descriptions when image understanding is off
prs.body:
Closes #181980

## What Problem This Solves

An uncached static Telegram sticker triggers a separate image-description model request even when `tools.media.image.enabled: false`. Operators who explicitly disabled image preprocessing still pay for that extra request.

## Solution and user impact

Honor the existing switch in `describeStickerImage`, before model selection. Return no description when image understanding is disabled; normal sticker delivery and the agent reply remain available. Enabled/default behavior, searchable sticker descriptions, model selection, and stored cache formats are unchanged. No new configuration or plugin-SDK surface.

Thanks to @wr-web for the report, fix, regression, and original Windows Gateway proof; their commit is preserved.

## Evidence

Built main `61bd8a5ea12ea2531e61c3c41065309ef22d6a4a` and candidate `c970c4670c732bf5a59707d8cac8157d7f404038` once each in Linux Docker with Node 24.22.1. A leased QA user sent six distinct static WebP stickers over the real Telegram Test Server. Every run used a fresh built Gateway and state created through shipped CLI commands. TDLib recorded `messageSticker` / `stickerFormatWebp`; the bot replied in every run.

The provider was a deterministic OpenAI-compatible HTTP recorder. Requests are classified by the serialized sticker-description prompt, not inferred from reply timing:

| Build | Image understanding | Runs | Separate sticker-description requests per run | Other response requests | Embedding requests | Bot reply |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main | disabled | 2 | **1, 1** | 2 each | 2 each | yes, both |
| Candidate | disabled | 2 | **0, 0** | 2 each | 2 each | yes, both |
| Main control | enabled | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | yes |
| Candidate control | enabled | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | yes |

These are observed HTTP request counts, not a live billing benchmark. Fresh state and distinct sticker bytes avoid a cached-description false pass. The harness sends native TDLib stickers; it does not fabricate inbound Bot API updates.

Focused regression: the new disabled-image case fails against main with `expected 'Described by openai/image-b' to be null`. Candidate sticker selection and cache suites pass **9/9**. Candidate wrapper wall time: 57.48s including cold worker compilation; selection test bodies total 272ms, cache test bodies total 2.165s. Oxfmt and Oxlint pass on both changed files.

Separate real-provider scope check: the built candidate CLI used `openai/gpt-5.4-mini`, returned `LIVE_GATE_OK`, and recorded one successful assistant turn with no fallback. This check does not substitute for the Telegram A/B request-count proof.

Whole-diff simplification retained the existing owner and one discriminating regression. Production **+5/-0**, tests **+11/-0**: the added guard is necessary to enforce the existing setting; no parallel mechanism or test-only seam was introduced. Existing media-understanding documentation already describes the off-switch contract.

## Merge risk

Two-way door: reverting restores the old request behavior; there is no migration or persistent-format change. Blast radius is Telegram's separate sticker-description request when image understanding is explicitly disabled. Enabled descriptions and native sticker delivery remain protected by the control runs.

prs.title: refactor: separate steering delivery from policy preparation
prs.body:
Related: #181768

## What Problem This Solves

The retained-recovery-claim repair leaves steering delivery checks hidden inside tool-policy preparation and mixes recovery observations with execution settings, making binding lifetime and final admission difficult to review.

## User Impact

No intended user-visible behavior change. Same-requester steering, collaborative steering, refusal/followup behavior, queue ordering, and legacy plugin compatibility retain their existing contracts. No configuration, storage, or migration changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The message-join coordinator now explicitly composes delivery eligibility, execution settings, and caller policy. Settings and recovery observations remain attached to the exact selected policy binding, preserving the existing capture points and invalidation lifecycle across replies and native attempts. Generic policy preparation no longer prepares delivery as a side effect.

Final submission still checks cancellation, the captured owner/backend, policy, settings, and delivery eligibility. The retained-predecessor exception stays limited to same-requester human continuation. Existing fallback warnings retain the specific typed rejection message without changing public fallback reasons.

This is the separately requested architectural followup to the merged repair. It does not establish the cause of the historical production incident, whose admission/rejection observations were not retained.

## Evidence

Validated head: `1fb7cfea1e6f4b0eac13e9203d9a2c80541982e7`. Focused validation and both live-model native proof cases are complete.

- Fresh independent diff review completed with no actionable P0–P2 findings, including a second pass after the receiver-preserving lint repair.
- On one isolated AWS lease, all 159 baseline tests passed across eight commands. The candidate passed those eight files (164 tests) and four focused consumer commands, for 191 passing tests total. After the receiver-preserving callback repair, both affected suites reran successfully (48 tests). Complete source manifests verified before and after execution; the tested staged tree exactly matches the committed tree. No Testbox or shared Gateway was used.
- Existing boundary matrices are extended for failed binding cleanup, equivalent-policy attempt replacement, absent versus explicitly empty recovery capture, and delivery invalidation at final submission.
- Negative control confirmed the final-admission test detects removal of the delivery descriptor: the isolated mutant accepted the input and failed the unchanged rejection assertion. The candidate rejects before the delivery sink. The mutant source was restored and reverified (47.550 seconds command wall).
- Core production and all 29 selected test type graphs passed, as did formatting, targeted lint after repair, and the remaining applicable static guards. Two inherited failures remain: the deprecated-API guard reports an untouched performance script, and the three dead-export scans report 6/18/15 entries. Exact-baseline replay produced identical findings with zero candidate-only entries; no unrelated repairs are included.
- Two fresh live-model cases used the rendered Control UI and isolated Gateway on the exact committed source, with the existing fixture preparing recovery state through its owner. An unchanged predecessor claim allowed the correction into the original native task; a replacement claim produced `reply-owner-ended` and `followup-queued`, left the original task without the correction/effect, and consumed the correction once in a separately correlated subsequent task. Both harmless file effects had successful native tool results. Gateway run IDs, native threads/calls, direct task start/end records, claim checkpoints and actual effects were reconciled; transcript persistence and model claims were not treated as consumption proof.
- Serving source/runtime hashes stayed unchanged. The observed managed native binary was Codex 0.162.1, verified by executable hash and actual version command. Each cell preserved its authenticated browser connection and used `queue.mode: steer` with `allowCollaborativeSteering: false`; all eight exported screenshots were inspected. The replacement followup repeated the fixture's old barrier command and got exit 1 before its successful effect; that separate fixture/model outcome is retained in the evidence, not described as a clean tool run. Replacement occurred before correction preparation; focused tests cover later invalidation. These constructed cases do not establish the historical incident's cause.

<details>
<summary>Scope, test costs, and LoC churn</summary>

Candidate versus merged base `3de0f0007f6951bf283041c90ae415984f48d1d8`:

| Scope | Files | Added | Deleted | Churn | Net |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Production | 16 | 382 | 306 | 688 | +76 |
| Tests | 5 | 193 | 47 | 240 | +146 |
| Total | 21 | 575 | 353 | 928 | +222 |

Each command used `pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`. Measured wall seconds for the five changed test files:

| Test file | Baseline | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `session-controller.message-join.test.ts` | 49.456 | 50.601 |
| `session-controller.message-join.handoff.test.ts` | 37.583 | 37.839 |
| `tool-authority.runtime.admission.test.ts` | 50.150 | 50.003 |
| `tool-authority.runtime.continuation.test.ts` | 36.181 | 36.330 |
| `agent-runner-fallback-steering.test.ts` | 55.969 | 56.060 |

The eight matched commands totaled 393.024 seconds on baseline and 394.413 on the candidate. The four additional caller checks took 221.697 seconds; candidate total 616.110 seconds. The final receiver-fix replay took 39.734 seconds for message join and 37.583 for authority admission; lint, core types, formatting and whitespace also passed. These include wrapper/setup/compilation and are not a controlled runtime benchmark. CI timing is pending.

The runtime build took 123.382 seconds and browser preparation 18.194 seconds. Live case wall times were 56.269 seconds (unchanged claim) and 60.779 seconds (replacement). Summing each native thread's final cumulative usage gives 212,691 total tokens, including 157,626 cached input tokens; this is recorded usage, not a billing estimate. No new live suite is added to per-PR CI.

No new persistent state, public snapshot field, authority manager, or per-tool authority layer is added.

## What Problem This Solves

Single-consumer helpers, modules, and private type synonyms add unnecessary indirection to their owning paths.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior, configuration, CLI, protocol, or Plugin SDK change. Validation, authorization, resource bounds, shutdown settlement, and lazy-import boundaries remain intact. The standalone session memory backend is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep one-use preparation and rendering frames with their existing callers. Fold the internal tool/hook registrar module into its existing composer, and put plugin-service startup and QA timing preparation in their existing Gateway owners. Preserve all callback bodies and security scope policy; only private framing disappears. Remove one now-unused assertion allowance and migrate the affected QA code reference.

Net production reduction: **156 lines across 26 paths** (756 additions / 912 deletions against the branch base). Moved implementation is charged as added code, not counted as deleted behavior. Tests grow by 55 net lines: public-boundary coverage replaces the private timing parser tests, with bounded contact, status-target, and invalid-duration cases. No production test seam, suppression, timeout, retry, or skip is added.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

None added: no rare-failure guard is removed. Existing validation, live-authority checks, ownership, and error behavior stay at the same decision or effect point. The Gateway service import remains dynamic, with eligibility checked after the import yields.

## Evidence

Focused owner and consumer tests, targeted native typechecks, typed lint, format, and line-cap checks pass for each cut. The final Gateway additions include 187 startup/reload cases, five migrated diagnostics cases, and 112 scope/Gateway/UI-access cases. The latter run in 31.39 seconds across three focused shards; the diagnostics shard takes 26.65 seconds including worker preparation. Tests execute serially with one worker and isolated HOME/OpenClaw/XDG state. Independent scoped reviews through P2 have no accepted actionable findings.

Final push guards pass: format parity, assertion and lint-suppression ratchets, mock exports, wrapper/eager-import closure, frozen updater bindings, prompt-prefix stability, line caps, UI controller guards, and keyless i18n. Runtime and static import cycles are both zero. Hosted CI on the exact published head is the broad proof. No local build, broad suite, whole-graph typecheck, live channel/provider, pixel, performance, or native-device verification is claimed. Existing dependency and Vite warnings remain unsuppressed.

prs.title: fix(ui): replace stored secrets from config forms
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Control UI Form mode can type a new sensitive value, but a stored secret arrives as the server redaction sentinel and remains read-only. The disabled reveal button leaves no way to replace that credential from Form mode.

Sensitive scalar fields now offer an explicit **Replace stored value** action. It opens an empty, masked input without revealing or committing the sentinel. Abandoning the replacement restores the concealed state; typing replaces the stored value normally.

## User Impact

Operators can rotate a stored token from Settings and channel forms without switching to Raw mode or exposing the existing secret. Opening and abandoning the replacement does not clear the credential.

Structured `SecretRef` values remain raw-mode-only, and non-masked reveal behavior is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`getSensitiveRenderState` intentionally prevents the redaction sentinel from becoming editable. The scalar renderer now tracks a local replacement transition: the sentinel stays concealed, the input renders empty as `type=password`, and the first input marks the replacement as intentional. Blur without input cancels the transition.

The existing sensitive-field button becomes the explicit replacement entry point when the value is sentinel-redacted; otherwise it keeps its reveal/hide behavior.

## Evidence

Base-red on `origin/main` with the new browser coverage: 3 failures. The replacement action was absent, and the sentinel remained locked.

Head-green:

```text
config-form-scalar-integrity.browser.test.ts  36 passed
config-form.browser.test.ts                   43 passed (adjacent suites, 2 files)
```

- `pnpm test ui/src/components/config-form-scalar-integrity.browser.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`
- `pnpm test ui/src/components/config-form.browser.test.ts ui/src/components/config-form-union-integrity.browser.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json ui/src/components/config-form.node.scalar.tsx ui/src/components/config-form.node.shared.tsx ui/src/components/config-form-scalar-integrity.browser.test.ts ui/src/i18n/locales/en-settings.ts`
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check ui/src/components/config-form.node.scalar.tsx ui/src/components/config-form.node.shared.tsx ui/src/components/config-form-scalar-integrity.browser.test.ts ui/src/i18n/locales/en-settings.ts`
- `pnpm check:line-cap-ratchet --base origin/main`
- `git diff --check`

Browser proof covers replacement, masked keystrokes, focus retention, no sentinel disclosure, no reveal callback, and cancellation without clearing. The focused UI typecheck reached unrelated existing errors in `src/snapshot/local-repository-directory-policy.ts:351` and a missing local `libdeflate` declaration; neither changed file is involved.

Closes #163393

prs.title: fix(perf): report natural GC cost for paired RPC measurements
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

RPC benchmark results now distinguish **untraced GC timing** from **traced promotion**, normalize cost by validated completed work, and expose the heap state needed to interpret paired measurements. This corrects a measurement boundary: Node's GC event timer includes trace serialization/output after V8 stops its collection-pause clock. Traced GC and event-loop timings therefore remain attribution evidence, not eligible timing gates.

**Production source delta: 0 lines.** The change is confined to eight harness, fixture, test, and documentation files (+289/−10). No runtime owner, schema, configuration, timer, or production behavior changes. Related investigations: #181921, #181904, #181759. Merging this harness does not approve any allocation candidate.

## Final Behavior

`--diagnostics` reports per-round `naturalGc` with validated operation count, GC time/work by kind, and `timingGateEligible: true`. Adding `--trace-gc` supplies main-isolate promotion/work from independently named round windows, parsed after Gateway exit and log drainage, and marks timing ineligible. Allocation profiling remains separate because stopping it forces collection. Connection and background-polling workloads retain raw diagnostics without entering the single-RPC normalization path.

Diagnostics include Node/V8 versions, process age, before/after heap-space statistics, GC counts/tails/maxima, and event-loop sample counts. A shared `--start-file` supports synchronized warm starts. Offline fixtures provide 40 disabled announce/last cron jobs; the cron workload checks every expected job and delivery preview. The board workload prepares and checks three widgets.

The methods note requires matched A/A controls, fixed work, retained maintenance activity, untrimmed total cost, visible maxima, and explicit inconclusive outcomes. It does not subtract trace overhead or replace total GC cost with V8's narrower pause sum. The boundary follows the [Node callback timer](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v26.12.1/src/node_perf.cc#L166) and [V8 collection/epilogue ordering](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v26.12.1/deps/v8/src/heap/heap.cc#L1716).

## Verification

- Focused diagnostics and fixture tests passed (4 each), including persisted disabled cron jobs with no retained delivery route; the named sequential trace-window assertion passed. Changed-file format/lint and the tooling typecheck passed.
- Real isolated Gateway proof covered two cron rounds with distinct promotion windows and validated work counts. A reproduced mixed-polling failure now completes successfully, retaining all 11 RPCs and omitting `naturalGc`; that rerun also verified the shared start-file epoch. Separate two-RPC mode smokes verified untraced timing eligibility without promotion and traced promotion with timing ineligible. These are behavior checks, not performance claims.
- Independent subagent review (autoreview route unavailable): actionable findings were fixed; final scoped and integration reviews found no P2+ issue.
- Final head `0f8081b1afaac1c3eac9023dcd6b1b3f3d9d31d2` passed [CI 40043061563](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40043061563), including changed-test lanes and the CI gate; [artifact build](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40043061576) and [final PR-context gates](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40044003412) also passed. Merged as `34875012f54f9076336635977b99e6907704926b`.

Prior failure remains disclosed: an earlier [CI worker-profile test](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40033134998/job/120686661493) expected zero discarded-worker allocation bytes and observed 1,080. Five interleaved replays on the exact CI parent and five with the diagnostics change passed, with verified loaded-source hashes and the same Node 24.22.1 fixture runtime. The replay controller used Node rather than CI's Bun. This supports the bounded unrelated-flake classification; it neither reproduces nor fixes the original stochastic sample. No assertion was relaxed or CI rerun requested. An earlier local full profile run also had one retained-object failure (13/14 passed), and a stalled follow-up was stopped; neither is claimed as passing proof.

## Completed Original A/A Controls

All **16 primary pairs / 32 sides** completed successfully: four pairs per workload, with fresh synthetic state, validated counters, paired catalog response digests, swapped interleaved CPU placements, an exclusive quiet slot, and the unchanged shared guard. No completed pair was discarded. Historical cron/board and catalog drivers preserve their original process topology and work sequence; the generic child-Gateway scenarios do not substitute for those controls.

Every original capture was traced. The fixed-window calculations below preserve the historical rule arithmetic; **their timing classifications are instrumented evidence requiring untraced confirmation**. Promotion remains separately identified. The four-pair columns show mean absolute deltas and pooled percentage changes; these descriptive values are not gates.

| Workload; work per side/pair | Four-pair GC Δ: mean absolute; pooled % | Four-pair promotion Δ: mean absolute; pooled % | Paired window 1–2 | Paired window 3–4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plugin; 1,000 RPCs | +47.316 µs/RPC; +11.75% | +3,316.740 B/RPC; +19.29% | No adverse gate; GC instability and mixed promotion/loop signs are inconclusive | Promotion adverse: paired mean +27.43%; both pairs >10%. GC/loop inconclusive |
| Paced cron.full; 200 RPCs, 1,100 ms before each | +8,802.579 µs/RPC; +349.41% | +19,451.370 B/RPC; +27.80% | GC/promotion raw thresholds cross, but opposite signs make them inconclusive | GC inconclusive; promotion/loop below threshold; pair 4 maximum-event safeguard triggers |
| Board; 1,000 burst reads within the original five-flow sequence | +29.746 µs/RPC; +88.03% | +6,010.484 B/RPC; +23.24% | GC adverse: paired mean +47.88%; promotion +33.76% | GC adverse: paired mean +107.06%; promotion adverse because both pairs >10%, despite mean +12.89% |
| Catalog/roster; 4,000 persisted-update/catalog/two-roster cycles | +33.034 µs/cycle; +2.53% | +8,850.610 B/cycle; +0.71% | No adverse gate; mixed GC/promotion inconclusive; loop mean +3.22% (n=13,466–13,830/side) | No adverse gate; GC mean +2.68%; mixed promotion/loop inconclusive |

Four of the eight preselected windows produced an adverse historical signal on identical source. This is an observed count, **not an estimated population false-positive rate**. Pause tails remain context where sample counts are insufficient or the existing sub-millisecond exception applies; that exception is never applied to total GC/work. Board window 1–2 also lacks enough loop samples. No overlapping window or favorable subset replaces the preselected comparisons.

Cron pair 4 illustrates the boundary problem: callback GC-event maxima were **426.740 → 7,749.990 ms**, while exact-window main-isolate V8 collection maxima were **12.902 → 75.162 ms**. The 7.75-second event must not be called a V8-reported collection pause. Trace output is a demonstrated measurement hazard, not a proven cause of that stall; the narrower maximum also crosses the numerical safeguard and is retained as supplementary evidence. Board's consistently positive deltas have another unresolved confound: A always launched 11.508–17.777 seconds before B. CPU swapping did not counterbalance startup age. Neither observation establishes a production regression or exonerates a candidate.

## Revised Campaign Still Pending

**Current snapshot: 2/4 revised A/A pairs complete, 0/2 candidate pairs complete; promotion unmeasured. No candidate or landing verdict.** The frozen untraced protocol uses 7,500 plugin RPCs at 132 ms after 1,000 paced warmups, a common start five seconds after both sides are ready, swapped CPU placements, alternating launch order, and enabled maintenance. The approximately 990-second capture spans a maintenance interval; driver/controller hashes, runtime, and owner attestations are recorded.

The first revised window has no adverse timing gate, but GC/work is mixed-sign **inconclusive**: +8.51% and −11.74%. Its mean signed absolute change is +4.520 µs/RPC and pooled change +3.028%; neither substitutes for the paired rule. Loop p99 is below the gate (n=49,031/49,017 and 49,227/49,200). Minor p95 has 545/605 and 539/389 collections; its paired mean +0.880 ms makes it context under the existing absolute-shift exception. Neither maximum safeguard triggers: maxima are 590.648/452.886 ms and 13.781/16.232 ms. Each side observed 5–6 major collections, yet nursery capacity and maintenance work still differ; close start times do not prove equal heap state or a causal explanation.

The remaining controls and candidate comparisons are required. Proposed v5.4 preserves existing cost, promotion, loop, sample-count, and maximum safeguards while requiring calibrated measurement modes and predeclared resolution of ambiguous gates. Any favorable candidate recommendation additionally requires separate matched traced promotion proof. Unresolved controls or required gates remain inconclusive; four controls cannot establish absence of regression.
