prs.title: fix(matrix): only act on invites from the live rooms.invite sync section
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

The Matrix adapter re-fires `_on_invite` for historic invite events every time it connects.

1. `connect()` builds its client with a new `MemorySyncStore` and runs `sync(full_state=True)`, so every (re)connect is a full-state initial sync.
2. That sync re-sends each joined room's state and recent timeline.
3. mautrix's `MembershipEventDispatcher` turns every `m.room.member` event with `membership: invite` into `InternalEventType.INVITE`. It does this no matter which sync section carried the event or who it was addressed to.
4. `_on_invite` checks only the inviter allowlist.

So each connect logs a `rejecting invite ... from unauthorized user` WARNING for every replayed invite from a sender not on the allowlist. Every replayed invite from an allowed sender gets an `invited to ... joining` INFO line plus a join task that does nothing. This repeats for as long as the invite event is part of that sync response.

This PR adds three `debug`-level early returns at the top of `_on_invite`:

1. **The sync-stream stamp is not `INVITED_ROOM`.** `Client.dispatch_event` sets `event.source` on every event it dispatches. An invite carried in a joined room's timeline or state is history, never a live invite for us.
2. **The room is already joined.**
3. **The `state_key` target is someone else.** This is @kvnloo's guard from #111170: bridged rooms carry invites addressed to other users. It now compares through `_is_self_sender`, so a difference in localpart case between homeserver surfaces isn't mistaken for another user.

The reconcile pass now uses the same identity check to find our member event in `invite_state`. Without it, an invite whose `state_key` differs from the `whoami` id only in localpart case was never joined: mautrix's invited-room path matches `state_key == mxid` exactly and dispatches nothing, and reconcile's exact selector lost the inviter and logged a rejection with an empty inviter. The exact-id event still wins; the case-insensitive match is only a fallback when there is none. (Found by @kvnloo in review.)

Guard 3 alone does not close the bug. When the bot's own historic invite is replayed, its `state_key` is the bot, so it passes a target check and keeps logging on every connect. Guards 1 and 2 close that case.

Live invites behave as before:

- Unauthorized inviters are still rejected and authorized ones are still joined.
- The reconcile pass in `_schedule_pending_invite_joins` is untouched, including the allowlist gate from #87258 (landed via #117189).
- Guard 2 changes no join outcome, because `_schedule_invite_join` and the reconcile pass already skip rooms in `_joined_rooms`. What it removes is the log lines.
- An event that can't be classified (no `source` stamp, no `state_key`, or no resolved own user id) keeps the old path.

**Filtering at registration instead.** `add_event_handler(IntEvt.INVITE, ..., sync_stream=SyncStream.INVITED_ROOM)` also works. It would need `SyncStream` added to `_make_fake_mautrix()` in `tests/gateway/test_matrix.py`, because without it 11 `connect()` tests there fail. (Our earlier comments on #76292 and #111170 blamed the stub in `test_matrix_approval_reaction_fail_closed.py`. Re-checked on current `main`, it is `test_matrix.py`'s fake.) This PR keeps the checks in the handler so that all three guards sit in one place and can be unit-tested without the dispatcher. Happy to switch to the registration filter if you prefer it.

This is the fresh carrier on current `main` that @kvnloo asked for on #111170. It carries his `state_key` guard and tests with credit (`Co-authored-by`), plus the replay guards and tests from the branch posted there on 09-18.

## Related Issue

Fixes #76292
Supersedes #111170

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [x] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage)

## Changes Made

- `plugins/platforms/matrix/adapter.py`
  - New module-level `_is_invited_room_source(source)`. It imports `SyncStream` lazily and returns `True` for anything it can't classify.
  - `_on_invite`: adds the three guards above, ahead of the existing allowlist check, and a docstring on the replay mechanism.
  - `_extract_invite_dm_signal`: selects our member event by exact id first and falls back to `_is_self_sender` only when there is none.
- `tests/gateway/test_matrix_invite_replay.py` (new, 11 tests)
  - **8 unit tests** drive `_on_invite` with events stamped the way `Client.dispatch_event` stamps them. They cover:
    - the bot's own historic invite and a third-party invite, both replayed from a joined room's timeline;
    - a replay from a joined room's state section;
    - the stamp deciding on its own;
    - live invites from authorized and unauthorized users (joined / still rejected);
    - unstamped events (an invite to self still joins; a joined room stays quiet).
  - **Why a fixture:** CI installs no matrix extra, so a `sync_stream` fixture supplies the real `SyncStream` when mautrix is importable and otherwise patches a mirror of it into `mautrix.client`. The unit tests therefore run with or without mautrix.
  - **3 `TestRealDispatchPath` tests** feed synthetic sync payloads through a real mautrix `Client` + `MembershipEventDispatcher` into `_on_invite`, registered the way `connect()` registers it. They check the stamping those unit tests assume, and they skip when the real package isn't installed.
- `tests/gateway/test_matrix_invite_state_key.py` (new, from #111170, 5 tests)
  - an invite addressed to another user is skipped quietly;
  - an invite to self still joins;
  - an invite to self with different localpart case still joins (new);
  - an unknown own user id still gets the invite processed;
  - a missing `state_key` still gets the invite processed.
- `tests/gateway/test_matrix_dm_invite_recording.py` (from #111170): the fake invite event now carries `state_key` = the bot, as a real invite addressed to the bot does.
- `tests/gateway/test_matrix_pending_invite_auth.py`, 2 new cases:
  - a case-drifted own invite from an allowed inviter is joined, the DM is recorded, and no rejection is logged;
  - `exact-event-wins-over-case-folded-look-alike`, added to the fail-closed parametrization.

## How to Test

**Rebased 2026-10-08** onto `main` @ `38880bd2f`. The one conflict was `_CryptoStateStore` moving to `adapter_crypto.py` (2efd6961f), which left `_is_invited_room_source` without its old neighbour; it now follows `ensure_matrix_deps`. The change is otherwise byte-identical, and every number below was re-measured on the new head.

1. **With mautrix 0.21.1 installed:**
   - `pytest tests/gateway/test_matrix_invite_replay.py tests/gateway/test_matrix_invite_state_key.py tests/gateway/test_matrix_dm_invite_recording.py tests/gateway/test_matrix_pending_invite_auth.py -q` gives **28 passed**.
   - The two new files against unpatched `main`'s `adapter.py` give **7 failed, 9 passed**. The 7 failures are the four replay unit cases, the unstamped joined-room case, the real-dispatch timeline case and the other-user `state_key` case. The rest are green on both by design; they pin the behaviour this change keeps. In `test_matrix_pending_invite_auth.py`, the case-drift case fails against `main`, and the look-alike case passes on `main` because it pins main's behaviour.
2. **With mautrix unimportable, as CI installs it** (simulated with an import blocker for `mautrix*`):
   - The same four files give **25 passed, 3 skipped**. The skips are `TestRealDispatchPath`.
   - Against `main`'s adapter: **6 failed, 7 passed, 3 skipped**.
   - Every `tests/gateway/test_matrix*.py` file, run per file under the same condition: **0 failures**.
3. **Every `tests/gateway/test_matrix*.py` file, one pytest process per file:** 22 files, 225 passed, 4 skipped without mautrix (via `scripts/run_tests.sh`); 231 passed with mautrix 0.21.1. The two files under `tests/plugins/platforms/matrix/` pass both ways. `ruff check` is clean on the touched files, and both new test files are `ruff format` clean.
4. **Live, on the reporter's fleet:** four gateway profiles on one self-hosted homeserver (Tuwunel), no bridges, mautrix 0.21.1. The same three guards (identical logic, different comments) have run there as a local patch since 2026-09-17. On one profile, counting connects (each a full-state initial sync):
   - **Unpatched, 10 connects (09-15 to 09-17):** every connect logged 3 `rejecting invite` WARNINGs and 4-7 `invited to ... joining` INFO lines. The WARNINGs came from three historic invites by a non-allowlisted user in one room. The INFO lines came from historic invites by allowlisted users to other people.
   - **Patched, 25 connects (09-17 to 09-23):** 0 of either. On the WARNING side that covers 15 connects, because the room holding the unauthorized invites was retired on 09-22.
   - **Two connects during updates** ran stock `main` before the local patch was re-applied, and both brought the noise back: 3 WARNING + 4 INFO on 09-21, and 4 INFO on 09-23 (after that room was retired).

## Checklist

### Code

- [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.)
- [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate (#111170 is superseded at its author's request; #76308 is closed)
- [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature (no unrelated commits)
- [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass. **Not the full suite:** the gateway Matrix tests, as listed above.
- [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features)
- [x] I've tested on my platform: Linux / Python 3.11, with mautrix 0.21.1 and with mautrix unimportable; the live fleet runs the same guards as a local patch

### Documentation & Housekeeping

- [x] I've updated relevant documentation (README, `docs/`, docstrings): the `_on_invite` docstring
- [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys: N/A, no config keys
- [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows: N/A

This PR was prepared by AI agents (Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) working with the operator who hit the bug on his own fleet, where the live data above comes from. The models:

prs.title: fix(gateway): preserve final replies across idle and relay reconnect
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Keep a gateway awake until a completed messaging turn's final response has been recorded, sent and settled in the delivery ledger. Recover saved logical Slack/Discord replies through their hosted relay after boot or an authenticated WebSocket reconnect, without rerunning the model turn.

The runner releases its agent slot before the adapter finishes final delivery. Both the idle predicate and planned-restart drain previously treated that gap as no work. Recovery also filtered/resolved ledger rows by native platform registrations even when the connected transport was Relay, and an internal WebSocket reconnect did not notify the runner to sweep failed replies.

## Related Issue

No public issue; reproduced from a hosted support report using synthetic routes and a real SQLite ledger.

Related open work: #84288, #92589 and #84386 address delivery/drain accounting. The adapter-owner lifetime approach here follows Qixuan Cao's proposal in #84288, applied to the current split modules and both idle detection and planned restart. No source commits were cherry-picked. Those PRs do not cover logical-platform relay replay or same-adapter WebSocket reconnect notification. #107135 addresses adjacent Telegram polling/late-write/cancellation recovery and is companion work, not superseded by this PR.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- Count live adapter-owned session tasks across credential-owning profiles, deduplicate their runner slots, and retain a balanced task lease through replay sends and ledger settlement.
- Use the shared scoped transport resolver for boot claims and replay. Preserve the logical platform, thread and runtime profile; native adapters keep priority and unadvertised/offline profile routes remain excluded.
- Schedule a runner-owned recovery task once on the first authenticated descriptor of a reconnect generation. Do not await outbound I/O on the WebSocket reader or change its auth-revocation supervisor lifecycle.
- Preserve the existing atomic claims, retry budgets, recovery markers and resume-flag clearing. This does not introduce a new queue or exactly-once delivery guarantee.

## How to Test

The complete CI run on `314667aee012b3b095c0462749d5bd86a145021f` is green: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/actions/runs/40057988760

- Full Linux Python shards: **35,568 + 31,013 = 66,581 passed, zero failed** (938 skipped).
- Both macOS lanes and Windows x64/ARM64 lanes pass. All required checks pass.
- The original failing crash-recovery, served-profile recovery, cron delivery, restart-notice and profile-following cases pass in the full Linux run. Native cron/notification calling conventions are preserved; bare recovery fixtures now provide the real GatewayConfig required by transport resolution. No assertions were removed or relaxed.
- Local final Ruff and code-health checks pass with zero blocking/advisory health findings. Full configured ty comparison reports no new diagnostics; existing repository type debt remains. Tools match CI pins: Ruff 0.15.22 and ty 0.0.89. New Python files pass formatting; existing full-file formatting debt is not reformatted in this change.
- Nine regression cases failed against unchanged base production modules, covering the final-delivery lifetime and boot/reconnect relay recovery. The tests use a real SQLite ledger and synthetic connector routes.

Local exploratory runs are not claimed fully green: Windows cannot satisfy the POSIX SIGKILL/getuid harness assumptions; a WSL cron-worker probe missed its startup deadline before reaching the worker marker. The full Linux CI run passes these cases on this exact head. No live hosted instance was mutated or deployment acceptance claimed. Existing Telegram-specific late failure/cancellation races tracked by #107135 remain outside this change.

## Checklist

### Code

- [x] I've read the Contributing Guide
- [x] My commit messages follow Conventional Commits
- [x] I searched for existing PRs to make sure this isn't a duplicate
- [x] My PR contains only changes related to this fix
- [x] Full Python test suite passes in CI on the PR head
- [x] `python scripts/check` passes
- [x] I've added tests for my changes
- [x] I've tested on my platform: Windows

### Documentation & Housekeeping

- [x] Relevant internal docstrings updated
- [x] Config keys, tools and schemas unchanged
- [x] Cross-platform impact considered; no host-specific production operations added

## Screenshots / Logs

Synthetic behavior tests cover native priority, secondary credential ownership, independent runtime profile routing, unavailable targets, idle fail-awake behavior, duplicate reconnect descriptors, and completed versus cancelled delivery work. Private support logs and identifiers are omitted.

## What does this PR do?

Adds four macOS MCP servers to the `optional-mcps/` catalog so Hermes users can install them with `hermes mcp install <name>`:

- **apple-mail** — read, search, send, reply, forward, and organize Apple Mail
- **apple-notes** — create, search, read, update, and organize Apple Notes
- **apple-numbers** — read, write, search, and format Apple Numbers (`.numbers`) spreadsheets
- **apple-photos** — query, search, export, and inspect the macOS Photos library

All four are published, MIT-licensed npm packages maintained under [github.com/sweetrb](https://github.com/sweetrb), with CI on `macos-latest` (Node 20 + 22). Each manifest is a plain **stdio** entry that launches the published package via `npx -y <pkg>` — no `install`/clone step (per the npm/uvx note in the n8n manifest) and `auth: none` (everything is local). They already support Hermes today via `hermes mcp add`; this just makes them one-command installable from the catalog.

## Related Issue

None — new catalog entries.

- `optional-mcps/apple-notes/manifest.yaml`
- `optional-mcps/apple-numbers/manifest.yaml`

## How to Test

On **macOS**:

1. `hermes mcp install apple-notes` (or `apple-mail` / `apple-numbers` / `apple-photos`)
2. Start a new Hermes session.
3. The server launches via `npx -y apple-<app>-mcp`. First use prompts for macOS Automation access (AppleScript); `apple-photos` additionally needs Full Disk Access. Tools then load (e.g. `apple-notes`: `create-note`, `search-notes`, `list-notes`, …).

**Platforms tested:** macOS (each server's own CI runs on `macos-latest`, Node 20 + 22). `apple-numbers` and `apple-photos` use a Python 3.11+ sidecar (`numbers-parser` / `osxphotos`) that bootstraps a local venv on first run.

## Notes

- These are **macOS-only** by nature (AppleScript / the macOS Photos library), which each manifest's `post_install` calls out.
- `apple-mail` exposes send/delete/move tools that act on the real mailbox; the install-time checklist lets users prune to a read-only surface. The others are read-mostly (`apple-photos` is read-only except `export`).

Happy to adjust naming, descriptions, or split into separate PRs if you'd prefer.

prs.title: fix(plugins): key hook suppression by registration token, not id(cb)
prs.body:
## Summary

`id(cb)` keys the hook suppression map (`_hook_timeout_suppressed_until`, `_hook_abandoned`) by a CPython memory address. Addresses are reused after the callback object is collected, and list removals shift slots, so a **fresh** callback can inherit a **dead** one's back-off window and abandoned-worker budget and be skipped for reasons that belonged to its predecessor. Current `main` still keys by `id(cb)` (`hermes_cli/plugins_dispatch.py`, `suppression_key = (hook_name, id(cb))`).

## Change

- `register_hook()` mints a registration token (`itertools.count()` on the manager) and records it per callback; the lease removes token and callback together.
- The dispatcher keys suppression by `(hook_name, token)`; direct `_hooks` writes without a token fall back to `id(cb)`.
- The in-flight marker is renamed `run_token` so it is not confused with the registration token.

## Test plan

`tests/hermes_cli/test_hook_suppression_key.py`: distinct tokens per callback; a removed callback loses its token; a fresh same-named callback never inherits a dead key; slot shift after a mid-list removal keeps keys distinct; tokenless callbacks fall back to `id()` and still run; the second callback runs after the first times out; the suppression window sticks to the same callback. Not run locally on this rebase (no pytest in our runtime) — CI is the check. `tests/hermes_cli/test_plugins.py` seeds callbacks through `register_hook`. Observed in a live fleet as a hook family skipped at ~1760/h while the process-wide gate looked healthy; we carry this as a local patch.

## Related

Supersedes #123188 (closed unmerged during a triage sweep; rebased onto current `main` as one commit). Follows #111177 (call identity in `gate_key`).

prs.title: fix(shell-hooks): support transform_tool_result replies and matcher
prs.body:
## Problem

Shell hooks can be registered on `transform_tool_result`, but they can't do what the event exists for:

- **No replacement.** The hook's stdout goes through the default context parser, so the callback always returns `None`. A reply like `{"result": "..."}` never reaches `_apply_transform_tool_result_hook`, which takes the first string return. A shell hook therefore can't withhold or rewrite a tool result.
- **No per-tool scoping.** A `matcher` is dropped at config parse time with the warning "will be ignored at runtime". The hook then fires, and spawns a process, for every tool result.

## Change

- `transform_tool_result` honors `matcher` like `pre_tool_call` / `post_tool_call`. This applies to the runtime callback and to `hermes hooks test --for-tool`, which share one event set (`_MATCHER_EVENTS`).
- A new response dialect: `{"result": "<string>"}` replaces the tool result. As with a Python hook, `""` blanks it. `{}`, a missing key, or a non-string `result` keeps the original.
- `hermes hooks test` prints an empty replacement instead of reporting that the hook contributed nothing.
- Return annotations now allow the string reply. The docs and the module docstring describe the dialect, and the `matcher` note mentions `transform_tool_result`.

## Tests

- New tests in `tests/agent/test_shell_hooks.py` cover the parser, the matcher kept at parse time, and the callback, which honors the matcher and returns the replacement. `tests/hermes_cli/test_hooks_cli.py` covers `--for-tool` filtering and a result-dependent hook under `hooks test`. Of the 10 new tests, the 8 that exercise the new behaviour fail on `main`. The 2 "keep the result" guards (`{}` and non-string `result`) pass there too.
- I ran `test_shell_hooks.py`, `test_hooks_cli.py` and every test file that mentions `transform_tool_result`: 9 failed / 427 passed before the change, 1 failed / 435 passed after. The one remaining failure, `test_tool_defs_cache_key_sees_config_replacement_with_pinned_mtime`, fails on `main` too.
- End to end: `test_handle_function_call_applies_shell_transform` registers a real shell hook through the config path. The hook is a script run with `sys.executable` that prints `{"result": "withheld"}`, with `matcher: web_search`. The test stubs only the tool itself: `handle_function_call("web_search", {})` returns `withheld` and `"terminal"` stays raw. On `main` the same test gets `raw`. I ran it on Windows only.

## Notes

- The hook's exit code doesn't gate the reply: exits 0, 1 and 2 are all parsed (blocking stays `pre_tool_call`-only). A spawn error or a timeout keeps the original result (fail-open).
- Related: #128683 / #128688, the sequential-path hook order. This PR is independent of that fix.

prs.title: feat(plugin-catalog): add codex-theme plugin (v1.0.0)
prs.body:
## Add `codex-theme` (desktop theme plugin) — v1.0.0

**Plugin:** https://github.com/ethanz-code/hermes-codex-theme @ `5a96907a63c1d83b801c0e754123f1bf2bc5b09f` (tag `v1.0.0`)

Reworked v1.0.0 submission replacing #143006 (closed with notes). The plugin repo history has been rebuilt as a clean 7-commit linear story so this first public version is `1.0.0` end to end — entry, manifest and runtime log string all agree, no re-pin chain to review.

A graphite-on-paper theme for the Hermes Desktop chat, after the design language of the OpenAI Codex app and ChatGPT: dual light/dark palettes that follow the system appearance, a 10px radius system, hairline borders instead of shadows, the 6/10/16/24 spacing rhythm, 1.7 root line height, and an 880px reading column with 768/880/992px presets.

### Surfaces used

Desktop plugin SDK only (`desktop/plugin.js`, `plugin.yaml` manifest):

- `THEMES_AREA` — one theme (`colors` + `darkColors` + `typography` + `customCSS`, the same theming surface user skins use)
- `PALETTE_AREA` — two quiet rows (reapply theme / open settings)
- `ctx.registerSettingsPage` — appearance mode (follow system / dark / light) + reading-column width (Narrow 768px / Standard 880px / Wide 992px)
- `ctx.i18n` — en + zh strings for the settings page

### Validation

`hermes plugins validate . --install-deps` at the pinned commit is green (real output):

```text
✓ manifest — plugin.yaml parses
✓ manifest fields — name, version, description present
✓ requires_hermes — spec '>=0.22.0' parses
✓ config schema — not declared
✓ requires_env — all entries UPPER_SNAKE
✓ oauth — not declared
✓ loadable — entry: desktop/plugin.js
✓ python dependencies — none declared
✓ capability probe — skipped (no __init__.py)
✓ built-in tool collisions — no tools to check
✓ security scan — safe
✓ no core override — no runtime rebinds of Hermes core
✓ desktop surface — stays inside the plugin SDK surface
⚠ no __init__.py — capability probe skipped (manifest-only plugin)
◆ Isolation — portable plugin (no Python): runs anywhere

Validation passed.
```

### Disclosure (rule 13)

- No network calls, no telemetry, no credentials, no background processes.
- One plugin-scoped `ctx.storage` record for settings-page choices (appearance mode + reading-column width); a first-install flag in the same store is written once to decide whether the theme takes over on first load.
- `customCSS` is injected by the app's own theme engine from the theme object, like user skins — visual only, no behavior changes.
- No core patching: everything registers through the Desktop plugin SDK only (`THEMES_AREA`, `PALETTE_AREA`, `ctx.registerSettingsPage`, `ctx.i18n`).
- The theme deliberately does **not** write user-configurable settings (e.g. `--chat-text-scale` stays owned by Settings → Appearance) and applies itself only on first install, never overriding a later manual theme choice.

### Screenshots

`assets/cover.png` (2:1 banner) and `assets/theme-{light,dark}.png` (rendered specimens, referenced by `image:` / `screenshots:` at the pinned sha). The README renders from the pinned tree.

> Note on rule 15: this is a community-tier theme *inspired by* the Codex/ChatGPT design language, not a vendor-lookalike shipped under Nous branding — the README carries an explicit "independent community theme, not affiliated with OpenAI" note. Happy to rename if maintainers prefer a non-vendor name.

prs.title: catalog: add adaptive-reasoning-router (community)
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds one catalog entry: `plugin-catalog/adaptive-reasoning-router.yaml`, pinning [linyubin/adaptive-reasoning-router](https://github.com/linyubin/adaptive-reasoning-router) @ `3d9feb42153cf7ebd3f0e923bc33dc06c389eb95` (validated at exactly this pinned commit with `hermes plugins validate` — all checks green, security scan safe, no core override, isolation host).

## What the plugin does

Per-turn reasoning-effort routing. Today Hermes has a single global `agent.reasoning_effort`: set it high and trivial questions burn deep-thinking tokens and latency; set it low and hard problems get shallow answers. This plugin routes per turn:

- **light** (greetings, acks, time/date/weather lookups, "remember X", bare arithmetic) → `reasoning_effort: low`
- **medium** (short factual questions like "还有多少空间") → `medium`
- **complex / unrecognized** → untouched, keeps the user's configured effort

Classification is pure in-process regex (Chinese + English patterns), zero added latency, no extra LLM calls.

## Hermes surfaces used

- `ctx.register_middleware("llm_request", ...)` — the public behavior-changing middleware only. The rewrite happens after Hermes assembles the provider payload (so the plugin edits the exact wire fields the provider emits: top-level `reasoning_effort`, `reasoning.effort`, `extra_body.reasoning.effort`).
- No tools, no hooks, no provider profiles, no env vars, no Desktop SDK surface.

## Safety properties (relevant to rules 3/6/9/12)

- **Rule 6 (capabilities match reality):** `provides_middleware: [llm_request]` only; verified by the capability probe.
- **Rule 9 (no core overrides):** the plugin never touches Hermes internals — `no core override` check green. The original request dict is never mutated; the middleware returns a rewritten copy per the contract.
- **Prompt-cache safe by design:** the rewrite applies only when `api_call_count == 0` (the main loop's first call of a turn). Tool-loop follow-ups keep the session's configured effort, so mid-turn reasoning continuity is preserved.
- **Rule 12 (approvals/unattended):** fail-open — any error leaves the request untouched; nothing waits on a person.
- **GLM-5.x nuance:** GLM rejects disabled thinking, so the plugin only moves the effort knob and leaves `thinking` enabled.

## Rule 13 disclosures

- No network calls to third-party services. No telemetry or usage reporting. No background processes. No stored credentials, no reads outside the plugin's own scope — pure in-process string matching and payload rewrite.
- Known limitation (also in the README): heuristics are conservative — short ambiguous messages ("帮我看看这个") stay at the configured effort rather than being downgraded.

## Checklist

- [x] Public repo, owner-submitted (I own `linyubin/adaptive-reasoning-router`)
- [x] Full 40-char SHA pin, `version` quoted
- [x] `hermes plugins validate` green at the pinned commit (ran locally against a fresh clone checked out at the pin)
- [x] Entry schema fields per `plugin-catalog/README.md`
- [x] License: MIT; English-first README

prs.title: feat(plugin-catalog): add yandex-disk entry
prs.body:
## What this adds

One catalog entry, `plugin-catalog/yandex-disk.yaml`. The catalog key is `yandex-disk`, the manifest name, as with `yandex` and `yandex_calendar`. The plugin is MIT-licensed and registers **up to fifteen tools** in one toolset, `yandex_disk`. They browse, search, read, write, upload, download, copy, move, share, delete and restore files on the user's Yandex Disk over its REST API.

- Repository: https://github.com/akinfold/hermes-yandex-disk (public, MIT, owner submission).
- Pinned commit: `0d4e8b293bb64322def34d94f1bd52424ce73ea5`, the commit of the annotated tag `v0.6.1`. It is released as **v0.6.1** on GitHub Releases and on PyPI as `hermes-yandex-disk` 0.6.1. The plugin lives in `hermes_yandex_disk/`, hence `subdir`.
- The tier is self-declared `community`. This is my third Yandex entry, after `yandex` (#141797) and `yandex_calendar` (#142267). Unlike those two, this plugin touches **local files**: `yadisk_upload` can read one and `yadisk_download` writes one. Most of the disclosure below is about that and about deleting.

0.6.0 and 0.6.1 were made for this listing (akinfold/hermes-yandex-disk#16 and #17):

- `yadisk_search` is declared (rule 6).
- An undeclared alias for the token is gone (rules 6 and 11).
- `plugin.yaml` carries `requires_hermes: ">=0.21.5"` (rule 14).
- Every local path goes through Hermes' shared file-safety rules and then through the plugin's own rules (below).
- A settings lookup that Hermes refuses comes back as an error result.
- `YANDEX_DISK_BASE_URL` must be HTTPS.

## Hermes surfaces used

- `ctx.register_tool(...)`, called once per tool, all in toolset `yandex_disk`, with `requires_env=["YANDEX_DISK_OAUTH_TOKEN"]`. The tools are `yadisk_disk_info`, `yadisk_list`, `yadisk_search`, `yadisk_read_file`, `yadisk_trash_list`, `yadisk_download`, `yadisk_mkdir`, `yadisk_write_file`, `yadisk_upload`, `yadisk_copy`, `yadisk_move`, `yadisk_trash_restore`, `yadisk_publish`, `yadisk_delete` and `yadisk_trash_empty`.
  - Each tool has a `check_fn` that only checks the token is set, without a network call. A lookup Hermes refuses counts as "not set".
- `register()` reads `YANDEX_DISK_ACTIONS` and registers only the tools it allows; unset means all. A tool left out is never registered, so the agent never sees it, rather than seeing it refused at call time.
- `yadisk_search` has one more gate. Yandex grants its search endpoint per application, not per token scope. So when `search` is allowed, `register()` sends one search request to find out, and registers the tool only if Yandex answers it successfully.
  - The probe is a single attempt with no retries. httpx's connect, read and write timeouts are each capped at 2 seconds. That is chosen to fit well inside Hermes' default 10-second plugin load deadline.
  - It is a per-phase cap, not a total, and DNS resolution is outside it. If a load did overrun, Hermes would drop all of the plugin's tools until the next start.

No hooks, no middleware, no config schema, no slash commands, no web provider, no Desktop surface. `kind: standalone`, manifest name `yandex-disk`. `client.py` and `paths.py` import nothing from Hermes. The Hermes imports are all inside `try/except ImportError`:

- `get_provider_env` from `agent.web_search_provider` (in `_compat.py`);
- `get_read_block_error`, `get_write_denied_error` and `is_write_approval_required` from `agent.file_safety` (in `local_files.py`; see "Things I'd rather flag");
- `get_hermes_home` and `get_default_hermes_root` from `hermes_constants` (in `local_files.py`).

## Disclosure (rule 13)

- **Network calls to a third-party service.** All REST over HTTPS to `https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk`, with `Authorization: OAuth <token>`.
  - **Transfers.** Uploads and downloads take two steps. The API hands out a single-use URL on a Yandex transfer host, and the bytes then go to that URL **without** the token.
  - **Deferred operations.** Yandex may defer copies, moves, deletes, restores, bin operations and uploads. The plugin then polls, with the token, the operation URL the API returns (or, for a local-file upload or `yadisk_write_file`, one it builds from the base URL and the operation id), every 0.5 seconds. After 60 seconds the tool returns an error saying the operation is still being processed; it may still complete on Yandex's side.
  - **Upload from a URL.** `yadisk_upload` with a `url` makes **Yandex** fetch that public URL into the Disk. The plugin never downloads it.
  - **Retries.** Responses 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504, and transport errors such as a refused connection or a timeout, are retried up to three times. `Retry-After` is honoured up to 30 seconds; otherwise the waits are 1, 2 and 4 seconds. This covers API calls, operation polls and the upload PUT of `yadisk_write_file`. It does not cover the load-time probe, which is one attempt, or the download byte stream. A local-file upload whose PUT fails after bytes have gone out returns an error instead of retrying, because the retry would resend an already-read file; that is a bug I'll fix in the next release.
- **Load-time request.** Loading the plugin sends at most one `GET /resources/search?query=a&limit=1&offset=0` with the configured token, to the API base. Nothing is sent when no token is configured, when `YANDEX_DISK_ACTIONS` leaves `search` out, or when the same process already holds a verdict for that token.
- **Local files.** `yadisk_upload` with `local_path` reads a file on the machine Hermes runs on and sends its bytes, unredacted, to the user's Disk. `yadisk_download` writes one there. Two sets of rules apply, and either can refuse a path. Symlinks are resolved first, and a download destination is checked before it is even probed. A refusal comes before the first request to Yandex, so nothing is left behind on the Disk.
  - **Hermes' shared rules.** These are the rules in `agent.file_safety`, the deny-lists Hermes' file tools share. Reads are checked with `get_read_block_error`. Writes are checked with `get_write_denied_error`, then `is_write_approval_required`, which is treated as a refusal because a tool cannot ask a person. In Hermes v2026.9.24 through `main` they refuse:
    - for upload: Hermes' credential stores (`.env`, `auth.json` and the like) and any `.env` file;
    - for download: credential files (Hermes' `.env`, SSH and cloud-provider keys and logins, `~/.netrc` and so on), Hermes' `sessions`, `mcp-tokens`, `pairing`, `vault` and `browser-profile` directories, `~/.ssh/config`, and anything outside `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT` when that is set.
  - **The plugin's own rules.** Hermes' `write_file` checks more than the shared rules, and sending a file off the machine is more than reading it into the conversation. So the plugin also refuses:
    - for upload: anything in Hermes' own directory (the active `HERMES_HOME` and the root above its profiles), which holds `config.yaml`, sessions and memories, and anything in the home directories that hold keys and logins (SSH, AWS, GnuPG, Kubernetes, Docker, Azure, and the GitHub and Google Cloud CLIs);
    - for download: anything in Hermes' own directory (`config.yaml` with the approval settings, profiles, plugins, skills, memories, cron jobs), anything in a project's `.hermes` directory, files agents read as instructions (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `SOUL.md` and `.cursorrules`, in any directory and any letter case), and system locations (`/etc/`, `/boot/`, `/usr/lib/systemd/`, the macOS `/private` equivalents and the Docker socket).
  - **Docker.** The official Docker image keeps the agent's home and workspace inside `HERMES_HOME` (`/opt/data/home` and `/opt/data/workspace`). Those two folders count as the agent's, not Hermes', and the other rules still apply in them; the key directories under `/opt/data/home` are refused for upload too.
  - **What is not covered** (the README states the first point's first sentence and the last point):
    - Any other file the Hermes process can read can be uploaded, unredacted. Hermes' `read_file` would mask a private-key block or a credential value it recognises.
    - Any other path the Hermes process can write can be created by `yadisk_download`, and with `overwrite=true` an existing file there can be replaced, for example a shell start-up file such as `~/.bashrc`. Hermes' `write_file` has the same reach, but here the bytes come from the Disk.
    - Hermes' `write_file` also honours `security.protected_instruction_extra_patterns` from `config.yaml`, which the plugin does not read.
    - Anything else the agent runs as the same user, such as a terminal, reaches the same files.
  - **Without `agent.file_safety`** (outside Hermes, or on a Hermes that moves it), a stand-in refuses `.env` files in both directions. The plugin's own rules apply either way.
  - **Withholding the tools.** The README shows how to withhold both tools. The `write` group includes `upload`, so it names the write tools one by one.
  - `YANDEX_DISK_ROOT` confines Disk paths only, not local ones. The README says so; versions before 0.6.0 said "every path".
- **Default scope.** Every tool is registered unless `YANDEX_DISK_ACTIONS` narrows the list (`yadisk_search` only when the load-time probe allows it). That includes:
  - `yadisk_delete` with `permanently=true`;
  - `yadisk_trash_empty`, which destroys bin items or the whole bin;
  - `yadisk_publish`, which creates a public link anyone with the URL can open;
  - the write tools, which with `overwrite=true` replace existing files.

  The variable takes groups (`read`, `download`, `write`, `share`, `delete`, `all`) and single tools. A name that matches nothing is dropped, so a typo can only withhold a tool. Deletes go to the bin unless `permanently` is set. Writes, copies, moves and uploads refuse an existing destination unless `overwrite` is set.
- **`YANDEX_DISK_ROOT`.** When set, every Disk path, whether invented by the model or copied from an earlier result, resolves inside that folder, and an escape is refused before any request. The bin is filtered by origin, and emptying the whole bin is refused because the bin is account-wide.
- **Endpoint override.** If set, `YANDEX_DISK_BASE_URL` replaces the API base; it is documented for testing against a stub. It must be an `https://` URL with no user name, password, query or fragment, and anything else is refused before any request. The host is not checked, so the token goes to whatever HTTPS host it names.
- **Credentials.** The only credential is `YANDEX_DISK_OAUTH_TOKEN`, which is required.
  - It and the optional settings are read through `get_provider_env`, which resolves through Hermes' config layer and the profile secret scope.
  - On Hermes v0.21.6 and later, under a multiplexed gateway with no profile bound, that lookup raises `UnscopedSecretError`. Since 0.6.1 every handler returns it as an error result.
  - On v2026.9.24 (0.21.5), the entry's floor, `get_provider_env` swallows that error and falls back to the process environment.
  - The plugin never logs, stores, refreshes or rotates the token.
- **Reads outside its own data:** only the local files the agent names to `yadisk_upload`, as above. The plugin itself opens no `.env`, no `auth.json` and no credential store.
- **Untrusted input.** File names and contents on the Disk can be written by other people, through shared folders or files saved from public links. They reach the model as tool output from `yadisk_list`, `yadisk_search`, `yadisk_read_file` and `yadisk_trash_list`. `yadisk_read_file` returns text only, up to 1 MiB by default, and downloads are capped at 256 MiB by default.
- **Shell commands / subprocesses:** none.
- **Long-running background processes:** none.
- **Telemetry / usage reporting:** none, and no update check (rule 3).
- **Caching / storage.** The search verdict is cached in memory, per token, for the life of the process. A download is written to a temporary `.yadisk-<uuid>.part` file beside the target and moved over it once complete, so a failed transfer never destroys the existing copy.
- **Unattended runs (rule 12).** Nothing waits for a person.
  - Each HTTP request has a 30-second connect, read and write timeout by default (`YANDEX_DISK_TIMEOUT`). That bounds a stalled connection, not a whole call, and nothing limits a call's total time. One request with its retries can take several minutes, and deferred-operation polling adds at least 60 seconds. An upload (no size limit) or a download (up to 256 MiB by default) runs for as long as its bytes keep moving.
  - API, path, local-file and settings failures all come back as `{"error": ...}`.
  - The write and delete tools do not ask for confirmation themselves. Under cron or the gateway, an agent that has them acts with no one watching; that is what `YANDEX_DISK_ACTIONS` is for.

## Facts a reviewer will want

- **Dependencies:** none declared. `plugin.yaml` has no `python_dependencies`, and an install from `subdir` never reads the root `pyproject.toml`. The only third-party runtime import is the `httpx` that Hermes core ships; everything else is the standard library or the Hermes modules listed above.
- **No core overrides, no self-updater, no binaries, no committed bytecode** (rules 3, 9, 17). The plugin directory holds nine `.py` files, `plugin.yaml` and an empty `py.typed`.
- **Capabilities match the code:** up to 15 tools, 0 hooks, 0 middleware, `requires_env: [YANDEX_DISK_OAUTH_TOKEN]` — the same lists as `plugin.yaml`.
  - With a token whose application may search, all fifteen register. Without one, as in the admission CI, there are fourteen, and `validate` warns that `yadisk_search` was declared but not registered.
  - `YANDEX_DISK_ACTIONS` can only remove tools.
- **Validation at this pin.** A clean `git archive` export of `hermes_yandex_disk/` at the pinned commit was checked with Hermes `main` (`5894e750c3`). It ran in a fresh environment built from Hermes' `uv.lock` with core dependencies only and no extras, as the admission CI builds it:

  ```text
  $ hermes plugins validate --install-deps hermes_yandex_disk
  ✓ manifest — plugin.yaml parses
  ✓ manifest fields — name, version, description present
  ✓ requires_hermes — spec '>=0.21.5' parses
  ✓ config schema — not declared
  ✓ requires_env — all entries UPPER_SNAKE
  ✓ oauth — not declared
  ✓ loadable — entry: __init__.py
  ✓ python dependencies — none declared
  ✓ capability probe — register() ran in isolation
  ✓ declared tools — matches registrations
  ✓ declared hooks — matches registrations
  ✓ declared middleware — matches registrations
  ✓ built-in tool collisions — no collisions
  ✓ security scan — safe
  ✓ no core override — no runtime rebinds of Hermes core
  ⚠ provides_tools declares yadisk_search but register() did not register them
  ⚠ private core imports (catalog rule 9: public surfaces only; these can break on
  any release): local_files.py:88 agent.file_safety.get_read_block_error; 
  local_files.py:88 agent.file_safety.get_write_denied_error; local_files.py:88 
  agent.file_safety.is_write_approval_required. Use ctx.* / documented plugin 
  APIs, or open an issue for the seam you need.
  ◆ Isolation — runs in the plugin host (plugins.isolation: host)

  Validation passed.
  ```

  `scripts/scan_plugin_payloads.py` exits 0 on a fresh export of the same tree. `scripts/validate_plugin_catalog.py` passes on this file and on the whole directory with it. The install scanners of Hermes v2026.9.24 and `main` both rate the plugin directory and the repository root `safe`.
- **`requires_hermes: ">=0.21.5"`** is set in the entry and in `plugin.yaml`. It is the oldest Hermes the plugin's CI covers. The plugin's CI runs on every pull request, every week and before every release. It installs the build with Hermes' official installer into three Hermes versions: v2026.9.24 (0.21.5), the latest release, and `main`. Each time it checks that Hermes lists the plugin as enabled, loads it and gives the agent its tools. The GitHub Release and the PyPI upload wait for that check.
- **Tests:** 298 unit tests at the pinned commit, offline and keyless, run on Python 3.11–3.14 with 99.9 % coverage.
  - They run against an in-memory fake of the API that speaks the real protocol: deferred operations, the two-step transfers, the error envelope and the search 403.
  - 22 hand-picked single-guard mutations of the local-path rules, the base-URL check and the settings-error handling each turn the suite red. Not every guard has a test of its own yet: the suite stays green when any of these is removed: the base-URL fragment check, the user-name check (the test URL also carries a password), the Docker-socket check, the `/private/etc/` prefix, `CLAUDE.md`, or any key directory other than SSH and AWS. I'll add those tests with the retry fix.
  - The rules were also exercised against the real `agent.file_safety` and `hermes_constants` of Hermes v2026.9.24 and `main`.
  - The live end-to-end suite ran on 0.6.1's tree inside Hermes v0.22.5, and on 0.6.0's inside v0.22.5 and `main`. It creates, publishes and permanently deletes throwaway files on a test account. The ten file tests passed every time, including the check that a `.env` file is never uploaded.
  - The three search tests never passed in these runs. Yandex was not indexing new files that day, so they skipped, with one exception. On 0.6.0's tree in v0.22.5, the confinement test failed before it searched: Yandex reported the upload of its marker file as a failed operation, although the file had been saved intact. `yadisk_write_file` and `yadisk_upload` pass such a report on as an error.
  - A manual check found a new file still unindexed after three minutes, while older items were found. The search tests passed on 0.5.2, and the search code has not changed since.
  - `ruff`, `radon` (nothing rated C or worse), `bandit` and CodeQL are clean.

## Things I'd rather flag than have found in review

1. **A private import, on purpose.** `local_files.py` imports `get_read_block_error`, `get_write_denied_error` and `is_write_approval_required` from `agent.file_safety`, and `validate` warns about it under rule 9.
   - I chose it over a home-grown copy of Hermes' deny-lists, which would drift from them. With it, upload refuses what Hermes' shared read check refuses, and download refuses what its write checks refuse, including anything outside `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT`; that variable does not limit what is uploaded. Hermes' bundled `openai-codex` image plugin calls the same read check on local files, and `krea` (on `main`), `openai`, `openrouter` and `xai` call it through `agent.file_safety.raise_if_read_blocked`.
   - The plugin's own rules on top of it are its own copies: the instruction-file names, the system prefixes and the key directories, taken from `tools/file_tools_write_guards.py` and `agent/file_safety.py`.
   - If you'd rather expose these checks as a documented plugin surface, I'll open an issue for them, together with one for `to_agent_visible_cache_path`, which my mail plugin imports.
2. **Every tool is on by default, permanent delete included.** The bin is the default and `permanently` is an explicit argument, but an agent with the `delete` group can still destroy files and empty the bin, and `yadisk_publish` makes a link anyone can open. The description says `read` gives a read-only Disk, and the first known issue and the README's quick start point new users at it. If you'd rather a catalog install start read-only, I'll change the default in a release and re-pin. Existing users would then lose tools on update until they set the variable.
3. **Upload sends what it reads, unredacted.** The key and login directories and Hermes' own directory are refused. Any other readable file, for example a project config with a token in it, can still go to the user's Disk byte for byte, where Hermes' `read_file` would mask credential values it recognises. With `yadisk_publish`, the file could then be shared. The README and the third known issue say so and show how to withhold the tool. If you want something stricter, such as content sniffing for private keys, I'll add it.
4. **`YANDEX_DISK_BASE_URL` accepts any HTTPS host,** and the deferred-operation poll sends the token to whatever operation URL the API returns, also unchecked. Whoever can set the variable already holds the token in the same profile, and with the default base the operation URL comes from the API the token is for. If you want the base pinned to `https://cloud-api.yandex.net` and the poll to the same origin, I'll do that in a release.
5. **The load-time probe:** one request to Yandex during `register()`, as described above. A 2xx, 401 or 403 is a verdict and is cached per token for the life of the process. Any other failure — a network error, 429, 5xx or another status — hides search for that load only. In the admission CI there is no token, so no request is made.
6. **`get_provider_env`, not `get_secret`,** as in my other two entries. Rule 11 names `agent.secret_scope.get_secret` for declared secrets, so this is a deviation from its text, and it matters on the floor. On v2026.9.24, `get_provider_env` falls back to the process environment where `get_secret` would raise. From v0.21.6 on, both raise. If you want `get_secret`, I'll switch in a release.

prs.title: fix(a2a): keep late replies and refuse a shared port
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Two bugs in the A2A platform adapter that we hit on a Windows host with several agents talking over A2A.

**1. A reply that comes after the server stops waiting is lost.** When a blocking `message/send` runs longer than
`A2A_REPLY_TIMEOUT`, or a `message/stream` client disconnects, the task is marked `TASK_STATE_FAILED`. The agent
keeps working, the gateway logs the finished response, but the task is already terminal, so `GetTask` keeps
returning FAILED and the reply is gone. The docs said the opposite ("a late reply is stored, not discarded").

With this change the task is detached instead of failed: it stays `TASK_STATE_WORKING`, the caller gets that task
back, and a daemon thread records the reply when it arrives, so `GetTask`, `ListTasks` and push notifications see it.
A task that never gets a reply still fails, at the existing orphan ceiling (24 h).

**2. Two profiles can share one A2A port on Windows.** The server is a stdlib `ThreadingHTTPServer`, which sets
`SO_REUSEADDR`. On Windows that lets a second socket bind a port that is already listening; with multiplex profiles
we saw two gateways on 9902 and requests split between them. The server now binds with `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` on
Windows, so the second bind fails loudly (the existing `bind_failed` path). Elsewhere the stdlib behaviour is kept:
there `SO_REUSEADDR` only lets a restart reuse a port in TIME_WAIT. A restart right after closing a server with
TIME_WAIT connections still binds on Windows (checked).

## Related Issue

Related to #91687 (long A2A jobs). This PR does not add non-blocking sends (#91688, #94880, #103453 cover that);
it only stops losing the work when the server gives up waiting. The question this raises for the spec (a blocking
send MUST wait for a terminal state, a server cannot always keep waiting) is in
https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/discussions/2277.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- `plugins/platforms/a2a/adapter.py`: `_detach()` / `_finish()` replace "fail on timeout or disconnect" in
  `message/send` and `message/stream`; `_ExclusiveHTTPServer` for the listener.
- `tests/plugins/test_a2a_plugin.py`: the timeout test now expects WORKING and then the late reply; a ceiling test;
  a test that a second server on the same port fails to bind.
- `tests/plugins/test_a2a_phase23.py`: the stream-disconnect test now expects the task to stay WORKING, then complete
  with the late reply and release the active request.
- `website/docs/user-guide/messaging/a2a.md`, `plugins/platforms/a2a/README.md`: what happens past
  `A2A_REPLY_TIMEOUT`.

Behaviour change to note: a blocking caller whose request outlives `A2A_REPLY_TIMEOUT` now gets a WORKING task
instead of a FAILED one, and has to follow it with `GetTask`.

## How to Test

1. `pytest tests/plugins/test_a2a_plugin.py tests/plugins/test_a2a_phase23.py tests/plugins/test_a2a_tools_gate.py plugins/platforms/a2a -m ""`
   (the round-trip tests are marked `integration`, so plain `pytest` skips them): 160 passed, 1 skipped.
2. Without the adapter change, the four new or updated tests fail.
3. We run this on a live gateway: a reply after the timeout lands in the task; a second profile on a used port fails
   to start its A2A platform.

prs.title: plugin-catalog: add kinocut (local video editing)
prs.body:
Adds Kinocut to the plugin catalog. I maintain Kinocut through KyaniteLabs.

Kinocut gives agents video editing tools through a local MCP server. The plugin contains the configuration and skills; FFmpeg and ffprobe do the local media processing. Ordinary local edits don't need an account or API key.

- Source: [2bb755d191ea00885a6861d61bb39965b13122f4](https://github.com/KyaniteLabs/kinocut/tree/2bb755d191ea00885a6861d61bb39965b13122f4/plugins/kinocut), subdirectory `plugins/kinocut`.
- Plugin bundle: `1.16.7`. Runtime: `uvx kinocut==1.16.4` over stdio.
- Format: Portable Agent Plugins v1. No native Hermes tools, hooks or middleware.

First launch downloads Kinocut and its dependencies from PyPI. It requires uv and FFmpeg on PATH. URL inputs download the requested media, and some font and model features download assets from GitHub. Revideo's explicit install/render workflow runs `npm ci` and may download renderer dependencies.

Kinocut's optional vision calls are off by default; an inherited API key or `use_ai=true` cannot enable them. The docs explain how to use Hermes's image tools with the user's chosen provider, including local models. When explicitly configured in local or remote mode, Kinocut's legacy product adapter sends the selected image to an Anthropic-compatible endpoint; it doesn't inherit Hermes's model settings. The separate QC worker sends sampled frames to Anthropic, requires remote mode and cannot be enabled by a local or custom product configuration. Color grading itself runs locally through FFmpeg.

Revideo telemetry is off by default. Hyperframes child processes receive telemetry opt-outs, skip update checks and have known provider credentials removed. Capture and snapshot commands disable the optional vision/description step. Without explicit telemetry consent, previews are limited to the two versions whose browser opt-out was verified (`0.8.104` and `0.8.140`), and Docker rendering is refused. These controls aren't a network sandbox; requested downloads and explicit consent still matter.

Existing outputs require explicit `overwrite=true`. Existing non-media files are refused unless Kinocut can verify that the same job created them. The output checks protect agent configuration directories, including `.hermes`. Shipped skills avoid unpinned installers and host-configuration changes. The README also includes an optional Hermes tool allowlist to reduce the schemas loaded into context.

The [1.16.4 runtime](https://github.com/KyaniteLabs/kinocut/releases/tag/v1.16.4) was published before updating the launcher pins and catalog commit. PyPI, npm, GitHub releases and the official MCP Registry agree on the runtime version; compatibility package `mcp-video==1.6.19` pins it too. Source CI and a fresh Python 3.14 install passed, including rendering, explicit overwrite, protected-path, default-off vision and Hyperframes child checks. The official catalog validator reports zero errors or warnings. Upstream GitHub checks are held for maintainer action.

prs.title: feat(plugins): support native browser-login backends
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Adds `PluginContext.register_login_backend()` so third-party password managers can use the existing browser autofill tools. Integrations remain standalone plugins rather than in-tree backends.

The implementation reuses the plugin manager's ownership and unload lifecycle. It adds no model tool or dependency. An optional login-destination hook lets plugins implement their manager's website-matching policy for passwords and saved one-time codes without adding vendor-specific domain rules to core.

## Related Issue

Addresses the core extension point requested in #110759. The Proton Pass integration itself is not included.

## Type of Change

New feature, with regression tests and documentation.

## Changes Made

- **Registration and routing** — `agent/vault_backends/registry.py` and `hermes_cli/plugins.py` register concrete backend classes per profile. Built-in names, duplicate names, and overlapping handle prefixes are rejected. Unloading a plugin releases its registrations.
- **Availability and configuration** — `agent/vault_backends/base.py` adds constructor-free `is_available(config)` checks. Probes and constructors receive separate copies of the complete `vault.<name>` subsection, including plugin-defined keys. Third-party sources require literal `enabled: true`; local-first ordering and built-in opt-out behavior are preserved.
- **CLI and Desktop integration** — `hermes_cli/vault.py`, `tui_gateway/methods_vault.py`, and the existing unlock tool discover plugin sources and support explicit activation. Token-based providers do not receive an unlock prompt. Unknown, disabled, and non-unlockable sources are rejected before prompting.
- **Credential destinations** — `LoginBackend.matches_origin()` defaults to exact-origin matching. Password and saved-handle OTP fills share the same predicate for tab selection and the pre-retrieval check. Empty saved origins, including `allowed_origins=("",)`, deny without invoking the predicate or retrieving a credential.
- **OTP authorization** — fixes the saved-handle `browser_vault(action="enter_code", handle=...)` path, which previously retrieved a handle’s code without authorizing its destination. Unknown handles, non-login records, metadata errors, and disallowed destinations now refuse before code retrieval or a fallback prompt. Reported retrieval failures return a safe error; the user can explicitly choose `manual: true` with the same handle, preserving fresh metadata and destination checks. Absent/disabled OTP still permits a manual prompt. Existing 1Password/Bitwarden fallback behavior is unchanged. The host advertises `LoginBackend.otp_origin_bound` so plugins can refuse automatic OTP on older unsafe cores.
- **Origin normalization** — preserve IPv6 brackets when converting a saved website URL to an origin. Regression tests cover default and explicit ports and repeated normalization.
- **Documentation** — the developer guide specifies registration, configuration, authentication, lifetime, thread behavior, and credential handling. The user guide retains its existing walkthroughs and examples. Changes cover plugin activation and matching policies, with targeted corrections to storage, headless authentication, and security statements.

## Security boundaries

Only literal `True` from a destination predicate authorizes a fill. Predicate failures deny without exposing exception text. The final fill script still checks the **selected origin and inspection nonce**: navigation to another origin rejects the write, even when that origin also satisfies the plugin's policy.

Cards and addresses remain exact-origin. Saved-handle OTP routing now obeys the login’s destination policy; manual entry without a handle remains available through a prompt naming the destination. Reported OTP metadata/retrieval/transport failures return fixed diagnostics rather than raw provider or secret-bearing transport errors. Native plugins are trusted Python code, not a sandbox. Providers must keep credentials out of metadata, logs, and errors. General provider-error sanitization is outside this PR. Invalid non-string registration names are rejected without logging their values.

## How to Test

```sh
scripts/run_tests.sh \
  tests/agent/test_login_backend_discovery.py \
  tests/agent/test_vault_backend_plugins.py \
  tests/agent/test_vault_backends.py \
  tests/agent/test_vault_store.py \
  tests/hermes_cli/test_vault.py \
  tests/hermes_cli/test_vault_sources_shape.py \
  tests/hermes_cli/test_plugin_ownership_ledger.py \
  tests/tui_gateway/test_vault_methods.py \
  tests/tools/test_browser_vault.py \
  tests/tools/test_vault_plugin_unlock.py \
  tests/tools/test_vault_origin_policy.py \
  tests/tools/test_vault_otp.py \
  tests/tools/test_browser_eval_supervisor_path.py \
  tests/tools/test_browser_supervisor_healthcheck.py \
  tests/tools/test_browser_supervisor_reconnect.py \
  tests/tools/test_bot_desktop_browser_fence.py

cd website
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build -- --locale en
```

### Initial local verification

Verified locally on macOS with Python 3.13.15:

- **200 focused core tests passed**, including real temporary-profile discovery, A → B → A isolation, ownership lifecycle, activation, unlock handling, and origin-policy behavior. The canonical per-file runner used an isolated home and a temporary scratch-path override; that runner-only change was excluded from commits and restored before pushing.
- The empty-origin and registration-log regressions both failed with the pre-fix behavior and passed after the fixes. The IPv6 normalization regressions also failed before their fix and passed afterward.
- Real Chrome/CDP tests in the standalone plugin’s synthetic suite exercised password, automatic single/split OTP, and explicitly requested manual OTP fills, related-subdomain selection, an untouched decoy tab, deceptive-hostname refusal, non-disclosing results, and rejection after navigation to another permitted origin. The core suite separately verifies empty-origin and non-login refusal, default/custom matching, safe errors, and explicit manual retries that repeat metadata/origin checks and cannot bypass a refusal.
- The standalone Proton companion passed **101 tests** with both current and minimum dependencies, including RFC 6238 vectors, built-in-only TOTP selection, explicit default-off opt-in, compatibility refusal on older cores, and fresh profile/identity/vault/item/origin checks. This private companion and its dependencies remain outside the PR. No real Proton account or Keychain access was used.
- Project-configured Ruff, plugin-compatibility checks on changed Python files, and `git diff --check` passed.
- The English documentation production build passed. It reported two broken anchors on unchanged pages: `bot-mode` and `codex-app-server-runtime`.

### Merge revalidation

Merged upstream `main` at `ea114c3e98c3339e13004adfc6098cf28ed7d754` without rewriting existing commits. The OTP handler retains upstream's Bot Desktop lease fence and passes the explicit manual-entry option through it. The write-time takeover check remains intact. Two PR tests now use `hermes_yaml`, matching upstream's removal of PyYAML.

- **206 focused core tests passed** on Python 3.14.7 with a fresh PM-built environment from the merged lockfile. This includes the new manual-entry dispatch regression and upstream's human-takeover/write-refusal tests.
- **101 plugin tests passed** on Python 3.13.15 against the merged core, including real Chrome automatic/manual OTP and navigation checks.
- Ruff, the PR-scoped whitespace check, and a secret scan of the committed PR diff passed. The temporary test-runner scratch override was restored before committing.

### Current-main conflict resolution

Merged upstream `main` at `63d0b94120027d487c9a5235b9ec64b696af1b26` in `0741d45269fc11c40548757ce7bb38d417c62ee5`, preserving existing commits and contributor authorship. GitHub now reports this head as **MERGEABLE** (no merge conflicts).

- Kept upstream's single deferred `browser_vault` tool with its `action` dispatcher, rather than restoring the five removed model tools. Plugin backend names are accepted by `action="unlock"`; `action="enter_code"` retains explicit `manual: true`, destination authorization, the handler lease fence, and write-time takeover checks.
- Combined upstream's modern type annotations with the PR's local-first explicit plugin activation and supervisor origin-matching hook. Updated the PR's registry-dispatch tests and manual-OTP documentation to the consolidated interface.
- Extracted scoped provider registration and OTP metadata validation into small sibling modules to meet current upstream file-size/complexity limits. Deliberate credential-bearing exception suppression uses documented health exemptions; it does not log raw exceptions.
- **220 tests passed** on macOS / Python 3.14.7: the 207-test focused core suite plus 13 shared TTS/transcription provider and plugin-host regressions. Used a fresh PM-built environment from the merged lockfile, isolated test homes, and the canonical per-file runner. The temporary scratch-root runner adjustment was restored and excluded from the commit.
- All **12 `scripts/check --base origin/main` gates passed**, including Ruff and the code-health ratchet; the PR-scoped whitespace check passed.

At readback, GitHub still marked the PR **BLOCKED**, with no CI checks reported for this head. Local verification is not a claim of upstream CI approval. The PR has been updated, not merged.

The full test suite, Linux/Windows execution, and real-manager authentication have not been verified in this review. No live credentials were used. Upstream CI must be checked before merging.

## Attribution

Preserves @fangliquanflq's three registration/discovery commits from #110767 and adopts the constructor-free availability approach credited to @KoNit-K in #110764. These overlapping proposals still need maintainer coordination.

prs.title: Use the kernel's starttime for process birth on Linux (WSL2 clock drift kills all managed workers)
prs.body:
## Problem

`process_birth()` only uses a monotonic clock on macOS; on Linux it still returns
`psutil.Process.create_time()`.

`create_time()` is `boot_time + starttime / HZ`, and **`boot_time` is cached per process**. On
WSL2 the host clock steps after resume, so a long-lived gateway and a freshly spawned worker
disagree about the **same pid's** birth by whole seconds (measured 1.0 s, later 3.0 s on one host).

## Impact

`gateway/session_worker.py::_claim` compares births with strict equality:

```python
if (process_birth(process) != birth or ...):
    raise RuntimeStoreError('permission_denied')
```

Every `worker.persist` was denied → the turn lease could not be renewed → the turn was
hard-interrupted → **all managed Kanban workers crashed** (`crashed=N`, `reaped zombie worker(s)`,
`Session DB append_message failed: permission_denied`).

## Fix

On Linux, return `/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22 (`starttime`, ticks since boot) — independent of the
wall clock and identical for every reader. All four identity checks (pid / birth / secret / user)
stay intact; only how *birth* is computed changes. Falls back to `create_time()` when `/proc` is
unreadable (restricted containers), i.e. current behaviour.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Same pid, two samples 5 s apart | `birth` delta **0.0** (was 1–3 s after a clock step) |
| Returned value | kernel ticks (e.g. `126890337`), not epoch |
| End-to-end | a 4-step multi-turn Kanban card completed, `worker_result exit_code=0`, zero `worker.persist` denials |
| Regression | 6 services up, 16 cron jobs scheduled, both API bridges healthy |

prs.title: fix(managed-worker): keep the route's credential pool so a 401 refreshes an expired OAuth token
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Kanban runs (key-less managed workers) on a pooled OAuth route now refresh an expired access token on a 401, as an in-process turn on the same route already does.

The worker resolves its route through `route_runtime()`, the resolver the in-process turn shares, but `_construct_agent()` kept only the `api_key` and built the `AIAgent` without the credential pool. When the native-Anthropic OAuth access token expires mid-run:

1. `recover_with_credential_pool()` returns at once (`agent._credential_pool is None`), so nothing refreshes the entry;
2. `_try_refresh_anthropic_client_credentials()` re-resolves the token read-only and gets back the same expired token;
3. the 401 is non-retryable, so the run fails and Kanban books it `terminal_provider` (exit 78), blocking the card until someone releases it.

It recurs at every expiry of the shared token: any worker whose next call lands after the expiry and before some other process refreshes dies this way. In our deployment that was seven runs in a week, about 20 minutes of work lost on the worst one.

## Related

- Same seam as #142453, which threads the resolved `api_mode` into the worker agent through a `worker_runtime()` helper. This PR uses the same helper name and shape and threads `credential_pool`. Whichever lands second is a small rebase, and I'm happy to rebase onto #142453 if it goes first.
- Follows #139472 (key-less workers resolve their route key) and keeps its #139155 rule: a fallback entry's credential never reaches the primary.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- `gateway/session_worker_construct.py`: `worker_api_key()` becomes `worker_runtime()`, returning the primary route's runtime dict (still `{}` when resolution landed on a fallback entry).
- `agent/managed_worker.py`: `_construct_agent()` passes the runtime's `api_key` and `credential_pool` to the agent. A bound launch key is unchanged.
- `tests/gateway/test_managed_worker_route_key.py`: one behaviour test.

## How to Test

`scripts/run_tests.sh tests/gateway/test_managed_worker_route_key.py`

The new test builds a key-less worker on a pooled Anthropic OAuth route (temp `HERMES_HOME`, fake tokens, refresh POST stubbed), then drives the real `recover_with_credential_pool()` for a 401 with the agent the worker built. Results:

| Tree | Result |
|---|---|
| `main` (fix removed) | FAILS: `recovered` is `False`, no refresh attempted |
| this branch | passes: the entry refreshes and the new token is swapped in |

prs.title: fix(zai): list models at /v1/models on the Anthropic-compatible endpoint
prs.body:
## Problem

Users who route Z.AI through its Anthropic-compatible endpoint (`GLM_BASE_URL=https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic`, or a `model.base_url` relay pointing there; that wire is the one that honors thinking-block replay) never get a live model list. Z.AI has no bare `/models` route on that endpoint. It answers **HTTP 200** with an error envelope:

```
GET https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic/models     -> 200 {"code":500,"msg":"404 NOT_FOUND","success":false}
GET https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic/v1/models  -> 200 {"data":[{"id":"glm-4.5",...}, ...]}   (11 models)
GET https://api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4/models -> 200 {"object":"list","data":[...]}          (same 11 models)
```

`ProviderProfile.fetch_models` parses the envelope as an empty catalog, so `provider_model_ids("zai")` falls to its no-live branch and the picker serves the profile's `fallback_models` (`glm-5.2`, `glm-5`, `glm-4-9b`). The disk cache then re-probes that placeholder every 60 s, forever. Same key, same account: the live catalog is right there under `/v1/models`.

## Fix

`ZaiProfile.fetch_models` appends `/v1` when the base URL's path ends in `/anthropic`, then delegates to the generic fetch (same Bearer auth, same response parsing). OpenAI-compatible bases (`/api/paas/v4`, `/api/coding/paas/v4`, `open.bigmodel.cn/...`) are untouched.

All Z.AI catalog paths go through `profile.fetch_models`, so the one override covers them: the picker (`_profile_live_catalog` → `probe_profile_catalog`), the configured-relay path (`_relay_model_catalog`), and the setup flow's profile probe.

## Overlapping PRs

This is the endpoint half only. It does not touch the fallback behaviour other open PRs address:

- #115173 makes the static `_PROVIDER_MODELS` row lead over `fallback_models` when the live fetch is empty (and refreshes Z.AI's tuple). That fixes what users *see* when listing fails; this PR stops listing from failing on the Anthropic wire.
- #136987 refreshes Z.AI's `fallback_models` tuple.
- #46724 also adds a `ZaiProfile.fetch_models` override (it appends free Flash models). The two compose: if it lands first, this becomes a few lines inside its override, and I'm happy to rebase onto whichever merges first.

Supersedes my earlier #96444, which bundled both halves and went stale.

## Tests

`tests/plugins/model_providers/test_zai_profile.py::TestZaiModelListing`, with the real profile resolved through plugin discovery and `open_credentialed_url` stubbed:

| Test | Fix applied | `zai/__init__.py` at `main` |
|---|---|---|
| `test_anthropic_endpoint_lists_under_v1` | pass | **fail** (requests `/api/anthropic/models`) |
| `test_openai_compatible_endpoint_keeps_models_path` (control) | pass | pass |

`scripts/run_tests.sh tests/plugins/model_providers/test_zai_profile.py tests/providers/test_fetch_models_base_url.py`: 59 passed. `scripts/check --base upstream/main`: 12 checks ok, 0 code-health findings.

Live verification: with the override in place, `provider_model_ids("zai")` under an `/api/anthropic` base returns 13 ids as a plain list (the curated row plus the live-only `glm-4.5-air`, `glm-4.6`, `glm-5.3-flashx`) rather than the 3-id `CuratedFallbackModels` placeholder.

## Risk

Only bases whose path ends in `/anthropic` change URL. A user-supplied base that already ends in `/anthropic/v1` is passed through unchanged (it doesn't end in `/anthropic`).

## Model Used

Anthropic `claude-opus-5-5`, extended thinking, tool use via Hermes.

prs.title: fix(desktop): mark the picked endpoint from the gateway's is_current, not the provider name
prs.body:
## What

The Desktop model picker decided "this row is the current one" with

```ts
const isCurrent = model === currentModel && catalogProviderMatches(provider, currentProvider)
```

`catalogProviderMatches` compares `slug` / `name` / `aliases` only — never the endpoint. Two things make that ambiguous in practice:

1. **Every named `providers:` entry resolves to the bare `custom` provider class**, so the provider string carries no endpoint identity (`gateway/session_mutation_model.py:23`; the model pill renders `custom: <model-id>`).
2. **Relays routinely serve the same model id** — e.g. `claude-opus-5.5` on two endpoints, `deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` on another.

Result: picking a model under endpoint A can leave the ✓ on endpoint B's row (or on none), even though the request was routed correctly (gateway log: `provider=custom base_url=https://a.example/v1 model=<shared-id>`).

## Fix

The gateway **already** computes the answer: `inventory.build_models_payload` sets each row's `is_current` from `endpoint_is_current(..., url_norm)`, i.e. a base-URL comparison. So use that verdict when it is present, and keep the name match only as a fallback for payloads without the field:

```ts
// lib/model-options.ts
export function catalogProviderIsCurrent(provider, currentProvider) {
  if (provider.is_current === true) return true
  if (provider.is_current === false) return false
  return catalogProviderMatches(provider, currentProvider)   // payloads without is_current
}
```

`components/model-picker.tsx` uses it for the row highlight. The other `catalogProviderMatches` call sites are untouched — they legitimately resolve a provider *id* to its catalog row.

Verified the flag really does separate two endpoints that share a model id (built the payload against a two-relay config):

```
relay-a  current=True  user=True api_url=https://a.example/v1 models=['shared-model-id']
relay-b  current=False user=True api_url=https://b.example/v1 models=['shared-model-id']
top-level: model=shared-model-id provider=relay-a
```

## Tests

```bash
cd apps/desktop
npx vitest run src/lib/model-options.test.ts src/components/model-picker.test.tsx   # 35 passed
npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json                                                   # clean
```

New cases cover: two endpoints sharing a model id stay apart; `is_current: false` outvotes a stale provider name; fallback to name matching when the field is absent; no highlight without a provider string.

## Not covered here

This only fixes the highlight. The provider *identity* being flattened to `custom` in session state is a separate change (see #66367 and the discussion in #66329) — that one is needed for the pill/tooltips to name the endpoint, not for the checkmark.

I did not build the Electron bundle locally (no packaged-build verification), so this is validated by the unit tests + typecheck only.

Refs #66329
