prs.title: fix(sop): match step scope groups to registered tool names
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - The SOP step scope groups `fs`/`filesystem` and `web`/`network` expanded to `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, and `web_search`. The tool registry registers `file_read`, `file_write`, `file_edit`, and `web_search_tool`. `resolve_excluded` matches expanded group members against registry names, so those four members never matched a tool.
  - With `sop.step_scope_enforce = true`, `deny-tools: fs` removed nothing, `deny-tools: web` removed only `http_request`, and `allow-tools: fs` removed every tool except the mandatory ones. This corrects the four names.
  - `expand_group` now reads one group table, and new tests build the production tool registry and check every group against it, so a renamed tool or a mistyped member fails a test instead of silently disabling a scope. Master now registers `web_search_tool` only in builds with the external tools, so a member listed in `zeroclaw_config::builtin_tools::EXTERNAL_TOOL_NAMES` is left out of the expected sets while the `tools-external` feature is off; the `Test (opt-in tools)` job builds with that feature and checks it there, and every other member stays strict.
  - The resolver unit tests in `scope/mod.rs` used a fake registry with the same wrong names, which is why they passed. The fixture now uses real tool names.
  - The registry-building test helper keeps both config arguments in its temp dir, so the test never touches the developer's real `~/.zeroclaw`; the first revision of this PR opened the session store there.
- **Scope boundary:** Group membership is unchanged (see open questions). No change to resolver semantics, SOP parsing, config, schema, or docs. No validation or warning is added for scope entries that match no registered tool. Other tests that use `read_file` as an arbitrary name in their own fake registries are left alone, because they do not go through group expansion.
- **Blast radius:** SOP step turns (live and headless) and child or delegated runs that inherit a step scope, only when `sop.step_scope_enforce = true` and a step's `allow-tools:`, `deny-tools:`, or legacy `tools:` list names `fs`, `filesystem`, `web`, or `network`. Steps that list explicit tool names, and every install with enforcement off (the default), behave as before.
- **Linked issue(s):** None.

### What this does, simply

An SOP step can carry a tool scope: an allow list, a deny list, or both. When an operator turns on `sop.step_scope_enforce`, the runtime removes tools from the step according to that scope. Entries can be tool names or short group names such as `fs` or `web`, which stand for several tools.

The group table spelled four tools differently from how the runtime registers them. A step told to deny `fs` kept its file tools, a step told to deny `web` kept web search, and a step told to allow only `fs` lost every tool except the SOP lifecycle tools that are always kept, including the file tools it asked for.

This PR corrects the four names and adds tests that compare the group table with the tool registry the runtime actually builds.

### Open questions for maintainers

1. **Group membership.** Should `fs`/`filesystem` also cover `glob_search` and `content_search`, and should `web`/`network` also cover `web_fetch`? All three are registered by default. After this fix, `deny-tools: fs` still leaves the local discovery tools `glob_search` and `content_search`, as well as other default tools that touch files, such as `shell`, `git_operations`, `deliver_file`, and `image_info`; `deny-tools: network` still leaves `web_fetch` and any other tool that can reach the network. Changing membership changes what operators get from a group, so it is left out of this fix.
2. **Unmatched scope entries.** A scope entry that matches no group and no registered tool is ignored without a warning, which is how this went unnoticed. Should SOP load or save warn or reject? Note that the tool-call parser accepts `read_file` and similar spellings from models as aliases for `file_read`, which can make those spellings look valid in a scope.
3. **Documentation.** The group names are not in `docs/book/src/sop/syntax.md`. They could be documented once membership is settled; that note should also say that `web_search_tool` exists only in builds with the external tools.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A`. No interface changes, and the new unit tests run the resolver against the production tool registry.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The `Test` job runs the `zeroclaw-runtime` lib tests in the default build, and `Test (opt-in tools)` runs them with `--features tools-compat`, which includes `tools-external`; both include the new `sop::scope::groups::tests`. The Lint, Format, and compile-check jobs cover the two changed files.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No Windows job runs the new tests: the advisory Windows lane needs the `ci:windows` label, `Check x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` runs `cargo check` without test targets, and `Test Windows task-owner recovery`, when its change detection selects it, compiles the runtime lib test target but runs only its two control-plane tests. No group member name is platform-specific.
- **Commands run and tail output:** macOS (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64), rustc 1.97.1, at commit `5415a8ac3f` (origin/master `8f03c962dc` merged on top of `2bd6255d60`, which is `3a73f5f7a9` plus an earlier master merge and one test-only commit). Cargo commands ran with `CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=0 CARGO_PROFILE_TEST_DEBUG=0` to keep the build small.

```text
$ cargo deny check advisories
advisories ok
exit=0

$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
exit=0

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib sop::scope
running 8 tests
test sop::scope::tests::deny_scope_subtracts_from_allow ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::mandatory_infra_survives_empty_allow ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::allow_scope_excludes_everything_else ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::security_policy_can_only_narrow ... ok
test sop::scope::tests::mandatory_infra_cannot_restore_policy_denied_tools ... ok
test sop::scope::groups::tests::every_group_member_is_a_registered_tool_name ... ok
test sop::scope::groups::tests::denying_a_group_excludes_exactly_its_registered_tools ... ok
test sop::scope::groups::tests::allowing_a_group_keeps_exactly_its_registered_tools ... ok

test result: ok. 8 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5824 filtered out; finished in 0.03s
exit=0

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib --features tools-external sop::scope
test result: ok. 8 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5829 filtered out; finished in 0.04s
exit=0

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib sop
test result: ok. 803 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 5028 filtered out; finished in 5.83s
exit=0

$ printf '%s\0' crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/scope/groups.rs crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/sop/scope/mod.rs > files.nul
$ python3 scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.py files.nul
Comment hygiene gate passed.
exit=0

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 1m 27s
exit=0

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets --features tools-external -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized] target(s) in 1m 50s
exit=0
```

Earlier revisions of this PR recorded a strict clippy failure on an unused import in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs`; that came from the old base, and master gates the import correctly (PR 11314), so the command passes on this head.

The registry-building tests also ran with an empty temporary `HOME` and no `ZEROCLAW_CONFIG_DIR` (the `tools-external` test binary):

```text
$ HOME=<empty temp dir> target/debug/deps/zeroclaw_runtime-<hash> sop::scope::groups
test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5834 filtered out; finished in 0.02s
(nothing was created under that HOME)
```

The new tests fail without the fix. At `5415a8ac3f` in a default build with the four names reverted to `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, and `web_search`:

```text
test sop::scope::tests::deny_scope_subtracts_from_allow ... FAILED
test sop::scope::groups::tests::every_group_member_is_a_registered_tool_name ... FAILED
test sop::scope::groups::tests::denying_a_group_excludes_exactly_its_registered_tools ... FAILED
test sop::scope::groups::tests::allowing_a_group_keeps_exactly_its_registered_tools ... FAILED

assertion `left == right` failed: deny scope `fs`
  left: []
 right: ["edit_file", "read_file", "write_file"]

scope group ["fs", "filesystem"] lists `read_file`, which the test registry did not register: fix the name, or switch on its config gate in registered_tool_names(); a member behind the tools-external feature must be listed in EXTERNAL_TOOL_NAMES

test result: FAILED. 4 passed; 4 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5824 filtered out; finished in 0.05s
```

`deny_scope_subtracts_from_allow` fails there because its fixture now uses real names and expands `fs`. With only `web_search_tool` misspelled as `web_serch_tool`, still in a default build, the three group tests fail (`5 passed; 3 failed`), because a name that is not in `EXTERNAL_TOOL_NAMES` stays strict:

```text
assertion `left == right` failed: deny scope `web`
  left: ["http_request"]
 right: ["http_request", "web_serch_tool"]
```

With `--features tools-external` and only `web_search_tool` reverted to `web_search`:

```text
assertion `left == right` failed: deny scope `web`
  left: ["http_request"]
 right: ["http_request", "web_search"]

scope group ["web", "network"] lists `web_search`, which the test registry did not register: fix the name, or switch on its config gate in registered_tool_names(); a member behind the tools-external feature must be listed in EXTERNAL_TOOL_NAMES

test result: FAILED. 5 passed; 3 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5829 filtered out; finished in 0.07s
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Traced every production caller of `resolve_excluded`. It is reached only through `resolve_active_step_scope`, which returns early unless `sop.step_scope_enforce` is set, and every caller passes names taken from `Tool::name()` (`collect_callable_tool_names` in the turn loop and per tool call, and the delegate tool's own registry). Checked that the SOP docs and cookbook examples use only real tool names and never use a group name other than `shell`, which expands to the tool of the same name. Ran the three registry-building tests with an empty temporary `HOME` and no `ZEROCLAW_CONFIG_DIR`; nothing was created under it. Not verified: an end-to-end SOP run against a live provider.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A`. No user-visible interface state changed.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `5415a8ac3f`; no user-facing interface is involved, and the evidence is the command output above.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** `N/A`. No interface change.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** `N/A`. No interaction or transition changed.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Full-workspace `cargo test` and `cargo clippy` were not run. The change is confined to one module of `zeroclaw-runtime`.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? (`No`)
- New external network calls? (`No`)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? (`No`)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? (`No`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? (`No`)
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: None are `Yes`. The change restores a restriction that was failing open: with enforcement on, a step that denied `fs` or `web` kept tools the operator meant to remove. Agent security policy, workspace confinement, path guards, rate limits, and approvals were not affected by the bug and are not changed here. In the allow direction, with enforcement on, `allow-tools: fs` and `allow-tools: web` steps now keep `file_read`, `file_write`, `file_edit`, and `web_search_tool`, which the shipped table excluded by mistake; that is the group's intended meaning, and those tools remain subject to the agent's security policy.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? (`Yes`) SOP definitions and config parse as before. Behavior changes only for steps that name these groups in `allow-tools:`, `deny-tools:`, or the legacy `tools:` list while enforcement is on: `deny-tools: fs` and `deny-tools: web` now remove the tools they name, and `allow-tools: fs` and `allow-tools: web` now keep them. A step that relied on `allow-tools: fs` removing everything will now have the three file tools.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? (`No`)
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? (`No`)

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** `sop.step_scope_enforce = false` turns step scope enforcement off entirely.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** A scoped step reports a tool as unavailable that the operator expected it to have, or the reverse.

prs.title: fix(channels/lark): parse image elements in Feishu post messages
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:** Feishu/Lark **post** (rich-text) messages that contain an image were silently dropped before reaching the agent, so the bot never answered them. Two gaps in `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/lark.rs`: `parse_post_content_details` required a `zh_cn`/`en_us` locale wrapper (flat bodies that keep `title`/`content` at the top level returned `None`), and `img` elements were never converted into image markers. The change accepts flat bodies and downloads each `img` element through the existing `download_image_as_marker` path in both receive modes.
- **Scope boundary:** Only the Lark/Feishu channel implementation. No other channel, provider, config schema, or CLI surface changes. Plain image messages (`msg_type = "image"`) and file messages are untouched.
- **Blast radius:** Feishu/Lark posts that previously produced no inbound message now reach the agent, carrying an `[IMAGE:data:...]` marker per downloaded image. This reuses the marker format from plain image messages. Wrapped text-only posts keep their existing behavior; flat text-only posts are also newly accepted.
- **Linked issue(s):** No tracker entry yet (reported out-of-band from a live deployment); happy to link or file one if that is preferred.
- **Labels:** `bug`, `channel`, `channel:lark`, `risk:medium`, `size:S`.

### What this does, simply

Feishu clients can send one message that mixes text and a picture (the "图文" composer). ZeroClaw read those bodies only in the shape some clients produce (a `zh_cn`/`en_us` wrapper), and it never looked at the picture element at all. The result was the worst possible failure mode: the message was skipped without a reply and without an error.

This PR teaches the post reader the flat body shape, collects the `image_key`s of `img` elements, and hands each image to the channel's existing download helper so the agent receives the picture as a normal image marker, exactly like a plain image message does today.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes — this is channel-level behavior that needs a live Feishu app.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` `lark` (Feishu endpoint), WebSocket receive mode.
- **Setup / preconditions:** `[channels.lark.<alias>]` with `use_feishu = true` and default `receive_mode = "websocket"`, an agent bound to that channel, and a Feishu app subscribed to `im.message.receive_v1` with the `im:resource` scope.
- **Steps to run:** Send **one** message that contains both an image and text.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the agent receives the post (image marker + text) and answers it.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the same message produces no inbound event at all — no reply, no error.

### How I tested

- `cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --features channel-lark --lib flat_post_with_image` — new unit test using a real flat post payload (image + text): `test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed`.
- `cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --features channel-lark --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo fmt -p zeroclaw-channels -- --check` — clean.
- Manual smoke on a live Feishu bot (v0.8.5 source plus this patch): before the change a mixed image+text message left no inbound trace and no reply; after the change the same message reaches the agent and the reply describes the picture.
- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the `zeroclaw-channels` unit tests plus the workspace fmt/clippy gates.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** webhook receive mode was patched to match the WebSocket path but was not exercised against a live Feishu webhook.
- **Beyond CI, what did I manually verify?** Live WebSocket receive on a Feishu tenant (image+text post answered). I did **not** verify webhook mode end to end.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A` (no rendered-interface change).

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No`
- New external network calls? `Yes`. Post images now trigger resource downloads through the existing `GET /open-apis/im/v1/messages/{message_id}/resources/{file_key}?type=image` endpoint already used for `msg_type = "image"` messages.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No` — the test uses a synthetic `image_key`.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `Yes`. Content that used to be silently discarded (post text and images) is now delivered to the agent, matching the existing trust boundary for `text`/`image`/`file` messages. `LARK_IMAGE_MAX_BYTES` limits each accepted image to 10 MiB; `[multimodal]` limits apply during downstream provider preparation and do not bound aggregate channel download work.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: no new trust boundary or endpoint is introduced; posts are the same operator-visible channel input as other message types. Downloads retain the existing authentication, MIME checks and per-image byte guard. Posts with several images can increase receive latency and temporary memory because there is no post-level download budget.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `Yes`
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `No`
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <squash-sha>` (single-file change; no data migration).
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** `None`
- **Observable failure symptoms:** image posts stop producing inbound messages again, or trace logs show `failed to download image in post` (WARN) alongside `[IMAGE:<key> | download failed]` bodies.

---

## 中文说明

**问题：** 飞书「图文」消息（`msg_type = "post"`，一条消息里同时有图片和文字）会被**静默丢弃**——机器人既不回复也不报错。原因是 Lark 频道的 post 解析器要求内容带 `zh_cn`/`en_us` 语言包裹层，而这类消息的内容是平铺结构（`title`/`content` 在顶层），解析直接返回 `None`；即使解析成功，`img` 元素也从未被转换成图片标记。

**修复：** 接受平铺格式的 post 内容；从 `img` 元素提取 `image_key`，并复用频道已有的 `download_image_as_marker` 下载路径，把图片作为 `[IMAGE:data:...]` 标记交给 agent。WebSocket 与 webhook 两条接收路径都做了同样处理，下载失败的兜底标记与既有 image 分支保持一致。

**测试：** 新增单元测试（使用真实的平铺 post 报文，含图片与文字）通过；改动 crate 的 `clippy -D warnings` 与 `fmt --check` 干净；并在真实飞书机器人上做了手工验证——修改前图文消息无任何入站记录、无回复，修改后同一条消息能正常到达 agent 并回答图片内容。webhook 模式仅代码对齐，未做线上验证。

prs.title: feat(channels/whatsapp-web): save inbound images and mark them like Telegram
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - An inbound WhatsApp Web image was downloaded into a `MediaAttachment { marker: None }`, and the message said `[Image]`. The bytes lived for one turn. With `media_pipeline` on, the model saw them once, inlined as base64; with it off (the default, see #10975), it saw nothing. Either way the agent had no file afterwards, so a tool that archives a receipt or attaches a photo to a report could not reach the original.
  - The channel now does what Telegram does with `telegram_files/`. When it has a workspace, each provider-loadable image of the message is written to `<workspace>/whatsapp_files/<phone>_<message id>_<n>.<ext>`, its attachment's `marker` is set to that absolute path with `MarkerKind::Image`, and the content carries `[IMAGE:<path>]` in place of the `[Image]`/`[Sticker]` placeholder (or ahead of any text). The pipeline already defers to a channel-rendered marker (`channel_rendered_owned_disposition`), so the image reaches the model exactly once, as an image, and does so whether or not the pipeline is enabled.
  - The file-name prefix is the sender's phone number, digits only, never the LID. It is the sender JID when that is a phone-number JID (device suffix dropped), else the alternate JID, else the LID-to-phone mapping the allowlist check already resolves. Files from one person share a stable prefix, and two senders never collide. The message id is reduced to ASCII alphanumerics.
- **Scope boundary:** images and stickers that `provider_loadable_image_mime()` accepts, on the message itself. Quoted attachments stay in memory. No change to video, audio, documents, retention/cleanup of `whatsapp_files/` (Telegram keeps its files too), the Cloud API channel, or config. Reading WhatsApp caption fields remains separate in #11257/#11757; this PR preserves text already supplied to the save step.
- **Blast radius:** the WhatsApp Web inbound path for messages carrying an image, when the channel has a `workspace_dir` (the daemon always sets one). Such messages now write one file per image and render a path marker instead of `[Image]`.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11255. Related: #10975.

### What this does, simply

Photos sent to the bot over WhatsApp Web are now kept as files in the agent's workspace, and the agent sees them as images it can open and show to the model, the same way Telegram already works. Before, a photo lived in memory for one turn, and with the media pipeline off the model only saw the word `[Image]`.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Optional, if a spare WhatsApp account is available.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` = `whatsapp_web`.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a Web-mode `[channels.whatsapp.<alias>]` channel bound to an agent with a vision-capable model.
- **Steps to run:** send the bot a photo without a caption from an allowed number. Caption extraction is covered separately by #11257/#11757.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** `<agent workspace>/whatsapp_files/<number>_<id>_0.jpg` exists with the photo's bytes, the inbound content is `[IMAGE:<that path>]`, and the model describes the photo, with `media_pipeline` on or off.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** no file; content `[Image]`; the model sees the photo only with `media_pipeline.enabled = true`.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the Lint job, which runs clippy with `--all-targets --features ci-all` and so compiles this code and its tests.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the tests are linted in CI but not run there: the required Test job uses default features, and `whatsapp-web` is not one of them. I ran them locally with the feature on (commands below).
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
$ ./scripts/ci/rust_quality_gate.sh
==> rust quality: provider dispatch gate clean
gate exit=0

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --features whatsapp-web --lib --tests -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --features whatsapp-web --lib
test result: ok. 2253 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - New tests: `sender_phone_digits_never_uses_the_lid` (phone JID with a device suffix, LID plus phone alt, LID plus mapping, LID alone gives no name), `inbound_file_stem_keeps_only_safe_message_id_characters`, `save_inbound_images_writes_and_marks_loadable_images` (bytes on disk equal the attachment, absolute marker target, `MarkerKind::Image`, a video in the same list left alone), `save_inbound_images_failure_leaves_the_attachment_in_memory` (a file where the directory should be: no marker, bytes still delivered), and `content_with_image_markers_replaces_only_the_placeholder`.
  - Mutation checks: making `sender_phone_digits` fall back to the sender JID whatever its server, and dropping the `attachment.marker` assignment, each make the matching test fail.
  - The no-double-image behavior rests on the pipeline's existing `image_already_marked_by_channel_is_not_double_described`, which this change relies on rather than reimplements.
  - **Paired-account result at `7764d4a10`:** [Linux daemon run](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11259#issuecomment-6180211137), with a linked WhatsApp account, self-chat enabled, `media_pipeline.enabled = false`, and `gpt-4o-mini` with vision enabled. A received photo produced a valid saved JPEG, a marker-only user turn, and a model response describing the image. Caption handling was not tested and remains separate in #11257/#11757.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** the pre-push hook was skipped with `--no-verify`. It runs `cargo test --workspace`, and on this machine it failed in `zeroclaw-hardware` on `subprocess::tests::execute_returns_success_before_descendant_closes_output_pipes` ("fixture must record a positive PID before the readiness deadline"), a timing-sensitive test in a crate this PR does not touch. Run alone, it passes 3 of 3 times. Every crate the hook reached before it, `zeroclaw-channels` included, passed.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? Yes
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No (tests use `1555…` numbers)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation:
  - The channel now writes bytes received from chat participants to disk, as Telegram already does. The directory is fixed (`<workspace>/whatsapp_files/`), and the file name is built only from digits, ASCII alphanumerics of the message id, an index and an extension from `mime_extension` (which already rejects path characters), so a crafted message id or MIME type cannot leave that directory. Only images the provider loader accepts are written.
  - The file name carries the sender's phone number, which the channel already treats as the sender identity. Write failures are logged without the path, so the number does not reach the log sink.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes. Content for image messages changes from `[Image]` to `[IMAGE:<path>]`, the form Telegram and Discord already deliver.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` the squash commit. Files already written are inert.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None. A channel built without a workspace keeps the old behavior.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** warnings `failed to create whatsapp_files directory`, `failed to resolve whatsapp_files directory` or `failed to save WhatsApp image attachment`; the message is still delivered with the in-memory image, as before.

prs.title: fix(config): accept tagged declarative cron schedules
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes #11237. `cron.<alias>.schedule` is a tagged object, not a string enum. Config PATCH/PUT and `/config/cron` now save it; PATCH `test` compares typed schedules. Existing TOML works unchanged. `/api/cron` database jobs and scheduler startup/reload behavior are unchanged. Labels: `config`, `gateway`, `web`, `size:S`; maintainer requested to add `risk:medium`.

### What this does, simply

The config editor could read a schedule but could not save one. It now sends the object ZeroClaw expects.

## Testing

### How you can test

In `/config/cron/daily`, save `{"kind":"cron","expr":"0 9 * * *"}`. This branch persists it to `config.toml`; `master` reports `invalid type: string`.

### How I tested

`cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib --locked --quiet` (**1,752 passed**); gateway equivalent (**623 passed**), covering PUT/PATCH, all schedule variants, saved TOML and failed conditional writes. `cargo run -p xtask --bin web -- check`, `npm test`, `npm run build`, and formatting passed. Current-head CI Lint, Test, build and MSRV passed. No visual layout change; no browser screenshot.

Upstream fixed the unrelated Wasmtime security gate in #11253. Fresh CI is running on the branch synced with current `master`.

## Security & Privacy Impact

No new permissions, network access, credential handling, personal data or model-visible text.

## Compatibility

Existing config needs no migration; this property's metadata changes `enum` → `object` and its form value becomes JSON text. Runtime activation still follows the existing scheduler startup/reload path. No toolchain change.

## Rollback

Revert the squash commit; already-saved tagged TOML remains readable.

prs.title: fix(runtime): preserve interrupted requests and refuse scoped service termination
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- A shell tool that runs `zeroclaw service restart` can kill its own daemon before its result or final reply is persisted. Refuse scoped-agent stop, restart and uninstall at the runtime service entrypoints, before platform commands or service-file deletion.
- Replace the terse restored-session closure with actionable localized text: the original request is preserved, effects may already have occurred, and state/receipts must be checked before retry. The transcript remains the sole request record.
- **Scope boundary:** no automatic resumption, tool replay, new approval authority, or proactive channel notification. The environment marker is accident prevention, not a security boundary or ancestry proof; arbitrary termination tools are outside this guard.
- **Blast radius:** service control invoked with the existing nonempty `ZEROCLAW_SESSION_ID` marker; trailing user-only transcripts during startup or cold-cache restoration.
- **Linked issue:** Related atorenherrinton/zeroclaw-helpers#25. The installed upstream release remains unchanged in that deployment.
- **Labels:** `bug`, `docs`, `channel`, `runtime`, `service`, `channel:core`, `risk:medium`, `size:M`.

### What this does, simply

An assistant trying to repair its own service must finish its reply before an independent operator restarts it. Interrupted requests keep an honest recovery record instead of silently saying they will not continue. Recovery does not assume a missing reply means a write failed.

## Testing

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, for deployment-specific shell attribution.
- **Interface:** CLI service control invoked from a scoped channel tool.
- **Setup:** disposable service instance and a shell tool carrying `ZEROCLAW_SESSION_ID`.
- **Steps:** request `service restart` from that tool, inspect the returned error and daemon PID, then run the same command from an independent operator terminal without the session marker.
- **After:** the tool attempt refuses before service effects; operator control is unchanged.
- **Before:** the tool can terminate its daemon and lose the enclosing turn's final result.

### How I tested

- `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib --no-default-features scoped_service_termination`: isolated subprocess regression passed. It invokes real service entrypoints with fake platform commands and verifies no platform command ran; marker-absent checks exercise only the guard, never a real service stop.
- `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-channels --lib --no-default-features hydration_`: 12 passed. Consecutive interruptions preserve original requests and append one closure each; repeated hydration adds none. A manually completed retry remains intact. This proves persistence and idempotence, not automatic resumed-tool execution.
- Formatting, diff checks, docs quality and docs links gates passed.
- `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-channels --no-default-features --lib interrupted_channel_retry_checks_receipt_without_repeating_effect`: one passed. Three real `process_channel_message` turns use isolated SQLite session storage and a fake durable receipt. Two tasks are aborted after tool execution and before a final response; the retry checks the receipt and produces one final channel reply and one durable assistant result. The synthetic mutation happens once; repeated restoration never executes tools. This proves the scripted recovery path, not exactly-once behavior for arbitrary model decisions.
- **CI relied on:** [Quality Gate run 36737465133, attempt 2](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36737465133/attempts/2) passed on current head `004f32e91befe896a86d43cdf3267599a484fee8`, including the required gate, workspace tests, parallel runtime tests, Windows service smoke, lint, security, macOS/Windows compilation, Linux build, and declared MSRV.
- **CI rerun:** the initial 32-bit job timed out installing Ubuntu packages before compilation. The failed jobs passed on rerun. The current PR risk report also passed.
- **Known gap:** no live platform service stop, automatic task recovery, or Discord notification delivery was exercised. The full workspace suite ran in CI; local validation was scoped to the changed behavior.
- **Visual evidence:** exact unstyled CLI error from the guarded entrypoint; English locale, no width-dependent rendering: `Service stop, restart, or uninstall was not performed because this command is running inside an active agent turn.` The remainder directs an independent operator restart and prohibits bypassing the marker.
- **Locally tested revision:** `b10e8ac94dc5a8ad03d93e3633fe24ca487a72a4`. Local recovery-loop and hydration tests passed at this head. The service subprocess regression also passed on its unchanged implementation at parent `073751751591b46719950a8529e7d283b82de57a`; all three service APIs were exercised inside the fixture.
- Generated translations were not changed; English Fluent is the source and existing fallback resolves the new keys.

## Security & Privacy Impact

- New permissions, capabilities or filesystem access scope: No.
- New external network calls: No.
- Credential handling changed: No.
- PII, real identities or personal data in diff/fixtures: No.
- Model-visible text changed: Yes. The restored synthetic assistant record now instructs verification before retry; it does not authorize action or incorporate external text.

## Compatibility

- Backward compatible: Yes for independent operator control and stored-session schemas. Scoped tool processes now receive an intentional error instead of stopping their parent service.
- Config/env/CLI surface changed: No new surface; the existing scoped-session environment marker is consumed.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed: No.

## Rollback

- Revert this change and rebuild. Keep session databases and current configuration.
- No new feature flag. Independent operator service control remains available.
- Failure symptom: unexpected service refusal should be investigated by checking whether the process inherited a scoped-session marker; do not clear it inside an active turn to bypass the guard.

prs.title: fix(memory): reject unknown backends instead of selecting markdown
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** the `MemoryBackendKind::Unknown` arm in `crates/zeroclaw-memory/src/lib.rs` logged a WARN and built a `MarkdownMemory`, so any `memory.backend` the classifier did not recognise wrote durable memory into workspace Markdown files. It now returns an error naming the rejected value and every selectable backend. `classify_memory_backend` matches six names (`sqlite`, `lucid`, `postgres`, `qdrant`, `markdown`, `none`) with no `cfg` gates, so the names reaching this arm are typos (`"sqllite"`), stores ZeroClaw has no memory backend for at all (`"redis"`, `"lancedb"`, `"faiss"`), dotted references whose prefix matches none of them (`"custom.default"`), and any kind a future commit adds to the factory without adding to the classifier.
- The removed WARN also carried no information: `record!` formats with `message = %$msg` and accepts no format arguments, so the message was the constant `Unknown memory backend '', falling back to markdown` whatever was rejected. The name existed only in structured attrs, which the formatted log line an operator reads does not show.
- Empty or whitespace-only `memory.backend` now means disabled persistence, matching `Config::resolve_active_storage`, which already defines an empty value as no storage. It previously produced a Markdown store.
- The follow-up rejects non-empty references with an empty backend kind, such as `.default`, before they can be interpreted as disabled memory. The gateway installs `FailedMemory` when construction fails, so memory API writes return errors while the config editor remains available. The daemon RPC startup warning now retains the construction error in its structured attributes.
- **Scope boundary:** recognized backend construction and explicit Markdown behavior remain unchanged. The follow-up adds a failed-backend implementation of the existing `Memory` trait, gateway selection and API tests, complete-reference validation, and the daemon diagnostic. It does not reconcile the Quickstart backend lists or change heartbeat's best-effort memory handling.
- **Blast radius:** every `create_memory*` construction path. Gateway construction failures now install `FailedMemory`; intentionally disabled memory and the existing no-agent case retain `NoneMemory`. The default memory API returns errors from the failed handle, and per-agent API construction errors already propagate. CLI, migration, and RPC explicit memory writes also fail rather than report success after construction fails. Repairing the config and reloading recreates daemon-owned backends.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11208
- **Labels:** `bug`, `config`, `daemon`, `gateway`, `memory`, `runtime`, `principal contributor`, `memory:backend`, `risk:medium`, `size:L`.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw chooses where an agent's durable memory lives from `memory.backend`. If that name was wrong, the program did not complain: it wrote memory into Markdown files in the agent's workspace directory and printed a log line that read `Unknown memory backend ''` no matter what had been typed. So a typo meant agent history accumulated somewhere other than where the operator thought it was, with nothing in the logs to explain where it went, and the normal cleanup command (`zeroclaw memory clear`) refuses to operate on a Markdown store (`src/memory/cli.rs:321-326`).

This PR makes an unknown name a construction error that quotes the value and lists the valid names, and makes an empty `memory.backend` mean "no persistence", which is what the config layer already says it means. Choosing Markdown deliberately is unchanged and still fully supported.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes — the A/B is one command, and the behaviour change is the point of the PR.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli`; daemon boot path.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a workspace config with `memory.backend` set to a value the classifier does not know (`sqllite`, or `redis`). No provider, model, or network needed.
- **Steps to run:** set `memory.backend = "sqllite"` in the config, then run `zeroclaw memory list`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the command fails, with an error naming `"sqllite"` and the selectable list `sqlite, lucid, postgres, markdown, none`.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the command succeeds against a Markdown store in the workspace directory, and the only diagnostic reads `Unknown memory backend '', falling back to markdown`.

### How I tested

The command results below are the original factory-change validation report, before the gateway and malformed-reference follow-up. They do not establish a local rerun of that follow-up. [CI Required Gate](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36763482034/job/110055866761) passed at `99aa354a09a4`.

Original command results:

```sh
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-memory --lib
test result: ok. 539 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib
test result: ok. 1720 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw --lib
test result: ok. 277 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(no output)

$ cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)
```

Tests added or removed in the original factory change:

- `factory_unknown_backend_fails_closed` (new) — `backend: "redis"` must error, and the error must name `"redis"` and contain every key from `selectable_memory_backends()`.
- `factory_markdown_remains_selectable` (new) — `backend: "markdown"` still builds a Markdown store.
- `factory_empty_backend_is_disabled_memory_not_markdown` (new) — `backend: ""` yields `none`.
- `factory_bare_qdrant_reports_its_own_storage_defect` (new) — a bare `qdrant` still reports its missing `[storage.qdrant.<alias>]` entry and is not swallowed by the new unknown-backend message.
- `migration_factory_unknown_backend_names_its_context` (new) — the migration path's error identifies its context.
- `factory_unknown_falls_back_to_markdown` (deleted) — it asserted the substitution, so removing it is the inversion itself, not an oversight.

The follow-up adds tests for full-config malformed-reference rejection, migration rejection, blank/`none` controls, `FailedMemory` operations, gateway backend selection, and the production memory-store handler's HTTP 500 response versus a healthy control. These are separate selection and handler tests; no full daemon reload smoke is reported here.

The following validation notes describe the original factory-change session:

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `fmt`, `clippy --all-targets`, and the library suites above cover the changed factory, classifier, and profile lookup, and the root package suite covers the `zeroclaw memory` CLI surface that consumes the classifier.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the full-workspace `cargo test` and `typos` were not run in this session, and the gateway/daemon suites were not executed — their handling of this error is confirmed by reading the call sites, not by running them. The `container-test` lanes were not run.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** I did not boot a daemon or run the built binary; the runtime behaviour above is asserted by the unit tests and the call-site reads, not observed in a live process. I verified no other consumer in-tree depends on the old fallback: the only remaining `assert_eq!(mem.name(), "markdown")` cases construct with `backend: "markdown"` explicitly (`crates/zeroclaw-memory/src/lib.rs:1882`, `:2269`, and `markdown.rs:379`).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A — no presentation-sensitive state changed.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** whole-workspace `cargo test` and `typos` were skipped in the original session. The later follow-up also changes the gateway and daemon; current required CI is linked above.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **No**
- New external network calls? **No**
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No**
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **No**
- Notes: the rejected value is operator-authored config, echoed into an error message with `{:?}` so quotes and newlines are escaped rather than injected into the log line. No memory content is included in the message.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **No** — intentional fail-closed change.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? **Yes** — `memory.backend` gains a rejection case and `""` changes meaning.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? **No**
- **Upgrade steps:** check the value with `zeroclaw config get memory.backend`. Any value outside `sqlite`, `lucid`, `postgres`, `qdrant`, `markdown`, `none` (or a dotted `<backend>.<alias>` form of those, where supported) was previously degraded to Markdown and now errors. Set it to the backend you meant, or to `none`/empty if you meant no persistence. **If your memory was silently stored as Markdown, do not delete it:** the substituted store used the same constructor as the selectable `markdown` backend, so pointing `memory.backend` at `markdown` keeps that history readable; moving it into SQLite is a separate deliberate step.

## Rollback

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <merge sha>`
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None. Reverting restores the silent fallback; nothing gates it.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** an unknown backend error names the rejected value and selectable backends; a malformed reference error names the invalid reference. Gateway construction failure logs explain that memory operations will return errors until the backend is fixed, with instructions to fix `[memory]` and reload. Memory-store requests then return HTTP 500 rather than `status: ok`.

prs.title: fix(tool-call-parser): recover DeepSeek DSML tool calls
prs.body:
> Maintainer note: I carried forward the contributor's DSML support and added the declaration, argument-boundary and example-context repairs. I updated this description to match the structural reader and retained `Refs #11130` because runtime classification and streaming remain separate work.

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- **What changed and why:** Recover complete DeepSeek DSML tool calls from response text. Read the structural tags directly so DSML saved inside JSON arguments or existing tool payloads does not become a separate invocation. Preserve DSML string values, including whitespace, literal quotes, marker-shaped text and empty strings; accept whitespace around attribute equals signs.
- **Scope boundary:** Only `crates/zeroclaw-tool-call-parser/src/lib.rs`. No provider, runtime, configuration, dependency or permission changes. Mixed-format call retention/order, malformed-output classification and streaming suppression remain follow-ups.
- **Blast radius:** The shared `parse_tool_calls` text-fallback entry point. Responses without DSML use the existing parser path. Recovered calls still enter the runtime's known-tool filter and normal approval and execution flow.
- **Linked issue(s):** Refs #11130.

### What this does, simply

Some DeepSeek models write a tool request into their reply instead of returning the API's native `tool_calls` field. DSML wraps that request in tags such as `<｜DSML｜ calls>`, `<｜DSML｜ invoke>` and `<｜DSML｜ parameter>`. ZeroClaw needs to recognize those tags to recover the reported non-streaming shell request.

Removing marker prefixes throughout a reply is unsafe. For example, a legitimate `file_write` request can contain DSML as text to save. Scanning that text as another invocation can turn the saved example into a tool call, while normalizing its markers can change the file's contents.

This PR reads DSML structure separately from argument data. It skips existing JSON values and tool-payload boundaries before looking for DSML. Within a DSML call, a parameter's value remains data through its reserved closing delimiter. A value marked `string="true"` keeps its exact bytes rather than being trimmed or decoded as JSON. A genuine call after an enclosing declaration or JSON wrapper remains recoverable. Example cues come only from surrounding prose, not descriptions or argument contents inside skipped payloads. Genuine teaching prose still suppresses example calls.

Complete valid calls use the existing tool registry and approval flow. Runtime handling of malformed DSML and live streaming output is unchanged. Mixed DSML and legacy formats can still lose or reorder calls, as identified in the existing reviews.

### Scope and maintenance tradeoff

The reader stays in the shared parser and reuses its call representation, wrapper boundaries, JSON deserializer and GLM-line admission. It adds no general XML parser or provider-specific dispatcher. Direct parameter reading is needed because the older normalization path cannot distinguish structural tags from literal parameter contents. The parameter's own closing delimiter remains reserved, and existing global thinking-tag preprocessing is unchanged.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. Deterministic parser-entrypoint tests exercise the changed data-versus-call boundary without depending on a model emitting a particular response. The broader runtime and streaming behavior is not established by these tests.

### How I tested

```sh
cargo test --locked --offline -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-api --features tokio/time --lib -- --quiet
# Parser: 215 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored. API: 310 passed; 0 failed.
cargo clippy --locked --offline -p zeroclaw-tool-call-parser -p zeroclaw-api --features tokio/time --all-targets -- -D warnings
# Passed with no warnings.
rustfmt --check --edition 2024 crates/zeroclaw-tool-call-parser/src/lib.rs
# Passed.
git diff --check
# Passed.
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh
# Passed.
```

Nine added regressions cover DSML inside JSON and legacy arguments; literal markers, empty strings and spaced attributes; incomplete spans; strict tag names; ordinary prose quotes; GLM-line argument data; and preservation of a genuine following call. Two further regressions cover example/sample words inside skipped declarations and arguments, teaching prose before and after those payloads, and separate prose fragments that must not join into an example cue. Existing tests cover the reported fullwidth and ASCII DSML calls, declaration rejection, examples, literal quotes and whitespace. The one ignored test is the unchanged `close_alias_inside_arguments_should_not_expose_nested_call` regression outside the `<tools>` alias.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Required Rust CI supplies workspace compilation, lint and consumer/test coverage. Its results must be checked against the published repair head; the local results above establish the parser-level behavior.
- **Known CI coverage gap:** No end-to-end DSML model/channel or streaming smoke was performed. Runtime classification and streaming remain on #11130.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Source tracing confirmed that the existing runtime caller filters recovered calls against known tools and sends them through normal approval preparation. I did not run a live model or channel smoke.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A. No visual interface state changes.
- **Tested revision:** `5c00f9bd00bcdb24fec78f4f2c14276600dec2e7`; parser-file SHA-256 `a329c10eb1f997b7c8ca47a363bbc1fcdcc5404759dd0f4f98b034473b90b97e`.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No additional local workspace build was run because the focused crate checks cover the edited parser and required CI supplies broader build coverage.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No. No new tools or execution permissions; DSML requests use the existing registry and approval path.
- New external network calls? No.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No. The repair fixtures use synthetic tool requests and paths.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? Yes. DSML is untrusted model output that can request tool execution. The extraction scan preserves existing argument boundaries, parameter contents are not recursively parsed, and incomplete recognized DSML does not expose its payload to legacy executable fallbacks. Ordinary tool approvals remain in effect.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes for existing supported protocols. Complete DSML calls gain parsing support; malformed recognized DSML is consumed by the parser rather than offered to legacy fallbacks.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- Upgrade steps: None.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the landed squash commit for this PR with `git revert <squash-merge-sha>`.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** No new toggle. Existing `strict_tool_parsing = true` disables text-protocol fallback when the provider supplies native tool calls; it also disables other text-only tool protocols.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** A DSML-emitting model returns markup without a recovered call, a recovered call has altered arguments, or unexpected additional calls appear. Inspect the response and tool-call records with sensitive argument content redacted.

prs.title: docs(skills): enqueue squash merges through the merge queue
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - `master` now requires the GitHub merge queue (squash, batched). The queue tests each PR against the exact result it will land on, so it is the freshness check. The skill's freshness rules are removed, including this PR's first-version rule that required checks start after the `master` head.
  - The squash commit is now title-only: the repository's squash settings are PR title (GitHub appends ` (#N)`) and a blank body. The commit-history body, its scratch file, and the `--subject`/`--body-file` flags are removed. The PR title must be conventional before enqueuing.
  - The preflight stays: open, not draft, review decision, required CI, `do-not-merge`/`status:blocked`/`release-gate` holds, milestone and release-line placement, closing issues, and the last-moment release recheck.
  - New Step 2: refuse to enqueue when the PR title or commits carry bot or AI attribution (the same pattern the skill already used for the squash body).
  - The final step enqueues with `gh pr merge <N> --squash --auto --match-head-commit <sha>`. Verification waits for `MERGED`, or reports the `RemovedFromMergeQueueEvent` reason and stops without enqueuing it again.
  - Bypassing the queue (`--admin`) happens only on the user's explicit request for that PR, and the skill states the stale risk first. It never falls back to a bypass on its own.
  - Batches: enqueue each PR after its own preflight and confirmation; the queue serializes them.
- **What changed from the first version, and why:** The first version added a rule that every required check start after the current `master` head. That disqualified green checks after every unrelated `master` commit and did not prove which base was tested, as RFC #11096 pointed out. With the merge queue back on, the queue answers that question on the exact result, so this PR now removes the freshness rules instead of tightening them.
- **Scope boundary:** Skill text only. No workflow, ruleset, or CI changes.
- **Blast radius:** Maintainers and agents using the squash-merge skill. Merges go through the queue; commit messages on `master` are the PR title plus ` (#N)`.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11096. Related #10815. Related #11066.
- **Labels:** `docs`, `type:docs`, `risk:medium`, `size:XS`, `needs-author-action`

### What this does, simply

The merge checklist still checks that a PR is approved, green, not on hold, and on the right release line, and now also that its title and commits carry no AI attribution. Then, instead of merging, it puts the PR in the merge queue, which tests the exact result and lands it or kicks it out, and the checklist reports which.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A — skill text; the new snippets are reproducible from the file.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Docs gates on the changed Markdown; no code paths change.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The local docs gates lint `docs/` and do not select `.claude/skills/squash-merge/SKILL.md`, so the changed file relies on CI's markdown checks. No PR has gone through the queue yet (the newest `merge_group` run predates it being re-enabled), so the enqueue and removal paths are checked against the API schema and live PR data, not an actual queue run.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh      # exit 0
scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh        # exit 0
scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh   # exit 0
git diff --check                     # exit 0
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Ran the new snippets verbatim against the live repo. The attribution check is silent on #11084 and prints #11106's `Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>` trailers. The queue status query returns `state`, `isInMergeQueue`, `mergeQueueEntry`, `autoMergeRequest` and the removal timeline for #11084. Confirmed the queue (`mergeMethod: SQUASH`) and the repository squash settings (`PR_TITLE` / `BLANK`) before writing the text. `gh pr merge --help` confirms that on a queue branch it enqueues when checks pass and enables auto-merge otherwise.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A — no user-visible interface.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No Rust checks; no Rust changed.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

Rollback: `git revert <sha>`.

prs.title: fix(security): block high-risk shell commands even when allowlisted
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:** `validate_command_execution_for_shell` skipped the `block_high_risk_commands` gate when a command was a literal `allowed_commands` entry, so the reported profile with the hard block on and `rm` in its allowlist could execute `rm -rf` after shell auto-approval. The gate now applies to every high-risk command, which is what the config schema documents the field to do. The Balanced and Locked Down preset help and the PowerShell sandboxing guidance are reworded in the same change, because they promised an explicit-allowlist exemption the code no longer gives.
- **Scope boundary:** The allowlist itself, the medium-risk approval gate, and the supervised high-risk approval gate are unchanged. The `"*"` + `block_high_risk_commands = false` escape hatch is unchanged.
- **Blast radius:** `SecurityPolicy::validate_command_execution_for_shell`, which the shell tool, the skill shell tool, and cron shell jobs all call. A profile that allowlists a high-risk command with the hard block on now gets it blocked instead of executed.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11058
- **Labels:** `bug`, `config`, `domain:security`, `needs-maintainer-review`, `risk:high`, `runtime`, `security:policy`, `size:S`, `tool:delegate`.

### What this does, simply

A profile lists the commands an agent may run in `allowed_commands`. Putting a command there used to do two things at once: it allowed the command, and if the command was high-risk it also switched off the `block_high_risk_commands` hard block for that command. Only the first effect is documented, and the second is how an allowlisted `rm` ran silently while the profile had the hard block turned on.

The config schema documents `block_high_risk_commands` as "Block high-risk commands even when allowlisted", so this makes the code match that sentence. The allowlist still decides whether a command may run at all; the hard block just applies on top of it. If you do want a high-risk command to run, `block_high_risk_commands = false` is the switch for that, and it's untouched.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `N/A` — this is a pure policy function covered by the crate's own unit and integration tests; a manual agent run would exercise the same function without adding signal.

### How I tested

On `master`, before the change, the existing `validate_command_explicit_rm_bypasses_high_risk_block` passed. It builds a policy with `autonomy = Full`, `allowed_commands = ["rm"]`, `block_high_risk_commands = true` and asserts `validate_command_execution("rm -rf /tmp/test", true)` returns `Ok(CommandRiskLevel::High)`. That is the silent-execution path from the issue: the command clears validation and the shell tool runs it.

I added `validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk` (its comment quotes the schema sentence) and ran it before touching the code:

```
running 1 test
test policy::tests::validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk ... FAILED

---- policy::tests::validate_command_blocks_explicitly_allowlisted_high_risk stdout ----
thread '...' panicked at crates/zeroclaw-config/src/policy.rs:6588:13:
expected the hard block, got: Command requires explicit approval (approved=true): high-risk operation
```

That failure is the bug. The allowlist entry cleared the hard block, so an unapproved call fell through to the approval gate instead of being blocked; with `approved = true` the call returns `Ok` and the command runs.

After the change, on the tested revision:

```
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config
test result: ok. 1775 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out   (lib)
     Running tests/comment_writer.rs        — 8 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/migration.rs             — 99 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/nodes_mdns_config.rs     — 5 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/powershell_policy_probe.rs — 9 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/repro_8636.rs            — 1 passed; 0 failed
     Running tests/schema_v4_external_saas.rs — 1 passed; 0 failed

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib validate_command
test result: ok. 15 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1760 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib independent_delegate_denies_prompt_required_skill_tools_without_approval_route
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5698 filtered out

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib tools::shell::tests
test result: FAILED. 64 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 5634 filtered out
# shell_child_cannot_open_owners_controlling_terminal is the failure: its own
# openpty() call returns EACCES in this sandbox before any ZeroClaw code runs,
# and the same denial reproduces with a standalone libc call outside the repo.
# The other 64 pass.

$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
(clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings
(clean)

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
(clean)

$ scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh

$ scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh

```

The `validate_command` set covers the three cases the issue names: a high-risk command with an explicit allow entry is blocked for both `approved` values; an ordinary allowlisted command (`ls`) still returns `Ok(Low)` without approval; a high-risk command that is not allowlisted still fails with `Command not allowed by security policy`. One test also pins the opt-out: with `block_high_risk_commands = false`, an allowlisted `rm` still returns `Ok(High)`.

Five existing tests needed to move with the policy. Three asserted the old exemption directly and now assert the block. Two PowerShell allowlist-path tests set `block_high_risk_commands = false` so they keep exercising the path-match rule they exist for rather than the high-risk gate. `independent_delegate_denies_prompt_required_skill_tools_without_approval_route` used an allowlisted `rm` to reach the approval gate, so its fixture now turns the hard block off; with it on the command would stop at the high-risk gate instead of the prompt.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the Rust quality gate (fmt + clippy) and the workspace test job cover the changed crate and its callers.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None.
- **Commands run and tail output:** listed above.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** I confirmed the risk classifier and the allowlist both live in `SecurityPolicy`, so the change sits in the function that owns the decision and covers all three callers (`tools/shell.rs`, `tools/skill_tool.rs`, `cron/mod.rs`) rather than one entry point. I did not run a live agent turn against a real model.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A`
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `c29e071cfd325c5b7bb6e6e14d016c54b21e8bba`, `zeroclaw-config` and `zeroclaw-runtime`, Linux x86_64, Rust 1.97.0. The branch is rebased onto current `master` (`d03325172eb6c64272f01042b60fd7f66d74c711`), so these runs are against the merged result rather than the old base.

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No`
- New external network calls? `No`
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: `N/A`

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `No`
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `No`
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: keep `block_high_risk_commands = true` to retain the hard block. Profiles that previously relied on an explicit high-risk exemption will now receive `Command blocked: high-risk command is disallowed by policy`, with no process spawned. Choosing `block_high_risk_commands = false` permits allowlisted high-risk commands subject to the remaining approval, path and sandbox checks, but is an explicit security opt-out rather than an equivalent migration. With `"*"` in the allowlist, it also admits other high-risk commands and disables the existing shell syntax restrictions. Removing the wildcard and enumerating intended commands avoids that wildcard syntax bypass, but changes the previous broad low-risk allowance. This also affects allowlisted PowerShell executables classified as high risk.

  The Windows default profile is where a stock install feels this. `runtime.shell` defaults to PowerShell on Windows (#10956), and under PowerShell a command name the classifier doesn't recognize is high risk. 18 of the 27 entries in the Windows default allowlist are high risk, including `python`, `node`, `grep`, `find` and `where`. The `default` and `locked_down` profiles set `block_high_risk_commands = true`, so on Windows those 18 move from an approval prompt to a hard block that approval can't override, and a stock Windows install can no longer run them. POSIX defaults are essentially unaffected: the same names classify as low risk under the POSIX classifier. `block_high_risk_commands = false` restores them under the ordinary approval gates.

- **Fast rollback command/path:** revert the merged change using its landed commit SHA
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** none beyond the existing `block_high_risk_commands`; reverting restores the old allowlist exemption.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** shell tool results containing `Command blocked: high-risk command is disallowed by policy` for a command the profile previously allowlisted, with no process spawned.

milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

prs.title: fix(channels/whatsapp-web): queue a forced reply outside a voice chat
prs.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Stacked on #11057, which is the other half of the same decision point: that PR makes `suppress_voice` win, this one makes `force_voice` reach the channel at all. The diff below is against that branch. Merge #11057 first, or say the word and I will squash both.

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (stacked on #11057)
- **What changed and why:**
  - `SendMessage.force_voice` was never read by the WhatsApp Web sender. The automatic path asked one question, whether the chat's last inbound message was a voice note, so a producer asking for *this* reply to be spoken was ignored and nothing was logged to say so.
  - The reachable consequence: `send_via` maps `OutputModality::Voice` onto `force_voice`, so an agent that decided its answer should be spoken, or a peer group declared `voice`, got the ordinary text reply. Per-turn output routing did not reach this channel.
  - The chat's state is now the default rather than the rule, which is Telegram's gate exactly: `if (!force && !self.is_voice_chat(recipient)) || self.tts_manager.is_none()`.
  - Forcing does not override the refusals that mean something. `suppress_voice` still wins, as the field documents ("Ignored when `suppress_voice` is also `true`"), and the content heuristic still applies, so a forced URL or JSON blob is no more speakable than an unforced one. Telegram checks the heuristic after the force gate too, which is what keeps #10689's class of problem from returning through a new door.
  - A chat that is simply not speaking no longer logs a skip for every message: that refusal is the normal state of a text conversation, and logging it per message would bury the ones worth reading.
- **Scope boundary:** this is the queueing half only. Whether a forced voice note should also *replace* the text, as it does on Telegram, is the open question on #11059 and is deliberately not decided here. On Telegram that early return also drops the reply's attachments, which is the part I would rather not copy without your call. No change to the content heuristic, to the inbound path, or to when a chat becomes a voice chat.
- **Blast radius:** one gate in the WhatsApp Web sender. A deployment without TTS is untouched. A deployment with TTS sees a difference only for messages that carry `force_voice`, which nothing sets unless an agent calls `send_via` or a peer group declares `voice`.
- **Linked issue(s):** Part of #11059. Depends on #11057. Related #10922, #7361.
- **Labels:** none applied yet.

### What this does, simply

The agent can already say "answer this one out loud" — that is what `send_via` with a voice modality means, and it is how a peer group gets declared voice-first. On Telegram it works. On WhatsApp the request was dropped on the floor: the channel only ever spoke when the person had spoken first, so an agent that wanted to answer by voice, in a conversation that had been typed so far, simply could not.

Now it can. What it still cannot do is talk its way past the two guards: a message marked as never-to-be-spoken stays silent, and a reply that is a link, a JSON blob or three words long stays written, because forcing a route to voice is not a claim that anything can be read aloud.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, with a paired Web alias and TTS configured.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` = `whatsapp_web`.
- **Setup / preconditions:** a Web-mode alias with `tts.enabled` and the owning agent's `tts_provider` set, an agent allowed `send_via`, and a chat that has only ever exchanged text.
- **Steps to run:** have the agent answer a typed message with `send_via(modality: "voice")`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** the text reply, plus a voice note about ten seconds later.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** the text reply only, and no log line about the dropped flag.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** the required gate builds and tests `zeroclaw-channels`. `whatsapp-web` is not a default feature, so the default clippy pass does not compile this code; I ran clippy with `-D warnings` and the feature on.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the debounce task that follows the queue decision is not covered, as on #11057; the tests cover what decides whether it is spawned.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
$ ./scripts/ci/rust_quality_gate.sh
gate exit=0

$ cargo clippy -p zeroclaw-channels --features whatsapp-web --lib --tests -- -D warnings
clippy exit=0

$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-channels --features whatsapp-web --lib
test result: ok. 2203 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 13.38s
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Each behavior was checked against the defect it guards, by restoring the defect and confirming the test fails:

```text
force_voice ignored again (the reported bug)
  a_forced_reply_is_spoken_in_a_chat_that_never_sent_a_voice_note ... FAILED

forcing allowed to skip suppression and the heuristic
  suppression_outranks_a_forced_reply ... FAILED
  the_content_heuristic_survives_a_forced_reply ... FAILED
```

  - `a_forced_reply_is_spoken_in_a_chat_that_never_sent_a_voice_note` — with the control that the same reply unforced is still refused with `not_a_voice_chat`.
  - `suppression_outranks_a_forced_reply` — both flags set, suppression wins.
  - `the_content_heuristic_survives_a_forced_reply` — a forced URL is still refused.

  **Not verified live:** I have not driven `send_via(modality: "voice")` through a paired account on this branch. The voice path itself I did exercise live on a deployment carrying this channel's TTS code: an inbound voice note came back transcribed and answered with a synthesized voice note, which is the machinery this change decides to enter.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `N/A`. Nothing rendered changes; the difference is whether a voice note is sent at all.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `ca8f9e8c0`, `whatsapp_web` channel, local test run.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** test output above.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** a forced reply is queued for synthesis in a chat that has never sent a voice note.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** the pre-push hook was skipped with `--no-verify`; on this machine it fails on two tests unrelated to this branch that pass when run serially, as described in #10980.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: n/a. A forced reply reaches the same synthesis path an ordinary voice reply already uses, behind the same suppression and content guards.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`; forced replies go back to being text-only.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None; a deployment that never sets `force_voice` is unaffected.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a voice note arriving in a chat that expected text, which would mean a producer is setting `force_voice` where it should not.
